DETAILED ANALYSIS OF THE LINUX OPERATING SYSTEM

Preface

In the world of computer systems, booting is the starting point of all operations. From the exact moment of power-on until the execution of the first user-space process concludes, the system undergoes a complete transition from a piece of "silent silicon" to a "runnable operating system." Although this process appears brief, it embodies the collaborative orchestration across multiple layers, including hardware architecture, bootloaders, kernel initialization, memory management, scheduling mechanisms, and user-space architectures. However, for many beginners and even experienced engineers, what exactly occurs inside the system the moment the power turns on and the screen flashes often resembles a "black box" hidden beneath binary code.

The original intention behind writing this book is to dismantle this black box. We will lead readers starting from the first line of assembly instructions at hardware reset, through the initialization labyrinth of U-BOOT, and witness how the Linux kernel takes over the baton of control from the bootloader, until it ultimately starts the first process (init), drawing back the curtain on user space.

In the realm of embedded development, the combination of the ARM architecture and the Linux operating system has long been the core pillar of industrial control, the Internet of Things (IoT), and mobile devices. This book centers around ARM-based Linux, systematically parsing the complete technical lineage from the bootloader to the conclusion of the first process (init).

The core content of this book encompasses the following four major sections:

Part I: Environment Construction and Preparation (Chapters 1–3): Starting with the Linux architecture, this section elaborates on the U-BOOT bootloader—the bridge of embedded systems—and the Device Tree mechanism. This is the key to understanding hardware-software decoupling.

Part II: The Dawn Era of Kernel Booting (Chapters 4–14): This stage is often referred to as the "barren period" of the kernel. We will deeply analyze CPU mode configuration, page table initialization, Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP) configuration, and the layer-by-layer parsing of command-line arguments, witnessing how the kernel establishes basic operational order on blank hardware.

Part III: Deep Construction of Core Subsystems (Chapters 15–25): This is the hardcore soul of this book. It covers complex memory management (red-black trees, memory migration, compaction, and merging), task scheduling (CFS policies, runqueues), the RCU mechanism, and the establishment of the interrupt and time subsystems. Furthermore, it specifically explores modern kernel security features such as kernel hardening (stack canaries, latent entropy acquisition).

Part IV: System Operation and Functional Closed-Loop (Chapters 26–31): This section discusses how the kernel transitions into a multitasking state, establishing process credentials, namespaces, and container capabilities, and ultimately launching the init process. Finally, through the practical porting of the operating system and OP-TEE, theory is brought back to a real platform.

Every chapter of this book strives to strike directly at the essence. Through the analysis of advanced features such as jump label performance optimization, memory encryption, and deadlock detection, readers will not only master "how it boots," but also gain a profound understanding of the "art of trade-offs" in kernel design.

The book primarily covers:

  • The boot flow and source code structure based on U-BOOT

  • The boot and initialization phases of the Linux kernel

  • Call chain analysis of various initialization subsystems (memory management, interrupts, scheduling, driver frameworks, etc.)

  • The creation and execution path of the first user-space process (init)

  • System behaviors and mechanism analyses up to the end of the init lifecycle

Whether you are a driver engineer wishing to deeply understand the low-level system, or an application developer needing to quickly set up an environment, this book aims to build a complete knowledge system for you, helping you find a clear navigation route through the jungle of embedded Linux. Furthermore, to provide developers with a complete closed-loop experience, we have simultaneously launched a supporting Linux development platform that accommodates low-level IEEE 802.15.4 and MAC protocols. This platform perfectly integrates QML graphical interface programming and is specifically engineered for smart product development and Linux porting, lending wings to your research and development efficiency.

chapter 1 Introduction to Linux

The Evolutionary History of Linux

1.1 The Evolutionary History of Linux

During the late 1980s and early 1990s, the computer industry was undergoing a transition from mainframes to personal computers. Unix systems held a dominant position in scientific research and server domains; however, their commercial licensing fees were exorbitant, and their source code was not fully open. Concurrently, the Free Software Movement was gradually emerging, advocating for the free sharing and modification of software.

In 1991, Linus Torvalds, a student at the University of Helsinki in Finland, became dissatisfied with the expensive Unix systems and the functionally constrained MINIX system while using MINIX for educational purposes. Driven by learning and practical objectives, he wrote a Unix-like kernel capable of running on the Intel 80386 processor and publicly released it on internet forums; this kernel was subsequently named Linux. He posted in the comp.os.minix newsgroup, stating that he was developing an operating system kernel that was "just a hobby, won't be big and professional like GNU." Linus released the Linux kernel under the GPL (GNU General Public License), which permitted anyone to freely use, modify, and distribute it, while inviting developers to participate collectively. This decision attracted thousands of developers worldwide to contribute code.

Linux did not fight this battle in isolation. Because the GNU Project, initiated by Richard Stallman in 1983, had already developed most of the essential operating system software components except for the kernel itself (such as the Emacs editor, GCC compiler, and Shell), the emergence of the Linux kernel perfectly filled the final vacancy of the GNU operating system. Linus ingeniously combined his work with the GNU Project initiated by Richard Stallman (which provided tools like compilers and Shells) and the GPL license. This "kernel + tools" paradigm constitutes what we commonly refer to today as GNU/Linux. With the integration of the GNU toolchain, Shell, compiler, and system libraries, a complete and free operating system gradually took shape. The GNU General Public License model laid the foundation for the rapid expansion of Linux in the years that followed.

With the initial public offering (IPO) of Red Hat and IBM's announcement of a $1 billion investment in Linux, Linux shed its label as an "amateur hobbyist project" and began replacing expensive, closed-source Unix platforms on a massive scale in the server market. Today, Linux is far more than just an operating system; it serves as the digital foundation of modern civilization.

Strictly speaking, Linux itself is merely a kernel. It acts as the core of the operating system, responsible for managing computer hardware resources (such as the CPU, memory, and hard drives) and providing system call interfaces for upper-layer software. What we typically call "Linux" actually refers to GNU/Linux distributions (such as Ubuntu). This is because the Linux kernel must be combined with the system tools and libraries provided by the GNU Project (such as Shell, Coreutils, and compilers) to form a complete, usable operating system.

In simple terms, the kernel is an open-source, low-level computer resource management software system whose file management methods and basic operational commands are similar to those of the Unix operating system, and it forms the baseline architecture for countless operating systems.

The birth of Linux was not only a technological milestone but also a revolution in collaborative paradigms. Developers across the globe maintain and improve the kernel collectively via the internet, allowing it to achieve industrial-grade quality within a short period. In the evolutionary history of computer science, no other operating system matches Linux in simultaneously embodying the idealism of the hacker spirit while demonstrating dominant vitality in the commercial realm. From a few lines of experimental code in a Finnish university dormitory to the core driving force running on 100% of the world's supercomputers, the story of Linux itself is the history of the evolution of the modern internet.

Today, Linux runs on almost all platforms, ranging from supercomputers and servers to smartphones (Android is based on the Linux kernel) and embedded devices, making it one of the most popular and critical operating systems in the world. Linux comprises numerous distinct distributions, each tailored to specific user cohorts and use cases, primarily divided into three major mainstream lineages alongside several specialized variants.

The three major mainstream lineages include:

Desktop-Oriented Distributions:

  • Ubuntu: One of the most popular desktop distributions, renowned for its user-friendliness and robust community support.

  • Linux Mint: Based on Ubuntu, it provides a more traditional and streamlined desktop experience, making it exceptionally friendly to beginners.

  • Fedora: At the bleeding edge of technology, it incorporates the latest open-source software and serves as the upstream "testing ground" for the commercial Red Hat enterprise platform.

  • Debian: Famous for its absolute stability and massive software repositories, it serves as the foundational bedrock for numerous distributions, including Ubuntu.

Server and Enterprise-Oriented Distributions:

  • Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL): A commercialized, enterprise-grade Linux distribution that offers long-term stability and professional technical support.

  • CentOS Stream / Rocky Linux / AlmaLinux: Free alternatives to RHEL designed to maintain strict, production-ready compatibility with RHEL binary targets.

  • Ubuntu Server: Universally and extensively deployed across cloud infrastructures and enterprise Web servers.

Specialized and Purpose-Driven Distributions:

  • Kali Linux: Purpose-built for digital forensics and penetration testing, pre-installed with a vast suite of security auditing tools.

  • Raspberry Pi OS: Optimized specifically for ARM-architecture single-board computers, such as the Raspberry Pi.

  • Android: Although it features a distinct user-space experience, its low-level underlying core is powered directly by the Linux kernel.

Specialized Sub-variants include:

  • Puppy Linux / Lubuntu: Lightweight and minimal resource footprints, highly suited for legacy or low-specification hardware.

  • SteamOS: Gaming-centric operating system, utilized as the native system for the Steam Deck hardware platform.

  • Tails: Privacy-focused with high-anonymity configurations, leaving zero forensic footprints on the local machine.

Other Major Distributions include:

  • openSUSE: Engineered in Germany, it is widely acclaimed for its powerful integrated system administration framework, YaST.

  • Gentoo: A source-based compilation distribution built for achieving maximum, hyper-optimized hardware performance tuning.

  • Deepin: A prominent representative of domestic Chinese Linux engineering, sporting a highly polished and aesthetically designed desktop environment.

  • Alpine Linux: Extremely minimal and lightweight, commonly utilized as the baseline distribution for Docker container technologies.

Linux is far more than a mere technical commodity; it represents an entire collaborative development paradigm and architectural philosophy characterized by the following design attributes:

  • Open Source and Software Freedom: Anyone can inspect, modify, and enhance the Linux source code. This transparency implies that security vulnerabilities can be rapidly identified and remediated. Developers can customize the system architecture to meet precise requirements or port the Linux kernel directly onto proprietary hardware platforms. Because the vast majority of Linux distributions are free to download and deploy, enterprise and individual IT expenditure is drastically minimized.

  • Stability and Reliability: Linux systems are globally recognized for their capability to achieve continuous operational uptime for years without requiring a system reboot. This reliability is the primary driver behind its dominance as the premier choice for server infrastructure. In the server domain, Linux maintains an overwhelming market share.

  • Security Architecture: Inheriting the strict user segregation and discretionary access control models of Unix (such as the explicit separation between the root superuser and unprivileged accounts), Linux fundamentally prevents malware from easily escalating privileges and hijacking control of system resources. Furthermore, the massive global developer ecosystem ensures rapid response times to zero-day security threats through the swift distribution of upstream patches.

  • Multi-user and Multitasking Capabilities: In alignment with standard UNIX architecture, Linux was architected from inception as a true multi-user system, allowing multiple distinct users to log in concurrently and consume system resources without cross-session interference. Simultaneously, its preemptive scheduler executes complex multitasking environments with high efficiency.

  • Structural Flexibility: Whether deployed as a full graphical user interface desktop, a headless server instance, or a highly constrained embedded system consuming only a few megabytes of memory, Linux scales across all barriers. Users can select, strip, or fully customize entirely distinct distributions to match target operational envelopes.

Today, Linux holds a dominant, monopolistic position across the broader operating system landscape. Over 90% of public cloud infrastructure (such as AWS, Azure, and Alibaba Cloud), along with the overwhelming majority of global web platforms (including Google and Facebook) and enterprise databases, execute on top of Linux. 100% of the world's top 500 supercomputers (TOP500) run Linux exclusively. From Android smartphones, smart televisions, and automotive in-vehicle infotainment (IVI) systems to network routers, the ARM-based Android ecosystem—which holds the number one global market share in embedded deployments—is powered at its core by the Linux kernel. Moreover, due to its powerful command-line utilities, native support for programming runtimes, and modern containerization technologies (such as Docker and Kubernetes), Linux is the premier environment for programmers and systems engineers alike. The open-source nature of Linux also renders it an ideal platform for computer science education and academic research.

Ultimately, Linux is an expansive ecosystem maintained collectively by a global community. Its open-source ethos, unmatched reliability, and granular flexibility make it the digital bedrock of the modern world. Whether you are a student learning to program, an administrator deploying enterprise web services, or an end-user seeking a secure, autonomous computing environment, Linux provides a reliable platform brimming with architectural possibilities. The inherent flexibility of Linux enables it to span from the cloud down to bare metal, covering enterprise backends, cloud computing, containers, embedded IoT, network security, scientific computing, and aerospace systems. It is, in every sense, the omnipresent penguin governing the digital realm.

Linux Architecture

1.2 Linux Architecture

The Linux kernel implements a monolithic architecture, yet it maintains high structural flexibility through its loadable kernel module mechanism. Linux consists of multiple relatively independent subsystems, with its core subsystems including:

  • Process Scheduling Subsystem: Linux utilizes the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). Its core paradigm is to measure task fairness through virtual runtime (vruntime). The scheduler maintains the runnable task queue using a red-black tree, keeping the time complexity at $O(log n)$. In multi-core systems, Linux introduces scheduling domains (Scheduling Domains) and load balancing mechanisms to optimize CPU utilization.

  • Memory Management Subsystem: Linux supports paging mechanisms and virtual memory management. Key features include demand paging, page cache, the Slab/Slub allocators, and Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) architecture support. Memory management not only impacts overall performance but is also directly tied to system stability.

  • File Subsystem: Linux supports a diverse range of file systems, such as ext4, XFS, and Btrfs. Its Virtual File System (VFS) layer implements a unified interface, rendering differences in underlying storage mediums completely transparent to application-layer software.

  • Network Subsystem: The Linux network stack is highly acclaimed for its performance, supporting numerous protocols and advanced features such as TCP/IP optimizations, zero-copy, and the eBPF extension mechanism. This architecture makes Linux the premier platform for high-concurrency server deployments.

  • Device Driver Module: Linux provides a unified device driver model and hotplugging mechanisms, supporting a vast array of hardware platforms. Its modular design allows drivers to be loaded dynamically on demand. Driver developers can provide full hardware support for Linux simply by authoring their code in accordance with the standard Linux device driver model.

Advantages and Limitations of Linux

1.3 Advantages and Limitations of Linux

The advantages of Linux manifest across multiple dimensions:

  • Open Source and Transparency: The source code is publicly accessible, facilitating auditing and deep customization.

  • High Stability: Server instances can maintain long-term, stable operations without degradation.

  • Superior Performance: The scheduling and networking stacks have achieved high architectural optimization and maturity.

  • Granular Scalability: Highly adaptable to both heavily constrained embedded profiles and massively parallel high-performance computing (HPC) scenarios.

While Linux is exceptionally outstanding, its technical limitations persist, primarily presenting as:

  • Relatively Deficient Desktop Ecosystem: Native support for certain proprietary commercial software suites and mainstream gaming remains constrained.

  • Fragmentation of Distributions: The vast number of individual distributions results in varying degrees of ecosystem standardization.

  • High Complexity of System Administration: The steep learning curve presents a high technical barrier for beginners.

Nevertheless, in server and cloud domains, these limitations have in no way compromised its dominant positioning.

Driven by stringent requirements for low power consumption, enhanced security, real-time responsiveness, and robust isolation capabilities, mobile and edge hardware place high demands on operating systems. Linux maintains a sharp competitive edge in the following areas:

  • Mature Driver Ecosystem and Hardware Support: Broad compatibility with diverse silicon vendors and peripherals.

  • Extremely Scalable Kernel Architecture: Easily stripped down to match the performance and memory profiles of varying device tiers.

  • Comprehensive Security Frameworks: Built-in access controls and hardening mechanisms.

  • Continuous Community Support and Long-Term Support (LTS) Releases: Guaranteed stability and security lifecycle maintenance.

Looking ahead, Linux will continue to spearhead technological paradigms across several key dimensions:

  • Edge Computing and the Intelligent Internet of Everything (AIoT): With the widespread proliferation of 5G and AIoT, lightweight, modular Linux profiles (such as Alpine or highly stripped embedded variants) will serve as the neural center for billions of edge devices.

  • Kernel Hardening and Rust Integration: The Linux kernel has actively integrated the Rust language for driver development, aiming to mitigate system-level vulnerabilities via compile-time memory safety. This represents a profound revolution in the kernel engineering paradigm.

  • Breakthroughs in Desktop Computing Environments: Powered by industrial catalysts like Valve (Steam Deck), the Linux gaming ecosystem has achieved a massive qualitative leap. The maturation of translation layers like Wine and Proton is turning the old adage "Linux is unsuitable for entertainment" into relic history.

  • Real-Time Capabilities and Low-Latency Performance: Enhancements targeting predictable execution and deterministic processing.

  • AI and Heterogeneous Computing Matrix: Highly optimized integration with neural processing units (NPUs), graphics processors (GPUs), and custom accelerators.

Future technological trajectories for intelligent devices encompass edge computing synthesis, localized on-device AI inference, smart automotive infotainment/telematics, and industrial IoT expansion. In these deployment scenarios, Linux functions seamlessly both as a full-featured operating system and as a low-level real-time control kernel core.

Furthermore, as the real-time patchset (PREEMPT_RT) fully matures into the upstream kernel mainline, Linux is now capable of satisfying strict, hard real-time industrial requirements. This development will aggressively expand its deployment footprint in autonomous driving and mission-critical industrial automation.

As of 2026, Linux maintains an absolute monopoly across the server and cloud computing landscapes. Its expansive ecosystem bridges thousands of global enterprise stakeholders with an unmatched worldwide developer community.

The overarching success of Linux lies fundamentally in its open collaborative model and its capacity for continuous technological evolution. As long as this paradigm endures, Linux possesses a rock-solid foundation for long-term progression.

From a solo hobbyist project in 1991 to the core baseline platform supporting global internet and mobile infrastructures today, the evolution of Linux stands as a monument to the power of open-source collaboration. It is not merely an operating system kernel; it is an engineering culture and a foundational philosophy of computing.

In the future data-driven society, whether deployed inside hyperscale cloud data centers, resting in your pocket as an intelligent mobile terminal, or operating deep within industrial assembly lines and autonomous vehicles, Linux will continue to serve as the silent engine driving global technology forward.

Linux Command Structure

1.5 Linux Command Structure

The universal syntax for Linux commands follows this format:

command [options] [arguments]

Where command is the name of the utility, options alter or tune the execution behavior of the command, and arguments target specific operational objects (such as files or directories).

Options are categorized into short options and long options. Short options begin with a single hyphen followed by a single character representing the option, for example:

$ ls -l   
(note:In this examples and below, we assume the shell prompt is $. )

A single command can invoke multiple options simultaneously, separated by spaces:

$ ls -l -a

Alternatively, multiple short options can be concatenated into a single block:

$ ls -la

Long options begin with a double hyphen, typically followed by an explicit, descriptive word or hyphenated phrase, for example:

$ ls --all

Throughout the command reference sections in this book, short options are primarily utilized.

Certain Linux command options accept optional arguments, while other options strictly require them, for example:

$ tar -f file.tar

Or alternatively, using the long option syntax:

$ tar --file=file.tar

Command Help and Query Mechanisms

1.6 Command Help and Query Mechanisms

Command usage documentation and summaries can be retrieved using the following syntax:

command --help

Or:

command -h

(Note: Not all commands support the short -h flag; the --help long option should be used as the definitive fallback).

Example invocation:

$ ls --help

To review the exhaustive user manual and interface descriptions for an application, use the man utility via the following format:

man command

Example invocation:

$ man ls

The Linux environment boasts an incredibly expansive utility set, estimated to exceed several hundred built-in and standalone binaries. The following sections outline the most frequently encountered commands.

File and Directory Operation Commands

1.7 File and Directory Operation Commands

ls — Directory Listing Utility

Format:

ls [options] [directory_or_file]

Common Options:

  • -l: Long listing format (displays file type, permissions, ownership, size, and modification date).

  • -a: Show hidden files (those starting with a dot .).

  • -h: Display sizes in a human-readable format (e.g., KB, MB, GB); must be used with -l.

  • -t: Sort content by modification time.

  • -r: Reverse the sorting order.

  • -R: Recursively list subdirectories.

  • -i: Display the file's index node (inode) number.

  • -S: Sort content by file size.

  • -d: List directories themselves, rather than their contents.

Examples:

$ ls

$ ls -l

$ ls -lh

pwd — Print Working Directory Utility

Format:

pwd

cd — Change Directory Utility

Format:

cd [options] [directory_name]

Common Options:

  • -L: Follow symbolic links / logical path (default behavior).

  • -P: Use the physical directory structure without following symbolic links (resolves real path).

  • -e: When used with -P, returns an error status if the directory change fails.

Examples:

$ cd /home  # Navigate to the home directory under root

$ cd ..     # Move up one directory level

$ cd ~     # Change to the home directory of the current user

$ cd -      # Switch to the previously occupied directory

mkdir — Make Directory Utility

Format:

mkdir [options] directory_name

Common Options:

  • -p: Recursively create parent directories if they do not exist.

  • -v: Verbose mode (print a message for each created directory).

  • -m: Assign specific permissions to the directory during creation.

Examples:

$ mkdir dir1

$ mkdir -p a/b/c

rmdir — Remove Empty Directory Utility

Format:

rmdir [options] directory_name

rm — Remove Files or Directories Utility

Format:

rm [options] directory_or_file

Common Options:

  • -r / -R: Recursively delete directories and their sub-contents.

  • -f: Force removal (do not prompt for confirmation).

  • -i: Prompt for confirmation before every removal.

  • -v: Verbose mode (display file names as they are deleted).

  • -d: Delete empty directories.

  • -I: Prompt once before removing more than three files or when removing recursively.

Examples:

$ rm file

$ rm -r dir

$ rm -rf dir \# Use -rf with extreme caution.

cp — Copy Files or Directories Utility

Format:

cp [options] source_file_or_directory destination_file_or_directory

Common Options:

  • -r / -R: Recursively copy directories and their sub-contents.

  • -a: Archive mode (equivalent to -dpR, preserves links, file attributes, and ownership).

  • -f: Force copy by removing existing destination files if necessary.

  • -i: Prompt for confirmation before overwriting an existing file.

  • -n: Do not overwrite an existing file.

  • -v: Verbose mode (show copy progress).

  • -u: Copy only when the source file is newer than the destination file or when the destination is missing.

  • -p: Preserve file permissions, timestamps, and ownership.

  • --preserve=ATTR: Preserve specified attributes.

  • --no-preserve=ATTR: Do not preserve certain specified attributes.

Examples:

$ cp file1 file2

$ cp -r dir1 dir2

mv — Move / Rename Utility

Format:

mv [options] source_file_or_directory destination_file_or_directory_name

Common Options:

  • -i: Prompt for confirmation before overwriting an existing file.

  • -f: Force move by overwriting existing files without prompting.

  • -n: Do not overwrite any existing file.

  • -v: Verbose mode (show progression).

  • -u: Move only when the source file is newer than the destination file or when the destination is missing.

  • -t DIR: Move all source arguments into the specified target directory DIR.

  • -T: Treat the target as a regular file instead of a directory.

Examples:

mv file /tmp

File Viewing Commands

1.8 File Viewing Commands

cat — Concatenate and Display File Content Utility

Format:

cat [options] file

Common Options:

  • -n: Number all output lines (including blank lines).

  • -b: Number non-empty output lines.

  • -s: Suppress repeated consecutive empty output lines into a single blank line.

  • -E: Display a $ at the end of each line.

  • -T: Display tab characters as ^I.

  • -A: Equivalent to -vET (shows all non-printing and formatting characters).

  • -v: Use ^ and M- notation to display non-printing characters, except for tabs and line breaks.

Examples:

$ cat file

$ cat -n file

more — File Pager Utility

Format:

more [options] file

Common Options:

  • -d: Display user prompts instead of ringing the system bell (e.g., [Press space to continue, 'q' to quit.]).

  • -c: Draw new pages from the top down instead of scrolling the terminal interface.

  • -f: Count logical lines rather than screen lines (avoids wrapping artifacts in long line counts).

  • -l: Do not pause after processing a form-feed character (^L).

  • -s: Squeeze multiple consecutive blank lines into a single empty line.

  • -u: Suppress underline formatting codes.

  • +n: Begin displaying file contents starting at line number n.

Interactive Controls:

  • Space: Advance down by one full page.

  • Enter: Advance down by one line.

  • b: Move backward by one full page.

  • /pattern: Search downward for the specified regular expression string.

  • n: Repeat the previous search.

  • q: Exit the pager utility.

  • =: Display the current line number.

  • f: Advance down by one full screen (on supported implementations).

  • Ctrl+D: Scroll down half a screen width.

  • Ctrl+B: Scroll backward one full screen.

Examples:

more file1

less — Advanced File Pager Utility (Recommended)

Format:

less [options] [file...]

Common Options:

  • -N: Display explicit line numbers.

  • -S: Disable line-wrapping (causes long lines to scroll horizontally).

  • -X: Prevent clearing the terminal screen upon exiting less.

  • -i: Ignore case patterns during searches.

  • -I: Enforce case sensitivity during searches (unless the search pattern contains uppercase characters).

  • -r: Output raw control characters directly (such as color codes).

  • -R: Render ANSI color escape sequences cleanly (highly recommended).

  • +F: Monitor active file expansion in real-time (similar to executing tail -f).

  • +G: Open the target file directly at the end of its contents.

Interactive Controls:

  • Space: Page downward by one full screen.

  • Enter: Scroll downward by one line.

  • b: Page upward by one full screen.

  • y: Scroll upward by one line.

  • G: Jump directly to the end of the file.

  • 1G or g: Jump directly to the beginning of the file.

  • /pattern: Search downward for the string pattern.

  • ?pattern: Search upward for the string pattern.

  • n: Repeat the previous search in the forward direction.

  • N: Repeat the previous search in the reverse direction.

  • q: Exit the pager utility.

Examples:

$ less -N file1

head — Output Beginning of File Utility

Format:

head [options] file...

Common Options:

  • -n NUM: Print the first NUM lines of the file.

  • -c NUM: Print the first NUM bytes of the file.

  • -q: Suppress file headers when tracking multiple files.

  • -v: Always print headers containing file names.

Examples:

$ head -n 10 file

tail — Output End of File Utility

Format:

tail [options] file...

Common Options:

  • -n NUM: Print the trailing NUM lines of the file.

  • -c NUM: Print the trailing NUM bytes of the file.

  • -f: Continuously output appended data as the file grows (ideal for log monitoring).

  • -F: Similar to -f, but tracks the file descriptor by name, surviving log rotations safely.

  • -q: Suppress file name header markers across multiple targets.

  • -v: Always display file name header markers across multiple targets.

Examples:

$ tail -n 20 file

$ tail -f logfile

Permission and Attribute Management

1.9 Permission and Attribute Management

chmod — Change File Mode Bits Utility

Format:

chmod [options] mode file...

Common Options:

  • -R: Recursively modify file permissions for directories and their sub-contents.

  • -v: Verbose mode (display a diagnostic for every file processed).

  • --reference=file: Set permissions to match those of the specified reference file.

  • --changes: Like verbose, but report only when a change is actually made.

  • --silent / --quiet: Suppress most error and informational messages.

File permissions are divided among the file owner, group members, and other users, represented by u, g, and o respectively. The standard permissions are read, write, and execute, represented by r, w, and x. Permissions can also be represented numerically via octal values as follows:

PermissionOctal Value
r4
w2
x1

Examples:

$ chmod u+x \~/bin/repo

$ chmod go-w \~/bin/repo

$ chmod 751 file

(Note: In the third example, octal 7 grants read, write, and execute permissions to the owner; 5 grants read and execute permissions to group members; and 1 grants execute-only access to other users).

chown — Change File Ownership Utility

Format:

chown [options] owner[:group] file_or_directory

Common Options:

  • -R: Recursively modify ownership across directories and all sub-contents.

  • -v: Verbose mode (display detailed output for every file processed).

  • -c: Report only when an actual ownership change takes place.

  • -f: Force mode (suppress most error messages regarding ownership modification failures).

  • --reference=file: Set ownership and group properties to match those of the specified reference file.

  • -h: Modify the owner/group of a symbolic link itself instead of the target file it references.

Examples:

$ chown david file.txt

$ chown -R david:users /project

chgrp — Change Group Ownership Utility

Format:

chgrp [options] group_name file...

Or:

chgrp [options] group_name directory

Common Options:

  • -R: Recursively modify group ownership for directories and all sub-contents.

  • -v: Verbose mode (display detailed processing diagnostics).

  • -c: Report only when a group ownership change takes place.

  • -f: Force mode (suppress most error messages regarding group modification failures).

  • -h: Modify the group of a symbolic link itself instead of the destination file it references.

  • --reference=file: Set group ownership to match that of the specified reference file.

Examples:

$ chgrp users file1 file2 file3

$ chgrp -R developers /project

$ chgrp --reference=template.txt newfile.txt

Search and Discovery Utilities

1.10 Search and Discovery Utilities

find — Directory Hierarchy Search Utility

Format:

find [search_path] [matching_criteria/options] [actions]

Common Options and Matching Criteria:

Name-Based Criteria:

  • -name: Match file names (case-sensitive).

  • -iname: Match file names (case-insensitive).

  • -path: Match against the full file path.

  • -regex: Match against a regular expression pattern.

Example:

$ find /home -name "*.txt"

Type-Based Criteria:

  • -type f: Regular file.

  • -type d: Directory.

  • -type l: Symbolic link.

  • -type b: Block device.

  • -type c: Character device.

Example:

$ find /etc -type d

Size-Based Criteria:

  • -size 10k: Exactly 10 KB.

  • -size +10k: Greater than 10 KB.

  • -size -10k: Less than 10 KB.

SizeUnits
cBytes
kKB
MMB
GGB

Example:

$ find . -size +100M

Time-Based Criteria:

  • -mtime: Modification time (measured in days).

  • -atime: Access time.

  • -ctime: Metadata status change time.

Time Syntax:

  • -mtime 3: Exactly 3 days ago.

  • -mtime +3: More than 3 days ago.

  • -mtime -3: Within the last 3 days.

Example:

$ find /var/log -mtime +7

Permission and Ownership Criteria:

find . -perm 644

find . -user david

find . -group users

Logical Operators:

  • -a: Logical AND (default behavior).

  • -o: Logical OR.

  • !: Logical NOT.

Examples:

$ find . -type f -a -size +1M

$ find . -name \"\*.c\" -o -name \"\*.h\"

Common Structural Actions:

  • -print: Print the absolute or relative file path to stdout (default behavior).

  • -exec: Execute a trailing shell command on the matched targets.

$ find . -name "*.log" -exec rm {} \;

(Note: {} represents the current matched file path, and \; terminates the execution pattern).

  • -delete: Remove the matched targets directly.
$ find . -name "*.tmp" -delete
  • -ok: Perform interactive execution, prompting the user prior to running the command.
$ find . -name "*.log" -ok rm {} \;

Hierarchy Constraints:

  • -maxdepth n: Descend at most n levels of directories below the starting points.

  • -mindepth n: Do not apply any criteria or actions at levels less than n.

$ find . -maxdepth 1 -type f

Common Practical Invocations:

$ find /var/log -type f -mtime +7 -delete # Purge logs older than 7 days

$ find / -type f -size +1G # Locate large files across root

$ find . -type f -name "*.sh" -exec chmod +x {} \; # Batch update
script permissions

$ find . -type f | wc -l # Count the number of total files

grep — Pattern Matching and Key String Search Utility

Format:

grep [options] "pattern" [file...]

Or when processing stream inputs via pipes:

command | grep [options] "pattern"

Matching Control Options:

  • -i: Ignore case distinctions in both the pattern and the input files.

  • -v: Invert the sense of matching, selecting non-matching lines.

  • -w: Select only those lines containing matches that form whole words.

  • -x: Select only those matches that exactly match the whole line.

  • -e: Specify multiple search patterns.

  • -f: Obtain patterns from the specified file, one per line.

Examples:

$ grep -i \"error\" log.txt

$ grep -v \"debug\" log.txt

$ grep -w \"main\" test.c

Display Control Options:

  • -n: Prefix each line of output with the 1-based line number within its input file.

  • -c: Suppress normal output; instead print a count of matching lines for each input file.

  • -l: Suppress normal output; instead print the name of each input file from which output would normally have been printed.

  • -L: Suppress normal output; instead print the name of each input file from which no output would normally have been printed.

  • -o: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of a matching line, with each such part on a separate output line.

  • --color=auto: Highlight the matching string fragments using ANSI escape sequences.

Examples:

$ grep -n \"error\" log.txt

$ grep -c \"error\" log.txt

Recursive Directory Traversal Options:

  • -r: Read all files under each directory, recursively.

  • -R: Read all files under each directory, recursively, and follow all symbolic links.

Example:

$ grep -r \"main\" .

Context Display Options:

  • -A n: Print n lines of trailing context after matching lines.

  • -B n: Print n lines of leading context before matching lines.

  • -C n: Print n lines of leading and trailing output context.

Example:

$ grep -C 3 \"error\" log.txt

Regular Expression Variants:
(Note: Basic Regular Expressions (BRE) are supported by default).

  • -E: Interpret the pattern as an Extended Regular Expression (ERE) (equivalent to egrep).

  • -F: Interpret the pattern as a fixed string, suppressing regular expression parsing (equivalent to fgrep).

  • -P: Interpret the pattern as a Perl-Compatible Regular Expression (PCRE) (on supported environments).

Examples:

$ grep -E \"error\|fail\" log.txt

$ grep -F \"a+b\" file.txt

Common Practical Invocations:

$ grep -i "error" /var/log/syslog # Search system logs for error tags

$ grep -rn "main" . # Recursively locate functions in source trees

$ grep -c "error" log.txt # Calculate total instances of matches

$ ps aux | grep nginx # Filter active process listings

$ grep -o "[0-9]\+" file.txt # Extract matched segments exclusively

Regular Expression Fundamentals:

ExpressionMatching Pattern
.Matches any single character.
*Matches the preceding element zero or more times.
^Anchors the match to the start of a line.
$Anchors the match to the end of a line.
[abc]Matches a bracket expression containing a, b, or c.
[^abc]Matches any single character not matching a, b, or c.

Examples:

grep "^root" /etc/passwd

grep "[0-9]\{3\}" file.txt

Historical Implementations vs. Modern Standards:

  • grep: Basic Regular Expressions (BRE).

  • egrep: Extended Regular Expressions (ERE), deprecated in favor of grep -E.

  • fgrep: Fixed String matching, deprecated in favor of grep -F.

Modern infrastructure favors explicitly passing the flag vectors:

grep -E

grep -F

Compression and Decompression

1.11 Compression and Decompression

tar — Tape Archive Utility

Format:

tar [options] archive_name [files_or_directories]

The typical structural arrangement is:

tar -options archive_file targets_to_archive

Common Options:

  • -c: Create a new archive.

  • -x: Extract files from an archive.

  • -t: List the contents of an archive (table of contents).

  • -r: Append files to the end of an archive.

  • -u: Only append files that are newer than the copy in the archive.

  • -f: Use archive file (mandatory). The -f option must be followed immediately by the archive file name.

OptionCompression MethodStandard Extension
-zgzip.tar.gz
-jbzip2.tar.bz2
-Jxz.tar.xz
-aAuto-detectbased on Automatic extension

Examples:

$ tar -cvf archive.tar dir/ # Create a tar archive (uncompressed)

$ tar -czvf archive.tar.gz dir/ # Create a gzip compressed tar archive

$ tar -cJvf archive.tar.xz dir/ # Create an xz compressed tar archive (high compression ratio)

$ tar -xvf archive.tar # Extract an uncompressed tar archive

$ tar -xzvf archive.tar.gz # Extract a gzip compressed tar archive

$ tar -xzvf archive.tar.gz -C /target/path # Extract to a designated target path

$ tar -tvf archive.tar # List archive contents verbosely

Common Control Options:

OptionArchitectural Meaning / Function
-vVerbose mode (display file progression details).
-CChange to specified directory before、executing operations.
--excludeExclude files matching a specified pattern.
-pPreserve original file permissions and
--strip-components=nStrip n leading components from file names on extraction.

Advanced Practical Invocations:

$ tar -czvf backup.tar.gz /project --exclude="*.log" # Exclude file pattern example

$ tar -xvf archive.tar file.txt # Extract a specific file from archive

$ tar -czvf backup.tar.gz . # Archive the current working directory

Standard Archiving and Extraction Examples:

$ tar -xvf file.tar

$ tar -czvf file.tar.gz dir

$ tar -xzvf file.tar.gz

$ zip -r file.zip dir

$ unzip file.zip

1.12 Process Management

ps — Report Process Status Utility

Format:

ps [options]

OptionArchitectural Meaning / Function

OptionFunctional Specification

df (disk free) — Report File System Disk Space Usage Utility

OptionArchitectural Meaning / Function

Pipes and Redirection

1.14 Pipes and Redirection

| — The Pipe Command

Format:

command1 | command2

Its architectural function is to direct the standard output (stdout) of the first command (command1) to serve as the standard input (stdin) for the second command (command2).

Example:

$ ps aux | grep nginx

> and >> — Output Redirection Commands

Examples:

$ ls > file.txt # Overwrites or creates file.txt with the stdout of ls

$ ls >> file.txt # Appends the stdout of the ls command to the end of file.txt

$ ps -ef | grep root | grep ssh | wc -l # Multi-stage pipeline
execution

Within a Linux / Unix Shell environment, every running process maps to exactly three default standard file descriptors:

Descriptor NameNumeric VectorArchitectural Meaning
stdin0Standard Input (file or hardware input device)
stdout1Standard Output (file or hardware display device)
stderr2Standard Error (file or hardware diagnostic logging device)

These three processing channels can be controlled via their symbolic descriptor descriptors or explicitly referenced by their numeric index values. Leveraging the redirection syntax (> or >>), standard I/O channels can be decoupled from default hardware and mapped to alternative devices or physical files. The implementation syntax is defined as follows:

command 2> error.txt # Redirects the stderr stream of a command into error.txt

Examples:

$ ls not_exist 2 > err.log

command > out.txt 2>&1

(Note: In the final example, the primary output stream is directed into out.txt. Simultaneously, the stderr stream (2>) is mapped to the exact same channel destination currently assigned to stdout (&1), which typically outputs directly to the screen terminal).

The & symbol acts as a dedicated file descriptor token, informing the Shell interpreter that the trailing argument integer is an active file descriptor rather than a literal, regular filename string. Without appending the & token (e.g., writing 2>1), the Shell would parse the instruction as a request to dump diagnostic error tracking outputs into a common text file literally named 1.

grep keyword file 2>/dev/null # Redirects stderr to the bit-bucket null device to suppress errors

Other Common Utilities

1.15 Other Common Utilities

echo — Display a Line of Text

Format:

echo [options] [string]

Common Options:

  • -n: Suppress the trailing newline character character.

  • -e: Enable interpretation of backslash escape sequences.

  • -E: Explicitly disable interpretation of backslash escape sequences (Default behavior).

Supported Escape Sequences:

SequenceArchitectural Meaning / Action
\nNewline character.
\tHorizontal tab character.
\\Literal backslash.
\rCarriage return character.
\bBackspace control sequence.
\aAlert (system bell or beep tone).
\cProduce no further output (terminates processing).

Examples:

$ echo david

$ name="My name is David"

$ echo $name

$ echo -e "Hello \nWorld"

(Note: Evaluation of escape sequences occurs explicitly when enveloped within double quote pairs).

The Functional Distinctions Between ' ' and " ":
Within a Linux Shell architecture (such as ), single quotes (' ') and double quotes (" ") both enclose string assignments, but their low-level translation behaviors differ strictly:

Technical Feature'Single Quotes'"Double Quotes"
Variable Expansion❌ Suppressed (Literal Interpretation)✅ Executed (Expands $VAR)
Command Substitution❌ Suppressed✅ Executed (Runs `cmd` or $())
Escape Character Processing❌ Suppressed (Except \'in raw terms)✅ Partially Interpreted
Wildcard Globbing❌ Suppressed❌ Suppressed

ln — Create Link Files Utility

Format:

ln [options] target link_name

Common Options:

  • -s: Generate a symbolic / soft link instead of a hard link.

  • -f: Force remove existing destination files.

  • -i: Prompt interactively prior to removing existing destination targets.

  • -v: Verbose mode (print file names handled by the utility).

  • -n: Treat the destination link name as a normal file if it points to a directory symbolic link (prevents deep resolution).

  • -d: Permit the superuser (root) to attempt hard linking directories.

Links are split architecturally into hard links and symbolic links. A hard link shares the identical index node (inode) entry as the original target; removing one link reference leaves remaining nodes unharmed. A symbolic link (or soft link) functions as a pointer path pointing to the original filename; if the source file is deleted, the soft link stays intact but breaks, resulting in a dangling link.

Examples:

$ ln file.txt file_link.txt # Instantiates a hard link pointing to the same inode

$ ln -s file.txt soft_link.txt # Instantiates a soft symbolic reference link

export — Set Environment Variable Attributes

Format:

export [options] [variable_name[=value]]

Common Options:

  • -p: Display a listing of all currently exported system environment variables.

  • -n: Strip the export attribute from named variables, reverting them to local shell scope.

  • -f: Treat the targeted arguments as names of shell functions to export.

Examples:

$ export -p

$ export PATH=$PATH:/opt/bin

$ export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-11

env — Display or Temporarily Modify the Execution Environment

Format:

env [options] [NAME=VALUE...] [command [arguments...]]

Common Options:

  • No Arguments: Dumps a listing of all currently active environment variables to stdout.

  • VAR=val: Appends a temporary environment entry strictly for the duration of the trailing command invocation.

  • -i: Start with an empty environment, fully discarding inheritance values.

  • -u VAR: Purge variable VAR from the localized active environment tracking block.

Examples:

$ env

$ env DEBUG=1 ./program

$ env -i

$ env -u PATH

Wildcards

1.16 Wildcards

Wildcards are utilized within the shell environment to match specified character ranges. The most frequently encountered wildcards are defined below:

SymbolArchitectural Meaning / Matching Pattern
*Matches zero or more arbitrary characters.
?Matches exactly one single arbitrary character.
[]Matches any one single character enclosed within the brackets (defines a range or set).

Examples:

$ ls *.c

$ ls file?.txt

Bracket Range Matching

PatternMatching Envelope Rules
[character_set]Matches any single character present within the specified set.
[character-character]Matches any single character falling within the sequential range defined by the hyphen boundaries.
[!character_set]Matches any single character not included within the specified set.
[^character_set]Anchors the pattern to match strings that begin with the character configurations specified.

Examples:

$ ls file[123].txt

Valid matches:

  • file1.txt

  • file2.txt

  • file3.txt

Invalid matches (will not match):

  • file12.txt
$ ls file[a-z].txt

Valid matches:

  • filea.txt

  • fileb.txt

  • ...

  • filez.txt

Standard Character Range Configurations

ConfigurationExplicit Matching Context Syntax
[a-z]All lowercase alphabetic characters.
[A-Z]All uppercase alphabetic characters.
[0-9]All single-digit numeric characters.
[a-zA-Z]All alphabetic characters regardless of case.
[a-z0-9]All lowercase alphanumeric characters.

Linux Directory Structure

1.17 Linux Directory Structure

In the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS), the directory structure is not a random collection of directories but follows a strict logic. For embedded systems such as the NXP i.MX6 Solo, understanding these directories helps you precisely locate kernel images, configuration files, and driver nodes.

Linux does not partition drives into distinct drive letters (such as C: or D:); instead, all devices are mounted at specific locations underneath the single root directory /. The following is a quick reference guide to the core directories.

Core Boot and System Files

  • /boot: Contains the essential files required for booting the system. The kernel image (zImage), Device Tree blobs (DTBs), initramfs, and bootloader files are typically stored here.

  • /bin: Contains basic, essential system binaries and commands required for system booting and operation (such as ls, cp, sh), which are accessible to all users. Typical commands like ls, cp, mv, cat, and are located here.

  • /sbin: Contains system administration binaries (System Binaries) such as ifconfig, fdisk, reboot, and addgrp. These tools are designated for hardware management and system maintenance routines.

  • /lib: Contains essential dynamic shared libraries (.so files) and kernel modules (modules) needed by the binaries in /bin and /sbin. Without this directory, the basic commands in /bin cannot execute.

Hardware and Configuration

  • /dev: The location of device files. In Linux, everything is a file. Serial ports (tty), SD cards (mmcblk0), and USB devices are all accessed via nodes in this directory. It contains numerous subdirectories corresponding to different devices, such as tty, sda, and null. These files are dynamically populated by the kernel and udev.

  • /etc: The system configuration directory. It houses network configurations, user passwords, startup scripts (such as rc.local), and kernel parameters (sysctl.conf) applied after Linux boots.

    • /etc/passwd: Stores user account details and credentials.

    • /etc/fstab: Defines the file systems to be mounted automatically at boot time, along with their respective mount options.

    • /etc/hostname: Stores the system network host name.

    • /etc/systemd/: Contains local systemd configuration and service unit files; it is the core configuration directory for system service management.

Virtual File Systems /sys and /proc

  • /proc: Reflects process and kernel runtime states (such as CPU metrics), allowing users to monitor active process state data by reading files within this path. It is a virtual file system (procfs) in Linux that consumes zero disk space, as all contents are generated dynamically in memory by the kernel. Each active process maps to a specific subdirectory named after its unique Process ID (PID).

  • /sys: Exports kernel objects and hardware topologies. Manipulating GPIO pins or adjusting LED brightness is commonly handled under this path. System administrators utilize files here for resource configuration and device management. The standard top-level subdirectories include:

    • /sys/block

    • /sys/bus

    • /sys/class

    • /sys/devices

    • /sys/firmware

    • /sys/fs

    • /sys/kernel

    • /sys/module

    • /sys/power

The /sys/devices subdirectory acts as the core repository for the live Device Tree representation; the complete hierarchical structural arrangement of all registered devices inside the running kernel resides here. It reflects the true physical hardware topology and serves as the primary root of sysfs (e.g., /sys/devices/pci0000:00/ and /sys/devices/system/cpu/). All entries under /sys/class and /sys/bus ultimately resolve back to files inside this directory via symbolic links. It can be understood as the definitive physical device topology tree.

The /sys/class subdirectory provides a logical view of devices grouped by function class. These entries are typically symbolic links pointing directly to the actual device nodes under /sys/devices, making this the most frequently accessed interface from user space. It primarily includes elements such as:

  • /sys/class/net/

  • /sys/class/block/

  • /sys/class/leds/

  • /sys/class/gpio/

For example:

  • /sys/class/net/eth0 corresponds to the primary Ethernet interface.

  • /sys/class/block/sda corresponds to the first storage disk.

The /sys/block subdirectory holds the nodes corresponding to block devices. For instance, /sys/block/sda/ maps to a disk drive, while the /sys/block/mmcblk0/ subdirectory represents the primary MultiMediaCard (MMC) storage device. These entries encompass files such as size, queue/, and stat. They are commonly utilized for storage performance profiling, I/O tuning, and flash storage management in embedded deployments.

The /sys/bus path houses devices organized hierarchically by their physical or virtual bus types, such as /sys/bus/pci/, /sys/bus/usb/, /sys/bus/i2c/, and /sys/bus/platform/. These match PCI bus devices, USB devices, I2C peripherals, and integrated platform devices, respectively. Each individual bus contains a device description subdirectory (devices/) and a driver tracking subdirectory (drivers/) (e.g., /sys/bus/pci/devices/ and /sys/bus/pci/drivers/). This layout represents the definitive boundary layer where the kernel executes device-to-driver matching.

The /sys/module subdirectory exposes active kernel modules, such as /sys/module/ext4/ and /sys/module/nvme/. The content includes diagnostic files and paths like initsize, parameters/, refcnt, and sections/, which allow users to inspect live module configurations or dynamically tweak exported module runtime variables.

The /sys/kernel interface handles core kernel subsystem parameters, hosting critical entries like /sys/kernel/debug, /sys/kernel/mm, and /sys/kernel/tracing. Here, /sys/kernel/debug exposes the debugfs boundary layer (requiring an explicit, separate mount operation), and /sys/kernel/tracing exposes the active ftrace engine interface.

The /sys/fs path maps to the file system subsystem interface layer (e.g., /sys/fs/cgroup, /sys/fs/ext4, and /sys/fs/bpf). It tracks and exposes operational state statistics specific to file systems active within standard cgroups.

The /sys/firmware path contains low-level firmware-related configurations and exports, including /sys/firmware/efi and /sys/firmware/devicetree. ARM-based embedded systems heavily leverage the /sys/firmware/devicetree/base directory directory to export the flattened device tree abstraction layer to user space.

The /sys/power interface handles system-wide power management parameters, exposing files like /sys/power/state and /sys/power/wakeup_count. For instance, executing:

echo mem > /sys/power/state

forces the hardware into a suspend-to-RAM state.

The /sys/devices/system path aggregates infrastructure-critical system-level hardware devices, including /sys/devices/system/cpu/, /sys/devices/system/memory/, and /sys/devices/system/node/. For instance, executing:

echo 0 > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu1/online

takes CPU1 offline.

User and Application Space

  • /usr: Houses user-space applications and secondary utilities, conceptually mapping to C:\Program Files in Windows architectures.

  • /usr/bin: Contains non-essential system-wide user binary commands.

  • /usr/lib: Contains shared libraries consumed by binaries located under /usr/bin and /usr/sbin.

  • /var: Stores highly dynamic variable data, such as system event logs (/var/log) or package manager cache indexes.

  • /home: Serves as the primary root hosting individual unprivileged user home directories.

  • /root: The dedicated private home directory of the system superuser (root). Note that it is isolated outside the /home directory tree.

Other Key Directories

  • /tmp: Temporary storage directory. Files housed within this path are generally swept and purged during system boot sequences.

  • /mnt: General purpose mount point used to manually mount temporary external file system volumes.

  • /media: Automatically managed mount points for plug-and-play removable storage devices (such as USB thumb drives).

  • /opt: Add-on repository designated for hosting third-party monolithic software application packages.

  • /run: Holds ephemeral runtime data tracking active system operations since boot, such as process ID files (.pid) and active domain sockets. This path exists entirely in volatile memory and is wiped during reboots.

  • /lost+found: A repository used by file system check utilities (like fsck) to deposit orphaned file fragments recovered after structural file system corruption.

Chapter 2: The U-BOOT Bootloader

U-BOOT is an acronym for the Universal Boot Loader, commonly referred to by developers as "Das U-Boot". It is a powerful system bootloader capable of initializing and booting a diverse range of operating systems, as well as launching bare-metal, non-OS applications. U-BOOT provides architecture support for various processors, including ARM, PPC, MIPS, x86, NIOS, and MicroBlaze. Hundreds of development and production system boards natively support U-BOOT, establishing it as the dominant mainstream bootloader in contemporary embedded engineering.

As a completely free and open-source software project, U-BOOT was initiated by Wolfgang Denk. Subsequently, a vast community of computer enthusiasts and open-source enterprise vendors—such as Siemens—joined the developer ranks. Due to its extensive feature set and outstanding system stability, it has been widely adopted by multiple operating system architectures, particularly embedded operating systems, as their primary boot mechanism. Developers can fetch the official U-BOOT source code repositories directly from the upstream infrastructure hosted at https://source.denx.de/u-boot.

Distinct from standard, minimalist bootloaders, U-BOOT provides a fully integrated command-line shell interface (command interpreter). This capability permits users to interrupt the automatic boot sequence before the operating system kernel is loaded. Once interrupted, users can leverage commands or environment variables to alter the system boot topology or modify the boot argument vectors passed to the operating system kernel. These modified commands, environment variables, and execution command sequences can be written directly to non-volatile storage media, allowing the platform to utilize the updated configurations for subsequent routine boot cycles.

The following sections analyze the implementation details of common U-BOOT utilities, environment variable structures, and the syntactical composition of U-BOOT scripting frameworks.

U-BOOT Commands

2.1 U-BOOT Commands

U-BOOT provides a vast array of commands dedicated to interacting with peripherals, memory, file systems, and networking devices. Users can leverage these commands to read data from storage components, write payloads to target devices, configure hardware peripherals, and display critical system information. U-BOOT implements two distinct command line interpreter backends: a legacy simple command line interface and a Bourne-shell-compatible command line parser known as HUSH. Interaction with the user is managed dynamically through this text-based command shell.

U-BOOT commands are structurally categorized into system information, memory operations, flash storage manipulation, execution control, network utilities, environment variable overrides, file system abstraction support, special-purpose routines, advanced configuration commands, and miscellaneous helpers. The subsequent sections outline these functional sets systematically.

2.1.1 Information Commands

Information commands are utilized to query various system metrics and hardware parameters. These commands include:

  • bdinfo: Displays system board information.

  • coninfo: Displays console terminal interface statistics.

  • flinfo: Displays flash memory configuration and layout details.

  • iminfo: Displays the header block details of an uncompressed image file.

  • imls: Lists boot images found across storage blocks in flash memory.

  • fatinfo: Displays metadata and statistics of a FAT file system partition.

  • mii: Inspects and controls Ethernet Media Independent Interface (MII) and PHY registers.

  • help: Displays online interactive help summaries for all supported shell commands.

The following output shows the structural execution metrics returned by running the bdinfo command, where => represents the interactive U-BOOT command prompt.

=> bdinfo

memstart = 0x00000000

memsize = 0x04000000

flashstart = 0x40000000

flashsize = 0x00800000

flashoffset = 0x00030000

sramstart = 0x00000000

sramsize = 0x00000000

immr_base = 0xFFF00000

bootflags = 0x00000001

intfreq = 50 MHz

busfreq = 50 MHz

ethaddr = 00:D0:93:00:28:81

IP addr = 0.0.0.0

baudrate = 115200 bps

=>

the execution results of the help command are presented below:

=>help

? - alias for \'help\'

If a user wishes to query the specific usage and syntax parameters for a particular utility, they can execute help <command>. For example:

=> help run

run var [...]

- run the commands in the environment variable(s) 'var'

The usage structure and syntax options for the mii command are defined as follows:

  • mii device: Lists all registered Ethernet interface devices.

  • mii device <name>: Sets the active target device to <name>.

  • mii read <addr> <reg>: Reads the value of register <reg> from the Media Independent Interface (MII) PHY address <addr>.

  • mii write <addr> <reg> <data>: Writes the payload word <data> into the MII PHY address <addr> register <reg>.

2.1.2 Memory Commands

This class of commands is dedicated to volatile memory manipulation and includes the following operations:

  • base: Displays or configures the baseline address offset, which serves as a global reference offset for subsequent memory access commands.

  • crc32: Computes a 32-bit Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC32) checksum over a memory buffer.

  • cmp: Performs a byte-by-byte comparison between two distinct memory regions.

  • cp: Executes a bulk memory copy operation from a source address to a destination buffer.

  • md: Displays (dumps) memory content in organized hex and ASCII views.

  • mm: Modifies memory contents interactively with automatic address auto-increment.

  • mtest: Performs a standard, non-destructive volatile memory stress test across a given range.

  • mw: Fills a specific memory boundary range with a fixed data pattern.

  • loop: Loops memory access infinitely across a given address envelope for hardware troubleshooting.

The usage conventions and execution results for the base and md utilities are presented below:

=> base

Base Address: 0x00000000

=> md 0 c

00000000: feffffff 00000000 7cbd2b78 7cdc3378 ........|. +x|.3x

00000010: 3cfb3b78 3b000000 7c0002e4 39000000 <.;x;...|...9...

00000020: 7d1043a6 3d000400 7918c3a6 3d00c000 }.C.=...y...=...

=> base 40000000

Base Address: 0x40000000

=> md 0 c

40000000: 27051956 50504342 6f6f7420 312e312e '..VPPCBoot 1.1.

40000010: 3520284d 61722032 31203230 3032202d 5 (Mar 21 2002 -

40000020: 2031393a 35353a30 34290000 00000000 19:55:04)......

=>

2.1.3 Flash Storage Commands

  • cp: Flash memory programming utility (copies chunks from RAM to flash configurations).

  • flinfo: Displays detailed flash sector layouts, banks, and hardware definitions.

  • erase: Erases explicit sectors or full ranges within flash storage arrays.

  • protect: Enables or disables hardware/software write-protection bits across flash memory blocks.

2.1.4 Execution Control Commands

  • autoscr: Executes standalone binary macro scripts from memory.

  • bootm: Boots a structured application or kernel system image resident in physical RAM.

  • bootelf: Executes a binary application image formatted as a standard Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) structure from memory.

  • bootvx: Boots a structured VxWorks operating system application image built as an ELF payload.

  • go: Jumps directly to a raw instruction address (addr) to start bare-metal execution sequences.

The standard execution syntax for the bootm command is defined as follows:

bootm [addr [arg ...]]

- boot application image stored in memory passing arguments 'arg ...'; when booting a Linux kernel, 'arg' can be the address of an initrd image.

2.1.5 Network Utilities

  • bootp: Leverages BOOTP/TFTP protocol interactions to fetch and boot a system image over the network.

  • cdp: Configures and processes the Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) topology metadata.

  • dhcp: Invokes the internal DHCP client routine to acquire a dynamic local IP address and poll global boot configuration vectors.

  • loadb: Loads a raw binary payload stream into memory using the serial console line via the Kermit protocol.

  • loads: Loads a text-based Motorola S-record firmware payload into target memory blocks via the serial line interface.

  • nfs: Restructures network storage calls to boot an operating system image using the Network File System (NFS) protocol layout.

  • ping: Transmits standard ICMP ECHO_REQUEST packets to network hosts to check end-to-end transport layer paths.

  • rarpboot: Combines RARP/TFTP server handshakes to pull and launch a system image over network environments.

  • tftpboot: Downloads and initializes a system image over network setups using the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP).

The configuration format for the bootp command is structured as follows:

bootp [loadAddress] [bootfilename]

The configuration format for pulling and booting software via the nfs client framework is structured as follows:

nfs [loadAddress] [host_ip_addr:bootfilename]

2.1.6 Environment Variable Commands

  • printenv: Displays the values of all currently defined environment variables.

  • saveenv: Writes the active environment variables from RAM to non-volatile storage.

  • askenv: Prompts the user via the standard input console to capture and assign a value to an environment variable.

  • setenv: Establishes a new environment variable or modifies/deletes an existing one.

  • run: Executes the command sequence or macro embedded within specified environment variables.

  • bootd: Initiates the default boot sequence, structurally equivalent to executing run bootcmd.

2.1.7 File System Support Commands

  • chpart: Changes the active target partition.

  • fsinfo: Displays fundamental metadata regarding the active file system type.

  • fsload: Loads a raw binary payload into memory from a generic supported file system.

  • ls: Lists the files and subdirectories resident within a specified path.

  • fatinfo: Displays low-level cluster and volume metadata for a FAT-formatted partition.

  • fatls: Lists the contents of a directory located on a FAT-formatted file system partition.

  • fatload: Loads a binary file from a DOS/FAT file system into physical memory.

  • nand: The NAND flash memory subsystem, encompassing an array of sub-commands for raw block operations.

  • reiserls: Lists the subdirectory layout and contents within a ReiserFS file system hierarchy.

  • reiserload: Loads a binary payload into memory from a ReiserFS file system.

2.1.8 Special-Purpose Commands

  • i2c: The I2C bus subsystem, providing tools to probe, read, and write to peripheral chips.

  • doc: Disk On Chip (DOC) storage subsystem interface routines.

  • dtt: Digital Thermometer and Thermostat telemetry subsystem.

  • eeprom: Subsystem for reading and writing to on-board EEPROM chips.

  • fpga: Subsystem designated for loading and configuring field-programmable gate array bitstreams.

  • ide: Integrated Drive Electronics (IDE) storage subsystem.

  • kgdb: Switches the system interface into Kernel GNU Debugger mode for low-level trapping.

  • diskboot: Initiates an operating system boot sequence from an attached IDE storage device.

  • icache: Enables or disables the processor's internal instruction cache (I-Cache).

  • dcache: Enables or disables the processor's internal data cache (D-Cache).

  • diag: Executes hardware board-level diagnostic monitoring sequences.

  • log: Manages and reviews device log configurations.

  • pci: Scans, displays, and modifies fields within the PCI configuration space layout.

  • regdump: Dumps the current hardware register states to the console interface.

  • usb: The Universal Serial Bus (USB) subsystem, managing bus enumeration and storage/peripheral access.

  • sspi: Synchronous Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) configuration and transfer utility.

Each of the subsystems detailed above contains specific sub-commands for execution. Using the help utility alongside any subsystem name exposes its structural formatting and syntax.

2.1.9 Miscellaneous Commands

  • bmp: Manipulates and renders BMP format image data. For example:
    bmp info <image address> displays file metadata for a bitmap image resident at the designated memory address, whereas bmp display <image address> [x,y] renders the bitmap located at <image address> onto the screen starting at coordinates (x,y).

  • date: Displays or sets the current real-time clock (RTC) calendar date and system time.

  • echo: Outputs explicit text strings or expanded environment variable values directly to the active console terminal interface.

  • exit: Exits the execution context of the currently running macro script.

  • kbd: Scans and captures raw keyboard matrix input sequences.

  • in: Reads a data byte or word from a hardware I/O port address space.

  • out: Writes a data byte or word to a hardware I/O port address space.

  • reset: Triggers a full system hardware reset and cold reboot cycle.

  • sleep: Pauses the execution sequence of the command interpreter for a specified duration of seconds.

  • test: Evaluates conditional statement expressions for shell script control flows (minimal implementation).

  • version: Displays the current compilation release and build version string of the running U-BOOT binary.

  • wd: Probes, triggers, or configures the system hardware watchdog timer parameters.

  • ?: Acts as a direct structural alias for the help instruction.

Environment Variables

2.2 Environment Variables

U-BOOT utilizes environment variables to adjust its own execution sequence and configure system hardware parameters. Environment variables are case-sensitive and are stored as character strings within non-volatile storage media, such as an EEPROM or flash memory. The environment consists of standard predefined environment variables and custom user-defined variables. The most frequently encountered standard environment variables are detailed below.

2.2.1 autostart

When autostart is set to yes, y, Y, t, T, or 1, image files imported via the bootp, bootelf, dhcp, diskboot, nboot, nfs, rarpboot, scsiboot, tftpboot, or usbboot commands will automatically boot. If autostart contains any value other than those specified above, the image payload is merely loaded into memory but will not automatically execute. Images passed to bootm are copied to the memory space designated by the load address for decompression; leveraging this architectural trait allows arbitrary data blocks to be loaded into memory and decompressed on demand.

2.2.2 baudrate

This variable configures the transmission baud rate for the serial console port. Because U-BOOT is primarily deployed on embedded systems, the interactive control terminal typically runs on a host computer, communicating with the embedded target via a serial interface. This environment variable defines the communication speed across the UART line linking the host and the embedded platform.

2.2.3 bootdelay

This variable defines the wait time (in seconds) before the automatic boot sequence is initiated. After U-BOOT initializes in memory, if bootdelay is not equal to 0, it pauses for the specified duration. During this countdown period, if the user registers a keystroke on the keyboard, U-BOOT breaks out of the autoboot sequence and enters the interactive command interpretation state, enabling users to enter any of the U-BOOT commands listed previously. If the delay expires without a keystroke, U-BOOT automatically begins booting the system.

If bootdelay is set to -1, automatic booting is fully disabled. If bootdelay is set to -2, the system boots immediately and disables any attempt to abort the sequence (e.g., via Ctrl+C).

2.2.4 bootcmd

This variable specifies the exact command sequence or macro executed by U-BOOT when initiating an automatic boot. bootcmd stores a series of concatenated U-BOOT commands. When the U-BOOT autoboot sequence fires, it executes the operations defined within bootcmd sequentially.

2.2.5 bootargs

This variable holds the command-line argument vector passed from U-BOOT to the operating system kernel or binary image payload during the boot invocation. The booted kernel or application parses these parameters to control its low-level operational paradigms and driver initializations.

2.2.6 bootfile

Specifies the default target filename to be downloaded when importing images via the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP).

2.2.7 bootm_low

Specifies the lowest physical memory boundary address accessible to the bootm initialization routine. This variable is typically omitted, defaulting to the baseline memory configuration.

2.2.8 bootm_mapsize

Defines the total size of the linear memory region mapped and accessible to the Linux kernel during its initial booting phase. This virtual window begins explicitly at the address defined by bootm_low.

2.2.9 bootm_size

Defines the maximum allocation space within memory available to the bootm routine for handling, relocating, and decompressing input image files.

2.2.10 updatefile

Designates the source file path and location on the TFTP server when performing firmware or software updates via network protocols.

2.2.11 autoload

When autoload is configured explicitly to no, the bootp and dhcp routines only poll the network BOOTP server to pull environment configurations and network definitions without actually pulling the primary system image from the server into physical memory.

2.2.12 fdt_high

Specifies the highest physical memory address boundary that the Flattened Device Tree (FDT) can occupy.

2.2.13 initrd_high

When this variable is omitted, the initrd image payload is automatically copied to the highest available region of physical memory. When explicitly configured, initrd_high restricts the maximum memory address ceiling available for the initrd allocation.

2.2.14 ipaddr

Configures the local IP address for the network interface. Note that this configuration is strictly valid while executing operations within the U-BOOT context. Once control passes to Linux or another operating system, the IP address will be dynamically acquired or statically bound based on user-space network configurations. The following sequence establishes an IP address of 192.168.1.1:

setenv ipaddr 192.168.1.1

Executing saveenv writes this environment configuration to non-volatile storage.

2.2.15 loadaddr

Defines the default baseline memory load address utilized by utilities like bootp, dhcp, rarpboot, and loadb. As analyzed in subsequent boot sequence chapters, the explicit load address of an image payload is typically governed by the loadaddr field embedded inside the uImage file header, or by properties defined within the Device Tree. When no destination load address is specified anywhere, the value of the loadaddr environment variable acts as the absolute fallback target.

2.2.16 serverip

Specifies the IP address of the remote TFTP server, queried directly by the tftpboot network infrastructure.

2.2.17 bootretry

Defines the maximum threshold of sequential boot attempts before U-BOOT declares a definitive boot failure condition.

2.2.18 image

Specifies the exact filename of the target application or kernel image to be executed via bootm.

2.2.19 fdtfile

On platforms with Device Tree support, this variable defines the filename of the compiled binary Device Tree Blob (DTB) describing the target system's hardware configurations.

2.2.20 fdt_addr

Specifies the physical memory destination address where the Device Tree Blob (DTB) is loaded.

2.2.21 ramdisk

Specifies the filename of the primary RAM file system (ramdisk) image payload.

2.2.22 ramdisk_addr

Defines the exact physical memory target address where the RAM file system is imported and mounted.

Note: U-BOOT supports numerous other standard environment variables which are omitted here for brevity.

2.2.23 User-Defined Environment Variables

Users can instantiate custom environment variables arbitrarily, bounded only by the physical storage capacity allocated for the environment block.
