U-BOOT variables are categorized into local variables and global variables (the latter commonly referenced as environment variables), and can be further subdivided into simple variables and recursive variables. A simple variable maps a unique literal name directly to a string literal value, using the following format:

setenv <varname> <variable_value>

For example:

=> setenv kernelName ubuntu

=> printenv kernelName

=> kernelName=ubuntu

=>

A recursive variable is defined when a variable's value payload itself references one or more embedded variables. Within a recursive variable definition, the nested variables are not expanded immediately; instead, they persist inside the string as raw variable references. Expansion occurs exclusively when the parent macro variable is executed via the run command, substituting the variable references with their live values. The following sequence shows how a recursive variable is declared and processed:

=> setenv displayBytes md.b \${addr} \${bytes}

=> printenv displayBytes

=> displayBytes=md.b ${addr} ${bytes}

=> setenv addr 0b000000

=> setenv bytes 10

=> run displayBytes

0b000000: 00 00 00 00

0b000004: 00 00 00 00

0b000008: 00 00

In this scenario, setenv displayBytes md.b \${addr} \${bytes} defines the recursive target macro variable displayBytes with the literal string content md.b ${addr} ${bytes}. The backslash \ escape token functions to suppress the immediate expansion of the addr and bytes variables during definition. The ${} token sequence acts as the runtime evaluation operator that replaces the symbolic name with its current data value. When the recursive variable displayBytes is evaluated via run, the variable references addr and bytes expand dynamically, forcing the underlying memory display routine md.b to execute using the live values of those variables rather than their literal names.

Recursive variables are heavily integrated within scripting architectures. Scripting provides exceptional programmatic capability, allowing engineers to enforce highly complex system-wide control flows. The subsequent section comprehensively details the mechanics of U-BOOT script engineering.

U-BOOT Scripting

2.3 U-BOOT Scripting

A script is composed of a sequence of simple variables and recursive variables. Each recursive variable embeds a group of U-BOOT commands separated by semicolons (;). When a script is executed via the run command, these commands are evaluated sequentially.

U-BOOT supports two distinct command interpreters. The simple command line interface provides rudimentary command interpretation, executing U-BOOT commands sequentially with individual lines separated by semicolons (;) or newline characters. This legacy simple parser does not offer programmatic, conditional runtime control flows.

Conversely, the HUSH interface provides a Bourne-shell-compatible command interpretation layer, offering structured test statements, conditional branches, and loop control blocks. The HUSH parser dynamically determines the execution path of U-BOOT commands based on conditional evaluation results. It supports conditional constructs such as if...then...else...fi alongside loop mechanisms including for...do...done, while...do...done, for...in...do...done, and until...do...done. Furthermore, it natively implements the short-circuit logical operators && and || common to the Linux command line. Because advanced script control flow relies heavily on these features, complex U-BOOT scripts must execute within a HUSH-enabled shell environment.

2.3.1 U-BOOT Variables

U-BOOT variables are broadly divided into local environment variables and global variables. Local environment variables are utilized to store volatile, temporary configurations and are never written to non-volatile storage. The syntax for declaring a local variable follows this format:

var=value

There must be no whitespace surrounding the assignment operator (=), and the value must strictly be a single unspaced token. If the assigned string contains whitespace characters, the entire payload must be enclosed within single or double quotes. Enclosing a string in single quotes suppresses variable expansion, whereas double quotes permit inline variable expansion. The following example instantiates a local variable named LocalVar with the string payload "I am a local variable":

LocalVar="I am a local variable"

Global variables are declared using the standard syntax format:

setenv varName varValue

The three components are separated by whitespace. When the value payload must explicitly contain special characters such as $ or ;, those characters must be escaped with a leading backslash (\). A global variable value can encompass an entire command string separated by semicolons (;); the initial token of each statement is interpreted as a U-BOOT command, followed by its whitespace-delimited arguments. If a global variable holds multiple commands concatenated with semicolons (;), the entire command sequence must be wrapped in single quotes.

Global variables defined via setenv can be invoked as executable macros using the run command. The following example establishes a global variable named infoDisp1:

=> setenv infoDisp1 echo

This is to show how to use global variable.

The macro variable infoDisp1 can now be executed by passing it to the run command:

=> run infoDisp1

This is to show how to use global variable.

The following example shows how to utilize setenv to construct a complex global variable containing multiple sequential commands:

=> setenv infoDisp2 'echo Hello world,; echo I am a robot.'

=> run infoDisp2

Hello world,

I am a robot.

2.3.2 Test Commands

Test commands evaluate expressions, strings, or integers to determine the truth value of their logical relationships. When combined with conditional branches or loops, they enable dynamic command combinations. The standard conditional expressions are evaluated as follows:

  • ( expression ): True if the inner expression evaluates to true.

  • ! expression: True if the expression evaluates to false (logical inversion).

  • -n string: True if the length of the string is non-zero.

  • -z string: True if the length of the string is zero.

  • string: True if the length of the string is non-zero.

  • string1 = string2: True if both strings are identical.

  • string1 != string2: True if the strings are not identical.

For integer evaluation, relational comparisons are expressed using the flags -eq (equal), -lt (less than), -gt (greater than), -ge (greater than or equal), -le (less than or equal), and -ne (not equal). For instance, integer1 -eq integer2 evaluates whether integer1 equals integer2, while integer1 -lt integer2 checks if integer1 is less than integer2.

The evaluation construct test -n string or its structural alias [ -n string ] returns a truth value of 1 if the string length is non-zero, and 0 otherwise. Similarly, [ var1 -le var2 ] returns 1 if the integer value of var1 is less than or equal to var2, and 0 otherwise.

2.3.3 Conditional Statements

The standard syntax configuration for conditional branches follows this structure:

if (condition);

then

  command list

elif (condition);

then

  command list

else

  command list

fi

In the following script block, conditional execution logic interacts with the test framework to select different system boot vectors based on the value of the net_boot variable. If the net_boot variable is unassigned, the system defaults to booting from the SD card. If net_boot equals 1, the platform switches to a network-based TFTP boot pathway. The itest command is leveraged here to explicitly handle integer comparison operations.

if test -n $net_boot; 
then 
     if itest $net_boot == 1; 
     then 
              echo !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!;
              echo ! Booting from TFTP      !;
              echo !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!;
              tftp $fpgadata soc_system.rbf;
     else 
              echo !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!;
              echo ! Booting from SD        !;
              echo !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!;
              fatload mmc 0:1 $fpgadata soc_system.rbf;
     fi
else 
     echo !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!;
     echo  Booting from SD         !; 
     echo !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!;
     fatload mmc 0:1 $fpgadata soc_system.rbf;
fi

2.3.4 Loop Statements

There are three types of loop control statements implemented within the HUSH interface: for...in...do...done, while...do...done, and until...do...done. Distinct from the standard C-language iterative for loop, the loop variable in a HUSH interpreter's for loop can only iterate over values explicitly supplied in a tokenized literal list. The usage models and syntactical arrangements for these three loop variants are defined below:

for var in a b c d;
do 
    echo $var;
done
setenv var 1
while test var -eq 0;
do 
    echo $var;
    setenv var 1;
done
setenv var begin;
until test var != finished;
do 
    echo I am doing something meaningless!;
    echo Just to show how to use until loop.
    setenv var finished;
done

2.3.5 U-BOOT Script Practical Example

The following block shows a structured, minimal U-BOOT deployment script configuration. Lines prefixed with the # symbol represent code comments.

# Address in RAM where the Linux device tree will be loaded.
fdtaddr=0x88000000
# Address in RAM where the Linux kernel image will be loaded.
kerneladdr=0x82000000
# Command to reset the board (TODO).
boardreset=echo “Resetting all images to factory defaults”
# Arguments for the Linux command line, this will be read by the bootz command.
bootargs=console=ttyS0,115200n8 root=/dev/mmcblk0p1 rootfstype=ext4 rootwait
# Command to load the Linux device tree from MMC
loadfdt=load mmc 0:1 ${fdtaddr} /boot/dev.dtb
# Command to load the Linux kernel image from MMC
loadlinux=load mmc 0:1 ${kerneladdr} /boot/uimage
# Command to boot Linux.  Load the required images into RAM, then begin
# running the kernel.  This is the last command that U-BOOT will run.
bootlinux=run loadlinux; run loadfdt; bootz ${kerneladdr} – ${fdtaddr}
# Read a GPIO to see if the reset button is pressed for 2 seconds.  Return
# true if it is.  The ‘exit’ command stops the current command, execution will
# go back to the caller.
resetrequested=if gpio i 27; then sleep 2; if gpio i 27; then true; exit; fi; false;fi
# Entry point, this is the first command U-BOOT will run on boot.
# Do a board reset if needed, then boot Linux.  In this command, bootlinux will
# always run.
bootcmd=if run resetrequested; then run boardreset; fi; run bootlinux

Chapter 3: Device Tree

The Device Tree is a structured data configuration that utilizes a text-based language to describe the layout and attributes of non-discoverable, static hardware systems via a hierarchical tree architecture. Originally engineered by Open Firmware, the Device Tree served as a foundational data-passing interface between the low-level Open Firmware interface and guest application software (the operating system kernel). Mainline Linux officially integrated Device Tree support starting with kernel version 3.5.7.

Prior to the adoption of the Device Tree architecture, platform-specific hardware details were hardcoded directly into the Linux kernel source code as C structures. These board files were compiled alongside the generic kernel code into a monolithic binary image, which was subsequently loaded into memory by U-BOOT during the system initialization sequence. Because Linux targets a vast taxonomy of disparate hardware platforms and vendors, managing thousands of board-specific configuration files created a massive maintenance burden for kernel developers; even a minor adjustment to a peripheral property necessitated a complete recompilation of the entire kernel binary. Furthermore, to adapt to subtle hardware variations, U-BOOT had to pass an excessively large array of parameter vectors to the Linux kernel via the bootargs variable.

The introduction of the Device Tree fundamentally revolutionized this paradigm. By decoupling the hardware abstraction layer from the operating system core, the hardware configuration and the Linux kernel executable now reside in two completely independent files. The hardware topography is compiled into a standalone binary blob file suffixed with .dtb (Device Tree Blob), while the executable kernel routines are stored within separate uImage, zImage, or FIT image structures.

Because the exhaustive layout of the platform's hardware components is encapsulated within the compiled Device Tree blob, U-BOOT no longer needs to pass a long list of hardware descriptors to the Linux kernel. Instead, the bootloader simply tracks the destination address where the .dtb payload resides in physical RAM and passes this memory reference pointer directly to the kernel upon execution. U-BOOT implements this handover by writing the blob's starting memory address into register r3 on PowerPC architectures, or register r2 on ARM and other processor architectures.

An additional architectural advantage of this dual-file decoupling occurs during hardware updates or peripheral tuning: when integrating a new device or modifying existing board parameters, a developer only needs to implement the specific device driver, update the target text file, and compile it down to a new .dtb binary. The core Linux kernel image remains entirely untouched and does not require recompilation.

The Linux kernel leverages the Device Tree abstraction layer to execute three primary system-level routines:

  • Hardware Platform Identification: Verifying the exact board vendor and SoC model.

  • Dynamic Hardware Configuration: Parsing baseline peripheral properties to initialize low-level clocks, interrupt controllers, and pin-multiplexing matrices.

  • Device Driver Binding and Loading: Matching structural device definitions to their corresponding driver modules.

Device Tree Architecture

3.1 Device Tree Architecture

The Device Tree uses a declarative text-based syntax to map out the interconnects, relationships, and localized electrical characteristics of the various integrated circuits and controllers composing the system. Structurally, a Device Tree is composed of a mandatory top-level root node, sub-nodes, and child nodes. Each individual node block is uniquely identified by its node name, alongside an optional node handle (phandle), addressing window descriptors, and an arbitrary list of explicit hardware properties.

A valid Device Tree must contain exactly one singular root node (/). The root node is strictly required to contain exactly one cpus container node and at least one memory description node. The cpus node block can host multiple individual cpu child nodes to accommodate modern multi-core Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP) processor architectures.

Standard Properties

3.2 Standard Properties

The Device Tree Specification defines a set of standard properties. These standard properties define attributes required by the vast majority of Device Tree nodes, and authors can simply implement them according to their standardized usage. Beyond these standard properties, device driver developers can define custom properties tailored strictly for their proprietary drivers or for developers working on identical classes of hardware.

When describing properties, the concept of a "cell" is frequently encountered. Within a Device Tree context, a cell is defined as a 32-bit unsigned integer.

3.2.1 compatible Property

The value of the compatible property is a list of strings, typically formatted as a "manufacturer,model" pair. The sorting sequence within the string list dictates that the more specific the configuration is, the earlier it must appear; the more generic the configuration is, the later it must appear. The Linux kernel parses this exact string matching list to select and bind the appropriate device driver to the hardware node. The string characters must strictly consist of lowercase letters, numbers 0–9, and hyphens, with the initial character being a lowercase letter. For example:

compatible = "fsl,mpc8641", "ns16550";

3.2.2 model Property

The model property specifies a string value that defines the exact model of the component. It should generally follow the "manufacturer,model" nomenclature. For example:

model = "fsl,MPC8349EMITX";

3.2.3 phandle Property

The phandle property value is a 32-bit unsigned integer. When a node explicitly declares a phandle property, other hardware nodes can cross-reference it via this unique numerical identifier. For instance, consider a scenario where an interrupt controller node pic is defined as follows:

pic@10000000 {
        phandle = <1>;
        interrupt-controller;
        reg = <0x10000000 0x100>;
};

This block defines a phandle equal to 1. Consequently, alternative hardware nodes can target the pic node using the integer value 1:

regulator@1 {
        interrupt-parent = <1>;
};

This relationship indicates that the parent interrupt controller for regulator@1 maps directly back to the pic@10000000 node.

3.2.4 status Property

The status property indicates the operational state of a device. The allowable values for the status property are strictly constrained to okay, disabled, reserved, failed, or failed-sss (where sss represents a specific error code payload). When the status property is omitted from a node definition, it defaults implicitly to okay. If a developer is composing a new system Device Tree derived from an existing upstream overlay or reference base, any peripheral nodes not physically routed or supported on the new target board can have their status property explicitly overridden to "disabled". This configuration ensures the kernel bypasses the initialization and probe routines for that device during system boot.

3.2.5 #address-cells and #size-cells Properties

A node's #address-cells and #size-cells properties define the addressing layout rules for its immediate child nodes. Because the Device Tree parses data packages in 32-bit word cells, #address-cells specifies how many 32-bit cells are required to encode the base address within a child node's reg property. Concurrently, #size-cells dictates how many 32-bit cells are required to encode the memory window length or size of that child node. For example, if a parent container node defines these properties as follows:

#address-cells = <2>;
#size-cells = <1>;

Then any immediate child node must format its reg property statement using exactly two cells for the address and one cell for the size parameter:

reg = <0x10000000 0x00000008 0x100>;

In this scenario, the 64-bit combined vector 0x1000000000000008 represents the physical base address of the child node (consuming two cells), and 0x100 represents the allocated memory address space boundary size (consuming one cell).

3.2.6 reg Property

The reg property maps out the physical base addresses and corresponding memory address range sizes for the given peripheral node. The explicit cell count allocated for the address components and size components is determined entirely by the #address-cells and #size-cells properties of its immediate parent node. If a single peripheral maps to multiple non-contiguous physical address windows, it can be defined using multiple grouped address-and-size blocks. For example, assuming a device maps to 100 bytes of address space beginning at 0x10000000 and an additional 200 bytes of address space beginning at 0x20000000, and assuming both the address and size targets are configured to consume exactly one cell each, the node's reg property is expressed as:

reg = <0x10000000 100 0x20000000 200>;

If the parent node defines #size-cells = <0>, the length fields within the child node's reg array are omitted entirely.

3.2.7 ranges Property

The ranges property defines the memory-mapped address translation vector from a child node's local address space to its parent node's address space. Its structural format is defined as follows:

ranges = <[child_address parent_address length] [child_address
parent_address length]...>;

The exact cell count allocated to represent the child_address is governed by the #address-cells property of the node containing the ranges property. Concurrently, the cell count allocated to represent the parent_address is governed by the #address-cells property configured in the parent node's immediate precursor (the grandparent node). If the ranges property is empty (declared as an empty property block with no cell tokens), it signifies that the child and parent memory maps are identical (a 1:1 direct identity mapping). Consider the following structural example:

bus {
	#address-cells = <2>;
	soc {
		compatible = "simple-bus";
		#address-cells = <1>;
		#size-cells = <1>;
		ranges = <0x0 0xe0000000 0x00000000 0x00100000>;
		serial@4600 {
			device_type = "serial";
			compatible = "ns16550";
			reg = <0x4600 0x100>;
			clock-frequency = <0>;
			interrupts = <0xA 0x8>;
			interrupt-parent = <&ipic>;
		};
	};
};

Within the soc node block, #address-cells equals 1; thus, in the ranges translation array, the local child address field for serial consumes exactly one cell (0x0). However, within the parent bus node, #address-cells is configured to equal 2. Therefore, the parent physical base address (the mapping destination address for the soc container) must consume exactly two cells (0xe0000000 0x00000000), yielding a consolidated 64-bit parent hardware boundary base address of 0xE000000000000000. By parsing this matrix, the true system-wide physical base address for the serial@4600 peripheral under the root architecture resolves cleanly to 0xE000000000004600.

3.2.8 dma-ranges Property

The dma-ranges property implements the identical structural format as the standard ranges property. It maps Direct Memory Access (DMA) address translation channels initiated by peripheral bus masters back into the upstream parent address space.

3.2.9 interrupts Property

The interrupts property is implemented by hardware nodes capable of generating interrupt lines. This property does not feature a single universal syntax specification; its cellular layout is instead strictly bound to the specific type of peripheral. Device vendors or driver authors define these parameter mappings inside matching documentation specifications, which are generally maintained within the Documentation/devicetree/bindings/ directory of the Linux kernel source tree. In the majority of configurations, the interrupts cell block encapsulates a unique hardware interrupt index (IRQ number) paired with an explicit interrupt trigger flag vector (such as edge-rising, edge-falling, level-high, or level-low indicators). For example:

interrupts = <0xA 1>;

Depending on the architecture's driver definition file, this cell configuration can be parsed to represent physical interrupt number 10 acting as an active-high edge-triggered line. Alternative interpretations are governed entirely by the device's explicit binding logic.

3.2.10 interrupt-parent Property

The interrupt-parent property defines the phandle or label reference pointing to the upstream interrupt controller routing the node's electrical interrupt signals. Modern system-on-chip architectures frequently isolate or cascade interrupt controllers inside complex hierarchical trees; the interrupt-parent attribute explicitly captures these routing dependencies. If the target upstream interrupt controller specifies a numeric handle, that value can be assigned directly to the property. Alternatively, if the parent node defines a textual label, the standard reference operator syntax (&) can be utilized. The following blocks show both implementation methodologies:

Assuming the upstream target interrupt controller node specifies an explicit handle vector of phandle = <1>;, the tracking attribute is declared as:

interrupt-parent = <1>;

Alternatively, if the upstream controller specifies a symbolic node label like intc1:, the property references it via the label lookup syntax:

interrupt-parent = <&intc1>;

3.2.11 interrupt-cells Property

This property is declared strictly inside hardware nodes functioning as an interrupt controller. It specifies how many 32-bit cells are required to encode a single interrupt descriptor within the controller's routing domain (defining the width of the interrupts property described in Section 3.2.9). In the example featured in Section 3.2.9, the interrupt descriptor consumes exactly two cells.

3.2.12 interrupt-controller Property

This is an empty boolean property applied directly to an interrupt controller node to declare that the containing node acts as an upstream system interrupt controller. It requires no accompanying cell data or value pairs. The standard syntax is defined as follows:

intc1: intc@100 {
        interrupt-controller;
};

3.2.13 Nexus Nodes

A nexus node is defined as a node that implements a #<specifier>-cells property, which dictates the exact number of 32-bit cells required to encode a specific resource specifier. A specifier typically identifies a functional hardware module; for instance, the specifier in #gpio-cells maps to a GPIO module. The value assigned to #<specifier>-cells defines the cell count required to target a single resource unit within that specifier domain. If a node defines a property such as #gpio-cells = <1>;, it functions as a nexus node, and its associated resource indicator consumes exactly one cell.

The following analysis of the i.MX6Q gpio1 module shows the practical application and architectural design of nexus nodes. Within the unified Linux Device Tree include file imx6qdl.dtsi supporting both the i.MX6Q and i.MX6DL SoCs, the gpio1 node is structured as follows:

gpio1: gpio@209C000 {
        compatible = "fsl,imx6q-gpio", "fsl,imx35-gpio";
        reg = <0x0209C000 0x4000>;
        interrupts = <0 66 IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_HIGH>, <0 67 IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_HIGH>;
        gpio-controller;
        #gpio-cells = <2>;
        interrupt-controller;
        #interrupt-cells = <2>;
};

In this block, the interrupts property indicates that this module can generate output interrupt signals. The interrupts array contains groups of three cells each, indicating that its parent interrupt controller defines #interrupt-cells = <3>. Therefore, the upstream controller requires three cells to map a single interrupt routing channel. On the i.MX6Q architecture, the first cell dictates the target GIC interrupt group/SPI index descriptor, the second cell specifies the raw interrupt number, and the third cell defines the interrupt trigger type.

The empty boolean property gpio-controller declares this hardware block as a functional GPIO controller. Operating system device drivers parse this property to identify and register the block's GPIO management capabilities.

The property #gpio-cells = <2> specifies that targeting an individual resource unit (a GPIO pin) within this controller requires exactly two cells. The first cell encodes the raw GPIO pin index number, and the second cell defines the initial electrical state or configuration flags, such as GPIO_ACTIVE_LOW.

The boolean property interrupt-controller indicates that this GPIO module also functions as an independent, downstream interrupt controller for user-space lines. Its companion property #interrupt-cells = <2> dictates that targeting any interrupt line managed by this module requires two cells: the first cell identifies the pin-specific interrupt number, and the second cell defines the signaling trigger type. Because the context implicitly locates the interrupt within the gpio1 block, a third cell to declare a GPIO module index is unnecessary, contrasting with the upstream parent controller's formatting.

Furthermore, properties such as <specifier>-map, <specifier>-map-mask, and <specifier>-map-pass-thru can also be applied to nexus nodes to handle complex cross-bus translations. Because their deployment footprints are less pervasive than the baseline #<specifier>-cells attribute, they are omitted here; developers can consult the official Device Tree Specification for extended edge-case documentation.

The standard properties detailed above represent only the baseline elements defined by the core Device Tree specification. Because the Device Tree format is inherently flexible, and because custom, vendor-specific attributes do not affect the parsing engines of unrelated devices, modern hardware descriptions rely heavily on custom provider-specific attributes.

Device Tree Nodes

3.3 Device Tree Nodes

Nodes within a Device Tree can represent a physical hardware component, an entire system subsystem, or an interconnect bus. A node description is structurally defined by its node name, localized unit address, absolute hierarchical path, and node label.

The node name specifies the technical identifier of the block, typically naming the node after the explicit device class it represents. The naming convention follows the format name@address, where the name segment is a string of 1 to 31 characters selected from 0-9, a-z, A-Z, ,, ., _, +, and -. The trailing address segment defines the base address or unit identifier of the component. This address can correspond to the device's physical layout within the CPU's memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) space, or it can represent a bus-specific coordinate system; its low-level interpretation is governed entirely by the Device Tree parsing routines compiled within the operating system driver.

Similar to file system folder structures, the absolute path of a node represents its full hierarchical lineage starting from the root node, separated by forward slashes (/), and formed by the corresponding node names (including their unit addresses). For example, the absolute path for the cpu0 node illustrated previously is:

/cpus/cpu0

A node label is an arbitrary string token suffixed with a colon (:) that resides immediately before the node name, isolated by whitespace characters. System software can reference or cross-access a target node either by invoking its symbolic node label or by referencing its full absolute path.

3.3.1 Root Node

The root node is represented by a single forward slash (/), mapping to the absolute path /. It can host the #address-cells, #size-cells, model, compatible, and serial-number properties. The serial-number property is optional, whereas the remaining properties are strictly mandatory. The #address-cells property is configured as one or more 32-bit integer cells. It specifies the exact cell count required to encode the unit address of its immediate child nodes. The #size-cells property maps to a 32-bit integer cell defining the cell count needed to represent the memory allocation length or address space size of those child nodes. The compatible property contains a string list identifying the target platform architectures compatible with the given Device Tree, typically structured as a "manufacturer,model" pair separated by a comma.

The direct child tree underneath the root node typically encapsulates specific structural container nodes, including /aliases, /memory, /reserved-memory, /chosen, and /cpus.

3.3.2 /aliases Node

The aliases node is utilized to define shorthand alternate names for fully qualified paths, allowing client software to locate or query complex nodes via abbreviated terms. An alias string consists of 1 to 31 characters drawn from 0-9, a-z, and -. The assigned property value maps directly to the absolute path of the targeted node. For example:

/ {
    aliases {
        serial0 = "/simple-bus@fe000000/serial@llc500";
    };
};

In this block, serial0 = "/simple-bus@fe000000/serial@llc500" binds the symbolic reference alias serial0 directly to the serial@llc500 node. Operating system routines can subsequently query serial0 to interact with that peripheral.

3.3.3 /memory Node

The memory node defines the physical layout of the system's volatile random-access memory (RAM). Every valid Device Tree must contain at least one operational memory node. If the physical memory architecture consists of multiple non-contiguous memory regions, the Device Tree can instantiate multiple independent memory nodes to capture the layout. Each individual memory block supports four properties: device_type, reg, initial-mapped-area, and hotpluggable. The device_type and reg properties are strictly mandatory, while the remainder are optional. The device_type string value must be explicitly set to "memory". The reg property contains one or more <address size> arrays mapping the base address and length vectors of the target memory banks. The hotpluggable property is an empty boolean flag; its presence indicates that the associated memory block supports dynamic hot-plug hardware operations. The following example shows a dual-bank memory topology configuration:

memory@0 {
	device_type = "memory";
	reg = <0x000000000 0x00000000 0x00000000 0x80000000>;
};
memory@100000000 {
	device_type = "memory";
	reg = <0x000000001 0x00000000 0x00000001 0x00000000>;
	hotpluggable;
};

3.3.4 /reserved-memory Node

The reserved-memory node declares specific regions of memory that must be protected and isolated from standard operating system memory management use. The reserved-memory container defines these protected blocks through dedicated child nodes. The container node must explicitly declare three attributes: #address-cells, #size-cells, and ranges. The value fields for #address-cells and #size-cells are 32-bit unsigned integers, while the ranges attribute must be left completely empty.

Each immediate child node under the reserved-memory block maps to a distinct reserved memory layout. These sub-nodes support seven optional properties: reg, size, alignment, alloc-ranges, compatible, no-map, and reusable. The array encoding rules for the reg property are determined by the #address-cells and #size-cells parameters established in the parent container, while the word width of the size property matches the parent's #size-cells directive. The alignment property dictates the boundary allocation constraint for the region, encoded using the cell size mandated by the parent's #size-cells. The format for the alloc-ranges property mirrors the structure of the standard reg array.

The no-map and reusable properties are empty boolean flags. When a child node declares the no-map attribute, the operating system kernel is strictly prohibited from instantiating a virtual memory mapping (such as a page table entry or cacheable kernel map) over that physical region. Conversely, the presence of the reusable attribute indicates that the operating system can temporarily leverage the memory block for general purposes; however, when the underlying peripheral driver explicitly requests the allocation, the kernel must yield the region back to its primary hardware owner. The following block outlines a complete structural example implementing standard memory and reserved memory allocations:

/ {
	    #address-cells = <1>;
	    #size-cells = <1>;
	    memory {
		    reg = <0x40000000 0x40000000>;
	    };
	    reserved-memory {
		    #address-cells = <1>;
		    #size-cells = <1>;
		    ranges;
		    linux,cma {
			    compatible = "shared-dma-pool";
			    reusable;
			    size = <0x2000000>;
			    alignment = <0x1000>;
			    linux,cma-default;
		    };
		    display: framebuffer@88000000 {
			    reg = <0x88000000 0x800000>;
		    };
		    multimedia: multimedia@70000000 {
			    compatible = "acme,multimedia-memory";
			    reg = <0x70000000 0x4000000>;
		    };
	    };
	    fb0: video@12300000 {
		    memory-region = <&display>;
	    };
	    codec: codec@12600000 {
		    memory-region = <&multimedia>;    
	    };
};

3.3.5 /chosen Node

The chosen node does not represent a physical hardware device; instead, it passes runtime parameters directly to the operating system. This node can contain three attributes: bootargs, stdin-path, and stdout-path. The bootargs property passes the command-line initialization string directly to the Linux kernel. The stdin-path and stdout-path properties designate the default standard input and standard output devices, respectively. All three attributes are stored as string types. The values for stdout-path and stdin-path specify either the absolute hierarchical path or the symbolic phandle referencing the standard input/output terminal hardware. The following example outlines the standard implementation framework for the /chosen node:

/ {
	chosen {
		bootargs = "root=/dev/nfs rw nfsroot=192.168.1.1 console=ttyS0,115200";
		stdout-path = &uart3;
		stdin-path = &uart3;
	};
	bus@20000000 {
       		uart3: uart3@20000000 {
                ...
       		};
	};
};

In this configuration, uart3 functions as a symbolic label pointing to a specific peripheral node within the Device Tree structure.

3.3.6 /cpus Node

The cpus container node describes the system's central processing units (CPUs). The top-level root node is strictly required to contain exactly one /cpus node. The cpus block houses multiple sequential cpu child nodes, and it must explicitly implement the #address-cells and #size-cells properties to define the address encoding scheme for its children. The cpus node can also host optional standard properties; when defined at this level, these properties represent common attributes shared universally across all child CPU cores.

3.3.7 /cpus/cpu* Child Nodes

A cpu* child node represents an independent hardware execution core capable of running an operating system context without interfering with sister CPU nodes, where * denotes the unique numerical index or identifier of the processing core. Hardware structures sharing a common Memory Management Unit (MMU) topology should be encapsulated within the same cpu node boundaries to ensure distinct CPU configurations remain mutually independent.

ARM architectures frequently deploy multiple decoupled CPU blocks. For example, the NXP i.MX6Dual integrates two Cortex-A class cores, the i.MX6Quad hosts four Cortex-A class cores, and the high-performance i.MX8 platform features a heterogeneous configuration comprising four Cortex-A72 cores, two Cortex-A53 cores, two Cortex-M real-time microcontrollers, a dedicated DSP, and two GPUs. Because these processing elements can operate independently, they are partitioned into distinct cpu nodes within the layout.

A valid cpu* node must contain the device_type, reg, clock-frequency, and timebase-frequency properties. Additional attributes can include status, enable-method, cpu-release-addr, power-isa-version, and mmu-type, alongside other standard metadata properties. The device_type string value must be set to "cpu", identifying the block as a core execution unit. The reg property defines the core's relative index mapping inside the parent cpus address space, formatted according to the parent's #address-cells and #size-cells properties.

The clock-frequency property is stored as a 32-bit or 64-bit unsigned integer, specified in Hertz (Hz), defining the current operating frequency of the CPU. Similarly, the timebase-frequency property is a 32-bit or 64-bit unsigned integer that specifies the operating frequency of the low-level system timebase generator.

The status property is a string value typically set to either "okay" or "disabled", where "okay" indicates the core is fully functional, and "disabled" denotes that the core is forced into a sleep, offline, or hard reset state. The remaining secondary attributes are less pervasive in standard configurations and are omitted here; readers can refer to the official Device Tree Specification for granular edge-case tracking. The following block show a complete Device Tree configuration for a dual-core system implementing a unified three-tier (L1, L2, L3) cache hierarchy:

cpus {
	#address-cells = <1>;
	#size-cells = <0>;
	cpu@0 {
		device_type = "cpu";
		reg = <0>;
		cache-unified;
		cache-size = <0x8000>; // L1, 32 KB
		cache-block-size = <32>;
		timebase-frequency = <82500000>; // 82.5 MHz
		next-level-cache = <&L2_0>; // phandle to L2
		L2_0: l2-cache {
			compatible = "cache";
			cache-unified;
			cache-size = <0x40000>; // 256 KB
			cache-sets = <1024>;
			cache-block-size = <32>;
			cache-level = <2>;
			next-level-cache = <&L3>; // phandle to L3
			L3: l3-cache {
				compatible = "cache";
				cache-unified;
				cache-size = <0x40000>; // 256 KB
				cache-sets = <0x400>; // 1024
				cache-block-size = <32>;
				cache-level = <3>;
			};
		};
	};
	cpu@1 {
		device_type = "cpu";
		reg = <1>;
		cache-unified;
		cache-block-size = <32>;
		cache-size = <0x8000>; // L1, 32 KB
		timebase-frequency = <82500000>; // 82.5 MHz
		clock-frequency = <825000000>; // 825 MHz
		cache-level = <2>;
		next-level-cache = <&L2_1>; // phandle to L2

		L2_1: l2-cache {
			compatible = "cache";
			cache-unified;
			cache-size = <0x40000>; // 256 KB
			cache-sets = <0x400>; // 1024
			cache-line-size = <32>; // 32 bytes
			next-level-cache = <&L3>; // phandle to L3
		};
	};
};

Cache-specific sub-properties encompass compatible, cache-unified, cache-size, cache-sets, cache-line-size, and next-level-cache. Out of these, cache-unified, cache-size, cache-sets, and cache-line-size explicitly define the internal physical topology layout of the cache controller; developers familiar with microarchitecture specifications can parse these properties without extended commentary. The next-level-cache property holds the unique phandle referencing the subsequent lower level of the memory cache hierarchy, allowing an upstream cache controller to cleanly map and traverse downstream cache nodes.

Property Bindings

3.4 Property Bindings

Property bindings define the explicit usage syntax, constraints, and methodologies mandated by hardware vendors or device driver architects when implementing a new attribute. They also encompass the standard formatting rules for standard and widely adopted properties, typically supplied as plaintext documentation or structured YAML schemas. Within the Linux kernel repository, these property binding specification files are maintained within the Documentation/devicetree/bindings/ directory under the git/ root, where git/ represents the baseline root directory of the fetched Linux kernel source tree.

For NXP Linux distributions targeting the i.MX family of application processors, if the platform project is compiled using the Yocto Project framework (which will be detailed in subsequent chapters), the localized Linux kernel source code resides within the active working workspace under the following explicit path:

build/tmp/work/<board_name>-poky-linux-gnueabi/linux-imx/<version_number>/git

Concurrently, the U-BOOT source tree is extracted and managed under:

build/tmp/work/<board_name>-poky-linux-gnueabi/u-boot-imx/<version_number>/git

Where build/ represents the centralized compilation and deployment output directory specified during the initial creation and setup of the project configuration workspace.

Flattened Device Tree (DTB) Format

3.5 Flattened Device Tree (DTB) Format

The Device Tree source text file (.dts) is formatted as plaintext, which is inefficient for the operating system to parse directly. Therefore, it must be compiled into a binary format (.dtb) using the Device Tree Compiler (dtc). This optimization flattens the source tree text into a structured binary payload commonly referred to as a "blob." During the boot sequence, the bootloader loads this binary blob alongside the kernel executable image into distinct regions of physical memory. Operating system device drivers parse this runtime memory block to resolve registered peripherals, device constraints, and low-level parameters, ensuring precise hardware initialization.

The DTB file features a strict, linear architectural topology consisting of a standardized file header followed by three sequential block modules: the memory reservation block, the structure block, and the strings block. The memory reservation block catalogs explicitly protected physical memory margins, providing an architecture-enforced mechanism to prevent user-space applications or general kernel allocations from corrupting critical software or hardware buffers. The structure block stores the actual hierarchical arrangement of the Device Tree; by executing a linear traversal across this module, the kernel reconstructs and accesses all nodes within the hardware tree. The strings block aggregates the explicit names of all properties utilized across the Device Tree into a single contiguous pool; individual nodes inside the structure block map to their textual property keys by maintaining numerical offset vectors pointing into this string database.

3.5.1 DTB File Header

The DTB file header occupies exactly 40 bytes of memory, divided into ten sequential 32-bit (4-byte) fields. The structural layout is mapped out in the following schematic:

  • Magic Number: A constant signature used by parsing routines to validate the payload as a definitive DTB structure. Its value is fixed to 0xD00DFEED and is encoded strictly in big-endian format.

  • Total Size: Defines the absolute linear length of the DTB payload in bytes, encompassing the 40-byte header block.

  • Offset to Structure Block: The explicit byte offset from the start of the file header to the baseline memory address hosting the structure block.

  • Offset to Strings Block: The explicit byte offset from the start of the file header to the baseline memory address hosting the strings block.

  • Offset to Memory Reservation Block: The explicit byte offset from the start of the file header to the baseline memory address hosting the memory reservation block.

  • Version Number: Specifies the version of the Device Tree Specification governing the compiled blob layout. The current baseline version tracks to 17.

  • Last Compatible Version: Defines the lowest historical specification version with which the current blob format maintains structural backward compatibility (typically fixed to version 16). Versions below 16 are deprecated and unparseable.

  • Boot CPU ID: Specifies the physical hardware index or core ID of the primary CPU core tasked with coordinating system boot routines. This value maps directly to the reg property assigned to that specific execution core under the /cpus tree path.

  • Size of Strings Block: The absolute linear width of the strings database module measured in bytes.

  • Size of Structure Block: The absolute linear width of the node structure module measured in bytes.

3.5.2 Memory Reservation Block

This module maintains an array of physical memory margins reserved for explicit use cases; all allocations specified within upstream memory-reserved nodes are consolidated here. The memory reservation layout is structured as an array of <physical_address region_size> coordinate pairs, where both the base address boundaries and length fields are stored as 64-bit unsigned integers. The following diagram shows the sequential binary formatting for a payload enclosing exactly three distinct memory isolation windows:

3.5.3 Structure Block Format

The structure block describes the actual topology and contents of the Device Tree, composed of a series of contiguous data fragments that are initialized via specific token markers. Each token identifier can be followed by a variable payload data segment whose structural formatting rules are governed entirely by the token class. The linear byte displacement linking any token back to the baseline origin of the structure block must be aligned precisely to a 32-bit (4-byte) word boundary. If a variable-length token sequence leaves a trailing address misaligned, compiler routines insert null-byte (0x00) padding to enforce explicit alignment.

The structure block relies on five primitive 32-bit token constants: FDT_BEGIN_NODE (0x00000001), FDT_END_NODE (0x00000002), FDT_PROP (0x00000003), FDT_NOP (0x00000004), and FDT_END (0x00000009).

  • FDT_BEGIN_NODE: Marks the structural initialization entry of a new Device Tree node. It is followed immediately by the node's name stored as a null-terminated ASCII string. If the node includes an explicit unit address identifier, the coordinate string is appended directly after the name block (e.g., name@address). A FDT_BEGIN_NODE token can accept any subsequent tokens except FDT_END_NODE. This allows a child node statement to open nested inside a parent block by injecting a nested FDT_BEGIN_NODE token sequence. The DTB architecture leverages this nesting rule to linearly map out the multi-dimensional tree topology.

  • FDT_END_NODE: Marks the termination boundary of the active node description block. It accepts no parameter arguments; the next contiguous byte region corresponds directly to the subsequent token.

  • FDT_PROP: Used to embed an explicit hardware attribute block into the active node context. It is followed by two mandatory 32-bit parameter words. The first word defines the payload length of the property data segment in bytes. The second word contains the numerical byte offset referencing the precise location of the attribute's text key inside the strings block. The raw property data payload is written directly after this second parameter word; its storage configuration within physical memory is detailed in the diagram below:

  • FDT_NOP: A structural no-operation marker. It carries no operational meaning and is skipped by kernel parsing engines.

  • FDT_END: Explicitly marks the termination of the entire structure block. The structure module must contain exactly one FDT_END token, which is required to reside at the absolute end of the block. The physical tracking layout of the structure block within memory is presented in the following schematic:

Within the upstream Linux kernel source tree, the following C structural definitions describe the binary layout of the FDT_BEGIN_NODE header and the FDT_PROP components: 
struct fdt_node_header {
	fdt32_t tag;
	char name[0];
};
struct fdt_property {
	fdt32_t tag;
	fdt32_t len;
	fdt32_t nameoff;
	char data[0];
};

3.5.4 Strings Block

The property names utilized across all hardware descriptors are structured as standard, null-terminated ASCII strings. The strings block is formed by concatenating these text keys sequentially into a contiguous memory pool. The baseline starting memory address allocated to store each discrete string identifier must be aligned to a 4-byte boundary.

Device Tree Source (.dts) File Format

3.6 Device Tree Source (.dts) File Format

Device Tree Source files are distinguished by the .dts filename extension suffix. The initial line of a valid source file must strictly contain the exact token declaration /dts-v1/;, where v1 identifies compliance with the first version of the Device Tree Specification. Leveraging the compilation preprocessor directive #include "file", a Device Tree Source file can reference and incorporate external hardware description layout files suffixed with the .dtsi extension. Except for omitting the standalone /dts-v1/; tag and the leading #include directives, the internal syntactical formatting rules for a .dtsi file match those of a standard .dts file. The following snippet illustrates a representative configuration slice extracted from the imx6dl-sabresd.dts platform file:

/dts-v1/;
#include "imx6dl.dtsi"
#include "imx6qdl.dtsi"
/ {
	model = "Freescale i.MX6 DualLite SABRESD Smart Device Board";
	compatible = "fsl,imx6dl-sabresd", "fsl,imx6dl";
	&battery {
       		offset-charger = <1485>;
        	offset-discharger = <1464>;
        	offset-usb-charger = <1285>;
	};
	/* ... */
};

In this context, offset-charger, offset-discharger, and offset-usb-charger represent proprietary hardware properties defined by NXP (formerly Freescale); their explicit parsing semantics and validation rules are mandated within matching vendor binding specifications.

3.6.1 Labels

Nodes or individual property definitions within the Device Tree can be preceded by a unique label identifier. A label must be 1 to 31 characters in length, consisting strictly of alphanumeric characters (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) or underscores (_), with the constraint that numeric digits 0-9 are prohibited from occupying the initial character slot. A label definition is declared by appending a colon (:) directly to the token string, typically isolated from the trailing node name or property declaration via whitespace.

When source code routines must target an absolute hierarchical path or resolve a specific node handle (phandle), developers can leverage a node's defined label as an abbreviated shorthand reference. This referencing mechanism is executed by prefixing the target label token with the ampersand character (&), as demonstrated by the &battery reference block in the preceding example. During the flattening process executed by the compiler, labels are translated into matching numeric phandle entries; consequently, raw textual label names do not persist inside the compiled binary .dtb blob.

3.6.2 Node and Property Definition Layout

A standard Device Tree node is composed of an optional label, a mandatory node name, an optional unit address, child nodes, and a localized block of properties. The universal layout syntax is defined as follows:

[label:] node-name[@unit-address] {
	[label:] property1 = value;
	[label:] property2 = value;
	[label:] child-node-name[@unit-address] {
            /* ... */
	};
};

A node block can encapsulate both explicit property strings and sub-nodes simultaneously. When mixing both types within a single node boundary, property definitions must precede child node declarations.

Hardware properties are classified into two primary presentation categories. If an attribute requires an explicit parameter assignment, its definition is formatted using the assignment operator (=):

[label:] property-name = value;

The assigned value payload can be expressed as an ASCII text string wrapped within double quotes (""), an array of 32-bit unsigned integer cells enclosed within angle brackets (<>), or a stream of raw hexadecimal byte values bound by square brackets ([]). If a node attribute requires a 64-bit integer allocation, it is represented as a sequence of two contiguous 32-bit cells (e.g., <0x7FFFF000 0x00000000>).

Property values can incorporate mathematical expressions, bitwise manipulations, and logical operations utilizing standard operators derived from C-language syntax rules. These operators include:

  • Arithmetic Operators: +, -, *, /, %

  • Bitwise Logical Operators: &, |, ^, ~, >>, <<

  • Logical Operators: &&, ||, !

  • Relational Operators: >, <, ==, >=, <=, !=

  • Conditional Ternary Operator: ?: (Format: Condition ? Value_If_True : Value_If_False)

An attribute can accommodate multiple distinct values or data types separated by a comma. For example:

compatible = "fsl,imx6qdl", "fsl,imx8";

The ampersand character (&) handles cross-references to phandles, labels, and paths. When an ampersand reference is nested inside a cell array (<>), the compiler maps the text label or absolute path to its underlying numeric phandle. Conversely, when an ampersand reference targets a node outside of a cell array context, the label expands to its fully qualified, absolute file system path string. The following blocks show the two equivalent syntactical pathways used to link the uart@1 peripheral to its upstream controller node intc@4000:

/* Method A: Reference via explicit symbolic node label */
uart1: uart@1 {
	interrupt-parent = <&intc1>;
};
/* Method B: Reference via full absolute path resolution syntax */
uart1: uart@1 {
	interrupt-parent = <&{/soc/intc@4000}>;
};
intc1: intc@4000 {
	interrupt-controller;
};

If a hardware attribute serves as an empty boolean indicator requiring no parameter data, it is declared as follows:

[label:] property-name;

The presence of an empty property string informs the operating system kernel that the target subsystem natively supports the associated hardware feature or peripheral configuration.

Chapter 4: The Boot Process of the Operating System

Computer systems generally comprise various components, including the central processing unit (CPU), memory subsystems, and peripherals. Upon system power-on, the reset circuit forces the program counter (PC) of the CPU to point directly to a fixed, predetermined memory location. Under the management of control logic circuitry, the central controller fetches the initial instruction from this absolute address, kicks off program execution, and performs the diverse computations and operations specified by the software logic.

Storage mediums can be broadly classified into two primary categories: volatile memory and non-volatile memory. Volatile memory completely loses its stored contents when power is disconnected, whereas non-volatile memory retains its data state in the absence of power. To enable system execution, the computer's hardware reset vector must map directly to a non-volatile memory space. These non-volatile memory components store pre-compiled software code tasked with executing low-level baseline hardware initialization, pulling the primary bootloader from a designated external storage medium into physical random-access memory (RAM), and then handing over control to that bootloader. The bootloader subsequently loads the operating system kernel into memory and triggers its execution sequence.

Desktop infrastructures running the Linux operating system typically leverage bootloaders such as GRUB, GRUB2, or LILO to introduce the operating system into RAM. Conversely, embedded Linux deployment pipelines generally employ the U-BOOT bootloader to import the Linux kernel, while BareBox stands out as a highly regarded alternative Linux bootloader within the Internet of Things (IoT) engineering ecosystem.

The Operating System Boot Process

4.1 The Operating System Boot Process

Traditional BIOS-Based Boot Process

The boot sequence of a legacy operating system utilizing a basic input/output system (BIOS) can be broadly divided into the following sequential stages:

  1. Power-On: Power is supplied to the system components.

  2. Power-On Self-Test (POST): Low-level routines hardcoded within the system's non-volatile ROM execute diagnostic hardware self-tests.

  3. Master Boot Record (MBR) Execution: The system reads and executes the primary stage-1 bootloader code from the Master Boot Record sector of the designated boot device.

  4. Stage-2 Loading: The stage-1 bootloader identifies the active boot partition, loads the secondary stage-2 bootloader code from that partition into random-access memory (RAM), and hands over execution.

  5. Operating System Bootloader Discovery: The stage-2 bootloader determines the explicit path of the definitive operating system bootloader within the active file system structure and loads it into memory.

  6. Kernel Initialization: The final operating system bootloader—commonly referred to simply as the bootloader—imports the operating system kernel image into RAM and relinquishes system control to the kernel itself, concluding the boot sequence.

Modern UEFI-Based Boot Process

Modern desktop and server firmware implementations follow the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) standard. Booting a UEFI-compliant operating system requires that the underlying hardware platform's firmware adheres strictly to the UEFI specification. This boot lifecycle is structured into the following operational phases:

  • Power-On: Power is supplied to the platform circuitry.

  • Security Phase (SEC): Initial security enforcement configurations and pre-RAM health checks are executed.

  • Pre-EFI Initialization (PEI) & Driver Execution Environment (DXE): System firmware initializes foundational hardware, and the system executes platform device drivers.

  • Boot Device Selection (BDS): The firmware evaluates configuration rules to choose the target boot device.

  • EFI System Partition Discovery: The firmware reads the /boot/efi directory tree on the selected storage device to locate the operating system's bootloader or boot manager.
    (Note: To support UEFI-compliant booting, the target drive—regardless of whether it utilizes a GUID Partition Table (GPT) or legacy MBR layout—must contain a dedicated EFI System Partition (ESP) formatted to hold operating system boot binaries and configuration profiles).

  • Boot Manager Invocations: The system launches the boot manager retrieved in the previous step, which orchestrates the final launch of the operating system kernel.

The first five steps are handled completely by the platform's non-volatile system firmware. The low-level partition architecture of the boot device itself is simplified under this paradigm; it no longer relies on complex stage-1 and stage-2 sector splitting, requiring only that the appropriate operating system bootloader application binary be populated within the standard /boot/efi target directory path.

Operating System and Hardware Interfaces for Desktops and Laptops

4.2 Operating System and Hardware Interfaces for Desktops and Laptops

4.2.1 BIOS Interface Program

Early computers possessed proprietary boot routines; for instance, the IBM PC hardcoded its bootloader directly into the non-volatile read-only memory (ROM) hosting the BIOS. After performing the necessary power-on self-tests and initial system provisioning, this integrated routine read the operating system from an external floppy disk or hard drive into memory for execution.

Conversely, the primary bootloader of a modern computer exists as an independent, standalone binary entity. Rather than residing within the machine's motherboard-bound non-volatile flash storage chips, it is saved on the designated boot device itself. The BIOS program stored in the computer's onboard non-volatile memory initializes baseline hardware subsystems so that the target storage controllers function correctly. It then reads a block of raw sector data from the Master Boot Record (MBR) region—the absolute first sector—of the media. This sequence determines whether a valid stage-1 boot string is present and resolves its physical deployment location and layout footprint. Once the BIOS confirms the presence of a viable bootloader payload on the media, it loads the binary into random-access memory (RAM) and jumps to its entry point to begin execution.

4.2.2 UEFI Interface

UEFI is an acronym for the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, which defines the standard software interface layer bridging the platform firmware with the client operating system. The UEFI specification standardizes platform-related system data tables and formalizes an array of discrete services—categorized into boot services and runtime services—provided by the firmware to the operating system kernel. Under this architecture, the operating system loader (OS Loader) can safely abstract away low-level silicon and platform details, relying entirely on these abstract data frameworks and firmware-exported calls to successfully initialize and load the operating system.

An operating system boot process compliant with the UEFI specification no longer depends on physical, hardcoded partition boot sectors. Instead, an integrated, non-volatile Boot Manager calls firmware-provided runtime infrastructure to fetch the explicit file pathways and metadata matching the target bootloader. The platform firmware then invokes its internal UEFI boot service function LoadImage() to load both the primary operating system bootloader (Boot Loader) and any necessary standalone UEFI hardware drivers into physical RAM. Once loaded, execution jumps directly to the entry point address exposed by the operating system bootloader, driving kernel initialization forward.

Because UEFI provides native backward compatibility for legacy MBR boot methodologies, a modern UEFI-compliant system firmware implementation is fully capable of parsing and executing bootloader blocks stored on storage media configured with an MBR table layout.

4.2.3 Partition Tables

Standard desktop and laptop computers leverage partition tables to orchestrate the system boot process. A partition table catalogs the structural boundaries of a storage medium—such as a hard drive, SD card, or flash memory array—alongside the low-level logical organization of the data resident on that medium, allowing system software to locate and interact with stored blocks efficiently. In personal computing infrastructures, partition tables predominantly follow one of two layout specifications: MBR or GPT. MBR remains the most historically pervasive partition format, whereas GPT represents a modern architectural standard that is systematically replacing the legacy MBR specification.

4.2.3.1 MBR Partition Table Format

MBR is an acronym for Master Boot Record. It resides strictly within the absolute first physical sector of the storage medium, consuming exactly 512 bytes of space. The internal layout of the MBR is divided into three distinct operational blocks: the bootloader code segment, the primary Partition Table, and the Boot Signature validator byte sequence. The bootloader code segment encapsulates both the primary stage-1 bootloader string (main boot code) and the secondary stage-2 helper blocks.

The address range from 0x01B8 to 0x01BB contains a 4-byte unique disk signature key, which system firmware parses to distinguish whether the operating system hosted on the drive maps to Linux, Windows, or another UEFI-compliant platform interface. The subsequent 2 bytes, located at addresses 0x01BC and 0x01BD, hold a fixed value of either 0x0000 or 0x5A5A, where the signature 0x5A5A explicitly designates that the target operating system volume is protected under copyright enforcement hooks.

Immediately following the signature block lies the primary MBR Partition Table. It registers up to four distinct primary partition entries, allocating exactly 16 bytes of data to encode each structural partition slot. These entries map out the absolute starting and terminating boundary layouts of the partitions, the total sectors allocated to each block, and the corresponding Logical Block Addressing (LBA) coordinates. Under legacy tracking setups, physical geometry tracking parameters are represented explicitly using cylinder-head-sector (CHS) indexing coordinates. The four dedicated partition entry slots are hardcoded to align with the following fixed memory address offsets: 0x01BE, 0x01CE, 0x01DE, and 0x01EE.

The final two bytes of the 512-byte MBR block hold the Boot Signature word, which functions as a definitive integrity check to verify if the medium contains a valid, bootable system application. If the drive is bootable, address offset 0x01FE holds the byte value 0x55, and address offset 0x01FF holds the byte value 0xAA (forming the standard 0xAA55 big-endian word). The system BIOS reads these specific memory bytes to determine whether to advance or halt the execution pass on the selected drive.

Because the primary master boot string and its companion secondary stage-2 code are supplied directly by the active boot media rather than the motherboard firmware, this architecture injects massive flexibility into the system lifecycle, enabling different operating systems to implement custom boot managers and execution hooks. Certain advanced bootloaders leverage this flexibility to present interactive, multi-boot menu interfaces on startup, allowing developers to choose dynamically between launching a Linux environment or a Windows instance.

However, due to structural constraints built into the legacy format, an MBR table is strictly limited to managing a maximum of 4 primary partitions and cannot address a total storage capacity exceeding 2 TB.

4.2.3.2 GPT Format

GPT is an acronym for GUID Partition Table. As an integral component of the Extensible Firmware Interface (EFI) standard, GPT defines the structural partitioning layout of hard disks. Compared to MBR, GPT offers greater architectural flexibility and cleaner compatibility with modern hardware. It is natively engineered for UEFI-based operating systems while maintaining backward compatibility hooks for legacy BIOS system interfaces.

Modern computer operating systems universally support GPT, including macOS and x86-based Windows implementations; however, booting Windows from a GPT-formatted storage medium strictly requires an operating system that supports the UEFI interface. Conversely, both FreeBSD and Linux are capable of booting from GPT-formatted storage media regardless of whether the underlying hardware implements a legacy BIOS or a modern UEFI platform interface.

GPT utilizes 64-bit Logical Block Addressing (LBA), enabling it to address up to 2⁶⁴ sectors. On storage media featuring a standard 512-byte sector size, GPT theoretically scales to support a maximum capacity of 8 ZiB, whereas on storage devices configured with 4096-byte (4 KB) advanced format sectors, its capacity boundary reaches 64 ZiB.

LBA0 (Sector 0) stores a Protective MBR structure, while the primary GPT Header resides explicitly at LBA1. The GPT Header contains a pointer vector targeting the Partition Entry Array, which typically begins at LBA2. The Partition Entry Array allocates a minimum allocation table size of 16,384 bytes, where each constituent entry layout is constrained to exactly 128 bytes.

To guarantee backward compatibility and prevent legacy MBR-bound disk utilities from misinterpreting a GPT disk as unpartitioned space—which could lead to catastrophic data overwrite or loss—GPT implements a structural modification over the traditional MBR layout. The modified MBR encapsulates a single partition entry defined explicitly with a partition type indicator of 0xEE. This placeholder partition spans the entire maximum address space manageable under standard MBR formatting rules. Consequently, legacy disk utilities that lack GPT awareness perceive the entire disk as a single, protected, unmanageable volume, preventing accidental data modification unless explicitly forced by the user. Conversely, modern GPT-compliant operating systems can reject processing a storage medium if it detects an invalid or corrupted protective block configuration that does not cleanly match the 0xEE signature.

For operating systems that feature native GPT parsing capabilities but are forced to boot via a legacy BIOS instead of a native UEFI firmware layer, the stage-1 bootloader string can still be embedded directly within the MBR area; however, this custom bootloader sequence must be explicitly coded to traverse and parse the underlying GPT partition structures.

4.2.4 Master Boot Record (MBR) Bootloader Code

Within traditional or legacy operating system architectures, the primary master boot code comprises a minimalist binary sequence tasked with locating the physical sectors hosting the Volume Boot Record (VBR) and reading that downstream VBR boot loader into memory. This initial stage-1 block occupies exactly 218 bytes of memory starting at address zero. Immediately following this primary execution string lies the disk timestamp payload, situated between addresses 0x00DA and 0x00DF. The secondary stage-2 boot code is written directly after the timestamp, spanning from 0x00E0 to 0x01E7. Once the stage-1 bootloader copies this stage-2 code block into random-access memory (RAM), it relinquishes system execution to the secondary block, which subsequently resolves and imports the definitive final-stage operating system bootloader into physical memory.

For modern operating systems such as Windows, the Master Boot Record bootloader code resides entirely within the primary MBR boot region at the absolute beginning of the first physical sector, consuming up to 440 bytes of space. The core architectural responsibility of this integrated boot routine is to identify the active boot sector, parse its boundary coordinates, copy the secondary-stage bootloader into RAM, and jump to its execution entry point.

4.2.5 Secondary Bootloader

The secondary bootloader, also referred to as the partition boot loader or Volume Boot Record (VBR), resides within a specific sector inside the designated boot partition; this physical sector is defined as the boot sector. Depending on the target operating system's filesystem architecture, the exact location of this boot sector within the partition layout may vary, though it typically occupies the absolute first sector of the boot partition.

The very first memory slot of a boot sector usually contains an explicit branch or jump instruction. Upon execution of this instruction, the partition boot loader kicks off its routine. The primary task of this code block is to parse the low-level filesystem headers, resolve the precise logical block address hosting the final-stage operating system bootloader on the storage medium, load that definitive boot loader binary into physical memory, and transfer system execution control over to it.

Embedded System Hardware and Operating System Interfaces

4.3 Embedded System Hardware and Operating System Interfaces

4.3.1 i.MX6 Solo/DualLite Processor

The core architecture of the i.MX6 Solo/DualLite features a single- or dual-core ARMv7 processor context. Around this processing core, NXP has integrated a vast matrix of multimedia and infrastructure modules, including hardware cryptographic acceleration engines, Vivante 2D and 3D GPUs, a Video Processing Unit (VPU), dual USB controllers, MMC/eMMC host interfaces, a multi-channel DDR memory controller, an LVDS display interface bridge, an HDMI transmitter, MIPI DSI/CSI interfaces, S/PDIF and EASI digital audio engines, an Enhanced External Interface Module (EIM) and General Purpose Media Interface (GPMI) supporting NOR and NAND flash variants, an enterprise Gigabit Ethernet controller, an Electronic Paper Display Controller (EPDC), a FlexCAN controller, and an ARM Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC), alongside generic I2C and SPI interfaces. The processor natively supports an expansive taxonomy of boot peripherals—including NOR flash, NAND flash, OneNAND, SD/MMC, eMMC, serial (I2C/SPI) NOR flash/EEPROM, and USB paths—and provides high-assurance hardware-enforced image authentication and decryption, resulting in a highly capable multimedia applications processor.

The primary bootloader code is embedded directly within the processor's on-chip boot ROM. This ROM bootloader features the following design attributes:

  • Granular support for a diverse taxonomy of storage boot devices.

  • Support for serial image downloading and bare-metal recovery via the USB OTG interface.

  • The capacity to parse Device Configuration Data (DCD) tables structured within the boot media to provision internal registers and memory sub-blocks.

  • Support for the execution of user-supplied initialization plugins stored on the boot medium.

  • High-Assurance Boot (HAB) digital signature validation and symmetric/asymmetric image decryption algorithms.

  • System wake-up routines from ultra-low-power suspend states.

  • Inter-Processor Interrupt (IPI) multi-core orchestration to wake secondary execution cores.

The ROM bootloader interrogates internal boot mode configuration registers and the hardware eFUSE matrix to isolate the designated primary boot device. During the prototyping and validation phases of a project, engineers can route specific GPIO lines to override these eFUSE definitions, streamlining low-level board development and hardware debugging.

Leveraging these native ROM routines, developers can initialize unprovisioned storage media; for instance, a raw firmware image can be injected into physical RAM via a host USB connection and subsequently written directly to an unformatted on-board storage chip.

The underlying ROM supports exactly three distinct boot pathways: eFUSE boot, serial downloader mode, and internal boot. The eFUSE boot path relies exclusively on the blown states of the on-chip fuse array to map the hardware initialization envelope. The serial downloader mode converts the USB OTG interface into a client endpoint to pull and run recovery payloads. The critical functional distinction between the eFUSE boot path and the internal boot path is that the internal boot mode evaluates physical GPIO pins on startup, allowing developers to manually override fuse settings. If an unrecoverable fault or timeout occurs during an eFUSE or internal boot sequence, the ROM state machine defaults to serial downloader mode.

During the hardware reset phase, the processor latches the electrical states of the dedicated boot configuration pins into internal registers. Upon release of the reset line, the execution pointer jumps directly to the on-chip ROM block. After performing essential baseline processor provisioning, the ROM code evaluates the latched status of the eFUSE, GPIO, and boot mode fields to determine the target storage interface. It then fetches a fixed allocation of blocks from a hardcoded offset on the boot media. This data chunk encapsulates the Image Vector Table (IVT), which acts as the definitive binary structural guide used to locate the Device Configuration Data (DCD) array, boot data parameters, and the primary application entry point addresses. The on-chip bootloader processes these tables to tune peripheral controllers and initialize the DDR controller, copies the primary U-BOOT binary from storage into physical RAM, and finally jumps to U-BOOT to drive the operating system initialization sequence forward.

4.3.2 On-Chip Bootloader

Upon system power-on reset, the power management and reset circuit forces the CPU into a deterministic baseline state, driving the primary program counter (PC) to align with a fixed physical address vector. This vector addresses the absolute starting instruction of the on-chip ROM, which typically contains a branch instruction leading into the primary ROM bootloader entry point. The fundamental objective of this low-level code block is to execute minimal, essential system initializations—such as configuring basic clock trees and initializing the external DDR memory interface—and transition the CPU core into its optimal execution mode. Once memory is available, the routine loads the initial boot data blocks and the primary U-BOOT stage binary from the initial boot sectors of the target storage media into RAM, then hands over execution to U-BOOT. The following analysis profiles the operational workflow of this on-chip bootloader using the NXP i.MX6 DualLite/Solo multimedia applications processor as a reference model.

Following a power-on reset (POR) cycle, the i.MX6 DualLite/Solo hardware samples the electrical levels of the BOOT_MODE0 and BOOT_MODE1 pins, latching these values directly into bits [1:0] of the internal BOOT_MODE register. The configured bit-pattern of BOOT_MODE[1:0], paired with the blown configurations of specific eFUSE registers and the real-time logic states of a defined subset of GPIO selection lines, strictly dictates the platform's boot pathway and execution topology. The integrated ROM layout provides native driver support to initialize and fetch payloads across SD/MMC cards, parallel/serial NOR flash, raw NAND flash, OneNAND arrays, high-speed SPI/I2C EEPROMs, and memory chips. The internal i.MX6 DualLite/Solo boot ROM provides the following technical capabilities:

  • Streamlined serial payload down-streaming and flashing via the integrated USB OTG controller interface.

  • The capacity to parse structural Device Configuration Data (DCD) matrices and execute short, pre-boot initialization software snippets (plugins).

  • Cryptographically sound digital signature verification (High-Assurance Boot) and encrypted secure boot mechanics.

  • System state restoration and execution tracking when waking up from low-power power-saving modes.
