  • Multi-core initialization routines to bring up the secondary CPU core.

The on-chip ROM framework also supports directly downloading external payloads into internal RAM and executing them in place.

The capability to parse local configuration parameters (DCD) and execute standalone plugin code blocks represents two of the most critical design attributes of the on-chip bootloader layer. By leveraging these mechanisms, system engineers can achieve highly optimized hardware timing register configurations and bring up external DDR memory blocks before launching the primary U-BOOT binary, ensuring U-BOOT has a stable, high-capacity memory footprint available for its boot routines.

The i.MX6 Solo/DualLite platforms support exactly three operational boot configurations:

  • eFUSE Boot Mode: Hardware configuration parameters and interface choices are governed entirely by the internal non-volatile fuse array.

  • Serial Downloader Mode: Forces the chip to pause routine boot checks and wait for an incoming software payload via the USB OTG port.

  • Internal Boot Mode: Peripheral parameters and interface selections are driven by the logical values sampled from external physical GPIO pins.

The definitive difference between the eFUSE boot mode and the internal boot mode is that the eFUSE mode completely locks down the boot flow, preventing developers from overriding the hardware parameter matrices via external strap pins; conversely, the internal boot configuration evaluates real-time GPIO logic states to dynamically adjust hardware behaviors.

The serial downloader configuration allows developers to connect a host machine to the board's USB OTG port to inject binary payloads directly into volatile memory or program non-volatile flash storage blocks. The foundational operational flow chart governing the i.MX6 Solo and i.MX6 DualLite on-chip boot ROM sequence is mapped out in the schematic diagram below:

If an unrecoverable data corruption fault, communication timeout, or execution error occurs during the execution of either the internal boot or eFUSE boot pathways, the on-chip bootloader state machine automatically executes a fallback branch, shifting the processor into serial USB downloader mode to ensure the system can be successfully recovered and booted via the serial communication interface.

4.3.3 Image Bootloader Structure

The so-called image program refers to the executable binary software stored on the boot device. The storage layout of the image program must conform strictly to a specific format. Otherwise, the on-chip boot ROM and U-BOOT cannot determine the physical locations of the various components on the storage media, nor can they resolve the destination execution addresses in memory or locate the program's primary entry point. For the i.MX6 Solo/DualLite processors, a valid image program is composed of the following four sequential blocks:

  • Image Vector Table (IVT)

  • Device Configuration Data (DCD)

  • Boot Data

  • Application Code and Data

Among these components, the Image Vector Table is stored at a fixed, deterministic offset on the boot device. It consists of a precise array of pointer vectors that the on-chip boot ROM utilizes to locate the remaining sections of the program across the storage media blocks. The DCD block encapsulates a specialized group of registers and value pairings readable by the on-chip ROM to tune internal silicon parameters and configure peripheral controllers. The Boot Data table stores the absolute physical location of the image, its exact linear size, and explicit configuration flags indicating whether a pre-boot initialization software plugin is active. Together, these three introductory blocks are collectively defined as the Initial Program Loader (IPL) or initial import region. Upon completing its low-level internal resets, the on-chip boot ROM must copy this initial import block into internal RAM before processing any other routines. Finally, the application code and data section contains the actual compiled U-BOOT instructions and structural environment data tables.

4.3.4 Image Vector Table (IVT)

After performing the necessary hardware initialization and identifying the primary boot medium, the on-chip ROM bootloader first copies the data within the initial boot region into the on-chip RAM and subsequently parses the Image Vector Table (IVT). Based on the parsing results, it relocates the initial boot region data from the on-chip RAM to the target destination address and loads the remainder of the image program into the target address space. For the i.MX6 family of processors, the explicit storage offsets of the IVT across different boot media are defined as follows:

Table 4-1 Storage Offsets of the IVT on Different Media

Boot MediumAbsolute Storage Offset/Address
NOR Flash0x0000_1000 (4 KB)
NAND Flash0x0000_0400 (1 KB)
SD / eMMC / MMC0x0000_0400 (1 KB)
SPI / I2C EEPROM0x0000_0400 (1 KB)

The IVT must be stored at a fixed, deterministic offset on the boot device; this represents the sole structural constraint enforced by the on-chip boot ROM.

The IVT consists of eight distinct 4-byte fields: the header, the entry pointer, reserved region 1, the DCD pointer, the boot data pointer, the self pointer, the Command Sequence File (CSF) pointer, and reserved region 2 (see the diagram below).

Table 4-2 IVT Format

Word OffsetField NameDescription
0x00HeaderDefines tag, length, and version of the IVT.
0x04Entry PointerAbsolute address of the application entry point.
0x08Reserved 1Reserved for future architectural expansion.
0x0CDCD PointerAbsolute memory pointer targeting the DCD block.
0x10Boot Data PointerAbsolute memory pointer targeting the Boot Data block.
0x14Self PointerAbsolute memory pointer targeting the IVT itself.
0x18CSF PointerAbsolute pointer targeting the Command
0x1CReserved 2Reserved for future architectural expansion.

Each component occupies exactly 4 bytes of memory. The structures and specific use cases of these fields are detailed below.

The Header resides at the absolute beginning of the IVT, describing the length and version specification of the structure. Its format is defined as follows:

Table 4-3 Header Format

FieldWidthFixed Value / Encoding Rules
Tag1 Byte0xD1 (Identifies the block as a valid IVT structure)
Length2 BytesBig-Endian integer encoding the total width of the IVT
Version1 Byte0x40 series (e.g., 0x41, 0x42, 0x43)

Within this header block, the Tag field holds a constant value of 0xD1, indicating that the data structure is an IVT. The Length field consumes 2 bytes, encoded in big-endian format, representing the absolute length of the IVT structure itself including the header word. The Version field spans 1 byte, carrying values such as 0x41, 0x42, or 0x43; this parameter explicitly dictates the program entry type, mapping either to the primary application start address or directly to a hardware reset vector.

The Entry field specifies the execution entry point of the image program, corresponding to the initial address of the application or the absolute address of the reset vector.

The DCD Pointer targets the Device Configuration Data array, spanning a length of 4 bytes. The hardware configuration matrices contained within this pointer block are parsed to initialize essential on-chip peripherals, such as the MMDC memory controller and external DDR chips.

The Boot Data Pointer holds the absolute memory address of the standalone Boot Data structure after the image has been loaded into memory. The structural layout of the Boot Data block is defined as follows:

Table 4-4 Boot Data Structure

Field NameWidthArchitectural Meaning
Start Address4 BytesAbsolute destination memory address of the image
Image Length4 BytesTotal linear size of the image program in bytes
Plugin Flag4 BytesConfiguration indicator for pre-boot initialization plugins

In the structure mapped out above, the starting address defines the absolute destination target in physical RAM where the image payload is unpacked and copied, while the length field dictates the total volume of the image in bytes. The plugin slot specifies configurations for custom hardware initialization plugins; when the processor relies on baseline DCD tables instead of an active plugin to configure the SoC, this area is left empty.

The Self Pointer registers the absolute memory address hosting the IVT block itself, utilized dynamically by the on-chip ROM bootloader routines during validation steps.

The CSF Pointer points to the specific memory coordinates hosting the Command Sequence File (CSF) binary stream utilized during high-assurance encrypted secure boot operations.

The physical structural relationship mapping the U-BOOT bootloader's layout on the storage medium to its final expanded layout after being imported into physical RAM is illustrated in the diagram below:

i.MX6 DualLite/Solo Device Configuration Data (DCD)

Typically, after power-on, the default values of a computer's internal registers are not optimized for system performance, and certain peripherals cannot be used until they are explicitly configured. This requires developers to configure specific registers based on actual hardware conditions to meet system requirements. For example, the i.MX family of applications processors provides an EIM interface, but its default configurations are tailored for generic NOR flash; while NOR flash can be accessed immediately upon boot, the transfer speed is low. Furthermore, this family of chips provides a multi-mode memory controller to drive external RAM, but users must configure an array of register fields before the chosen DDR memory can be accessed. The on-chip boot ROM of the i.MX6 chip provides a built-in function to parse Device Configuration Data (DCD) directly from the boot device. As long as the developer provides the correct data structures at the designated offsets within the external boot image according to the specified formatting rules, the on-chip ROM can execute baseline hardware provisioning automatically.

The DCD structure encapsulates these device configuration parameters, and the on-chip ROM utilizes the pointer vectors resident inside the Image Vector Table (IVT) to resolve the physical location of the DCD payload on the storage medium. The binary storage layout of the DCD data is defined as follows:

Table 4-5 Storage Format of DCD Data

Byte OffsetField NameDescription
0x00DCD HeaderStandard 4-byte descriptor header block.
0x04Commands ArrayA contiguous sequence of configuration commands.

The DCD structure header occupies exactly 4 bytes of memory, organized according to the following layout:

Table 4-6 DCD Header Structure

FieldWidthFixed Value / Encoding Rules
Tag1 Byte0xD2 (Identifies the block as a valid DCD structure)
Length2 BytesBig-Endian integer encoding the total length of the DCD array including this header
Version1 Byte0x41

Within this header block, the Tag field holds a constant byte value of 0xD2, identifying the data structure as a DCD block. The Length field consumes 2 bytes, encoded in big-endian format, representing the absolute length of the DCD payload including the header itself. The Version field spans 1 byte and is fixed to 0x41.

The CMD (Commands) section contains the actual configuration instructions executed by the ROM engine. The interpreter supports exactly 4 distinct command variants: the Write Command, the Check Data Command, the No-Operation (NOP) Command, and the Unlock Command.

The layout syntax for the Write Command is defined as follows:

Table 4-7 Write Command Format

Word OffsetField NameDescription
0x00Command HeaderTag (0xCC), Length (2 Bytes, Big-Endian), and Parameter (1 Byte).
0x04AddressTarget physical or register address for the write operation.
0x08Value / MaskPayload data to be written or bit-mask to be applied.

In this layout, the Address parameter specifies the target register or memory address for the write operation, while the Value/Mask parameter provides the raw payload data to be written or the bitmask to be applied. The command header consists of three segments: the Tag spans 1 byte and holds a constant value of 0xCC to signify a Write command; the Length spans 2 bytes, encoded in big-endian format, defining the total byte width of the Write command sequence including the header; the Parameter field occupies 1 byte, structured as follows:

Table 4-8 Parameter Format

Bit FieldsDescription / Sub-field Encoding
[2:0]Bytes: Width of the target register access; can be set to
[4:3]Flags: Operational mode control fields (Bit 3 = Masked Write, Bit 4 = Set/Clear).

The operational modes defined by these flag bits are evaluated according to the table below:

Table 4-9 Write Command Operational Flags

Binary Bit PatternOperation TypeFunctional Specification
00Clear}Clear bits specified by the value payload.
01WriteDirect write operation (absolute value assignment).
10Clear/ResetExecute a bitwise clear operation using the mask.
11SetExecute a bitwise set operation using the mask.

The Check Data Command performs conditional polling over a target register address space. Its layout configuration is structured as follows:

Table 4-10 Check Data Command Format

Word OffsetField NameDescription
0x00Command HeaderTag (0xCF), Length (2 Bytes, Big-Endian), Parameter (1 Byte).
0x04AddressTarget memory or register address to be polled.
0x08MaskBitmask utilized to filter out unrelated data bits.
0x0CCountMaximum polling loop iteration threshold.

The Address field defines the register target to sample, the Mask field acts as a filter to mask out unrelated bits, and the Count word specifies the loop iteration limit. The ROM engine loops and samples the target address continuously until the specified bitwise conditional checks match the mask constraints or the iteration counter reaches the threshold defined by Count. If Count is initialized to 0, the command effectively functions as a no-operation statement.

The command header for this check utility contains three distinct fields. The Tag is fixed to a constant byte value of 0xCF, identifying the structure as a Check Data block. The Length field consumes 2 bytes, encoded in big-endian format, indicating the total length of the check sequence including its header. The Parameter field occupies 1 byte, formatted as follows:

Table 4-11 Check Data Parameter Header

Bit FieldsDescription / Encoding Specification
[2:0]Bytes: Width of the target access check window (1, 2, or 4 bytes).
[4:3]Flags: Operational evaluation logic selectors (Bit 3 = Masked, Bit 4 = Set).

The exact polling logic governed by these parameter flags is detailed below:

Table 4-12 Data Test Operations

Binary Bit PatternCondition RulesExecution Behavior
00Until All ZeroPoll continuously until all unmasked bits evaluate to zero.
01Until ClearPoll continuously until specified unmasked bits are cleared.
10Until All OnePoll continuously until all unmasked bits evaluate to one.
11Until MatchingPoll continuously until unmasked bits exactly match the target pattern.

The NOP Command occupies exactly 4 bytes of memory, matching the format below:

Table 4-13 NOP Command Format

Byte OffsetField NameFixed Value / Encoding Rules
0x00Tag0xC0 (Identifies a No-Operation token)
0x01LengthFixed to a value of 4 bytes (encoded across 2 bytes: 0x00 0x04).
0x03UndefinedReserved / Undefined trailing byte (can be safely ignored).

The Tag field spans 1 byte and holds the constant value 0xC0. The Length field spans 2 bytes and is fixed to 4. The final byte carries no definition and is ignored by the parsing engine.

The Unlock Command is implemented to prevent the internal secure boot sub-routines from locking out specific hardware engines upon exiting the ROM execution phase. Its structure is configured as follows:

Table 4-14 Unlock Command Format

Field SegmentWidthFunctional Specification
Tag1 Byte0xB2 (Identifies an Unlock token)
Engine ID1 ByteEng vector specifying the hardware cryptographic engine to remain active.
Unlock Value2 BytesValue payload specifying the configuration word needed

The Tag field occupies 1 byte, holding a constant value of 0xB2. The Eng sub-field defines the hardware engine component that must remain active and accessible after the ROM completes execution, while the trailing Value payload provides the exact configuration parameter word required by that engine. This command is primarily utilized within encrypted high-assurance secure boot deployment pipelines.

Bootloaders

4.4 Bootloaders

The application code and data section contains the final-stage bootloader, which is the most complex component among the primary segments. It is precisely this stage of the bootloader that imports the operating system kernel into physical memory and ultimately transfers system control to the operating system itself.

Different operating systems can implement different bootloaders, and a single bootloader can also be adapted to target diverse operating systems. The most prevalent bootloaders deployed across desktop systems include:

  • NTLDR

  • BOOTMGR

  • GRUB2

  • LILO (Linux Loader)

Conversely, the most popular bootloaders utilized within contemporary embedded operating system architectures include:

  • U-BOOT

  • BAREBOX

  • REDBOOT

NTLDR is utilized to boot legacy operating systems including Windows NT, Windows 2000, and Windows XP. A text configuration file named boot.ini resident inside the boot partition contains the operating system selection list alongside the physical storage coordinates of each instance. NTLDR must interact with NTDETECT.COM to collect hardware profiles before launching the operating system.

BOOTMGR is implemented to boot Windows Vista and subsequent Windows operating system releases. The available operating system options are maintained within a structured database file named BCD (Boot Configuration Data) stored in the active system partition. This bootloader operates independently and does not require secondary helper applications to orchestrate the kernel launch.

GRUB is capable of loading a vast, diverse matrix of operating systems and stands out as the most dominant, prevalent bootloader in the Linux ecosystem. The primary configuration script containing boot parameters is maintained within the grub.cfg file (for GRUB2 structures) or the menu.lst file (for legacy GRUB configurations).

U-BOOT is a powerful open-source bootloader extensively deployed across embedded environments. Globally known as "Das U-Boot," which is an acronym for the Universal Boot Loader, it provides broad processor architecture support for 68k, ARM, Blackfin, MicroBlaze, MIPS, Nios, SuperH, PowerPC (PPC), RISC-V, and x86 silicon targets. It supports a comprehensive taxonomy of storage interfaces—including SD cards, SATA drives, SCSI peripherals, EEPROMs, parallel/serial NOR flash, raw NAND flash, eMMC blocks, and USB storage volumes—alongside native network-based boot implementations.

BAREBOX is an alternative open-source bootloader framework supporting diverse architectures like ARM, x86, MIPS, and RISC-V. Initiated in 2007 as a fork derived from U-BOOT, it integrates multiple foundational components and design paradigms directly from the Linux kernel source code, resulting in a highly modular, Linux-style embedded boot platform.

REDBOOT is an acronym for Red Hat Embedded Debug and Bootstrap Firmware. It leverages the underlying Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) of the eCos real-time operating system to deliver a robust bootstrap environment for embedded systems. It supports serial line and network-based image downloading while providing complete trapping hooks for interactive GDB debugging. Furthermore, it exposes a comprehensive command-line interface that allows developers to execute manual firmware downloads and flash programming operations.

Because U-BOOT stands as the most pervasive, feature-rich, and industrially proven bootloader platform across contemporary embedded systems engineering, the subsequent chapter focuses explicitly on U-BOOT compiled for the NXP i.MX6Solo applications processor to systematically analyze its runtime execution pipeline, source code architecture, and core functional capabilities.

Chapter 5: U-BOOT Booting

U-BOOT Boot Flow

5.1 U-BOOT Boot Flow

U-BOOT is the definitive bootloader responsible for importing the operating system kernel into physical memory. It can function as both a first-stage and a second-stage bootloader, loaded into RAM by the primary initialization routines embedded inside the on-chip boot ROM (such as the ROM firmware within NXP's ARM-based i.MX6 family of multimedia applications processors). After loading the image program into memory, the on-chip ROM forces an execution jump to the absolute address specified by the entry pointer entry within the Image Vector Table (IVT), triggering the execution of the U-BOOT bootstrap pipeline. When the platform is configured to leverage the SPL boot methodology, the complete multi-stage system boot lifecycle is organized as illustrated in the schematic below:

The U-BOOT binary components can reside across an array of storage mediums, including SD cards, SATA drives, parallel/serial NOR flash, or raw NAND flash arrays. For a typical embedded target, the primary boot device is logically partitioned into four operational areas. The first partition stores the initial program loader and image vectors detailed in the preceding chapters (the boot image payload). The second partition holds the persistent environment block containing the runtime boot parameters passed by the bootloader to the operating system kernel. The third partition isolates the compressed Linux kernel image (zImage or uImage), and the fourth partition hosts the root filesystem (rootfs) matrix.

The execution flow of the U-BOOT bootstrap pipeline is divided into the following architectural stages:

As mapped out in the sequencing flowchart above, the U-BOOT startup pipeline supports several distinct boot modes, specifically: SPL (Secondary Program Loader), TPL (Tertiny Program Loader), or proper execution modes. These variants represent modular binary derivatives generated from a single consolidated U-BOOT source tree based on explicit compile-time configuration parameters. They can be freely stacked and combined like building blocks to adapt to localized silicon or memory boundary constraints.

These compilation targets maintain mutually independent operations yet execute sequentially based on system requirements. If the SoC features a high-capacity internal SRAM footprint, or if the hardcoded BootROM routines are explicitly engineered to initialize the external DDR layout before handing over execution, the platform can boot directly into the Proper image via a single-stage boot configuration. This single-stage approach is common among high-performance SoCs or system emulators. Conversely, if the physical internal RAM is highly constrained and the on-chip ROM lacks the capacity to initialize the external memory controller, the chip can initially parse and run only a minimal code footprint. In this scenario, a two-stage configuration joining U-BOOT Proper with an intermediary SPL (Proper + SPL) serves as the optimal layout; the on-chip ROM loads the lightweight SPL component into internal SRAM to initialize the system clocks and DDR lines, and the SPL subsequently fetches and unpacks the heavy U-BOOT Proper binary into the newly initialized external memory. Alternatively, the SPL can bypass the Proper stage entirely and branch straight into the Linux kernel initialization path (known as Falcon Mode). Under highly restrictive hardware constraints (for instance, a legacy layout exposing only 4 KB of internal SRAM where even a stripped SPL cannot fit), a three-stage boot pipeline joining U-BOOT Proper, SPL, and TPL (Proper + SPL + TPL) can be deployed, forcing the TPL to execute first from raw SRAM to bring up the core memory lines.

U-BOOT Proper represents the full-featured, standard variant of the bootloader. It encapsulates a highly complex command-line interface shell (CLI), granular environment variable parsing engines, a robust network protocol stack, and a comprehensive device driver model; its primary responsibility is loading the operating system kernel into memory. The SPL functions as a stripped-down, lightweight variant of U-BOOT, compiled without the text shell interpreter, environment subroutines, and superfluous peripheral drivers to optimize its binary size. Its exclusive objective is initializing foundational hardware blocks and loading the subsequent execution stage. The TPL represents a hyper-stripped, minimal variant of U-BOOT that typically isolates only the absolute baseline register loops needed to bring up the external DDR lines.

The selection of these U-BOOT boot stages is enforced at compile time using build flags (CONFIG_SPL=y, CONFIG_TPL=y), rather than being dynamically evaluated at runtime. Configuring these compilation switches is handled either via interactive menu-driven configuration utilities (menuconfig) or by editing the platform baseline configuration tables directly (such as defconfig templates or the active .config workspace).

While CONFIG_SPL and CONFIG_TPL act as global functional selection switches determining whether the compiler generates standalone SPL and TPL binary components, code blocks belonging to Proper, SPL, or TPL can coexist within a single function or source file. To isolate and separate these interleaved routines cleanly, the build system defines the CONFIG_SPL_BUILD and CONFIG_TPL_BUILD macro constants. If a block is bound by an #if !defined(CONFIG_SPL_BUILD) guard, it indicates that the enclosed code belongs strictly to the primary U-BOOT Proper image. An assignment matching #if defined(CONFIG_SPL_BUILD) wrapped alongside an inner #if !defined(CONFIG_TPL_BUILD) boundary indicates that the routine is compiled exclusively for the SPL layer. Finally, combining #if defined(CONFIG_SPL_BUILD) with an active #if defined(CONFIG_TPL_BUILD) filter designates that the target routine belongs exclusively to the TPL compilation pipeline. If code segments are written without these conditional macro envelopes, they are integrated globally into all three images.

When utilizing the Yocto Project compilation and build framework, the localized U-BOOT source tree leveraged by the NXP Linux release is extracted and tracked under the following workspace directory:

build/tmp/work/<board_name>/u-boot-imx/<version_number>/git/

Throughout all subsequent sections of this book, any explicit references detailing source code locations or file pathways are mapped assuming the git/ root directory as the absolute base path.

System Startup

5.2 System Startup

Upon receiving system control, the U-BOOT bootloader first initializes the exception vector table. For ARM systems, the source code for this low-level component is written in ARM assembly language and is maintained within the file git/arch/arm/lib/vectors.S. This file defines the following exception vector matrix. Once compiled into binary machine code, the linker mechanism places this exception vector table directly into the .vectors section starting at the global symbol _start. The linker script explicitly places this section at the absolute base entry point of the compiled U-BOOT binary image.

.macro ARM_VECTORS
b    reset
ldr    pc, _undefined_instruction
ldr    pc, _software_interrupt
ldr    pc, _prefetch_abort
ldr    pc, _data_abort
ldr    pc, _not_used
ldr    pc, _irq
ldr    pc, _fiq
.endm
.globl _start
    .section ".vectors", "ax"
_start:
    ARM_VECTORS

As shown in this assembly fragment, the absolute first instruction of the U-BOOT binary is an unconditional branch command jumping to the reset handler. The remaining exception vector slots utilize ldr instructions to load the starting memory addresses of their respective exception handlers directly into the Program Counter (pc) register, managing the corresponding hardware trap events. These underlying handlers and their target memory labels are fully declared within vectors.S. Because these routines are straightforward, they are omitted here for brevity; interested readers can review the source code in vectors.S.

It must be explicitly noted that if the platform is configured to leverage an SPL-based boot flow, this exception vector table definition is left empty, containing only a single unconditional jump instruction. Under this configuration, the final configuration of the active exception vector table is deferred and handled downstream by the running SPL routine.

The reset label is exposed globally within start.S, causing execution to branch directly into the code maintained inside start.S. For the i.MX6 Solo/DualLite processors, the start.S source file resides within the directory path git/arch/arm/cpu/armv7/.

The initial execution sequence in start.S forces the CPU core into Supervisor (SVC32) mode, masks out the IRQ and FIQ line interrupts, and modifies specific CP15 coprocessor control registers to configure internal caches, provision the memory management sub-blocks, and configure basic memory page translation tables. The following diagram charts the core assembly-level CPU initialization flow executed inside the start.S routine:

The introductory lines of assembly logic declaring the reset vector entry path within the start.S file are structured as follows:

.globl reset

.globl save_boot_params_ret

.type save_boot_params_ret,%function

reset:

b save_boot_params

save_boot_params_ret:

mrs r0, cpsr

and r1, r0, #0x1f @ mask mode bits

teq r1, #0x1a @ test for HYP mode

bicne r0, r0, #0x1f @ clear all mode bits

orrne r0, r0, #0x13 @ set SVC mode

orr r0, r0, #0xc0 @ disable FIQ and IRQ

msr cpsr,r0

bl cpu_init_cp15

bl cpu_init_crit

bl _main

ENTRY(save_boot_params)

b save_boot_params_ret @ back to my caller

ENDPROC(save_boot_params)

.weak save_boot_params

At the reset execution entry block, the code invokes an unconditional branch jumping into the save_boot_params subroutine to protect the boot registers handed down by the precursor ROM stage. In the default fallback path, this subroutine consists of a basic branch command that immediately returns back to the save_boot_params_ret marker, where the core proceeds to disable incoming asynchronous interrupts. Declaring the symbol as .weak save_boot_params allows system architects to override this routine. Developers can implement a custom save_boot_params implementation within board_init.c or alternative platform files to fully suppress or replace the baseline tracking code defined here. To strictly optimize the binary footprint, start.S relies extensively on preprocessor conditional compilation macros rather than runtime logical statements to initialize various system configurations.

If the platform build files do not define the configuration overrides CONFIG_SKIP_LOWLEVEL_INIT or CONFIG_SKIP_LOWLEVEL_INIT_ONLY, the system advances to call the lowlevel_init assembly routine. This code block resides within git/arch/arm/cpu/armv7/lowlevel_init.S and is responsible for carving out a temporary stack frame inside internal volatile storage. The target address parameters for this temporary stack differ significantly depending on whether the system is compiled under an SPL configuration or an ordinary non-SPL Proper build. The lowlevel_init routine subsequently invokes the s_init helper subroutine located within the same file. Upon completion, s_init returns control back to the original function block that initiated the call to lowlevel_init. This routine is exported with a weak linker attribute, permitting developers to easily substitute their own custom hardware initialization hooks.

Initializing the C Runtime Environment

5.3 Initializing the C Runtime Environment

The final instruction of the start.S utility is an unconditional branch command jumping to _main, forcing the CPU to jump to the _main entry point declared within crt0.S to process subsequent logic.

Before transitioning into the C programming execution state, the assembly logic in crt0.S coordinates the low-level, foundational allocation of resources. It first loads the absolute baseline starting address of the global_data structure into a dedicated processing register (specifically register r9 on ARM 32-bit architectures) and provisions the primary Stack Pointer (sp) required for C runtime execution, allowing downstream C functions to access parameters directly via gd->xxx. By invoking board_init_f_alloc_reserve(), it calculates and carves out the explicit memory margins required to accommodate the early stack frame and the gd tracking structure. It then invokes board_init_f_init_reserve() to clear and zero out the newly isolated gd memory region, ensuring all constituent structural members initialize cleanly to zero. Finally, it triggers board_init_f() to dynamically assign values to the internal tracking fields of the global_data layout.

The stack layout coordinates utilized by U-BOOT Proper align with the parameter CONFIG_SYS_INIT_SP_ADDR, whereas the SPL layer targets CONFIG_SPL_STACK and the TPL layer maps to CONFIG_TPL_STACK. These macro definitions reside inside the platform include files located within the directory tree git/include/configs/. For the NXP i.MX6 applications processor, the explicit parameter boundary for CONFIG_SPL_STACK is defined within the imx6_spl.h include file.

Within the U-BOOT architecture, the struct global_data structure (universally abbreviated as gd) acts as the primary global data repository tracking the platform lifecycle across the entire system boot sequence. Its core architectural declaration is maintained within the generic source file git/include/asm-generic/global_data.h. Because U-BOOT lacks an available global static variable block prior to executing the code relocation sequence (as the uninitialized data block, or BSS segment, remains completely uninitialized at this stage), the system routes this pointer tracking structure across active function boundaries by anchoring it within a dedicated processor register or specialized stack offset.

This global tracking framework encapsulates an array of metrics used to register physical hardware parameters, volatile memory distributions, and code relocation layout parameters, serving as the primary bridge to pass runtime data tables from the pre-relocation phase (board_init_f()) over to the post-relocation phase (board_init_r()). The primary structural members of this framework include:

  • bd_t *bd: Points to the platform-specific board information structure (board info), containing baseline hardware attributes such as memory starting addresses and bank capacities.

  • unsigned long flags: Status bitmask flags identifying the active runtime state of the system (such as tracking whether components are fully initialized, relocated, or running in silent mode).

  • unsigned int baudrate: Registers the active data transfer speed (baud rate) assigned to the primary serial console.

  • unsigned long relocaddr: Identifies the absolute destination target address in physical memory where the U-BOOT binary is relocated.

  • unsigned long reloc_off: Stores the explicit linear offset tracking the delta between the actual running address execution vectors and the default compile-time link addresses.

  • const void *fdt_blob: Stores the absolute physical memory address hosting the Flattened Device Tree binary (dtb) blob.

  • struct udevice *cur_serial_dev: Points directly to the structural driver instance managing the active serial communication port.

The crt0.S file resides within the directory tree git/arch/arm/lib/. The low-level assembly execution pipeline tracking the initialization sequence inside crt0.S is mapped out in the flowchart below:

The pre-relocation routine board_init_f() resides within the file git/common/board_f.c and acts as the universal hardware setup engine for standard U-BOOT Proper boot pathways. It invokes initcall_run_list() to execute a sequential array of initialization calls mapped out within the init_sequence_f array, which is declared inside board_f.c. Regulated by preprocessor build flags, init_sequence_f aggregates a wide array of architecture-specific and feature-dependent hardware setup loops. System architects choose the appropriate initialization sequence to match target hardware envelopes by toggling these configuration switches.

This execution array is divided into four distinct systemic phases: execution environment construction, core hardware initialization, memory allocation layout planning, and final pre-relocation preparation.

The Execution Environment Construction Phase relies primarily on the following functions:

  • setup_mon_len: Calculates the absolute linear footprint and size of the compiled U-BOOT binary image to prepare subsequent memory allocation and relocation tracking blocks.

  • fdtdec_setup: Sets up and validates the internal Device Tree Blob (DTB), exposing the baseline peripheral properties and target register base addresses (such as console UART base parameters) to the bootloader.

  • initf_malloc: Inits a lightweight, early memory allocation pool (Early Malloc). Because formal memory management and dynamic heap allocators are not yet active, this early heap block is required to manage temporary object instances.

  • initf_dm: Initialized the unified Driver Model (DM) architecture, bringing up U-BOOT's core device driver framework to enable the system to find and bind driver abstractions by name.

The Core Hardware Initialization Phase relies primarily on the following functions:

  • arch_cpu_init / mach_cpu_init: Coordinates low-level System-on-Chip (SoC) register configurations, tuning internal bus clocks and silencing asynchronous hardware blocks that could interfere with early boot routines.

  • timer_init: Initialized the low-level system hardware timer, ensuring microsecond delays (udelay()) and communication timeout checks compute deterministically.

  • env_init: Evaluates persistent storage links to resolve the exact physical location of the environment variables block (identifying whether parameters reside on an SD card, flash memory blocks, or fall back to default read-only memory arrays).

  • serial_init / console_init_f: A highly critical step that initializes the primary serial port driver, enabling text streams to output cleanly onto the host console terminal.

  • dram_init: A milestone function that handles volatile memory discovery. Within an SPL/TPL build, this routine handles the heavy lifting of tuning timing registers and bringing up the external memory controller to make DDR RAM usable. Within a Proper build, it typically reads pre-existing registers or parameters from the DTB to verify bank allocations.

The Memory Allocation Layout Planning Phase relies primarily on the following functions:

  • reserve_mmu: Reserves memory blocks to house the core MMU page tables, preparing the platform to enable cache engines to accelerate execution speeds.

  • reserve_uboot: Allocates the exact destination memory boundaries needed to accommodate the relocated U-BOOT binary image.

  • reserve_global_data: Carves out physical memory to hold the post-relocation global_data (gd) tracking structure.

  • reserve_stacks: Standardizes the absolute layout coordinates and memory margins required to anchor the main C execution stack.

The Final Pre-Relocation Preparation Phase relies primarily on the following functions:

  • setup_reloc: Sets the absolute target destination coordinates in physical RAM where the U-BOOT binary image will be copied.

  • clear_bss: Clears the uninitialized data section (BSS segment) by filling it with zeroes. At this stage, the system has successfully established a complete C runtime environment (the execution stacks are ready, the heap is operational, and the BSS block is cleanly initialized).

  • jump_to_copy (along with subsequent assembly routines): Within a U-BOOT Proper pipeline, this routine coordinates copying the active binary from flash storage into external DDR memory, then branches execution over to the relocated address space. Within an SPL or TPL pipeline, although the system traverses this identical initialization array, the board_init_r() phase typically bypasses relocation to locate and load the subsequent stage binary image.

For the NXP i.MX6 family of applications processors, when compiled under an SPL configuration to minimize the memory footprint, the universal board_init_f() sequence is replaced with a highly optimized, simplified execution block maintained within the board file git/board/freescale/mx6sabresd/mx6sabresd.c. Under this setup, the streamlined initialization sequence is defined as:

Depending on the chosen boot mode, crt0.S provides distinct initialization pathways. The Proper boot method requires shifting the execution location of the U-BOOT code within DDR memory; the invoked subroutines relocate_code and relocate_vectors are defined in the file relocate.S. Conversely, the SPL boot method requires relocating the active stack frame; the tracking stack relocation routine for SPL is located within the file git/common/spl.c.

The explicit function of relocate_code is to copy the contiguous code segment bounded between the symbols __image_copy_start and __image_copy_end into the physical RAM destination address pointed to by register r0. This copied section corresponds directly to the built-in.o object artifacts generated across the U-BOOT source tree, which represent the exact code blocks currently active in memory. The relocate_vectors subroutine is subsequently invoked to shift the system exception vectors to their designated runtime base.

The physical layout mapping U-BOOT memory allocation is structured as shown in the diagram below:

The linker script groups the vital execution paths needed during the core initialization lifecycle into the \_\_image_copy_start section. Conversely, the interface commands invoked via the interactive U-BOOT command line are treated as dynamically linkable runtime modules; the structural metadata required to parse and relocate these commands is isolated within the .rel.dyn section. Following the completion of the relocate_code routine, the updated memory layout of the U-BOOT image is partitioned as follows:

Based on the low-level configuration of the CPU core, relocate_vectors remaps the exception vectors either to base address 0x00000000 or to high address 0xFFFF0000. The ARMv7 architecture natively allows exception vectors to reside at either the low base (0x00000000) or the high base (0xFFFF0000); this boundary choice is governed explicitly by the V bit within register c1 of the CP15 coprocessor space. The updated structural layout of the exception vectors within memory is shown below:

If the system executes under a U-BOOT Proper boot pipeline, the routine subsequently invokes c_runtime_cpu_setup to invalidate the internal instruction cache (if the instruction cache has been explicitly enabled).

The code path directly following the execution of c_runtime_cpu_setup handles both the standard U-BOOT Proper sequence and any complex SPL pipelines that explicitly toggle the CONFIG_SPL_FRAMEWORK compilation flag. When an SPL implementation grows in complexity to support advanced subsystems, enabling the CONFIG_SPL_FRAMEWORK abstraction layer becomes structurally mandatory. The core objective of this final assembly block is to execute runtime environment cleanup, optionally re-anchor the active Stack Pointer and the global_data (gd) base tracking pointer, and execute the definitive jump into the post-relocation C entry function, board_init_r.

Post-Relocation Initialization (board_init_r)

type: basic-note

5.4 Post-Relocation Initialization (board_init_r)

5.4 Post-Relocation Initialization (board_init_r)

Following the code relocation phase, the system transitions into the definitive execution stage managed by board_init_r(). For the standard U-BOOT Proper boot pipeline, this function resides within git/common/board_r.c. Mirroring the pre-relocation phase, it invokes initcall_run_list() to parse and execute a comprehensive sequence of hardware initialization and software subsystem configuration loops defined within the init_sequence_r array.

The complete sequential execution matrix tracking the low-level functions within the post-relocation runtime phase is mapped out in detail in the following technical flowchart:

The system does not invoke all of the modules listed above during the booting sequence. Depending on the selected boot mode and the hardware configurations supported by the platform, developers configure specific compilation switches at build time to selectively couple and isolate the target modules required to initialize the system.

Running of U-BOOT

5.5 Running of U-BOOT

5.5.1 U-BOOT Top-Level Loop

The final pointer within the init_sequence_r array must target the run_main_loop function, shifting the system state into an infinite execution loop that waits for user command inputs. The run_main_loop() function is defined inside board_init_r.c and is structured as the following infinite for loop that sequentially invokes main_loop():

static int run_main_loop(void)
{
#ifdef CONFIG_SANDBOX
	sandbox_main_loop_init();
#endif
	for (;;)
		main_loop();
	return 0;
}

The main_loop() function is defined within git/common/main.c, and its implementation code is structured as follows:

void main_loop(void)
{
	const char *s;
	bootstage_mark_name(BOOTSTAGE_ID_MAIN_LOOP, "main_loop");
	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_VERSION_VARIABLE))
		env_set("ver", version_string); /* set version variable */
	cli_init();
	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_USE_PREBOOT))
		run_preboot_environment_command();
	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_UPDATE_TFTP))
		update_tftp(0UL, NULL, NULL);
	s = bootdelay_process();
	if (cli_process_fdt(&s))
		cli_secure_boot_cmd(s);
	autoboot_command(s);
	cli_loop();
	panic("No CLI available");
}

Its primary function is to initialize the command-line interface (CLI) routines, fetch the countdown delay duration via bootdelay_process(), and evaluate the target bootcmd environment variable. The bootcmd variable stores an execution macro or script composed of sequential U-BOOT commands that control how U-BOOT boots the Linux kernel. (The countdown delay can be tuned dynamically via the autodelay environment variable, or specified directly within the Device Tree using the bootdelay integer property, among other configurations). The operational flow of the main_loop() function alongside a streamlined representative slice of the underlying bootcmd script macro is presented below:

bootcmd=run findfdt;
run findtee;
mmc dev ${mmcdev};
if mmc rescan; 
    then if run loadbootscript; 
            then run bootscript; 
         else if run loadimage; 
             then run mmcboot; 
           else run netboot; 
           fi; 
         fi; 
else run netboot; 
fi
loadfdt=fatload mmc ${mmcdev}:${mmcpart} ${fdt_addr} ${fdt_file}
loadimage=fatload mmc ${mmcdev}:${mmcpart} ${loadaddr} ${image}
loadtee=fatload mmc ${mmcdev}:${mmcpart} ${tee_addr} ${tee_file}
mmcboot=echo Booting from mmc ...; 
run mmcargs; 
if test ${tee} = yes; 
    then run loadfdt; 
         run loadtee; 
         bootm ${tee_addr} - ${fdt_addr}; 
else if test ${boot_fdt} = yes || test ${boot_fdt} = try; 
	then if run loadfdt; 
             	then bootz ${loadaddr} - ${fdt_addr}; 
          else if test ${boot_fdt} = try; 
            		then bootz; 
          		else echo WARN: Cannot load the DT;
            	fi; 
            fi; 
	else bootz; 
	fi;
fi;

U-BOOT initially executes the statement run findfdt to process the findfdt macro script. The findfdt macro performs an array of sequential test criteria matching the live motherboard configuration to dynamically resolve and populate the baseline value for the fdt_file environment variable. For brevity, the granular algorithmic details of the findfdt script are omitted here. The fdt_file variable registers the corresponding compiled Device Tree Blob filename matching the physical board; for the imx6qp_sabreauto development board, this evaluates explicitly to fdt_file = imx6qp-sabreauto.dtb. Concurrently, bootcmd runs run findtee to invoke the findtee macro script, which checks for the platform-specific Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) binary payload filename, assigning it to tee_file. Because the imx6qp_sabreauto board implements the uTee-6qpauto hardware security manager firmware, this resolves to tee_file = uTee-6qpauto.

The explicit instruction mmc dev ${mmcdev} configures the active MMC host slot indexed by ${mmcdev} as the primary system boot media target.

When the platform executes a Linux kernel launch sequence originating from an SD card, U-BOOT shifts execution into the run mmcboot macro path. The underlying mmcboot macro runs the child loadimage script, invoking the standard U-BOOT fatload utility block to copy the kernel binary target defined by ${image} from the designated boot partition coordinates (specified explicitly via mmc ${mmcdev}:${mmcpart}) into the physical RAM destination address configured by ${loadaddr}. Following an identical operational framework, the overarching bootcmd macro pulls the target .dtb file and the secure .tee firmware payload into their designated physical memory targets. In this operational context, ${image} maps to a compressed zImage kernel envelope. The absolute boundary coordinates for ${fdt_addr}, ${loadaddr}, and ${tee_addr} are hardcoded or adjusted inside the board architecture configuration header files. Finally, the boot execution sequences handled by the trailing macros—specifically bootm ${tee_addr} - ${fdt_addr} or bootz ${loadaddr} - ${fdt_addr}—execute the definitive jump into the Linux kernel initialization path.

The bootcmd macro string is maintained directly within U-BOOT’s persistent non-volatile environment space; its default fallback string value is established at compile time within the generic platform configuration templates located at git/include/configs/<board_common>.h. End-users can interrupt the automatic autoboot countdown sequence to drop into the interactive U-BOOT command-line shell, modify the configuration properties of bootcmd manually, and commit the updated script permanently to flash blocks via the saveenv routine.

If the active Device Tree configuration implements a custom bootcmd node property block, the parsing routines inside main_loop() interrogate the tree to verify whether an explicit bootsecure enforcement flag has been enabled. If the bootsecure flag is active, the system branches immediately into an unreturned secure encrypted boot execution routine (cli_secure_boot_cmd). If the verification pass confirms standard booting operations, execution control passes to the autoboot_command() block. The autoboot_command() function evaluates the live tracking timer parameters alongside the console UART inputs to check if a user keystroke has been registered. If the timeout delay expires without catching an active keyboard interrupt vector, it calls run_command_list() to interpret and run the compiled bootcmd command sequence fetched by the bootdelay_process() routine. Conversely, if a valid keystroke is caught during the active countdown delay window, the state machine diverts into the cli_loop() function block, initializing the persistent shell loop to parse, interpret, and execute incoming text commands manually supplied by the developer.

5.5.2 U-BOOT Command Interpretation

The run_command_list function parses U-BOOT scripts. U-BOOT can evaluate scripts or commands using either the legacy simple parser or the HUSH parser (detailed in subsequent sections). When configured for the simple interpretation path, it invokes cli_simple_run_command_list to process the script. The C implementation code for run_command_list under this simple interpretation profile is structured as follows:

int run_command_list(const char *cmd, int len, int flag)
{
    int need_buff = 1;
    char *buff = (char *)cmd; /* cast away const */
    int rcode = 0;
    if (len == -1) {
        len = strlen(cmd);
        need_buff = strchr(cmd, '\n') != NULL;
    }
    if (need_buff) {
        buff = malloc(len + 1);
        if (!buff)
            return 1;
        memcpy(buff, cmd, len);
        buff[len] = '\0';
    }
    rcode = cli_simple_run_command_list(buff, flag);
    if (need_buff)
        free(buff);
    return rcode;
}

This code first calculates the length of the cmd string (passed dynamically to cmd via the bootcmd variable within the main_loop). If the cmd string encapsulates newline characters ('\n'), the routine allocates a dynamic buffer, replaces occurrences of '\n' with null terminators ('\0'), copies the command block into this isolated buffer memory, and finally invokes cli_simple_run_command_list to execute the script referenced by buff.

5.5.3 U-BOOT Command Execution

The functional role of cli_simple_run_command_list() is to split the script pointed to by cmd into distinct sub-units delimited by newline boundaries ('\n'), and then sequentially call cli_simple_run_command() to execute each unit's command string. cli_simple_run_command() parses the text stream provided by cli_simple_run_command_list and sections it into multiple tokens separated by semicolons (;).

If any tokens contain macros wrapped inside ${} or $(), the routine calls cli_simple_process_macro() to dynamically substitute the macros with their current expanded environment values. It then leverages cli_simple_parse_line() to tokenize the expanded string into an array of individual, whitespace-delimited argument variables.

These resolved variables are stored sequentially inside the argv array, where argv[0] holds the primary command binary string, and subsequent entries like argv[1] map to the trailing arguments passed to the utility; the total argument count is registered inside the integer variable argc. Finally, cli_simple_run_command() calls cmd_process() to execute the explicit command specified by argv[0].

The cmd_process() function first leverages find_cmd(argv[0]) to query the internal link-time command table for a matching tracking entry corresponding to argv[0]. If a valid entry is resolved, it passes the command's structural argument count and argument vector array over to the cmd_call() infrastructure to execute the operation. Within the source file git/cmd/bootm.c, a core macro declaration is defined as follows:

U_BOOT_CMD(bootm, CONFIG_SYS_MAXARGS, 1, do_bootm, 
  "boot application image from memory", bootm_help_text);

This macro architecture is defined within the core header file git/include/command.h. In this declaration, bootm specifies the text command string, CONFIG_SYS_MAXARGS defines the maximum argument threshold permitted by the utility, 1 indicates that hitting the carriage return key will repeat the execution of the previous command string, and do_bootm acts as the definitive C callback handler function pointer. When an operator issues the bootm string, U-BOOT handles the invocation by executing the underlying C function do_bootm. The string "boot application image from memory" provides a short summary description, while bootm_help_text stores the exhaustive help documentation.

Expanding this structural macro shows that the statement expands to the following link-time initialization code:

ll_entry_declare(cmd_table_t, bootm, do_bootm) = {
    "bootm", CONFIG_SYS_MAXARGS, cmd_always_repeatable, do_bootm, "boot application image from memory", bootm_help_text, NULL
};

The compilation layout defines a unique static tracking structure of type struct cmd_tbl named _u_boot_list_2_cmd_2_bootm, which is placed within the custom linker section .u_boot_list_2_cmd_2_bootm. The final generated variable assignment maps to the following definition:

struct cmd_tbl _u_boot_list_2_cmd_2_bootm = {
    .name       = "bootm",                                   // Command string token
    .maxargs    = CONFIG_SYS_MAXARGS,                        // Maximum parameter count threshold
    .repeatable = 1,                                         // Repeatable execution flag on Enter keypress
    .cmd        = do_bootm,                                  // Function pointer: target logic execution loop
    .usage      = "boot application image from memory",     // Short description string (shown by generic 'help')
    .help       = bootm_help_text,                          // Long description string (shown by 'help bootm')
    .complete   = NULL                                       // Auto-completion hook callback (Null assigned here)
};

This mechanism links the command registry key "bootm" directly to the do_bootm C routine. The structural execution architecture tracking the run_command_list function is mapped out in the technical flowchart below:

When launching a Linux kernel from an attached SD card, the cmd_call() infrastructure invokes cmd_always_repeatable(), which subsequently triggers the execution entry point of do_bootm(). Consequently, cmd_call() routes execution straight into do_bootm() to drive the final Linux booting sequence forward.

If the platform is compiled to leverage an early pre-boot environment pathway, the main_loop processes the pre-boot commands before parsing other variables. Furthermore, if network-based recovery configurations are enabled, the main_loop invokes upstream network protocols using the TFTP framework to pull down and flash updated U-BOOT and Linux kernel images before continuing routine execution loops.

5.5.4 Command Processing and Execution

At its termination phase, the main_loop function transitions into the interactive command-line interface framework loop (cli_loop), where it pauses to capture manual command strings supplied by the operator or awaits the expiration of the autoboot countdown delay vector to initiate the automated booting pathway.

The cli_loop() function is defined within the source file git/common/cli.c, and its technical implementation is structured as follows:

void cli_loop(void)
{
	bootstage_mark(BOOTSTAGE_ID_ENTER_CLI_LOOP);
#ifdef CONFIG_HUSH_PARSER
	parse_file_outer();
	/* This point is never reached */
	for (;;);
#elif defined(CONFIG_CMDLINE)
	cli_simple_loop();
#else
	printf("## U-BOOT command line is disabled. Please enable CONFIG_CMDLINE\n");
#endif /*CONFIG_HUSH_PARSER*/
}

The system is architected to parse operator commands utilizing either the Bourne-shell-compatible HUSH parser or the legacy simple interface engine; the targeted translation model is explicitly dictated at build time via preprocessor configuration flags. The structural parsing of an incoming command line string is a sequential process of stream scanning and string tokenization. Because the underlying logic is linear, it is omitted here; interested developers can audit the parsing routines maintained inside git/common/cli_hush.c or git/common/cli_simple.c. To establish a baseline reference model, the utility execution pipeline is illustrated here by analyzing the workflow of the cli_simple_loop() sub-routine.

The cli_simple_loop() function is implemented as an infinite for(;;) execution loop. Inside this infinite loop block, the engine polls the active console device to sample user inputs and subsequently parses the captured string. If the token validation pass confirms a legal command structure, the system triggers the underlying execution logic mapped to that utility. Concurrently, it commits the verified command string to a localized history buffer, enabling the user to traverse and re-execute historical command vectors using the terminal's up and down arrow keys. Once the routine concludes, it recycles its tracking flags and returns to a block-waiting state to catch subsequent text streams.

U-BOOT exports an exceptionally rich and comprehensive suite of native utilities, predominantly categorized into hardware telemetry information gathering, low-level memory block manipulation, non-volatile flash programming, runtime execution flow control, transport layer network stack management, and environment variable manipulation, alongside generalized hardware interface control and bare-metal debugging routines. Furthermore, the bootloader incorporates structural abstraction layers supporting standard Linux file systems.

Leveraging this combined framework of commands and environment variables, U-BOOT exercises absolute control over the Linux kernel loading topology and boot pathways, allowing developers to configure and test custom hardware setups interactively. When U-BOOT is resting in its command interpreter state, executing the printenv utility dumps a full listing of all active global environment variables to the console terminal, exposing the precise booting vectors under which the current platform is running.

The programmatic definitions declaring these U-BOOT commands are distributed across distinct C resource files clustered within the git/cmd/, git/lib/, and git/common/ directories of the source tree. A single source module can isolate a standalone monolithic command definition or aggregate multiple related sub-commands into a unified register table. Developers seeking deep structural details regarding particular command arrays can audit the corresponding C source targets contained within those paths.

Booting the Linux Kernel

5.6 Booting the Linux Kernel

The actual launch of the Linux kernel is orchestrated by commands such as bootm, bootd, bootefi, bootelf, bootz, bootvx, bootp, nfs, rarpboot, and tftpboot. Among these, bootm is used to boot application images from memory, bootd handles the default boot sequence, bootefi boots EFI-format image applications from memory, bootelf boots ELF-format image applications from memory, bootz boots images formatted as a zImage, and bootvx boots the VxWorks operating system, while the remaining commands are dedicated to booting Linux via network pathways. As seen in the bootcmd script, before the bootm command executes, U-BOOT first loads the Flattened Device Tree (DTB) blob and the secure TEE firmware file into memory. The following sections evaluate the process of U-BOOT booting Linux from an SD card, using the bootm command as a primary reference model.

For U-BOOT to successfully boot the Linux kernel, it must understand the specific storage and packaging format of the kernel on the storage medium. Prior to analyzing the execution path of the do_bootm function, the underlying kernel image file formats supported by Linux are detailed below.

5.6.1 Linux Image File Formats

When discussing Linux kernel formats, terms such as vmlinux, vmlinuz, zImage, bzImage, uImage, and FIT are frequently encountered. The vmlinux format is a statically linked executable ELF file of the kernel; it is a raw binary payload that can be loaded into memory and run directly, predominantly utilized for kernel troubleshooting and debugging. The vmlinuz format is a compressed version of vmlinux, which becomes runnable immediately upon decompression. U-BOOT does not directly consume raw vmlinux or standard desktop vmlinuz files.

The zImage and uImage formats represent the legacy image infrastructure, which remains heavily deployed in embedded U-BOOT pipelines. A zImage is a self-decompressing kernel container enclosing a specific magic number header, a lightweight decompression wrapper routine, and the compressed raw vmlinux payload. The binary structural layout of a standard zImage file is organized as follows:

Within this topology, the executable code block (code) occupies the first 36 bytes of memory, followed immediately by a 4-byte Magic Number used by boot loaders to validate the payload as a definitive zImage. For the ARM Linux architecture, this magic signature is fixed to 0x016F2818. The zi_start marker denotes the absolute beginning address of the nested zImage executable logic, and zi_end points to its absolute termination boundary.

1. Single-Image uImage File Format

A uImage file is generated by wrapping a standard zImage container with a specialized U-BOOT header using the companion mkimage host utility. The uImage acts as an entry-ready kernel file that U-BOOT can parse and execute directly from memory. Its structural binary layout is structured as follows:

The 64-byte structural file header encapsulates the magic number, file header CRC checksum, file creation timestamp, image payload size, destination memory load address, application execution entry point, data (the inner zImage) CRC checksum, target operating system identifier, target CPU architecture token, image wrapper type, compression method flag, and the image name string.

  • Magic Number: A constant signature fixed to 0x27051956, which software routines evaluate to distinguish a legacy uImage file container from modern flattened image trees (FIT).

  • Header CRC Checksum: A Cyclic Redundancy Check validation word protecting the integrity of the 64-byte header block.

  • Creation Time: A standard Unix epoch timestamp registering the exact moment the image file was packed.

  • Image Size: Encodes the exact linear volume of the embedded zImage payload in bytes.

  • Load Address: Defines the baseline physical target address in RAM where the kernel payload must be uncompressed and relocated.

  • Entry Point: Explicitly marks the absolute address of the first machine instruction executed to initiate the kernel boot.

  • Data CRC Checksum: A Cyclic Redundancy Check validation word protecting the integrity of the inner zImage binary payload.

  • Operating System ID: An architecture token identifying the target operating system environment, such as Linux, VxWorks, NetBSD, or FreeBSD. Contemporary versions of U-BOOT provide native support for 28 distinct operating systems and firmware targets.

  • CPU Type: An architecture token mapping the compiled payload to its designated silicon target. U-BOOT currently identifies 26 discrete processor configurations including ARM, PowerPC (PPC), and x86 architectures.

  • Image Type: Maps the payload to one of 40 functional software categories, including standalone, kernel, firmware, tee, script, ramdisk, or multi.

  • Compression Type: Registers the algorithm utilized to compress the underlying zImage, with native support covering uncompressed raw blocks, gzip, bzip2, lzma, lzo, and lz4 compression variants.

  • Image Name: A descriptive text string identifying the image, capped at a maximum length of 32 characters including the null terminator.

2. Multi-Image uImage File Format

When the embedded image type field is initialized to configuration value 05 (multi), the legacy uImage container is refactored to wrap multiple independent sub-images within a single contiguous file block. The multi-image payload architecture presented in the diagram below encapsulates a compiled kernel binary, a compressed root RAMDISK container, and the platform Device Tree Blob (DTB) payload:

3. Flattened Image Tree (FIT) Image Structure

FIT is an acronym for Flattened Image Tree. Sharing the identical architectural design as the standard Device Tree, a FIT program image file is generated from a hierarchical, tree-structured source document describing the component images. This tree-structured file is authored using the same text-based language syntax as the Device Tree, where configuration blocks within the tree define how each component of the consolidated image file should be utilized. The file describing this image tree structure uses the .its extension suffix and strictly opens with the /dts-v1/; token declaration.

The hierarchical tree topology is composed of structured nodes, anchored at the top by a mandatory root node represented as a forward slash (/). The root node encapsulates individual image descriptors (images) and configuration sets (configurations), alongside the global description and #address-cells properties. The description property supplies a text summary explaining the image container, while #address-cells specifies the exact number of 32-bit cells required to encode node addresses within this context. U-BOOT parses these node addresses to cross-access and extract nested content from the flattened image blob. Both the images container and the configurations container can host multiple distinct child nodes, which are accessed via their defined addresses or unit tags.

The individual child nodes nested inside the images block can encapsulate legacy uImage files, compiled Flattened Device Tree blobs (.dtb), or compressed RAM disk images. Each independent child node block supports the description, data, type, arch, os, compression, load, entry, and hash attributes:

  • description: A descriptive text summary identifying the specific sub-image component.

  • data: Specifies the source binary payload to include, typically injected using the raw binary inclusion operator (/incbin/).

  • type: Registers the functional category of the binary payload (e.g., kernel, flat_dt, ramdisk).

  • arch: Identifies the target instruction set architecture compatible with the payload (e.g., arm, x86, riscv).

  • os: Specifies the guest operating system type to initialize.

  • compression: Registers the compression algorithm used to compress the target binary sequence.

  • load: Defines the absolute target address in physical RAM where the binary payload must be unpacked or copied.

  • entry: Specifies the absolute memory execution vector where control is transferred to start the program.

  • hash: Dictates the integrity verification algorithm applied to validate the sub-image segment.

The configurations container block can host multiple child configuration nodes alongside a top-level default selection attribute to define how the different compiled image pieces are joined together at runtime. For example, in the reference schema provided below, the default selection pointer targets config@1. The configuration matrix under config@1 specifies that the system must boot using the primary kernel defined under the kernel@1 node paired with the Flattened Device Tree blob registered under the fdt@1 node:

/dts-v1/;
/ {
	description = "Marcus FIT test";
	#address-cells = <1>;
	images {
		kernel@1 {
			description = "My default kernel";
			data = /incbin/("./zImage");
			type = "kernel";
			arch = "arm";
			os = "linux";
			compression = "none";
			load = <0x83800000>;
			entry = <0x83800000>;
			hash@1 {
				algo = "md5";
			};
		};
		kernel@2 {
			description = "Rescue image";
			data = /incbin/("./zImage");
			type = "kernel";
			arch = "arm";
			os = "linux";
			compression = "none";
			load = <0x83800000>;
			entry = <0x83800000>;
			hash@1 {
				algo = "crc32";
			};
		};
		fdt@1 {
			description = "FDT for my cool board";
			data = /incbin/("./devicetree.dtb");
			type = "flat_dt";
			arch = "arm";
			compression = "none";
			hash@1 {
				algo = "crc32";
			};
		};
	};
	configurations {
		default = "config@1";
		config@1 {
			description = "Default configuration";
			kernel = "kernel@1";
			fdt = "fdt@1";
		};
		config@2 {
			description = "Rescue configuration";
			kernel = "kernel@2";
			fdt = "fdt@1";
		};
	};
};

The root node can contain images and configurations child nodes. Within contemporary U-BOOT trees, the properties currently supported under the images child nodes encompass data, data-position, data-offset, data-size, timestamp, description, arch, type, os, compression, entry, and load. The data property is predominantly utilized to establish the location or reference path of the program code or source binary block. Concurrently, a node under the configurations block supports properties such as kernel, ramdisk, fdt, loadable, default, setup, fpga, firmware, and standalone.

Furthermore, the FIT specification supports secure cryptographic verification layers through dedicated signature and key verification nodes, including hash, signature, and key. A key configuration node can host attributes such as hash, algo, value, u-boot-ignore, signature, required, and key-name-hint. A cipher block node accommodates the cipher data pointer and its accompanying algo selection. These cipher and hash nodes are nested as child nodes within individual images components to enforce hardware-level image authenticity checks and implement encrypted high-assurance secure boots.

U-BOOT cannot directly parse or execute a raw text-based .its file. The file must first be flattened into a single operational binary image tree blob suffixed with the .itb extension using the host mkimage compilation utility. The schematic diagram below illustrates the exact input components and compiled output artifact managed during this mkimage build step:

The diagram below shows the core structural design and header alignment of the final compiled .itb binary image payload. Mirroring the binary layout rules of standard flattened device trees, the hierarchical image tree topology uses nesting definitions to append child node name strings directly beneath their corresponding parent block structures. Properties declared within these child nodes point to specific string tokens and tracking lengths packed into a centralized strings block database; the parsing engine traverses this string block via numerical offsets to read property values. FIT leverages this layout to encapsulate multi-component execution trees cleanly. For granular formatting guidelines and syntactical specifications, developers can consult the official Devicetree Specification documentation.

5.6.2 Booting the Linux Kernel via the bootm Command

Following the analysis of the binary image structures, this section evaluates the technical workflow under which U-BOOT leverages the do_bootm function to boot the Linux kernel.

The do_bootm function initially parses the command line string to verify if specific bootm sub-commands are declared. If sub-commands are detected, U-BOOT processes them sequentially to advance the bootstrap sequence. A sub-command executes only a partial or fractional slice of the complete bootm pipeline rather than a monolithic full boot. The tracking framework registers exactly eight sub-commands: start, loados, ramdisk, fdt, cmdline, bdt, prep, and go. If multiple sub-commands are issued manually by an operator, they must strictly follow this listed order, although executing the entire set is not structurally mandatory.

The universal syntax for the bootm utility is structured as follows:

bootm [addr [arg1 [arg2]]]

Where addr specifies the location in memory hosting the primary kernel image (typically a uImage or FIT blob base address), arg1 defines the physical memory address of the initialization RAM disk (initrd), and arg2 targets the compiled Flattened Device Tree (fdt) blob. If the target operating system configuration bypasses the use of a RAM disk, a hyphen placeholder (-) must be explicitly passed in place of arg1. As parsed within the bootcmd script analyzed in preceding chapters, the typical runtime execution syntax is expressed as:

bootm ${tee_addr} - ${fdt_addr}

Expanding this environment variable string (e.g., executing bootm 0x20000000 - 0x18000000) instructs the bootloader to branch execution into the program image hosted at address 0x20000000 without packing an initrd payload, while mapping the active Device Tree structure from base offset 0x18000000.

If no explicit sub-commands accompany the bootm invocation, the state machine must execute a complete, monolithic boot pipeline from scratch. Upon completing early sub-command checks, if the platform configuration has enabled High Assurance Boot (CONFIG_HAB), the routine triggers validation loops to authenticate the cryptographic signature and integrity of the outer uImage envelope. Concurrently, if the build incorporates support for OP-TEE secure layers, secondary hooks execute to validate the underlying zImage integrity.

Finally, the engine routes execution into do_bootm_states(), which acts as a centralized coordinator to step through the core initialization states sequentially: BOOTM_STATE_START, BOOTM_STATE_FINDOS, BOOTM_STATE_FINDOTHER, BOOTM_STATE_LOADOS, BOOTM_STATE_OS_PREP, BOOTM_STATE_OS_FAKE_GO, and BOOTM_STATE_OS_GO.

If a RAM-disk-based filesystem is deployed, the system branches into BOOTM_STATE_RAMDISK right after the OS loading phase concludes. Furthermore, if the processing architecture targets legacy PowerPC or MIPS silicon, the state machine must step through the OS_CMDLINE sub-state to construct command line strings. For an NXP i.MX6 application processor running mainline Linux, the definitive operational block array requires processing BOOTM_STATE_START, BOOTM_STATE_FINDOS, BOOTM_STATE_FINDOTHER, and BOOTM_STATE_LOADOS. Each discrete sub-state maps directly to a localized helper routine. The final sequence tiers—encompassing BOOTM_STATE_OS_PREP, BOOTM_STATE_OS_FAKE_GO, and BOOTM_STATE_OS_GO—are inherently OS-dependent; their final low-level executions are managed dynamically by invoking the targeted function pointers resolved via boot_fn() and boot_selected_os().

The continuous runtime execution flow tracking the do_bootm() function is mapped out in the schematic flowchart below:

The technical implementations and internal objectives of each core module within this flowchart are detailed below:

1. uImage Authenticity Verification

For the i.MX6 Solo/DualLite processors, U-BOOT handles cryptographic verification and decryption by interfacing directly with the hardware Cryptographic Acceleration and Assurance Module (CAAM) hosted inside the on-chip High Assurance Boot (HAB) silicon block. This hardware engine parses the binary Command Sequence File (CSF) tables embedded within the image's IVT wrapper to validate the uImage payload block. The physical base coordinates where the target uImage is evaluated align with the memory reference value configured inside the ${tee_addr} environment variable.

2. zImage Parameter Configuration

The bootloader inspects the internal text headers of the raw compressed kernel payload to extract the explicit zImage boundary vectors, registering its absolute starting and terminating memory coordinates. The baseline memory alignment tracking this zImage structure header is determined by the physical address value assigned to the standard U-BOOT ${loadaddr} environment variable.

3. zImage Authenticity Verification

U-BOOT leverages the on-chip HAB validation infrastructure and the CAAM engine to evaluate the CSF signatures tracking the zImage container, executing hardware-enforced image decryption and decryption verification passes. It must be noted that this specific ROM-driven pipeline handles authentication strictly for legacy single-image or multi-image binary wrappers; modern FIT container structures bypass this pathway, utilizing integrated self-contained cryptographic nodes to declare and enforce their own verification algorithms.

4. Sub-state Orchestration via do_bootm_states

The centralized coordinator steps through the following technical operations sequentially:

  • Initialization: Zeroes out all structural members of the internal bootm_headers_t tracking layout. If the platform build parameters have toggled the Logical Memory Block (CONFIG_LMB) macro constraint to fence off the lower bounds of memory accessible to the guest Linux kernel, the routine allocates and provisions the necessary lmb memory reservation tables at this stage.

  • Kernel Image Discovery: Initiates a lookup routine inside the loaded image block to isolate and parse the primary operating system kernel payload. The linear structural pipeline governing this component discovery path is illustrated below:
