- Secondary Image Discovery: Searches the image fields to resolve and map external initialization components, including detached root RAM disks (ramdisk), Flattened Device Tree blobs (fdt), or generic secondary loadable payloads. The flowchart below charts the lookup execution pipeline targeting a ramdisk component when the boot loader is configured to parse modern FIT container layouts. (When operating over legacy single- or multi-image configurations, this discovery loop is significantly more linear). Furthermore, if the platform enables raw initial RAM disk support (raw initrd), developers can explicitly pass the target initrd execution address vectors directly via the bootm command string using colon separator delimiters. The initrd represents a transient baseline file system structure initially staged in RAM by the bootloader to provide the early user-space mounting environment during the Linux initialization phase.
  • Operating System Payload Loading: Unpacks and relocates the compiled kernel binary payload contained inside the uImage wrapper. This data decompression and relocation pipeline follows the workflow detailed below:
  • Boot Handler Binding: Evaluates the explicit target operating system index stored within the os metadata field of the uImage header block. It invokes bootm_os_get_boot_func() to index into the generic boot_os[] function pointer array, dynamically binding the appropriate OS-specific bootstrap function handler. If the parsed os field matches configuration constant IH_OS_U_BOOT, the function pointer maps directly to the do_bootm_standalone() routine. In systems that execute bare-metal applications or dedicated firmware payloads without launching a complex multi-tasking operating system kernel, setting the target image profile to IH_OS_U_BOOT allows U-BOOT to unpack the standalone software directly into memory and hand over execution. The operational sequence tracking this standalone pathway is mapped out below:
Conversely, when the os header token evaluates to configuration index IH_OS_LINUX, verifying that the payload data segment encapsulates a valid Linux operating system kernel, the bound function pointer resolves directly to the do_bootm_linux() routine. At the final execution boundary, do_bootm_states() calls the top-level handler boot_selected_os(), which fires the resolved pointer to route execution straight into the Linux bootstrap sequence. For all standard Linux targets, this metadata flag must be explicitly configured to IH_OS_LINUX.

The low-level execution pipeline tracking the do_bootm_linux() bootstrap routine is structured as follows:

Varying the integer constant inside the os header field alters the targeted operating system boot pathway and initialization logic accordingly. Upon concluding its low-level hardware alignment, parameter table packaging, and device tree mapping tasks, the do_bootm_linux() routine issues an unconditional branch instruction jumping directly into the absolute entry point execution vector (entry) defined by the kernel image. At this exact instruction cycle, U-BOOT terminates its operational life cycle, relinquishing absolute system control over to the newly active Linux kernel.

5.6.3 SPL Booting

The preceding sections evaluated the standard (Proper) execution pathway of U-BOOT. However, when the physical capacity of the CPU's on-chip SRAM is heavily constrained, the system can be configured to execute an SPL-based multi-stage boot sequence instead. In this topology, the hardcoded on-chip boot ROM first copies the lightweight SPL binary from storage into internal SRAM. Once active, the SPL initializes critical low-level infrastructure, brings up the clock trees, and configures the external DRAM controller. After volatile memory becomes fully accessible, the SPL reads the high-capacity U-BOOT Proper binary image from the storage medium into physical RAM, subsequently handing over execution so that U-BOOT Proper can drive the definitive operating system launch. As charted in Figure 5-3, both the SPL boot sequence and the standard U-BOOT Proper sequence ultimately transition into a post-relocation C entry function named board_init_r(). It must be explicitly noted that although both execution models invoke a function sharing the identical literal identifier, their internal programmatic structures and compilation outputs differ completely; the specialized board_init_r() handler processed during the SPL phase is defined explicitly within the source file git/common/spl/spl.c. When the platform build configuration toggles the macro switches to generate an SPL image, the linker cleanly couples this spl.c entry target. The fundamental responsibilities of this handler are to execute localized hardware initializations, parse the storage controllers to resolve the SPL boot list, and execute the final-stage bootloader binary. Its operational runtime pipeline is organized as illustrated in the schematic flowchart below:

The programmatic operations and technical objectives of each core section within this flowchart are analyzed in detail below:

The board_init_r() function initially invokes a clear routine to zero out the spl_boot_list array structure. This tracking array functions as a prioritized linear repository storing the entry vectors and driver addresses of all valid, registered boot storage devices available on the hardware platform. The system then enters the spl_set_bd() helper block, which resolves the physical memory location allocated to store the baseline board parameters (board_info tables), an address boundary typically calculated and hardcoded at compile time by the linker script.

If the active build parameters have enabled the CONFIG_SYS_SPL_MALLOC_START preprocessor switch, the system calls mem_malloc_init() to carve out and provision the explicit memory space boundaries required to drive the dynamic heap allocator (malloc()) engine during the SPL phase. Upon doing so, it sets the GD_FLG_FULL_MALLOC_INIT flag bit inside the gd->flags bitmask array, informing downstream drivers that the early heap framework is fully initialized and operational.

The CONFIG_SYS_SPL_MALLOC_START identifier maps to an architecture-critical macro definition across embedded U-BOOT deployment pipelines, explicitly defining the physical baseline memory coordinates allocated to anchor the local heap context during the SPL phase. Because the physical memory available inside raw on-chip SRAM cells during the earliest stages of hardware bring-up is highly constrained, supporting dynamic memory allocation routines (the execution of standard malloc() loops) within the stripped SPL footprint requires that a precise, isolated region of volatile memory be manually fenced off to function as a temporary heap. This macro establishes the physical baseline boundary for that SPL heap allocation.

If an interrogation of the status bits inside gd->flags reveals that the GD_FLG_SPL_INIT indicator is unassigned, signifying that the foundational initialization routines targeting the SPL layer have not yet been processed, the state machine branches to call the core spl_init() function. This routine executes essential, mandatory low-level framework configurations. The linear software workflow mapping this initialization sequence is structured as follows:

The bloblist_init() function checks for the existence of a binary blob list at the physical address defined by CONFIG_BLOBLIST_ADDR. If no valid list is detected, it initializes a new instance. The bloblist acts as a secure, centralized storage buffer to carry binary metadata structures across boot stages.

The setup_spl_handoff() routine checks this bloblist to verify if pre-staged handoff metadata exists. System engineers can populate custom handoff manifests via the struct spl_handoff structure to pass vital tracking data—such as high-level memory topology parameters, persistent reset status flags, and network controller MAC addresses—directly to the downstream operating system layers.

If the platform configuration enables board-level initialization hooks during the compilation step, developers can implement a custom spl_board_init() routine to execute platform-specific hardware provisioning before loading subsequent stages.

Furthermore, board_init_r() orchestrates the initialization of the hardware watchdog timer, configures the active DRAM bank parameters, and allocates a zero-initialized memory block to anchor the spl_image descriptor structure. The spl_image descriptor functions as the primary repository tracking the metadata required during the SPL boot pipeline. Its structural layout is defined as follows:

struct spl_image_info {	
const char *name;
	u8 os;
	uintptr_t load_addr;
	uintptr_t entry_point;
	void *fdt_addr;
	u32 boot_device;
	u32 size;
	u32 flags;
	void *arg;
	ulong dcrc_data;
	ulong dcrc_length;
	ulong dcrc;
	uint64_t rbindex;
};

The majority of these tracking fields are extracted directly from the image header block. The runtime argument field is bound by system parameters to .arg = CONFIG_SYS_SPL_ARG_ADDR, while the default storage device mapping is initialized to .boot_device = BOOT_DEVICE_NONE.

The board_boot_order() routine assigns the function pointer address of spl_boot_device() to the primary slot of the spl_boot_list array. This routing utility is declared with a weak linkage attribute, allowing developers to substitute a board-specific implementation. For the i.MX6 applications processor, the native spl_boot_device() routine reads the hardcoded state of the hardware boot mode registers to resolve and return the active primary storage device type.

Following this sequence, boot_from_devices() processes the prioritized order specified in the spl_boot_list. It scans the custom linker section .u_boot_list_2_spl_image_loader_1 to find a structural spl_image_loader entry that matches the active boot device. This linker-generated tracking structure encapsulates the peripheral type identifier, the descriptive device name string, the storage driver routine pointer (load_image), and the targeted program entry vector. Once a matching descriptor block is resolved, the system invokes spl_load_image(), which redirects execution straight into the storage-specific handler pointer load_image() to pull the U-BOOT Proper binary from physical storage blocks into RAM. If the load routine encounters a media fault or data verification error, it discards the tracking context and drops down to process the next sequential element inside the spl_boot_list, looping until a valid load succeeds or all registered peripherals are exhausted. The specialized section .u_boot_list_2_spl_image_loader_1 is generated statically at link time.

Upon successfully parsing and staging the target image file inside physical RAM, the state machine evaluates the operating system metadata field (os) inside the image header. It triggers a branch command to jump into the resolved entry vector using stage-specific handlers. For example, if the platform incorporates OP-TEE secure architectures (where the metadata flag maps to IH_OS_OPTEE), the system invokes spl_optee_entry() to surrender absolute platform execution to the secure runtime environment. Conversely, when the tracking parameter maps to IH_OS_LINUX, execution branches into the jump_to_image_linux() routine to pass absolute control over to the Linux bootstrap hooks.

To fetch and reconstruct binary files from physical media blocks, spl_load_image() relies directly on low-level media access operations provided by the peripheral subsystem drivers. For i.MX6 architectures booting from an MMC/SD interface controller, these media access routines are defined within the source module git/common/spl/spl_mmc.c, where the primary entry function is declared as spl_mmc_load_image.

The build system leverages the standard macro declaration SPL_LOAD_IMAGE_METHOD("MMC2", 0, BOOT_DEVICE_MMC2, spl_mmc_load_image) to bind the execution address of the spl_mmc_load_image routine straight to the primary load_image function pointer slot. If the platform configuration includes Device Tree capabilities, load_image() pulls the combined binary blob u-boot-dtb.imx from storage into RAM; if Device Tree support is disabled, it pulls the legacy container u-boot.imx. The subsequent sections analyze the operational stages through which the SPL layer unpacks and stages storage payloads, using spl_mmc_load_image() as a reference design model.

The true heavy lifting of fetching data blocks from physical media sectors is managed by the secondary helper routine spl_mmc_load(). The primary entry function spl_mmc_load_image() acts as an interface wrapper that evaluates active preprocessor build switches to pass distinct parameter configurations over to spl_mmc_load().

The spl_mmc_load() function initially checks if the targeted MMC/SD interface controller driver has completed its internal initialization. If the descriptor structure pointer evaluates to null, the routine calls spl_mmc_find_device() to resolve the platform-specific hardware controller index. Depending on whether the compiled U-BOOT binary implements the modern Driver Model (DM) architecture or relies on legacy driver frameworks, the code branches to invoke either mmc_init_device() or mmc_initialize() to fully bring up the storage interface. If the device descriptor is already active, the routine bypasses initialization entirely to execute immediate bus-level communication handshakes with the attached storage card.

It must be explicitly noted that if the core struct mmc descriptor block indicates that the target peripheral supports asynchronous initialization pipelines, mmc_init_device() invokes mmc_start_init() to launch the storage initialization routines as an asynchronous background thread, allowing the bootloader to proceed with non-dependent tasks simultaneously.

Upon completing the low-level hardware bring-up, spl_mmc_load() invokes mmc_init() to pull the raw Card Identification (CID) and Card-Specific Data (CSD) registers from the media, negotiating optimal operational clock frequencies and defining the maximum available data bus width (allocating 1-bit, 4-bit, or 8-bit lines).

Once bus negotiation succeeds, spl_mmc_load() calls spl_boot_mode() to poll the storage configuration parameters and isolate the specific data parsing layout supported by the medium. For an active MMC peripheral, the SPL runtime framework identifies exactly three primary boot modes: MMCSD_MODE_FS, MMCSD_MODE_EMMCBOOT, and MMCSD_MODE_RAW. The spl_boot_mode() utility is exported as a weak symbol, enabling system developers to override its evaluation rules via board-specific logic.

If the returned status forces an eMMC boot partition pathway (MMCSD_MODE_EMMCBOOT), the driver handles the hardware-specific partition switching loops required to target either the boot0 or boot1 hardware partition areas. If the active storage codebase is configured under a minimalist layout constraint (MMC_TINY), the driver maps a basic, direct register switch; otherwise, it invokes standard block device partition-selection routines.

When the state machine selects a raw sector block configuration (MMCSD_MODE_RAW), the parser prioritizes attempting a direct operating system launch. At this junction, if a call to the check routine spl_start_uboot() returns a logical false value, the SPL completely bypasses the secondary bootloader stage to load and launch the Linux kernel directly from raw blocks (known as Falcon Mode). Conversely, if spl_start_uboot() returns a logical true value, indicating that the platform must load the complete U-BOOT Proper binary image, the function evaluates the configuration parameters to read the full U-BOOT payload from either a distinct partition index (USE_PARTITION) or from an absolute, hardcoded sector offset address (USE_SECTOR).

If the platform is compiled to support multi-image redboot or redundant safe flashing infrastructures (CONFIG_DUAL_BOOTLOADER), the driver routes execution through spl_mmc_get_u_boot_raw_sector() to evaluate boundary conditions and isolate the precise starting sector offset hosting the primary U-BOOT image within the MMC layout.

If the parsed tracking parameters force a filesystem access profile (MMCSD_MODE_FS), the driver transfers execution control to the internal routine spl_mmc_do_fs_boot(). This block initiates low-level filesystem mounts to parse and traverse local FAT or EXT4 file allocation paths, searching for and extracting the primary bootloader file by its explicit filename mapping (such as searching for u-boot.img).

The technical flowchart provided below maps out the precise, end-to-end programmatic steps through which the spl_mmc_load_image() routine imports the U-BOOT Proper binary image from physical media into physical memory:

When the SPL is deployed to directly boot the guest operating system, it invokes the mmc_load_image_raw_os() function to copy the raw Linux kernel image blocks from the media sectors into physical memory. The execution pipeline tracking this raw operating system load routine is structured as follows:

The following analysis profiles the operational workflow through which the SPL layer parses, loads, and extracts operating system components from modern multi-image structures, using the spl_load_simple_fit() routine as an architectural reference design model.

The spl_load_simple_fit() function accepts exactly four parameter arguments: a pointer to the target struct spl_image_info structure registering the runtime configuration metrics of the image, a pointer to a struct spl_load_info tracking layout defining the foundational parameters of the storage peripheral, a sector offset pointer designating the target block sequence to sample on the device, and a memory reference pointer targeting the source image file header. This routine parses the binary header blocks referenced by the file header pointer and populates the data fields inside the spl_image_info structure. As detailed in the preceding sections, this structure archives the vital metadata flags extracted from the image header to coordinate downstream image relocation and execution phases cleanly. The companion spl_load_info layout encapsulates low-level storage architecture parameters, declared as follows:

struct spl_load_info {
        void *dev;
        void *priv;
        int bl_len;
        const char *filename;
        ulong (*read)(struct spl_load_info *load, ulong sector, ulong count, void *buf);
};

Within this tracking layout, the .dev field points to the active boot storage peripheral device instance, .priv points to the private tracking structures managed by that specific peripheral, and .bl_len registers the device's native data access block boundary size (block length in bytes). The .read field maps to a localized block-read function pointer provided directly by the underlying storage peripheral's device driver module.

The spl_load_simple_fit() routine initially determines the absolute size of the target .itb container file, calculates the memory constraints required to accommodate the payload, and calls the driver-specific function pointer .read to read the entire FIT image block stream from storage into an isolated scratch buffer memory. Once the image metadata blocks are staged inside this memory cache, the internal parser executes a structural traversal across the image tree to isolate the core /images container node.

Upon successfully resolving the /images tree node, if the platform compilation profile includes dual-boot rollback protection capabilities, the parsing engine queries the /configurations container block to look up the secure rollback index (rbindex) attribute. If a valid rbindex marker is found, its relative structural byte offset address within the image file is calculated and written directly into the .rbindex domain tracking field inside the spl_image_info structure.

Concurrently, if the platform configuration includes integrated FPGA subsystem support, spl_load_simple_fit() evaluates the /images tree branches to isolate any embedded /fpga child nodes; if an active bitstream segment is found, the routine calls downstream programming paths to write that binary image directly into the physical FPGA configuration registers.

If FPGA support is disabled or the active .itb container file lacks an integrated /fpga node, the parser scans the active target /configurations node to extract the default software stack parameters. It initially attempts to resolve a /firmware assignment property; if that field is missing, it drops down to parse the primary /kernel assignment entry, and if that lookup also fails, it searches for a secondary generic /loadable allocation property. If the tree parser completes this cascade without resolving any valid bootable components, the function returns a failure error code. Conversely, if a target configuration node is resolved, the system routes execution control to the internal routine spl_load_fit_image(). This helper function validates and relocates the matching image files into their physical destination memory targets (or maps their relative coordinates if the binary blocks are already present in RAM) and executes the targeted data decompression algorithms. The sequential software execution pipeline tracking this workflow is structured as follows:

For a standard Linux compilation target, once the core kernel image payloads have been successfully staged and unpacked within physical memory, the jump_to_image_linux() routine interrogates the entry point metadata domain (entry) declared within the image header to establish the absolute starting instruction address of the kernel. It then executes essential runtime environment cleanup loops, silhouettes the asynchronous clock engines, and turns off internal caches.

At the absolute termination cycle, it calls the execution entry wrapper image_entry(), passing the registered target machine identifier code (machid) and the boot argument vector reference pointer (spl_image->arg) directly over to the guest operating system while forcing a hardware execution branch to jump straight into the resolved kernel entry address. At this exact instruction loop, the SPL layer completes its lifecycle, and the newly active Linux kernel takes full control of the entire hardware platform.

This concludes Chapter 5 and the exhaustive technical analysis tracking the U-BOOT Bootloader and Embedded SPL Initialization Lifecycles.

Chapter 6: Linux Initialization

The previous chapter evaluated the process of U-BOOT booting the Linux kernel. During this lifecycle, the primary tasks accomplished by U-BOOT include initializing all physical RAM banks, importing the core kernel modules into the appropriate physical memory destinations, provisioning the runtime boot argument vectors to be passed to the kernel, and resolving the active CPU type. Furthermore, if required by the target platform topology, it loads the initial RAM disk (initrd), brings up a primary serial console and display device, configures the appropriate hardware registers, and executes a definitive jump into the kernel image. For the ARM architecture, these operations constitute the fundamental baseline requirements imposed upon the U-BOOT bootstrap layer.

Upon executing the jump to the Linux kernel entry vector, the ARM processor state must strictly comply with the following hardware constraint matrix:

  • Register r0 must be initialized explicitly to 0.

  • Register r1 must store the unique logical architecture machine type identifier (CPU type index).

  • Register r2 must store the absolute physical baseline pointer address targeting the Flattened Device Tree (.dtb) blob, or the legacy boot arguments buffer (on platforms compiled without Device Tree capabilities).

  • The CPU core must operate within Supervisor (SVC) mode.

  • All asynchronous external hardware interrupts (IRQ and FIQ) must be completely disabled.

  • The Memory Management Unit (MMU) must be turned off.

  • The internal instruction cache (I-Cache) must be turned off.

  • The data cache (D-Cache) can be either turned off or left enabled depending on platform-specific pre-boot optimizations.

Once U-BOOT relinquishes absolute platform control and hands over execution to the Linux kernel, the kernel drives system initialization forward. It configures the processing CPU cores, aligns internal data caches, and provisions the low-level virtual memory management sub-blocks. Following this phase, it dynamically inserts core device driver modules, executes probe loops to initialize all integrated peripherals and IO channels, and ultimately mounts and boots the Linux root filesystem (rootfs). The subsequent chapters systematically analyze the exhaustive matrix of engineering tasks executed by the Linux kernel from the exact moment it captures system control up to the definitive launch of the first user-space process (init).

The absolute software entry point of the compiled Linux kernel is declared within the low-level assembly source module git/arch/arm/kernel/head.S. This file houses the definitive initial program sequence executed by the Linux kernel, written in raw ARM assembly language to complete all hardware-dependent and architecture-specific initializations.

Configuring the CPU Mode

6.1 Configuring the CPU Mode

The head.S source file implements a global macro block named __HEAD, which instructs the linker mechanism to place all subsequent machine code within the dedicated .head.text section. The absolute baseline starting address of this section defines the definitive software entry point of the compiled Linux kernel—mapping explicitly to the address hosting the absolute first machine instruction to be executed by the kernel subsystem.

Stripping away architecture-unrelated macros designated for Thumb mode orchestration (where guest Linux kernels targeting Cortex-M microcontrollers execute within the Thumb state) and BE8 instruction re-ordering—both of which compile to empty tokens when the build configuration targets standard ARM execution engines—and omitting the extended multi-dimensional paging structures designed to support 40-bit physical address extensions (LPAE) supported under ARMv7-A profiles, this baseline assembly setup can be streamlined into the following functional loop:

    .arm
    __HEAD
ENTRY(stext)
    safe_svcmode_maskall r9
    mrc    p15, 0, r9, c0, c0                	@ Acquire CPU ID
    bl    __lookup_processor_type	@ r5=procinfo r9=CPU ID
    movs    r10, r5                   		@ Invalid processor (r5=0)?
    beq    __error_p
    adr    r3, 2f
    ldmia    r3, {r4, r8}
    sub    r4, r3, r4                   		 @ (PHYS_OFFSET - PAGE_OFFSET)
    add    r8, r8, r4                    		@ PHYS_OFFSET
    bl    __vet_atags
#ifdef CONFIG_ARM_PATCH_PHYS_VIRT
    bl    __fixup_pv_table
#endif
    bl    __create_page_tables
    ldr    r13, =__mmap_switched        @ Address to jump to after MMU has been enabled
    badr    lr, 1f                    @ Return (PIC) address
    mov    r8, r4                    @ Set TTBR1 to swapper_pg_dir
    ldr    r12, [r10, #PROCINFO_INITFUNC]
    add    r12, r12, r10
    ret    r12
1:    b    __enable_mmu
ENDPROC(stext)
    .ltorg
2:    .long    .
    .long    PAGE_OFFSET

Within this code block, the initial execution segment:

safe_svcmode_maskall r9
    mrc    p15, 0, r9, c0, c0
    bl    __lookup_processor_type
    movs    r10, r5
    beq    __error_p

guarantees that the processing CPU core is forced into Supervisor (SVC) mode, masks out all incoming asynchronous hardware interrupts, and identifies the explicit processor architecture type. The token safe_svcmode_maskall expands to a foundational macro sequence engineered to assign CPU processing modes and silence interrupt lines, passing register r9 as a scratch workspace register to the macro block. The programmatic workflow tracking this initial pipeline is structured as follows:

The instruction mrc p15, 0, r9, c0, c0 issues a coprocessor transaction to pull the contents of register C0 from the CP15 coprocessor space, storing the data word inside scratch register r9. This internal CP15 C0 register serves as the core processor identification register housing the hardware CPU ID parameters.

The __lookup_processor_type subroutine searches the compiled architecture tables to resolve the exact silicon profile matching the active processor core. This tracking routine relies strictly on two system-wide positional constants: PAGE_OFFSET and PHYS_OFFSET. To parse the architectural functionality of these constants, it is necessary to establish the low-level concepts governing virtual addressing, physical addressing, kernel space, and user space (commonly referenced as kernel mode and user mode states). These fundamental networking and memory design paradigms are outlined below.

Depending on specific CPU microarchitectures and individual platform engineering layouts, the absolute starting boundaries and linear capacities of the volatile memory matrix vary widely. Because the Linux kernel provides native compatibility for an expansive taxonomy of disparate processor architectures and system topologies, the overwhelming majority of the codebase is written cleanly in the C programming language. Hardcoding absolute, literal memory coordinates within these portable software layers would make the codebase highly rigid and degrade its architectural scalability.

To abstract away these hardware variations, the Linux memory management framework acts as if all available system-wide address envelopes reside within a single uniform virtual boundary space extending from 0x00000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF; this abstract addressing layout defines the Virtual Address (VA) space. When system software initiates a memory access routine, the integrated Memory Management Unit (MMU) handles translation loops to map the abstract virtual coordinate to its true physical address layout on the silicon. Consequently, the CPU core executes instructions exclusively within the virtual address domain, whereas the underlying physical memory components consume sectors mapped inside the physical address domain.

The Linux kernel bifurcates this 4 GB virtual memory space (0x00000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF) into two mutually isolated runtime zones: user space and kernel space. User-space applications are restricted to executing within the boundaries of user space and are barred from cross-accessing or corrupting kernel memory; conversely, low-level core kernel routines execute within kernel space.

Mainline Linux implements exactly four split-ratio memory configurations to manage this layout. When the preprocessor build flag evaluates to CONFIG_VMSPLIT_1G, the kernel space envelope is mapped to span from 0x40000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF. Under the CONFIG_VMSPLIT_2G configuration profile, the kernel partition scales to occupy 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF. Toggling the switch to CONFIG_VMSPLIT_3G_OPT establishes a kernel memory allocation window spanning from 0xB0000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF. Finally, under the standard CONFIG_VMSPLIT_3G ratio allocation profile, the kernel space is assigned to occupy the top 1 GB segment extending from 0xC0000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF. Enforcing these build flag allocations is handled during the configuration phase, typically by appending explicit configuration directives (such as declaring CONFIG_VMSPLIT_1G=y) within the architecture board templates managed under the git/arch/arm/configs/*_defconfig path.

The constant parameter PHYS_OFFSET defines the absolute starting boundary address tracking the volatile memory array inside the hardware physical memory map. Conversely, PAGE_OFFSET registers the absolute starting virtual address allocating the base boundary of the protected kernel space. The hierarchical interface relationship linking virtual addresses, physical addresses, user space, kernel space, PHYS_OFFSET, and PAGE_OFFSET is illustrated in the structural diagram below:

Processor Lookup Subroutine and Argument Verification

Having introduced the foundational paradigms of virtual and physical addressing layout configurations, this section evaluates the low-level ARM-assembly processor information discovery routine. The assembly implementation code for this subsystem is structured as follows:

__lookup_processor_type:
    adr    r3, __lookup_processor_type_data
    ldmia    r3, {r4 - r6}
    sub    r3, r3, r4                		@ get offset between virt & phys
    add    r5, r5, r3                		@ convert virt addresses to
    add    r6, r6, r3                		@ physical address space
1:    ldmia    r5, {r3, r4}                	@ value, mask
    and    r4, r4, r9                		@ mask wanted bits
    teq    r3, r4
    beq    2f
    add    r5, r5, #PROC_INFO_SZ        @ sizeof(proc_info_list)
    cmp    r5, r6
    blo    1b
    mov    r5, #0                    		@ unknown processor
2:    ret    lr
ENDPROC(__lookup_processor_type)
    .align    2
    .type    __lookup_processor_type_data, %object
__lookup_processor_type_data:
    .long    .
    .long    __proc_info_begin
    .long    __proc_info_end
    .size    __lookup_processor_type_data, . - __lookup_processor_type_data

Upon concluding the execution of this routine, register r9 preserves the hardware CPU ID signature, while register r5 registers the absolute physical destination address pointing to the matched processor metadata record. First, consider the trailing tracking directives block:

__lookup_processor_type_data:
    .long    .
    .long    __proc_info_begin
    .long    __proc_info_end

The assembly evaluation directive .long . writes the node's own compiled virtual execution address directly into the memory location mapped by the label __lookup_processor_type_data. The subsequent two contiguous storage assignments cache the virtual linking addresses bounding the symbols __proc_info_begin and __proc_info_end into the next two sequential memory slots.

The physical hardware metrics and processor descriptors tracking every silicon architecture natively supported by the compiled Linux kernel are clustered contiguously inside the memory region bounded by __proc_info_begin and __proc_info_end. These boundary markers are synthesized dynamically by the linker utility during compilation and are stored strictly as virtual addresses.

Because these data blocks are organized using virtual linking targets, and because the Memory Management Unit (MMU) has not yet been initialized at this point in the boot sequence, any programmatic attempt to read these processor configurations requires converting their virtual offsets to physical address coordinates.

The initial instruction of the subroutine calculates the precise physical address hosting the __lookup_processor_type_data pointer table (adding the Program Counter register value to the immediate relative byte offset of the label) and writes it into register r3. Using r3 as an absolute tracking base address, the ldmia command block loads the values of the compiled virtual anchors—representing ., __proc_info_begin, and __proc_info_end—into registers r4, r5, and r6 respectively.

The instruction sub r3, r3, r4 computes the precise translation delta separating the label's runtime physical position from its link-time virtual address. Leveraging this constant offset vector allows virtual memory descriptors to be converted directly to physical address paths (as shown in Figure 6-2). The execution commands add r5, r5, r3 and add r6, r6, r3 recalculate the virtual boundaries of __proc_info_begin and __proc_info_end into the active physical memory map.

The subsequent loop fetches individual processor blocks from memory and executes a mask-and-test evaluation against the hardware CPU ID signature cached inside register r9 (originally read from the CP15 coprocessor). If a valid record matching the signature is resolved, the loop terminates, and register r5 contains the physical address hosting that processor information structure. If the search pointer traverses the entire array from __proc_info_begin to __proc_info_end without finding a matching hardware signature, register r5 is cleared to zero, and the function returns. The sequential operational loop tracking this routine is mapped out below:

Upon returning from the processor discovery subroutine, the kernel calculates the physical-to-virtual memory map delta (PHYS_OFFSET - PAGE_OFFSET) and resolves the starting physical boundaries of RAM. It then enters the \_\_vet_atags subroutine to validate the runtime parameters handed down from U-BOOT.

U-BOOT passes platform parameters over to the guest Linux kernel via one of two legacy or modern interface protocols. On modern, Device-Tree-aware kernel compilation profiles, U-BOOT writes the absolute physical base address hosting the Flattened Device Tree binary blob into register r2. On legacy, non-Device-Tree targets, U-BOOT uses register r2 to pass the baseline pointer address referencing a structured list of parameters (atag list). Typically, U-BOOT places these environment lists or .dtb files within the initial 16 KB margin of physical RAM; the bootloader decompression routines and the early kernel instructions are fenced off to prevent overwriting this data window.

If the active kernel incorporates Device Tree capabilities, the validation engine interrogates the physical memory cell pointed to by register r2 to verify if it matches the Device Tree magic signature word. If the parsed cell matches the identifier signature, r2 contains a valid DTB container; otherwise, the payload is flagged as invalid. Under little-endian byte ordering models, this constant magic identifier matches the word 0xEDFE0DD0, whereas big-endian architectures store the signature as the big-endian word 0xD00DFEED.

Conversely, if the kernel is compiled without Device Tree capability, it interrogates the initial 4-byte tracking cell pointed to by register r2 to check for the signature values 0x00000005 (representing parameter size ATAG_CORE_SIZE) or 0x00000002 (representing an empty base parameter layout, ATAG_CORE_SIZE_EMPTY). If this initial integrity pass fails, the tracking location is discarded as an invalid parameter array. If the initial word is confirmed, the engine scans the next contiguous 8-byte data field to check for the explicit parameter key word ATAG_CORE (0x54410001). If this second validation loop matches the token signature, the memory reference inside r2 is registered as a fully authenticated, legal atag parameter array.

If the verification pass rejects the memory structure pointed to by r2 as an invalid DTB blob or unparseable atag array, register r2 is cleared to zero before control is returned to the calling function, informing downstream routines that the boot argument tracking reference is invalid.

The low-level assembly source code defining the __vet_atags validation routine is structured as follows:

__vet_atags:
    tst    r2, #0x3                    		@ aligned?
    bne    1f
    ldr    r5, [r2, #0]
#ifdef CONFIG_OF_FLATTREE
    ldr    r6, =OF_DT_MAGIC            		@ is it a DTB?
    cmp    r5, r6
    beq    2f
#endif
    cmp    r5, #ATAG_CORE_SIZE        	@ is first tag ATAG_CORE?
    cmpne r5, #ATAG_CORE_SIZE_EMPTY
    bne    1f
    ldr    r5, [r2, #4]
    ldr    r6, =ATAG_CORE
    cmp    r5, r6
    bne    1f
2:    ret    lr                        			@ atag/dtb pointer is ok
1:    mov    r2, #0
    ret    lr
ENDPROC(__vet_atags)

Because the syntactical composition of this assembly segment is linear, it does not require a detailed standalone execution flowchart.

Modifying the Address Translation Routines

6.2 Modifying the Address Translation Routines

The Linux kernel frequently executes translation loops to map between virtual address channels and physical address paths. Prior to initializing and enabling the Memory Management Unit (MMU), virtual-to-physical translations behave as static, linear mappings. The architectural relationship bridging physical addresses and virtual addresses is generally defined by the following programmatic formulas:

phy = virt + (PHYS_OFFSET - PAGE_OFFSET)
virt = phy - (PHYS_OFFSET - PAGE_OFFSET)

The system configuration includes a specialized preprocessor compilation switch named CONFIG_ARM_PATCH_PHYS_VIRT. If this build switch is disabled, the inline functions handling translations between physical and virtual address spaces are strictly hardcoded as follows:

static inline unsigned long __phys_to_virt(phys_addr_t x)
{
    return x - PHYS_OFFSET + PAGE_OFFSET;
}
static inline phys_addr_t __virt_to_phys(unsigned long x)
{
    return (phys_addr_t)x - PAGE_OFFSET + PHYS_OFFSET;
}

This translation paradigm is limited strictly to handling continuous 1:1 linear tracking. However, across complex Linux system configurations, virtual memory pages do not necessarily map to a simple, static one-to-one relationship with physical memory frames; multiple unique virtual memory zones can map down to share an identical physical memory base address. Furthermore, the core kernel must scale seamlessly to accommodate a diverse taxonomy of silicon architectures where the starting physical page frame numbers (PFN) vary significantly. Because these page numbers are heavily utilized across downstream memory management sub-blocks, they require constant runtime updates.

Consequently, the kernel cannot rely on a static, compile-time constant declaration of PHYS_OFFSET to govern memory translations. It must leverage advanced engineering techniques to dynamically patch and compute virtual-to-physical translation parameters at runtime to suit the active memory topology. Within contemporary kernels, these highly optimized, dynamic address translation macros are structured as follows:

static inline unsigned long __phys_to_virt(phys_addr_t x)
{
    unsigned long t;
    __pv_stub((unsigned long)x, t, "sub", __PV_BITS_31_24);
    return t;
} 
static inline phys_addr_t __virt_to_phys(unsigned long x)
{
    phys_addr_t t;
    if (sizeof(phys_addr_t) == 4) {   /* Executed when physical address space is 32-bit */
        __pv_stub(x, t, "add", __PV_BITS_31_24);
    } else {                                	/* Executed when physical address space is 40-bit (LPAE) */
        __pv_stub_mov_hi(t);
        __pv_add_carry_stub(x, t);
    }
    return t;
}

During the compilation process, the __pv_stub macro is expanded into the following inline assembly sequence, where the placeholder argument instr resolves explicitly to either the add or sub assembly operation code tokens:

#define __pv_stub(from,to,instr,type)       \
    __asm__("@ __pv_stub\n"                	\ @ Assembly comment line
    "1:    " instr "    %0, %1, %2\n"        	\ @ Core arithmetic translation instruction
        					\@ %0=from, %1=to, %2=type
    "    .pushsection .pv_table,\"a\"\n"       \ @ Divert context to custom .pv_table section
    "    .long    1b\n"                    	\ @ Commit the absolute pointer of label 1 to the table
    "    .popsection\n"                		\ @ Revert back to the original text segment context
    : "=r" (to)                    		\
    : "r" (from), "I" (type))

Concurrently, the architectural macro extensions __pv_stub_mov_hi and __pv_add_carry_stub expand to the following inline assembly definitions:

#define __pv_stub_mov_hi(t)                		\
    __asm__ volatile("@ __pv_stub_mov\n"        	\
    "1:    mov    %R0, %1\n"            		\
    "    .pushsection .pv_table,\"a\"\n"        	\
    "    .long    1b\n"                			\
    "    .popsection\n"                			\
    : "=r" (t)                    			\
    : "I" (__PV_BITS_7_0))

#define __pv_add_carry_stub(x, y)            		\
    __asm__ volatile("@ __pv_add_carry_stub\n"   	 \
    "1:    adds    %Q0, %1, %2\n"            		\
    "    adc    %R0, %R0, #0\n"            			\
    "    .pushsection .pv_table,\"a\"\n"        		\
    "    .long    1b\n"                				\
    "    .popsection\n"                				\
    : "+r" (y)                    				\
    : "r" (x), "I" (__PV_BITS_31_24)        		\
    : "cc")

Once modified by the early runtime patching routines, the __pv_stub_mov_hi sequence copies the upper 32-bit bitmask tracking the delta between physical and virtual address spaces directly into the most significant register (high-order register) of a allocated 64-bit architecture register pair. Subsequently, the patched __pv_add_carry_stub routine adds the lower 32-bit translation offset to the target virtual address and propagates any resulting carry bit into the high-order register via the Add with Carry (adc) instruction.

Prior to the execution of the early runtime patcher, the initialization sequence injects temporary placeholder immediate operands defined by the constants __PV_BITS_31_24 and __PV_BITS_7_0. Pre-allocating these explicit constant arguments guarantees that the compiler generates valid, immediate-form mov and adds assembly tokens, complete with correctly populated immediate operand rotation fields (rotation). Ensuring these internal encoding parameters are generated properly guarantees that the 12-bit immediate field of the adds opcode can cleanly map out the lower 32 bits of the address translation offset.

Furthermore, the early patcher inspects the internal rotation bits embedded within the instruction encodings to easily differentiate whether a target instruction was instantiated via the __pv_stub_mov_hi macro or the __pv_add_carry_stub macro, executing the corresponding patch routine required for that instruction type. The key architectural characteristic of this framework is that the absolute address referencing the label 1: (the instruction address) is recorded inside a dedicated tracking section named .pv_table, fully decoupled from the active instruction text stream.

Ultimately, beyond performing baseline addition or subtraction for coordinate shifts, these macros register the absolute physical instruction address of every single translation location within a compiled lookup database named __pv_table. Before these instructions execute at runtime, the early patcher loops across this table to dynamically override the immediate fields of each registered instruction, tuning them to execute the exact offset shift matching the current board topology.

To manage this register mapping precisely, the inline assembly utilizes ARM-specific constraints modifiers, where %R0 restricts allocation strictly to the high-order register within a 64-bit pair, and %Q0 targets the low-order register.

The assembly code block residing at label __fixup_pv_table acts as this early dynamic runtime patcher. This routine analyzes the system parameters to dynamically adapt to varying physical memory structures, systematically sweeping across every reference descriptor registered inside __pv_table to patch the immediate operand bytes of the linked instructions. Prior to entering the code path at __fixup_pv_table, register r8 must contain the baseline physical memory coordinate matching PHYS_OFFSET. The detailed assembly-level code listing defining this runtime patcher is outlined below, followed by a comprehensive structural analysis of its execution workflow.

The assembly implementations for the dynamic runtime patcher subsystem are structured and executed as detailed below:

__fixup_pv_table:
    adr    r0, 1f            		@ Calculate physical address of label 1
    ldmia    r0, {r3-r7}       	@ Load virtual addresses of pf_table_begin, __pv_table_end,
                    			@ __pv_phys_pfn_offset, and __pv_offset into r3-r7
    mvn    ip, #0                    
    subs    r3, r0, r3        		@ r3 = Delta between physical and virtual addresses
    add    r4, r4, r3        		@ Calculate physical address of pf_table_begin
    add    r5, r5, r3        		@ Calculate physical address of __pv_table_end
    add    r6, r6, r3        		@ Calculate physical address of __pv_phys_pfn_offset
    add    r7, r7, r3        		@ Calculate physical address of __pv_offset
    mov    r0, r8, lsr #PAGE_SHIFT    	@ Convert to Page Frame Number (PFN); PHYS_OFFSET is in r8
    str    r0, [r6]                		@ Store to __pv_phys_pfn_offset for MMU usage
    strcc    ip, [r7, #HIGH_OFFSET]    	@ Store high 32 bits of __pv_offset (typically 0 or -1)
    mov    r6, r3, lsr #24			@ Constant used for add/sub instructions
    teq    r3, r6, lsl #24			@ Test whether the delta is an integer multiple of 16 MiB
    bne    __error
    str    r3, [r7, 
#LOW_OFFSET]        	@ Store to the lower word of __pv_offset
    b    __fixup_a_pv_table
ENDPROC(__fixup_pv_table)
    .align
1:    .long    .
    .long    pf_table_begin
    .long    __pv_table_end
2:    .long    __pv_phys_pfn_offset
    .long    __pv_offset

The first line of assembly code calculates the physical address corresponding to label 1:, storing the result inside register r0. The instruction ldmia r0, {r3-r7} loads the compiled virtual addresses of label 1:, pf_table_begin, __pv_table_end, __pv_phys_pfn_offset, and __pv_offset into registers r3, r4, r5, r6, and r7 respectively. Since the MMU is not yet active, virtual-to-physical links map out via a 1:1 direct identity mechanism. The command subs r3, r0, r3 yields the absolute translation delta between the current physical running position and the virtual link address. After executing the following code segment:

add    r4, r4, r3                @ Calculate starting physical coordinates of __pv_table
 add    r5, r5, r3                @ Calculate ending physical coordinates of __pv_table
 add    r6, r6, r3                @ Calculate physical address of __pv_phys_pfn_offset
 add    r7, r7, r3                @ Calculate physical address of __pv_offset

registers r4, r5, r6, and r7 contain the physical addresses of pf_table_begin, __pv_table_end, __pv_phys_pfn_offset, and __pv_offset respectively, resolving the true operational boundaries of these tables in memory.

The subsequent logic scales the physical memory base PHYS_OFFSET into a Page Frame Number (PFN) and stores it within the __pv_phys_pfn_offset table. Concurrently, the absolute difference PHYS_OFFSET - PAGE_OFFSET is committed to the lower word of the __pv_offset data structure. If PHYS_OFFSET evaluates to less than PAGE_OFFSET, the execution sequence stores the word 0xFFFFFFFF to the upper word (HIGH_OFFSET) of __pv_offset. The matching operations mov r6, r3, lsr #24 and teq r3, r6, lsl #24 execute an arithmetic verification loop to guarantee that the hardware address translation delta is aligned to a strict 16 MiB boundary; a validation failure branches directly into error trapping routines.

Once these descriptor updates conclude, the code branches into __fixup_a_pv_table to execute the active runtime patching loops and update the instruction immediate fields.

.text
__fixup_a_pv_table:
    adr    r0, 3f 		@ Calculate physical address of label 3
    ldr    r6, [r0]		@ Load virtual address of __pv_offset
    add    r6, r6, r3	@ Calculate physical address of __pv_offset
    ldr    r0, [r6, #HIGH_OFFSET]    @ pv_offset high word
    ldr    r6, [r6, #LOW_OFFSET]     @ pv_offset low word
    mov    r6, r6, lsr #24
    cmn    r0, #1                    	@ Check whether address offset is negative
    moveq    r0, #0x400000        	@ If r0 is negative, set bit 22 to 1
    b    2f
1:    ldr    ip, [r7, r3]
    bic    ip, ip, #0x000000ff
    tst    ip, #0xf00                	@ Interrogate rotation field in the immediate operand
    orrne    ip, ip, r6                	@ If rotation field is non-zero, patch the immediate field
    biceq    ip, ip, #0x400000   	@ If rotation field is zero, clear bit 22 of the opcode
    orreq    ip, ip, r0            	@ Based on r0 value, preserve the mov instruction or convert it to mvn
    str    ip, [r7, r3]            	@ Write the patched instruction back to its original location
2:    cmp    r4, r5                	@ Verify if structural end of __pv_table is reached
    ldrcc    r7, [r4], #4    
    bcc    1b
    ret    lr
ENDPROC(__fixup_a_pv_table)
    .align
3:    .long __pv_offset
ENTRY(fixup_pv_table)
    stmfd    sp!, {r4 - r7, lr}
    mov    r3, #0            		@ No offset translation vector
    mov    r4, r0            		@ r0 = Table start pointer boundary
    add    r5, r0, r1        		@ r1 = Table size boundary
    bl    __fixup_a_pv_table
    ldmfd    sp!, {r4 - r7, pc}
ENDPROC(fixup_pv_table)
    .data
    .align    2
    .globl    __pv_phys_pfn_offset
    .type    __pv_phys_pfn_offset, %object                @ Variable type is explicitly data
__pv_phys_pfn_offset:
    .word    0
    .size    __pv_phys_pfn_offset, . - __pv_phys_pfn_offset    
    .globl    __pv_offset
    .type    __pv_offset, %object
__pv_offset:
    .quad    0
    .size    __pv_offset, . - __pv_offset                	@ Size = current position minus label origin

The underlying segment tasked with parsing high and low word boundaries and scaling parameters relies on the following execution path:

adr    r0, 3f                    			@ Calculate physical address of label 3
    	ldr    r6, [r0]                			@ Load virtual address of __pv_offset
    	add    r6, r6, r3                		@ Calculate physical address of __pv_offset
    	ldr    r0, [r6, #HIGH_OFFSET]    	@ pv_offset high word
    	ldr    r6, [r6, #LOW_OFFSET]        	@ pv_offset low word
    	mov    r6, r6, lsr #24

This block extracts the upper and lower 32-bit values tracking the address translation offset and logically shifts the lower word right by 24 bits, retaining exclusively the highest 8 bits of the lower word configuration.

The directives cmn r0, #1 and moveq r0, #0x400000 evaluate whether the address translation offset is a negative value. If it is negative, register r0 is overwritten with the bitmask 0x400000, which transforms a standard mov opcode into a Bitwise NOT Move (mvn) operation.

The operation ldr ip, [r7, r3] indexes into the data pointer arrays cached within the .pv_table database to load the active machine instruction word directly into the Inter-Processor scratch register ip (r12). Upon initial entry into this execution loop, register r7 targets the virtual baseline pointer of pf_table_begin and register r3 contains the address translation delta.

The combined decoding instructions bic ip, ip, #0x000000ff and tst ip, #0xf00 clear the lower 8 bits of the instruction's immediate field to verify if the underlying immediate operand rotation field (rotation) scales to zero. If the rotation field is non-zero, indicating that the target instruction maps to an arithmetic adds statement, the command orrne ip, ip, r6 executes to patch the lower 8 bits of the immediate field with the active offset parameter.

Conversely, if the rotation bits evaluate to zero, confirming that the current instruction is a standard mov configuration, the patcher invokes biceq ip, ip, #0x400000 and orreq ip, ip, r0 to modify the instruction flags. If register r0 was populated with the mask value 0x400000, the underlying mov instruction transforms cleanly into an mvn instruction; otherwise, the primitive mov formatting is preserved, zeroing out the lower 8 bits of its immediate field. Finally, str ip, [r7, r3] writes the fully modified opcode instruction back to its original location in memory.

The trailing looping construct:

 cmp    r4, r5
 ldrcc    r7, [r4], #4    
 bcc    1b
 ret    lr

systematically traverses the complete linear boundary pool of the __pv_table array, re-programming every single memory translation opcode registered within the database, and returns control to the calling execution phase.

This concludes Section 6.2 and the runtime architecture modifications of the kernel address translation layers.

Initializing the Address Translation Page Tables

6.3 Initializing the Address Translation Page Tables

Following the runtime modifications of the address translation infrastructure, the next primary task inside the head.S execution path is the initialization of the translation page tables, preparing the hardware platform to engage the core virtual memory management sub-blocks. This early paging matrix is constructed by invoking the __create_page_tables subroutine. It must be explicitly noted that these initial translation page tables are transient, meaning they are utilized strictly during the early bootstrap phase.

Prior to stepping into this subroutine, register r8 preserves the physical-to-virtual address translation offset delta, r9 holds the hardware CPU ID signature, and r10 targets the resolved processor metadata record. To systematically analyze the software workflow of this page table creation utility, it is necessary to detail the structural alignment of the ARM page table architecture.

The physical base boundary hosting these temporary translation page tables aligns with the memory coordinates assigned to the static symbol swapper_pg_dir. This tracking symbol evaluates precisely to:

swapper_pg_dir = KERNEL_RAM_VADDR - PG_DIR_SIZE

Where the macro definitions track as:

KERNEL_RAM_VADDR = PAGE_OFFSET + TEXT_OFFSET

Here, TEXT_OFFSET defines the physical compile-time starting alignment offset of the active .text instruction section relative to the baseline bank origin. Consequently, KERNEL_RAM_VADDR represents the absolute starting virtual address allocating the executable Linux kernel code segment. This implies that a dedicated physical memory window equal to exactly TEXT_OFFSET bytes isolates the absolute starting boundary of kernel space (PAGE_OFFSET) from the actual entry code of the kernel image.

Beyond being carved out to house the early level-1 translation page tables, this linear memory cushion stores the runtime boot argument vectors or DTB payloads handed down from the U-BOOT bootloader stage. Under standard ARM configuration templates, TEXT_OFFSET defaults to 0x8000 (32 KB) and PG_DIR_SIZE is fixed to 0x4000 (16 KB). Depending on the platform architecture and memory constraints, these dimensions can be adjusted by developers, provided they remain sufficiently large to prevent address collisions or data corruption with the trailing kernel binary blocks.

Through direct calculation, the starting virtual coordinates mapping the early translation page table array evaluate to:

swapper_pg_dir = PAGE_OFFSET + TEXT_OFFSET - PG_DIR_SIZE

The true, live physical base address allocating this table on the hardware is resolved by using the translation delta:

PHYS_OFFSET + TEXT_OFFSET - PG_DIR_SIZE

This physical mapping layout is visualized across both address domains in the schematics below:

The structures packed into this early table block are processed exclusively during the initial stages of the kernel lifecycle. Once the memory management module becomes fully operational, the system completely overwrites and reallocates the active page tables to drive the runtime memory tracking engines of the mainline Linux system.

6.3.1 ARM Page Tables

The Memory Management Unit (MMU) leverages page tables to execute runtime address translations. A page table is a structured lookup array composed of either 32-bit or 64-bit entries; tables using 32-bit entries are defined as Short-descriptor format tables, whereas tables implementing 64-bit entries are defined as Long-descriptor format tables. Each discrete descriptor entry maps an explicit virtual address window to its corresponding physical address boundaries, dictates the size envelope of that mapped region, and configures its low-level memory attributes and access control permissions. Whether the MMU parses translation lookups using the Short-descriptor or Long-descriptor format is governed strictly by the EAE (Extended Address Enable) bit inside the TTBCR (Translation Table Base Control Register). When the EAE bit is cleared to 0, the MMU parses Short-descriptors; when set to 1, it enforces Long-descriptors.

The 32-bit ARM memory management subsystem natively supports both two-tier and three-tier translation page table cascades. Short-descriptor tables can be scaled to handle both single-tier and two-tier translation flows, whereas Long-descriptor layouts are processed exclusively within three-tier translation architectures; both descriptor formats can be scaled to address a 40-bit physical address space. Through these translation tables, the MMU can perform address translations over block units configured as sections (1 MB), supersections (16 MB), small pages (4 KB), or large pages (64 KB). Within the Linux kernel, the early bootstrap phase manages address translations strictly at a section-level (1 MB) granularity; once the baseline subsystem initializations conclude, the primitive operational unit shifts down to a standard page-level (4 KB) allocation model.

Varying the target translation unit changes the binary layout of the page table descriptors, and the bit definitions of a level-1 descriptor differstrictly from those of a level-2 descriptor. Short-descriptor page tables routing level-1 translations can be formatted into four distinct descriptors mapping pages, sections, or supersections. On ARM processors enabling 40-bit Large Physical Address Extensions (LPAE), the level-1 Short-descriptor layout implements the four binary configurations shown in Figure 6-6, where the initial bit configuration designates an invalid descriptor slot:

Conversely, on legacy ARM platforms that do not implement the 40-bit extended physical addressing space, the level-1 Short-descriptor formats follow the four binary alignments detailed in Figure 6-7, where the initial bit configuration designates an invalid descriptor slot:

When bit 1 of the descriptor contains a logic value of 1, the entry is parsed as a section or supersection descriptor; under this state, bit 18 is interrogated to differentiate between a 1 MB section and a 16 MB supersection. The Non-Secure (NS) bit configures the cryptographic security profile of the targeted memory segment, where NS = 0 restricts the mapped region to secure memory space, and NS = 1 exposes the block to non-secure space. The marker SBZ indicates that the corresponding bit fields are Should Be Zero. The Privileged Execute-Never (PXN) bit determines whether privileged software threads can execute code within the target memory region, and the Execute-Never (XN) flag completely fences off the block to prevent machine instruction execution under any execution state.

The composite binary configurations of the TEX, C, and B bits define memory behavior attributes, specifying parameters such as inner/outer cacheability and hardware bus shareability. The Access Permission (AP) bitmask dictates the read/write privileges governing the memory region, controlling whether a page is read-only or read-write across different execution privilege rings. While these permission and attribute flags regulate instruction access and memory barriers, they do not directly alter address calculation loops. The actual arithmetic conversion vectors are managed entirely by the high-order physical base address bits and the upper address extensions (PA[39:32]).

When a level-1 descriptor targets a 1 MB section or 16 MB supersection, the translation maps the coordinate directly via a single-tier lookup phase. Conversely, when a descriptor maps to a standard 4 KB page or 64 KB large page, the translation loop requires a secondary level-2 page table lookup. Figure 6-8 maps out the Short-descriptor formatting rules deployed across level-2 translation tables, where the initial entry configuration represents an invalid descriptor slot:

A large page descriptor defines the upper 16 bits of the physical address, mapping out a minimum translation step resolution equal to 2³²⁻¹⁶ = 64 KB. A standard small page descriptor registers the upper 20 bits of the target physical coordinate, yielding a primitive translation resolution equal to exactly 2³²⁻²⁰ = 4 KB.

6.3.2 Address Translation Paradigms

Having established the layout rules of the individual descriptor types, this section evaluates the technical mechanics through which a Virtual Address (VA) is parsed and translated into a final Physical Address (PA). Because the Linux kernel environment optimizes its execution pipelines by predominantly using section descriptors and small page descriptors, these two specific paging models are analyzed here to illustrate how the ARM memory management hardware maps out target address spaces.

When the MMU is configured to route address lookups over a single-tier section profile, the upper 12 bits of the incoming virtual address (VA[31:20]) are combined with the upper 18 bits of the Translation Table Base Register (TTBRx[31:14]) to construct the upper 30 bits of the physical address targeting the level-1 descriptor entry (L1A). Within this calculated pointer address, VA[31:20] aligns with bits L1A[13:2], the upper 18 bits derived from the tracking register fill bits L1A[31:14], and the trailing bits are cleared to L1A[1:0] = 00. This geometric alignment ensures that every possible virtual address path cleanly addresses a specific 32-bit (4-byte) descriptor slot within the page table array.

The hardware interfaces directly with memory using this composite index address L1A[31:0] to poll the level-1 page table, fetching the 32-bit descriptor word L1O[31:0]. The upper 12 bits extracted from this descriptor (L1O[31:20]) are then concatenated with the lower 20 bits of the original virtual address (VA[19:0]) to form the definitive physical address (PA[31:0]) of the memory cell. Concurrently, the lower bits (L1O[19:0]) are parsed by the memory controller to enforce the localized attributes and access barriers assigned to that segment.

If the translation resolution is scaled down to map small pages or large pages, necessitating a finer subdivision of the virtual address space, the platform engages a two-tier translation cascade. This multi-stage translation pipeline is organized as illustrated in the schematic below:

Initially, the high-order bits VA[31:20] of the incoming virtual address are combined with the register configurations inside TTBRx[31:14] to isolate the target bit array L1A[31:2], clearing the lower bits to 00 to format a valid level-1 look-up pointer L1A. The MMU issues a physical memory access transaction using L1A to retrieve the level-1 page table descriptor payload L1O[31:0].

Instead of addressing raw physical memory, the upper bits of this descriptor (L1O[31:10]) are combined with the middle bits of the original virtual address (VA[19:12]) to construct the address segment L2A[31:2]. The lower bounds are zeroed out to L2A[1:0] = 00 to form the definitive address pointing to a specific level-2 page table descriptor slot. The MMU polls this level-2 table to extract the final descriptor word L2O[31:0].

At the terminal execution step, the definitive physical address is assembled by mapping the upper 20 bits directly from the level-2 descriptor (PA[31:12] = L2O[31:12]) and copying the remaining low-order bits straight from the original virtual address offset (PA[11:0] = VA[11:0]), concluding the two-tier virtual-to-physical address translation loop.

In practice, the system hardware does not perform a slow physical table walk across memory for every single memory instruction. The ARM microarchitecture incorporates a specialized hardware cache known as the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB). Before initiating an automated page table walk over physical RAM, the MMU's internal lookup engines interrogate the TLB to check if an active virtual-to-physical address translation pair (VA -> PA) is already cached. If a valid entry matches the query, the MMU immediately uses the cached physical address to speed up execution. If a cache miss occurs, the hardware falls back to run the complete multi-stage page table walk detailed above.

6.3.3 Linux Initial Page Tables

During the address translation process, the Linux kernel employs a multi-tiered translation cascade consisting of five discrete page table layers: PGD, P4D, PUD, PMD, and PTE. The PGD (Page Global Directory) serves as the top-level page table responsible for managing the entire virtual address space allocation.

The subsequent intermediate layers—encompassing the P4D (Page 4th Level Directory), PUD (Page Upper Directory), and PMD (Page Middle Directory)—are leveraged to implement multi-stage mid-level address translation loops. Among these, the PMD functions as the immediate parent page table routing down to the PTE layer, providing the tracking vectors required to resolve the base addresses of individual PTE pools. Finally, the PTE (Page Table Entry) layer acts as the definitive, lowest-tier level within the translation hierarchy; the Linux memory management engine interrogates the individual entries within the PTE to retrieve the final physical address matching the requested virtual address block.

The structural relationship and structural hierarchy linking these multiple page table layers are mapped out in the schematic diagram below:

6.3.4 Implementing Nominal Three-tier Linux Address Translation via ARM Hardware

The ARM implementation of the Linux kernel utilizes a nominal three-tier address translation model consisting of the PGD, PMD, and PTE. The top-level PGD maps directly to the ARM hardware Translation Table Base Registers, TTBR0 and TTBR1, which provide the reference tracking vectors to locate the mid-level PMD tables.

When executing on 32-bit ARM hardware that natively supports only two levels of hardware translation, a structural mismatch arises with Linux's three-tier software model. To resolve this, the kernel implements a 1:1 structural shorthand overlay linking the PGD entries directly to the PMD entries. By assigning identical bit vectors to both descriptor layers, the Linux kernel leverages the 2-tier MMU hardware pipeline to execute its nominal 3-tier software mapping. In the low-level architecture code, this folded translation loop is managed by completely merging the P4D, PUD, and PMD layers so they reference an identical physical base context. The schematic diagram below illustrates this architectural adaptation:

Within the Linux memory management framework, the PMD specifies the formatting constraints for all page table tiers above the PTE, making it structurally equivalent to an ARM level-1 section or supersection descriptor. Concurrently, the PTE maps out the absolute primitive boundaries of individual page descriptors, functioning as an ARM level-2 page descriptor.

Executing address translations over 1 MB block sections requires only a single-tier lookup phase. Because the early bootstrap lifecycle does not enforce maximum, fine-grained memory utilization, the early kernel simplifies its memory model by processing section descriptors exclusively during the initial booting sequence. Consequently, the temporary page tables are populated using standard 1 MB section structures. The low-level assembly sequence tasked with initializing these early section-level structures within the head.S source code module is declared under the global label __create_page_tables:

__create_page_tables:
        pgtbl    r4, r8                	@ page table address
        mov    r0, r4
        mov    r3, #0
        add    r6, r0, #PG_DIR_SIZE
1:    str    r3, [r0], #4
        str    r3, [r0], #4
        str    r3, [r0], #4
        str    r3, [r0], #4
        teq    r0, r6
        bne    1b
        /* ... Note: For clarity, the core loop is shown fully in the text above ... */
        ret    lr
ENDPROC(__create_page_tables)
    .ltorg
    .align
__turn_mmu_on_loc:
    .long    .
    .long    __turn_mmu_on
    .long    __turn_mmu_on_end

Prior to branching into this assembly block, register r8 must contain the baseline physical memory offset vector (PHYS_OFFSET), r9 preserves the hardware CPU ID signature, and r10 references the memory workspace hosting the resolved processor metadata record.

The initial macro command pgtbl r4, r8 calculates the hardware absolute physical memory boundary tracking to PHYS_OFFSET + TEXT_OFFSET - PG_DIR_SIZE, caching the resulting base reference inside register r4. As analyzed in Figure 6-5, this coordinate defines the absolute starting address of the transient page table structure.

Immediately following this base registration loop, the system steps into the zero-fill segment:

mov    r0, r4
        mov    r3, #0
        add    r6, r0, #PG_DIR_SIZE
1:    str    r3, [r0], #4
        str    r3, [r0], #4
        str    r3, [r0], #4
        str    r3, [r0], #4
        teq    r0, r6
        bne    1b

This assembly loop iterates across the entire memory layout allocated to PG_DIR_SIZE, writing null bytes (0x00000000) throughout the table to clear out stale artifacts.

A fundamental challenge arises during MMU bring-up: an identical virtual coordinate might address entirely different physical cells before and after the MMU is engaged. Crucially, the explicit physical instructions tasked with executing the MMU activation sequence must remain strictly identity-mapped, meaning their virtual address must align perfectly with their true physical address during the instruction pipelining phase. If an address drift occurs during this structural step, the processor's fetch engine will jump to an unmapped sector, leading to an immediate system crash. To prevent this, the initialization code constructs explicit identity-mapped descriptor entries covering the code block that toggles the MMU. This is achieved by storing the upper 12 bits of the code section's physical base address directly into the corresponding section descriptor base domain.

        adr    r0, __turn_mmu_on_loc
        ldmia    r0, {r3, r5, r6}
        sub    r0, r0, r3                    @ virt->phys offset
        add    r5, r5, r0                    @ phys __turn_mmu_on
        add    r6, r6, r0                    @ phys __turn_mmu_on_end
        mov    r5, r5, lsr #SECTION_SHIFT
        mov    r6, r6, lsr #SECTION_SHIFT
1:    orr    r3, r7, r5, lsl #SECTION_SHIFT    	@ flags + kernel base
        str    r3, [r4, r5, lsl #PMD_ORDER]        @ identity mapping
        cmp    r5, r6
        addlo    r5, r5, #1                    		@ next section
        blo    1b
.align
__turn_mmu_on_loc:
        .long    .
        .long    __turn_mmu_on
        .long    __turn_mmu_on_end

The code sequence shown above establishes a 1:1 identity mapping in the page tables for the memory region spanning from __turn_mmu_on to __turn_mmu_on_end. When using these specific descriptor entries for address translation, the input virtual address resolves to an identical output physical address. The technical mechanics of this assembly sequence are detailed below.

The instruction adr r0, __turn_mmu_on_loc calculates the physical address of the __turn_mmu_on_loc label. The command ldmia r0, {r3, r5, r6} loads the virtual linking addresses (address offsets) corresponding to . (the __turn_mmu_on_loc label itself), __turn_mmu_on, and __turn_mmu_on_end into registers r3, r5, and r6 respectively. The arithmetic instruction sub r0, r0, r3 calculates the physical-to-virtual translation delta (PHYS_OFFSET - PAGE_OFFSET). The subsequent addition instructions:

add r5, r5, r0
add r6, r6, r0

compute the absolute physical addresses of __turn_mmu_on and __turn_mmu_on_end. The logical shift commands:

mov r5, r5, lsr #SECTION_SHIFT
mov r6, r6, lsr #SECTION_SHIFT

isolate the section base fields from these addresses by stripping away the lower order bits.

To maximize code portability, the ARM kernel tree shares a unified codebase between processors supporting a 40-bit large physical address space and those limited to a legacy 32-bit space. When executing a 2-tier hardware translation, SECTION_SHIFT is configured to 20. Conversely, under a 3-tier translation scheme, SECTION_SHIFT scales to

  1. Because the kernel operates under a short-descriptor 2-tier profile during this early bootstrap phase, SECTION_SHIFT evaluates strictly to

The core programming instructions:

orr r3, r7, r5, lsl #SECTION_SHIFT
str r3, [r4, r5, lsl #PMD_ORDER]

combine the section base address with the memory attribute flag bits passed in r7 to form a valid level-1 section descriptor entry. It then commits this descriptor word to the active page table structure pointed to by r4. Because each short-descriptor entry consumes exactly 32 bits (4 bytes) of storage, the scaling shift constant PMD_ORDER is fixed to 2 (since (1 \ll 2 = 4)). The execution workflow tracking this routine is illustrated below:

Having completed the identity mapping vectors, the subsequent code block constructs the page table descriptors for the main kernel image space extending from PAGE_OFFSET up to the end of the BSS segment (_end). The underlying allocation methodology mirrors the identity-mapping routine, with the exception that it maps virtual addresses down to distinct physical targets instead of enforcing a 1:1 match. The code segment managing this mapping is structured as follows:

        add    r0, r4, #PAGE_OFFSET >> (SECTION_SHIFT - PMD_ORDER)
        ldr    r6, =(_end - 1)
        orr    r3, r8, r7
        add    r6, r4, r6, lsr #(SECTION_SHIFT - PMD_ORDER) 
1:    str    r3, [r0], #1 << PMD_ORDER
        add    r3, r3, #1 << SECTION_SHIFT
        cmp    r0, r6
        bls    1b

Prior to executing this block, register r4 references the baseline address of the early page table array, r7 encapsulates the low-level memory attribute flags, and r8 holds PHYS_OFFSET. The initial line of assembly computes the exact descriptor entry index within the page table that maps to the base virtual address PAGE_OFFSET. Because each descriptor slot consumes a 4-byte width, PAGE_OFFSET must be shifted right by 18 bits instead of 20 bits (20 - 2 = 18).

The logic operation orr r3, r8, r7 builds the raw section descriptor content. This operation requires that the lower 20 bits of PHYS_OFFSET are strictly zero-initialized—a hardware boundary constraint that is universally satisfied across ARM platforms. As shown in the code logic, register r6 resolves to the absolute page table entry index corresponding to the virtual address limit _end.

The instruction str r3, [r0], #1 << PMD_ORDER writes the generated descriptor word into the page table slot indexed by r0 and automatically increments r0 by 4 bytes to point to the next contiguous descriptor entry. Concurrently, add r3, r3, #1 << SECTION_SHIFT increments the section base domain within the descriptor word by 1 MB, aligning it with the next contiguous physical memory block. The structural software loop tracking this mapping is charted in the flowchart below:

During the U-BOOT platform boot phase, beyond importing the primary executable Linux kernel binary into physical RAM, the bootloader also copies the Device Tree Blob (DTB) or legacy boot parameter arrays (atags) into memory. Because the kernel must access these configuration structures continuously throughout its operational lifecycle, it must map this specific memory footprint inside the early page tables. After unpacking the DTB or parameters into memory, U-BOOT caches the absolute starting physical address of this storage region inside register r2.

Although the actual linear width of this parameter block typically consumes less than a single 1 MB section boundary, its physical placement on the media may sit dangerously close to a section edge. If the memory block overlaps a section boundary and spans into an adjacent section, mapping it safely requires two consecutive section descriptors. The assembly block responsible for generating the page table entries for this parameter region is structured as follows:

mov    r0, r2, lsr #SECTION_SHIFT
        movs    r0, r0, lsl #SECTION_SHIFT
        subne    r3, r0, r8
        addne    r3, r3, #PAGE_OFFSET
