        addne    r3, r4, r3, lsr #(SECTION_SHIFT - PMD_ORDER)
        orrne    r6, r7, r0
        strne    r6, [r3], #1 << PMD_ORDER
        addne    r6, r6, #1 << SECTION_SHIFT
        strne    r6, [r3]
        ret    lr

The initial bitmask operations:

mov r0, r2, lsr #SECTION_SHIFT
movs r0, r0, lsl #SECTION_SHIFT

isolate the 1 MB section base address fields (bits[31:20]) hosting the Device Tree or parameter block. The conditional execution block:

subne r3, r0, r8
addne r3, r3, #PAGE_OFFSET

computes the corresponding virtual address of this region by applying the transformation matrix (phys_addr - PHYS_OFFSET + PAGE_OFFSET). The subsequent line:

addne r3, r4, r3, lsr #(SECTION_SHIFT - PMD_ORDER)

calculates the target index offset within the page table matching that virtual address.

The bitwise instruction orrne r6, r7, r0 constructs the section descriptor word mapping the parameter block. Finally, the trailing two store operations commit these two sequential descriptor words into the calculated page table offsets to ensure complete boundary coverage, then branch back to the calling function.

The comprehensive spatial relationship mapping the physical address blocks to their respective virtual spaces after processing this early page table generation phase is illustrated in the diagram below:

This concludes Section 6.3 and the detailed technical analysis of the early page table initialization phase.

6.3.5 Enabling the Memory Management Unit (MMU)

Following the initialization of the early translation page tables, the next step in the boot sequence is provisioning the CPU to engage the MMU safely. The assembly logic first loads the post-MMU execution target address __mmap_switched into register r13 (which functions as the primary Stack Pointer, sp), and writes the absolute physical return vector address (label 1:) into the Link Register (lr).

The following assembly sequence implements the MMU preparation pipeline for platforms supporting a standard 32-bit physical address space. Prior to entering this code segment, register r4 preserves the early page table base reference, and r10 targets the absolute physical address of the resolved proc_info_list matching the active ARM processor core model:

        ldr    r13, =__mmap_switched
        badr    lr, 1f
        mov    r8, r4
        ldr    r12, [r10, #PROCINFO_INITFUNC]
        add    r12, r12, r10
        ret    r12
1:    b    __enable_mmu

The operation ldr r13, =__mmap_switched writes the virtual linking address of the __mmap_switched routine into register r13. The command badr lr, 1f calculates and stores the physical address of the fallback label 1: into lr as the baseline return address vector. The command mov r8, r4 copies the page table base address into register r8.

The instruction ldr r12, [r10, #PROCINFO_INITFUNC] resolves the explicit relative byte offset of the core processor initialization block (__cpu_flush) relative to the proc_info_list base address. The command add r12, r12, r10 computes the absolute physical execution address of this __cpu_flush routine, writing the vector into register r12. Finally, ret r12 fires an unconditional branch to jump straight into the processor-specific setup subroutine.

For ARMv7 Cortex-A9 MPCore application processors, this setup routine is defined as the core symbol __v7_ca9mp_setup within the low-level memory management architecture source module git/arch/arm/mm/proc-v7.S. The assembly code block is structured as follows:

__v7_ca9mp_setup:
        mov    r10, #(1 << 0)                	@ Cache/TLB ops broadcasting
        adr    r0, __v7_setup_stack_ptr
        ldr    r12, [r0]
        add    r12, r12, r0                    	@ Calculate local stack pointer
        stmia    r12, {r1-r6, lr}                	@ Save r1-r6 and lr to __v7_setup_stack
        bl      v7_invalidate_l1
        ldmia    r12, {r1-r6, lr}
        b    __v7_setup_cont

The technical objective of this routine is to back up the contents of registers r1 through r6 and the lr vector by pushing them into a temporary local stack allocation frame named __v7_setup_stack. It then calls v7_invalidate_l1 to completely purge and invalidate all stale entries within the level-1 data cache hierarchy. Upon restoring the original values of registers r1–r6 and lr from the temporary stack, the state machine branches to __v7_setup_cont to provision the hardware Translation Table Base Control Register (TTBCR) and the Translation Table Base Registers (TTBR0/TTBR1).

The following assembly-level subroutine implements the absolute level-1 data cache invalidation loop. This routine interrogates the CP15 coprocessor configuration registers to read the explicit number of sets and cache ways implemented by the silicon, and subsequently loops across every cache line to execute hardware-enforced invalidate steps by writing to the CP15 c7 register:

ENTRY(v7_invalidate_l1)
          mov     r0, #0
          mcr     p15, 2, r0, c0, c0, 0            	@ Write CSSELR (Cache Size Selection Register) to target L1 Data Cache
          mrc     p15, 1, r0, c0, c0, 0            	@ Read CCSIDR (Cache Size ID Register) metrics
          movw    r1, #0x7fff
          and     r2, r1, r0, lsr #13                	@ Extract total sets parameter (Assigned value = actual sets - 1)
          movw    r1, #0x3ff
          and     r3, r1, r0, lsr #3                  	@ Extract total ways parameter (Assigned value = actual ways - 1)
          add     r2, r2, #1                              	@ Calculate absolute number of sets
          and     r0, r0, #0x7                    	@ Extract cache line word width (Actual = log2(words) - 2)
          add     r0, r0, #4                      	@ Define set shift value for DCISW formatting
          clz     r1, r3                              	@ Calculate way shift value based on leading zeros of ways bitmask
          add     r4, r3, #1                      	@ NumWays total constant
1:        sub     r2, r2, #1                      	@ Decrement NumSets loop counter
          mov     r3, r4                            	@ Reset Temp counter back to NumWays
2:        subs    r3, r3, #1                      	@ Decrement Temp way index counter
          mov     r5, r3, lsl r1
          mov     r6, r2, lsl r0
          orr     r5, r5, r6                          	@ Synthesize final formatted DCISW command register value
          mcr     p15, 0, r5, c7, c6, 2           	@ Write DCISW (Data Cache Invalidate by Set/Way) to invalidate cache line
          bgt     2b                        		@ Loop until all associative ways within the active set are invalidated
          cmp     r2, #0
          bgt     1b                        		@ Loop until all sets across the L1 cache controller are invalidated
          dsb     st
          isb
          ret     lr
ENDPROC(v7_invalidate_l1)

The logical execution workflow and register decrement tracking loop implemented across the v7_invalidate_l1 assembly subroutine is visualized in the schematic flowchart below:

Upon returning from the invalidation path, the processor branches into __v7_setup_cont to proceed with secondary low-level register updates. The __v7_setup_cont code path is architected to optionally apply silicon errata workarounds and hardware bug patches. Since NXP applications processors do not utilize these specific errata workarounds, this software segment has been omitted for clarity.

Following these conditional checks, the routine clears out stale instruction pipelines and pre-fetch buffers by writing zero values into the CP15 coprocessor c7 and c8 registers, which completely flushes the Instruction Cache (I-Cache) and invalidates the Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLBs).

The routine then invokes the system macro v7_ttb_setup r10, r4, r5, r8, r3 to program the Translation Table Base Control Register (TTBCR) layout, and writes the early page table physical base address preserved in r8 straight into the primary hardware page table register TTBR1. Finally, it programs the primary memory region attribute and normal memory re-mapping registers (PRRR and NMRR) within the CP15 configuration block. For granular details tracking the bit definitions and access controls of these re-mapping registers, developers can reference the official ARM Architecture Reference Manual.

__v7_setup_cont:
    mov    r10, #0
    mcr    p15, 0, r10, c7, c5, 0        	@ Invalidate all instruction caches
    mcr    p15, 0, r10, c8, c7, 0        	@ Invalidate TLBs
    v7_ttb_setup r10, r4, r5, r8, r3        	@ Configure TTBCR and TTBRx
    ldr    r3, =PRRR    
    ldr    r6, =NMRR    
    mcr    p15, 0, r3, c10, c2, 0        	@ Configure Primary Region Remap Register
    mcr    p15, 0, r6, c10, c2, 1        	@ Configure Normal Memory Region Remap Register
    dsb
    adr    r3, v7_crval
    ldmia    r3, {r3, r6}
    mrc    p15, 0, r0, c1, c0, 0        	@ Read System Control Register (SCTLR)
    bic    r0, r0, r3
    orr    r0, r0, r6 
    ret    lr

The instruction ldmia r3, {r3, r6} loads the explicit bitmask configurations 0x0122C302 and 0x30C03C7D into registers r3 and r6 respectively. Prior to returning to the caller, the target bit values destined for the System Control Register (SCTLR) are temporarily preserved within register r0.

Because the Link Register (lr) preserved the physical base address of label 1: during the cache invalidation call, returning from the setup block automatically executes b __enable_mmu, which shifts the execution pipeline into the __enable_mmu subroutine to kick off MMU activation. Prior to entering the __enable_mmu code block, the hardware register matrix is aligned precisely as follows:

  • r0: Holds the prepared configuration bitmask to be written to the System Control Register (SCTLR).

  • r1: Preserves the machine type identifier code.

  • r2: Stores the absolute physical base pointer address referencing the atags or the Device Tree Blob (DTB).

  • r4: Holds the lower 32 bits of the level-1 Translation Table Base Register 0 (TTBR0).

  • r5: Holds the upper 32 bits of TTBR0 (processed exclusively within 40-bit large physical addressing pipelines where TTBR0 and TTBR1 scale to 64-bit widths).

  • r8: Holds the structural base value for TTBR1.

  • r9: Preserves the hardware processor ID signature.

  • r13: Stores the absolute virtual destination address targeted for execution once the MMU has been successfully engaged.

The low-level assembly sequence tasked with transitioning the CPU into virtual memory mode is structured as follows:

__enable_mmu:
        bic    r0, r0, #CR_A            	@ Clear alignment fault checking bits in SCTLR configuration
        mov    r5, #DACR_INIT 
        mcr    p15, 0, r5, c3, c0, 0        	@ Write Domain Access Control Register (DACR)
        mcr    p15, 0, r4, c2, c0, 0        	@ Write Translation Table Base Register 0 (TTBR0)
        b    __turn_mmu_on
ENDPROC(__enable_mmu)   

.align    5
.pushsection    .idmap.text, "ax"
ENTRY(__turn_mmu_on)
        mov    r0, r0
        instr_sync
        mcr    p15, 0, r0, c1, c0, 0        @ Write SCTLR: Enable the Memory Management Unit (MMU)
        mrc    p15, 0, r3, c0, c0, 0        @ Read Cache Size ID Register (CCSIDR)
        instr_sync
        mov    r3, r3
        mov    r3, r13
        ret    r3                    	@ Return/Jump to virtual address space inside __mmap_switched
__turn_mmu_on_end:
ENDPROC(__turn_mmu_on)
    .popsection

The compiled binary code for the __turn_mmu_on block is mapped directly into the .idmap.text section. This section resides strictly within the identity-mapped (1:1) translation boundary, meaning the virtual and physical address planes are completely identical for this execution window. Consequently, instructions fetched within this loop proceed smoothly without being disrupted or unmapped when the MMU configuration changes.

The enabling routine itself is direct: it enforces the global memory access permission domains inside the DACR, registers the base table tracking pointer within TTBR0, and updates the System Control Register bits to activate the MMU hardware. The implementation uses the Instruction Synchronization Barrier isb macro constant (instr_sync) to flush the execution pipeline, guaranteeing that all internal processor states align before branching to the virtual domain.

Once the MMU is fully engaged, the execution pipeline executes the jump into virtual space, landing at the __mmap_switched entry vector to run the following routine:

__mmap_switched:
    mov    r7, r1
    mov    r8, r2
    mov    r10, r0
    adr    r4, __mmap_switched_data
    mov    fp, #0
    ldmia    r4!, {r0, r1, sp}
    sub    r2, r1, r0
    mov    r1, #0
    bl    memset            		@ Zero out the uninitialized global data (.bss) segment
    ldmia    r4, {r0, r1, r2, r3}
    str    r9, [r0]            		@ Store processor ID parameters
    str    r7, [r1]            		@ Store hardware machine type index
    str    r8, [r2]            		@ Store boot parameters pointer or Device Tree base address
    cmp    r3, #0
    strne    r10, [r3]            	@ Store System Control Register (SCTLR) value
    mov    lr, #0
    b    start_kernel   
.align    2
.type    __mmap_switched_data, %object
__mmap_switched_data:
    .long    __bss_start                		@ Read into r0
    .long    __bss_stop                		@ Read into r1
    .long    . + THREAD_START_SP     	@ Read into Stack Pointer (sp)

    .long    processor_id                		@ Read into r0
    .long    __machine_arch_type        		@ Read into r1
    .long    __atags_pointer            		@ Read into r2
    .long    cr_alignment               		@ Read into r3
    .size    __mmap_switched_data, . - __mmap_switched_data

The fundamental purpose of the __mmap_switched routine is to clear the uninitialized global variable region bounded between the __bss_start and __bss_stop markers by filling the blocks with null bytes via memset. Following this runtime cleanup, it commits the runtime hardware processor ID, the machine architecture index, the absolute memory pointer referencing the Device Tree blob, and the active System Control Register state into their respective global kernel variables (processor_id, __machine_arch_type, __atags_pointer, and cr_alignment).

Having successfully finalized the execution stacks and established a valid C environment within the virtual memory domain, it clears the link register and invokes an unconditional branch to jump directly into the architecture-independent C language initialization routine: start_kernel().

This concludes Section 6.3.5 and the complete technical translation of the low-level assembly bootstrap phase.

Chapter 7: Kernel Booting — Initialization Preparations

The start_kernel() function executes as Linux's Process 0 (the idle task / init_task). Its primary responsibility is to orchestrate and establish the global execution environment for the Linux kernel. It bears the main burden of the Linux startup sequence and stands as the absolute first core Linux routine authored entirely in the C programming language. The start_kernel() implementation is maintained within the source file git/init/main.c. The subsequent sections detail the engineering objectives and low-level mechanics of each constituent subroutine in their exact execution sequence. Due to the exhaustive length of this master function, its full monolithic text definition is omitted here.

The functional modules and early architectural tracking workflows are introduced below:

Setting the Initialization Task Stack-End Magic Number

7.1 Setting the Initialization Task Stack-End Magic Number

The Linux operating system manages all transactional activities via an abstraction model known as tasks, with each individual task represented by a struct task_struct descriptor block. Linux drives these tasks forward through threads, assigning exactly one thread to track every active task instance. The primitive boot-stage task is globally defined as init_task, which is instantiated as a static global variable of type struct task_struct.

During compilation, kernel architects toggle the preprocessor build flag CONFIG_THREAD_INFO_IN_TASK to determine whether the low-level thread metadata structure (struct thread_info) is stored directly inside the main task_struct container block or allocated independently. If the system is compiled to house the thread metadata inside the task structure itself, the stack-end validation token is written directly to the memory boundary pointed to by the task's internal stack pointer field (stack). Conversely, if the thread_info block is allocated externally, this validation token is injected into the absolute first memory word immediately following the task's corresponding thread metadata structure. The Linux kernel implements this dedicated validation word as a robust, lightweight safety mechanism to detect stack overflows.

The programmatic task of writing this stack-end signature is managed by the following routine:

void set_task_stack_end_magic(struct task_struct *tsk)
{
   unsigned long *stackend;
   stackend = end_of_stack(tsk);
   *stackend = STACK_END_MAGIC;    /* for overflow detection */
}

This function is defined within the core subsystem source module kernel/fork.c. When thread_info is nested inside the task block, the macro helper end_of_stack() returns the absolute address value cached within the task's stack parameter field. When thread_info is configured externally, the macro instead resolves to the physical memory coordinates immediately succeeding the task's companion thread metadata block (as illustrated in Figure 7-1).

Every task structure encapsulates an internal stack pointer defined as an unsigned long word that tracks its execution frame. For the boot-stage init_task instance, this stack pointer targets the statically allocated array init_stack, whose absolute physical boundaries and memory limits are pre-determined at compile time by the linker script.

The execution of set_task_stack_end_magic() permanently seals this memory boundary by writing the specialized 32-bit validation word STACK_END_MAGIC (0x57AC6E9D) directly to the base of the init_stack array, providing the kernel with a deterministic guard value to trap stack-smashing events.

Initializing the SMP Logical-to-Physical CPU Core Mapping Table

7.2 Initializing the SMP Logical-to-Physical CPU Core Mapping Table

Within Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP) architectures, the Linux kernel allocates a global array named __cpu_logical_map to establish a clean translation matrix linking each execution core's contiguous software logical ID to its concrete hardware physical ID. The kernel requires a linear, unbroken sequence of logical IDs starting from zero. However, physical core indexing on contemporary silicon can be highly non-contiguous, often dictated by specific bit patterns or cluster assignments within hardware multi-processor topology registers.

The baseline element __cpu_logical_map[0] caches the physical ID of the primary boot core currently driving the initial bootstrap pipeline. Consequently, the i-th index within this array registers the hardwired physical ID of the core assigned to logical logical ID i. For example, a standard layout could yield __cpu_logical_map[1] = 1 and __cpu_logical_map[2] = 2. If the physical ID of the primary boot core evaluates to N, the corresponding index array element __cpu_logical_map[N] is mapped back to hold a physical index placeholder value of 0.

The early routine responsible for constructing this architectural lookup table is structured as follows:

u32 __cpu_logical_map[NR_CPUS] = { [0 ... NR_CPUS-1] = MPIDR_INVALID };
void __init smp_setup_processor_id(void)
{
   int i;
   u32 mpidr = is_smp() ? read_cpuid_mpidr() & MPIDR_HWID_BITMASK : 0;
   u32 cpu = MPIDR_AFFINITY_LEVEL(mpidr, 0);
   cpu_logical_map(0) = cpu;    // __cpu_logical_map[0] = cpu
   for (i = 1; i < nr_cpu_ids; ++i)
     cpu_logical_map(i) = i == cpu ? 0 : i;
   set_my_cpu_offset(0);
   pr_info("Booting Linux on physical CPU 0x%x\n", mpidr);
}

If the underlying processor context verifies as a Symmetric Multiprocessing environment, the variable mpidr captures the filtered, masked bits of the hardware Multiprocessor Affinity Register (MPIDR); otherwise, on single-core uniprocessor silicon, mpidr defaults directly to 0.

The macro call cpu = MPIDR_AFFINITY_LEVEL(mpidr, 0) executes bitmask extractions to isolate the core affinity level-0 index, identifying the physical hardware ID of the specific processing core executing this code segment. The subsequent programmatic statements loop across the platform bounds to construct the __cpu_logical_map lookup array and initialize the localized memory base offsets dedicated to managing per-CPU thread data storage variables.

Early Initialization of the Debug Objects Infrastructure

7.3 Early Initialization of the Debug Objects Infrastructure

Within the early C initialization phase of the Linux kernel, the debug_objects_early_init() routine acts as the primary initialization entry point for the global Object Life Cycle Tracking Framework (Debug Objects Infrastructure). The critical structural objectives of this early routine include establishing and partitioning the obj_hash array (the master debug container tracking tracked kernel objects), provisioning an independent, low-level architecture synchronization lock of type raw_spinlock_t for each constituent hash bucket, formatting the early static memory pool, and linking pre-allocated static object descriptors directly into the free tracking pool list (obj_pool).

By manually orchestrating these data blocks and memory tracking list parameters at this early junction, the kernel guarantees that the runtime object validation framework is functional and stable long before the primary virtual page allocators or dynamic memory subsystem managers (malloc / slab engines) are initialized and active.

Early Initialization of Control Groups

7.4 Early Initialization of Control Groups

Control Groups (universally abbreviated as cgroups) represent a fundamental subsystem within the Linux kernel architecture, designed to enforce fine-grained resource management, isolation, and telemetry. Leveraging cgroups, system administrators can explicitly configure resource allocation ceilings (such as maximum CPU core execution time boundaries, physical RAM constraints, or block I/O parameters) and assign granular processing priority vectors across different collections of processes.

The underlying engineering strategy of cgroup resource tracking relies on partitioning system resources into specific, functional hierarchies. These top-level resource blocks can be further broken down into secondary sub-groups, resulting in a multi-dimensional tree structure. This abstract data tree maps directly to the operational directory structure of the cgroup virtual filesystem (cgroupfs) exposed to user space. An administrator can dynamically throttle the runtime behavior of an application thread by binding its process context to a specific branch within this cgroup hierarchy, forcing the process to execute within the resource parameters assigned to that node. A process can be simultaneously attached to multiple independent cgroup paths to capture and constrain different system resources. The following schematic illustrates the structural mechanics and thread-binding relationships mapping a cgroup tree layout implemented under the legacy v1 cgroup specification:

The overall cgroup ecosystem is structurally defined by three core abstractions: the Control Group (cgroup), the Control Group Filesystem (cgroupfs), and the Resource Subsystem (subsystem). The underlying kernel modules leverage the structural metadata tables exposed by both the cgroup nodes and the virtual filesystem layer to coordinate low-level scheduling and resource enforcement loops. The design rules and structural characteristics governing contemporary cgroup frameworks are detailed below, using the modern cgroup v2 architecture standard as a reference model.

The Control Group (cgroup) and Virtual Filesystem

A control group defines a logical aggregation or set of running processes or execution threads constrained by an identical collection of resource thresholds and scheduling variables specified within a matching cgroupfs interface node. Internally, the kernel organizes cgroups as a hierarchical tree topology that mirrors the physical directory layout of the unified cgroup filesystem. System administrators can dynamically reshape or scale this tracking tree from user space simply by executing standard directory creation (mkdir), deletion (rmdir), or re-naming (mv) instructions under the mount point located at /sys/fs/cgroup.

Each discrete cgroup can host a collection of processes, an aggregation of standalone execution threads, or encapsulate multiple nested downstream child cgroups. The legacy cgroup v1 specification permitted resource budgeting to be granulated down to the individual thread level, meaning a single thread could be decoupled from its parent process and mapped to run inside an entirely separate cgroup. While this flexibility provided powerful, low-level tuning hooks, the architectural side effects and tracking overhead severely degraded system determinism.

To resolve these complexities, the unified cgroup v2 standard implements the strict "no internal processes" rule. Under this specification, a cgroup node is strictly prohibited from housing a mixture of both child cgroups and active process contexts; a node must either act exclusively as an internal container that routes down to secondary child cgroups, or function strictly as an end-node containing processes exclusively. Consequently, all standard user-space processes are forced to reside exclusively within the leaf nodes of the cgroup hierarchy.

Threaded Subtrees and Domain Classifications

While the structural constraints introduced by cgroup v2 significantly reduced kernel management complexity, they completely eliminated the capability to granularly budget resources down to individual threads in certain deployments. To restore this capability without compromising architectural stability, contemporary Linux kernels introduce the concept of Threaded Subtrees. A threaded subtree represents an isolated branch within the main cgroup tree where individual nodes are explicitly permitted to contain child cgroups, thread pointers, or a combination of both.

The root origin of a threaded subtree is defined as the closest ancestral node that complies with the standard process-only container layout, known as the Threaded Domain Root. Under this multi-domain architecture model, cgroup v2 classifies nodes into specific operational categories: nodes containing standard child cgroups or complete process clusters are categorized into the Domain Class, the structural root node anchoring a threaded branch is designated as a Threaded Domain Class, and all secondary downstream sub-nodes nested along that threaded branch are managed under the Threaded Cgroup Class.

Resource Subsystems (Resource Managers)

A subsystem—frequently referenced as a Resource Controller—is an internal, low-level Linux kernel module engineered to intercept and alter the operational behavior of tasks. For instance, a controller can throttle the maximum CPU execution time slices allocated to a cgroup, fence off the volume of physical page frames a group can pin in RAM, profile the runtime CPU cycles consumed across a collection of tasks, or execute global freezer hooks to freeze and resume process execution threads.

These resource managers leverage cgroup categorization loops to process groups of tasks collectively using specialized scheduling algorithms. Typically, each distinct system resource maps back to an independent hardware controller module. Under the legacy v1 specification, each resource controller maintained its own completely independent tree topology, forcing users to track and navigate separate filesystem trees to schedule individual resources and assign ceilings for a process.

The cgroup v2 architecture design resolves this fragmentation by enforcing a Unified Hierarchy, binding all resource controllers to a single, consolidated tree structure. This design allows administrators to coordinate all resource scheduling, budgeting, and performance tracking vectors globally through a single centralized cgroup filesystem interface.

The Ubuntu Linux distribution defines 18 distinct subsystems, mapping to 18 individual resource managers. Several of the most frequently deployed subsystems are detailed below:

  • blkio: Sets resource limits and throttling thresholds for block device access (such as disk I/O operations).

  • cpu: Regulates CPU time-slice distribution and processing bandwidth allocation using the kernel scheduler.

  • cpuacct: Automatically aggregates telemetry data to generate comprehensive CPU resource utilization reports for tasks within a control group.

  • cpuset: Isolates specific CPU cores and memory nodes (NUMA affinity mapping) to assign them exclusively to designated tasks.

  • devices: Restricts or permits access permissions to physical character and block device nodes.

  • freezer: Pauses (suspends) or resumes the runtime execution sequence of tasks enclosed within a control group.

  • memory: Enforces strict physical RAM and swap space usage ceilings for targeted tasks while automatically generating detailed memory tracking reports.

  • net_cls: Tags network data packets with a specific class identifier (classid), allowing egress network traffic shapers to trace data back to its origin control group.

  • net_prio: Dynamically assigns priority coefficients to network interfaces on a per-cgroup basis.

  • ns: The namespace subsystem, designed to route resource scheduling over isolated operational environments; different namespaces can implement entirely separate scheduling policies.

The cgroupfs interface functions as a Linux pseudo-filesystem, serving as the primary kernel boundary layer exposed to user space. System administrators can mount this virtual directory structure to any designated location within the filesystem tree. Under the legacy cgroup v1 standard, each individual resource controller maintained an independent pseudo-filesystem instance, permitting users to mount different resource managers to entirely separate directory endpoints. Conversely, the cgroup v2 architecture mandates that all integrated resource controllers share a single, unified pseudo-filesystem instance. In modern Linux distributions, the initialization manager systemd automatically mounts this consolidated filesystem to the absolute path /sys/fs/cgroup during the early boot phase; throughout all subsequent analyses, this filesystem is assumed to reside at /sys/fs/cgroup.

Every subdirectory nested beneath this root cgroup directory maps directly to a specific structural node within the control group tree topology. In frameworks deploying cgroup v1 mechanics, each distinct resource manager exposes a corresponding parent subdirectory inside the mount root. In architectures tracking the cgroup v2 standard, subdirectories do not necessarily correspond to a single standalone resource; instead, each container directory exposes two vital control nodes: cgroup.controllers and cgroup.subtree_control. By updating these control files, administrators toggle resource constraints over the sub-tree.

However, within current kernel implementations, because a subset of legacy resource controllers has not yet been fully refactored to support the v2 specification, the subdirectories nested under /sys/fs/cgroup often remain mapped to individual resource managers to guarantee backward compatibility with v1 layouts. Utilizing this virtual filesystem layer, administrators can create or destroy structural nodes along the cgroup tree, establish process-specific resource limits and execution priorities, extract precise resource tracking statistics, and maintain absolute control over task behaviors.

An administrator can instantiate a new child cgroup node along the hierarchy simply by executing standard directory creation steps to form a new subdirectory inside any active cgroup path; similarly, removing a directory deletes the corresponding control node from the execution tree. Each localized cgroup directory hosts an array of core control files, resource configuration descriptors, and diagnostic data files. Diagnostic data files are strictly read-only nodes dynamically populated by the kernel to provide administrators with clear telemetry tracking system resource behavior. Conversely, core control files and resource configuration descriptors are formatted as read-write files generated by the system.

When an administrator creates or modifies these files, the kernel utilizes them to schedule and manage the resources regulated by that specific resource controller. The files dedicated to resource constraint optimization restrict or enhance the behavior of the active processes mapped to the corresponding nested subdirectories.

Every localized cgroup subdirectory can host both core control files and resource configuration files. Core control files regulate the fundamental architecture of the control group hierarchy itself; they are designated with a cgroup prefix name string, and their trailing extension tags define their functional file type. Several of the most infrastructure-critical control files include cgroup.procs, cgroup.type, cgroup.threads, and cgroup.subtree_control.

The cgroup.procs file registers the absolute Process IDs (PIDs) of all processes assigned to the cgroup node matching that subdirectory. Reading this file outputs a clear list tracking all currently associated processes, while writing a specific process PID into it immediately rebinds and relocates that process into the control group context of the current directory. This file can be interrogated or modified via standard shell commands as shown below:

  • Create a new child cgroup named cg1:

    # mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cg1

  • Attach the current shell process to the cg1 control group:

    # echo \$\$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cg1/cgroup.procs

  • Display all processes currently contained within the control group:

    # cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cg1/cgroup.procs

The cgroup.type file specifies the runtime domain classification of the control group matching that subdirectory. The registered type can resolve to a standard resource domain (domain), a threaded domain root (threaded domain), a nested threaded control group (threaded), or an unvalidated domain (invalid domain). The first three configurations represent the production domain classifications detailed in the preceding cgroup v2 conceptual overview.

Conversely, the invalid domain flag functions as a transient tracking type deployed dynamically when setting up a threaded subtree hierarchy; it signals that the control group rests in an unvalidated, temporary state. An invalid control group is strictly prohibited from housing process contexts or running resource budget constraints; it must be converted into a validated production type before it can accept active tasks. The inclusion of this invalid state ensures the kernel layout can support subsequent architectural expansions of the threaded cgroup model.

The classification parameters tracking a control group's type can be audited or changed via the following operations:

  • Configure the cg1 control group to act as a threaded control group:

    # echo threaded > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cg1/cgroup.type

  • Configure the cg1 control group to act as a standard resource domain:

    # echo domain > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cg1/cgroup.type

  • Configure the cg1 control group to act as a threaded domain root:

    # echo "threaded domain" > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cg1/cgroup.type

The cgroup.threads file logs the specific Thread IDs (TIDs) of all individual execution threads contained within that control group. Attaching an individual thread to a designated cgroup is handled by writing its unique TID into the target cgroup.threads node, and removing a TID from this list unbinds and expels the thread from the group.

The cgroup.controllers file is configured as a read-only metadata node that catalogs all available resource controllers currently active for that specific cgroup. To remain valid, these controllers must be explicitly derived from and enabled by the parent ancestral cgroup node.

The cgroup.subtree_control file logs the specific resource controllers that are actively enabled for the children of that control group. The controllers configured inside this file must strictly be a subset of the entries exposed within cgroup.controllers; a control group can only activate a resource controller if it is explicitly whitelisted inside its cgroup.controllers metadata node. The following commands show the method for dynamically enabling or disabling resource controllers utilizing the cgroup.subtree_control node interface:

  • Create a new child control group named mycgroup:

    # mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/mycgroup

  • Enable the pids, cpu, and memory resource controllers for the nested subtree:

  $ echo '+pids + cpu +memory' > /sys/fs/cgroup/mycgroup/cgroup.subtree_control
  • Disable the pids controller within the mycgroup subtree:
  $ echo '-pids' > /sys/fs/cgroup/mycgroup/cgroup.subtree_control

Beyond the primary core control files introduced above, each control group directory hosts an array of secondary tracking nodes, including cgroup.events, cgroup.max.descendants, cgroup.max.depth, cgroup.stat, cgroup.freeze, cgroup.kill, cgroup.pressure, and irq.pressure. Interested developers can consult the corresponding system documentation or Linux cgroup manuals for granular bitwise definitions of these blocks.

Resource Control Interface Files

Except for the absolute root cgroup container directory, every nested subdirectory exposes an array of dedicated resource control interface files. The naming standard for these interface nodes generally follows the explicit syntax format resource.parameter.

For instance, the cpu resource controller tasked with managing CPU clock-cycle and processing bandwidth distribution provides nine control nodes, including cpu.stat, cpu.weight.nice, cpu.max, cpu.max.burst, cpu.pressure, and cpu.idle. Concurrently, the memory resource management infrastructure maps out twenty-one control interface files, including memory.current, memory.min, memory.low, memory.high, memory.max, memory.reclaim, and memory.oom.group.

A subset of these nodes functions strictly as read-only diagnostic counters to aggregate memory execution metrics, whereas the majority serve as read-write variables to establish the definitive memory limits for the control group. Generally, each distinct file regulates a single structural parameter. For example:

# echo "2M" > /sys/fs/cgroup/mycgroup/memory.min

This statement establishes a strict minimum memory guarantee threshold of 2 MB for the mycgroup control group. As long as the memory footprint consumed by this group drops below the 2 MB boundary, the kernel's memory management tracking engine is completely barred from reclaiming or purging its pages under any physical memory pressure state.

Varying the target resource manager shifts the applicable parameter options, and the total count of interface files changes strictly based on the subsystem's architectural complexity; full listings are available within the upstream cgroup manual.

Core Cgroup Data Structures

The internal kernel code implementing the cgroup resource budgeting infrastructure relies on a decoupled network of data structures, predominantly encompassing struct cgroup, struct cgroup_root, struct cgroup_subsys, and struct cgroup_subsys_state.

  • struct cgroup: Describes the hierarchical node architecture of the control group tree topology. Every active directory path across the cgroup hierarchy maps to an individual cgroup structure instance inside the kernel, guaranteeing that all processes and execution threads linked to that node share identical resource ceilings and configuration variables. This structure is defined within the core header file git/include/linux/cgroup-defs.h. Its primary fields track the localized state of individual child subsystems, the absolute root pointer of the host tree, the relative depth or tier of the node along the hierarchy, the maximum depth limits of the subtree, the precise counter parameters tracking child nodes by category, and the active bitmask filters regulating enabled or disabled controllers. It also encapsulates an array of pointers routing to the individual controller states, the linked virtual filesystem virtual tracking nodes, and a master linked list connecting all associated subsystem states.

  • struct cgroup_root: Represents the absolute root container of a cgroup hierarchy tree. Declared within git/include/linux/cgroup-defs.h, it bridges the cgroup tree to the virtual filesystem infrastructure by embedding the .kf_root field, which points to the unified struct kernfs_root directory node. It also implements the .subsys_mask bitmask tracking globally enabled or disabled controllers, embeds the primitive struct cgroup structure (.cgrp) allocated to anchor the root block itself, and maintains a collection of tracking lists to manage the root mappings of various resource controllers (retained to ensure compatibility with legacy cgroup v1 environments).

  • struct cgroup_subsys: Defines the operational behavior and callback hooks of a specific resource controller subsystem. Maintained within git/include/linux/cgroup-defs.h, it exposes an array of low-level scheduling and resource enforcement function pointers, references the primary hierarchy tree root via the .root field, stores the descriptive system key string (.name), and sets the .implicit_on_dfl boolean flag to indicate whether the subsystem initializes by default. It also implements the .threaded flag bit to verify thread-level cgroup capability and tracks resource-specific virtual configuration nodes via the .cfts metadata arrays and the default .dfl_cfts property collections.

  • struct cgroup_subsys_state: Captures and maintains the runtime execution state of a specific controller module associated with an individual cgroup. These subsystem state blocks form a parallel tree hierarchy that mirrors the layout of the primary control group tree. Each state tree node references a matching node on the cgroup hierarchy, serving as the definitive database used by resource managers to tune scheduling parameters. The structure primarily contains a direct pointer referencing its parent control group, a pointer tracking its target resource controller subsystem, and standard layout fields to anchor the node within the hierarchy (including indicators routing to its parent node, list fields tracking sister nodes, and links mapping its immediate child branches).

Early Cgroup Initialization (cgroup_init_early)

The primary objective of the early initialization function cgroup_init_early() is to construct the default global cgroup root node (cgrp_dfl_root), initialize its master root list tracking parameters, and hook the early startup process into the cgroup framework. It accomplishes this task by writing the absolute physical address of the static initialization tracking set init_css_set straight into the .cgroups tracking pointer field inside the primary bootstrap task descriptor init_task.

The core initial tracking matrix is defined by the static init_css_set structure, which initializes with the following layout:

struct css_set init_css_set = {
	.refcount        	= REFCOUNT_INIT(1),
	.dom_cset        	= &init_css_set,
	.tasks            	= LIST_HEAD_INIT(init_css_set.tasks),
	.mg_tasks        	= LIST_HEAD_INIT(init_css_set.mg_tasks),
	.dying_tasks        	= LIST_HEAD_INIT(init_css_set.dying_tasks),
	.task_iters        	= LIST_HEAD_INIT(init_css_set.task_iters),
	.threaded_csets    	= LIST_HEAD_INIT(init_css_set.threaded_csets),
	.cgrp_links        	= LIST_HEAD_INIT(init_css_set.cgrp_links),
	.mg_preload_node    	= LIST_HEAD_INIT(init_css_set.mg_preload_node),
	.mg_node        	= LIST_HEAD_INIT(init_css_set.mg_node),
	.dfl_cgrp        	= &cgrp_dfl_root.cgrp,
};

Its architectural function is to configure and initialize the master list heads for tracking tasks across distinct execution boundaries, ensuring that tasks running through different behavioral cycles are isolated into separate linked lists.

The struct css_set structure acts as a centralized data repository required during the resource budgeting process, aggregating the state arrays of individual subsystems, referencing its associated control group nodes, and anchoring the various task linked lists. If a target node is classified as a standard resource domain or a threaded domain root, this structure also logs a comprehensive listing of all active nodes utilizing that specific domain. Furthermore, to seamlessly execute task migration routines—such as moving a running process or execution thread from one control group to an alternative branch—the structure caches the metadata and routing metrics tracking both the source and destination nodes during the migration cycle.

The primary design objective of implementing the css_set abstraction is not to manage the resources themselves, but rather to optimize system performance by drastically reducing the memory storage footprint of the task_struct arrays, which accelerates the execution speed of process cloning and termination routines (fork() and exit()). When a running task initiates a fork or exit routine, the kernel simply increments or decrements the reference counter field (.refcount) inside the corresponding css_set structure, followed by a fast list node insertion or deletion. This avoids the overhead of allocating or deep-copying massive blocks of duplicated data structures. Every active task in the Linux kernel accesses its associated subsystem states and node parameters indirectly by indexing through its own assigned css_set reference pointer.

Beyond establishing the default baseline control group root node, the cgroup_init_early() function performs early validation loops across the available resource subsystems, assigning unique names and unique identification indexes to every controller supported by the compiled kernel. If a specific subsystem registers a dependency requiring early lifecycle bring-up (indicated by the presence of an active .early_init flag bit inside its struct cgroup_subsys definition), the routine calls the controller's specialized early initializer to provision the subsystem.

The technical workflow executing this early subsystem initialization focuses primarily on setting the initial field states inside the target resource controller structure (struct cgroup_subsys). This sequence zeroes out the localized subsystem status identifiers, initializes the tracking list heads for the control group configuration files, and binds the subsystem's absolute root pointer field straight to the default global cgroup root node. It then generates a valid initial subsystem state descriptor layout (struct cgroup_subsys_state), configures its tracking identifier flags to 1, and registers this newly established state block directly into the centralized subsystem state array pool.

The interlocking network linking struct css_set, struct cgroup_subsys_state, and struct cgroup completely resolves the architectural challenge of tracking which running tasks belong to which control groups and defining the exact subsystem constraints bounding their execution.

  • struct cgroup: Represents an active, structural cgroup directory node inside the kernel. It coordinates and organizes various resource controllers (such as CPU bandwidth managers and memory fences) into a deterministic, hierarchical tree topology.

  • struct cgroup_subsys_state (css): Functions as the core status carrier. It encapsulates the precise resource limitations and scheduling configurations enforced by a concrete subsystem over an individual cgroup node; every valid cgroup node maintains a collection of these css pointers.

  • struct css_set: Serves as the high-speed operational bridge connecting the running process (task_struct) to its cgroup nodes. Because a single process context can be simultaneously bounded by multiple separate cgroups across disparate resource hierarchies, mapping individual processes directly to multiple separate cgroups would degrade kernel performance. The kernel resolves this by routing each process to point straight to a single consolidated css_set pointer. If two independent processes share an identical combination of cgroup bindings across all active resource controllers, they share a single, unified css_set instance in memory.

The multi-dimensional interface relationship linking these data structures is mapped out in the schematic diagram below, where the css_set exposes a continuous array of cgroup_subsys_state pointers, each routing to an individual state descriptor, which subsequently utilizes its internal .cgroup tracking pointer to map back to the parent cgroup container node:

Mainline Linux kernels provide native core definition support for up to 13 distinct resource subsystems declared within the include template include/linux/cgroup_subsys.h. These controllers encompass cpuset, cpu, cpuacct, io, memory, devices, freezer, net_cls, perf_event, net_prio, hugetlb, pids, rdma, and debug. The explicit subset of controllers actively built and supported by the running platform is selected at build time by kernel developers toggling target preprocessor compilation switches.

Disabling Local Interrupts

7.6 Initializing the Primary Boot CPU

The primary bootstrap lifecycle of an operating system kernel is coordinated and driven forward by a single central processing core—universally designated as CPU Core 0. Therefore, the kernel must explicitly initialize and register this initial execution core within its tracking matrices. The early optimization routine tasked with registering the primary bootstrap processor is declared as boot_cpu_init(), which is maintained within the core subsystem file linux/kernel/cpu.c with the following implementation:

void __init boot_cpu_init(void)
{
   int cpu = smp_processor_id();
   set_cpu_online(cpu, true);
   set_cpu_active(cpu, true);
   set_cpu_present(cpu, true);
   set_cpu_possible(cpu, true);
#ifdef CONFIG_SMP
   __boot_cpu_id = cpu;
#endif
}

The individual function calls encapsulated within this initialization routine update and manipulate distinct CPU bitmask topologies: __cpu_online_mask, __cpu_active_mask, __cpu_present_mask, and __cpu_possible_mask. Toggling the corresponding bit fields to true registers the active core state as online, active, physically present in the current system bus, and legally available for symmetric multiprocessing allocations, respectively.

The programmatic prefix token __init placed before the function return type specifies a specialized compiler section macro attribute. This token instructs the compiler to place the executable machine code of the routine exclusively inside the .init.text section. Memory blocks allocated to this temporary section are utilized strictly during early system architecture bring-up and are completely freed, purged, and recycled back into the global kernel memory pool once the system completes its booting cycles.

High-Memory Page Address Translation Initialization

7.7 High-Memory Page Address Translation Initialization

Operating systems deploy various technical layouts to model and optimize virtual-to-physical translation page lookup sequences, including flat tables, hierarchical architectures, hashed tables, or inverted page tables. When a platform architecture implements a hashed page table configuration to manage high-memory page address transformations, it must initialize the descriptor heads of each individual hashing bucket on startup.

The early routine page_address_init() executes this specific bucket configuration and list head alignment sequence. Conversely, on system compilation profiles targeting alternative hardware or virtual memory paging layouts that bypass hashed lookups, the page_address_init() function compiles down directly to an empty no-operation block (nop).

Early Initialization of the Linux Security Modules (LSM)

7.8 Early Initialization of the Linux Security Modules (LSM)

The Linux kernel maintains a global, consolidated tracking table infrastructure named security_hook_heads to archive individual hash list head descriptors. Every discrete list head within this database maps straight to a dedicated callback function vector (security hook), providing the subsystem with a centralized interface to locate and invoke active access control routines. The comprehensive taxonomy of security module callback hooks natively identified by the kernel is declared within the core header file include/linux/lsm_hook_defs.h. The architectural layout definition of the security_hook_heads structure is configured as follows:

struct security_hook_heads {
   struct hlist_head binder_set_context_mgr;
   int (*binder_set_context_mgr)(struct task_struct *mgr);
   struct hlist_head binder_transaction;
   int (*binder_transaction)(struct task_struct *from, struct task_struct *to);
   /* ... Additional subsystem definitions omit for brevity ... */
   struct hlist_head perf_event_write;
   int (*perf_event_write)(struct perf_event *event);
} __randomize_layout;

The initial operation executed by the early security initialization function early_security_init() is to iterate across this master database and cleanly initialize each embedded hash list head structure (struct hlist_head) to a null baseline state.

The Linux kernel infrastructure can simultaneously accommodate a multi-layered matrix of disparate security modules, with each discrete module described by a dedicated struct lsm_info tracking layout:

struct lsm_info {
   const char *name;            		/* Required: Unique identifier string */
   enum lsm_order order;       	 	/* Optional: Defaults to LSM_ORDER_MUTABLE */
   unsigned long flags;        		/* Optional: Operational flags describing the LSM */
   int *enabled;            			/* Optional: State control indicator driven by CONFIG_LSM */
   int (*init)(void);            		/* Required: Primary entry function pointer */
   struct lsm_blob_sizes *blobs;     	/* Optional: Tracks metadata requirements for blob sharing */
};

During the project compilation step, the linker utility aggregates all initialized lsm_info descriptor structures and writes them contiguously into a specialized, low-level link section bounded by the symbols __start_early_lsm_info and __end_early_lsm_info.

The secondary technical objective managed within the early_security_init() lifecycle phase is the orchestration and execution of the early security modules. The parsing loop initially verifies whether the targeted LSM exposes a proprietary, configurable initialization tracking state variable (enabled). Following this lookup, it passes the descriptor block context over to the internal helper utility prepare_lsm() to determine whether the target module complies with system policies and can be safely activated. If a module lacks an explicit status controller reference, the subsystem initializes its evaluation flags using standard system fallback variables (lsm_enabled_true and lsm_enabled_false).

If the evaluation phase flags the target module as explicitly disabled, or if the controller demands exclusive platform enforcement (LSM_FLAG_EXCLUSIVE) when another exclusive security infrastructure has already finished initialization, the current candidate module is blocked from activating. Conversely, if the check validation confirms that the candidate module is eligible for activation, the engine invokes its primary entry function pointer (.init) to bring up the subsystem hardware dependencies.

The low-level helper function tasked with verifying module eligibility is structured as follows:

static void __init prepare_lsm(struct lsm_info *lsm)
{
   int enabled = lsm_allowed(lsm);
   set_enabled(lsm, enabled);
   if (enabled) {
       if ((lsm->flags & LSM_FLAG_EXCLUSIVE) && !exclusive) {
           exclusive = lsm;
           init_debug("exclusive chosen: %s\n", lsm->name);
       }
       lsm_set_blob_sizes(lsm->blobs);
   }
}

The core function tasked with invoking the module's compiled entry handler to execute the early subsystem initialization loops is structured as follows:

static void __init initialize_lsm(struct lsm_info *lsm)

static void __init initialize_lsm(struct lsm_info *lsm)
{
   if (is_enabled(lsm)) {
       int ret;
       init_debug("initializing %s\n", lsm->name);
       ret = lsm->init();
       WARN(ret, "%s failed to initialize: %d\n", lsm->name, ret);
   }
}

This concludes Section 7.8 and the early initialization sequence of the Linux Security Modules.

Chapter 8 Kernel Booting — Framework-Based Hardware Configuration

Foundational Architectural Concepts

8.1 Foundational Architectural Concepts

8.1.1 Architectural Concepts of Linux Memory Management

The Linux kernel is engineered to scale across a vast taxonomy of disparate hardware platforms, which may utilize uniprocessor (single-core) layouts or symmetric multiprocessing (multi-core) topologies. Within uniprocessor environments, all physical memory banks may reside in close proximity to the CPU, guaranteeing uniform access latencies across the entire memory space; alternatively, a portion of the memory footprint may be physically closer to peripheral controllers to facilitate High-Speed Direct Memory Access (DMA) transactions, creating non-uniform latencies for CPU access loops. In symmetric multiprocessing infrastructures, physical memory is frequently partitioned into multiple discrete channels or groups. Certain blocks may be isolated for the exclusive use of a single execution core, others may be shared globally among all active processing cores, and some may be bridged adjacent to IO endpoints to optimize DMA transfers. Because the electrical tracing distances separating individual storage matrices from different CPU cores vary significantly, each core exhibits unique access latency parameters when addressing the same chunk of physical memory.

To model this variance in memory access latencies precisely, the Linux kernel architecture implements the Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) paradigm to define and manage low-level physical memory topologies. Any hardware architecture where disparate processing elements experience asymmetric latencies when addressing different physical memory regions is categorized as a NUMA structure.

To fulfill hardware modularity constraints, volatile physical memory is structurally deployed as memory banks (or modules). The CPU experiences uniform access latencies when executing read/write sweeps across a single memory bank. The Linux memory management subsystem treats each distinct bank or clustered group as a standalone NUMA Node, represented internally by the struct pglist_data descriptor block. Through a standard type abstraction, this structure is aliased as the pg_data_t type. The master definition for the pglist_data structure is maintained within the core zones header module git/include/linux/mmzone.h. It primarily encapsulates tracking fields such as the node identifier index, the memory zones array housed within the node (detailed in the subsequent section), the total count of valid zones (nr_zones), a collection of fallback lookup pointer lists tracking zones across all active nodes (node_zonelist[]), the absolute physical Page Frame Number (PFN) boundary marking the node's origin (node_start_pfn), the total linear virtual span of the node measured in pages (node_spanned_pages), the actual count of physical page frames physically populated within the node (node_present_pages), and linked reference lists tracking localized zone maps.

Depending on individual electrical attributes and device usage models, the Linux kernel subdivides the physical memory allocation of each distinct node into several discrete, specialized Zones (ZONE_DMA, ZONE_DMA32, ZONE_NORMAL, ZONE_HIGHMEM, ZONE_MOVABLE, and ZONE_DEVICE), represented inside the system by the struct zone descriptor block.

  • ZONE_DMA and ZONE_DMA32: Dedicated memory margins fenced off to safely drive legacy and standard peripheral Direct Memory Access (DMA) address channels.

  • ZONE_NORMAL: The direct-mapped, generic memory space utilized by the core kernel to fulfill standard persistent allocations.

  • ZONE_HIGHMEM: High-memory regions that are not permanently mapped by the kernel's virtual page tables; to read or alter contents cached within high-memory blocks, the kernel must instantiate temporary mapping vectors at runtime.

  • ZONE_MOVABLE: Behaves similarly to standard memory zones with the structural exception that pages are marked as relocatable, meaning an identical virtual memory coordinate can be safely re-mapped to point down to alternative physical page frames to facilitate hot-unplug and memory compaction routines.

  • ZONE_DEVICE: Abstract zones allocated to model and manage non-volatile storage or dedicated hardware memory blocks hosted directly on external peripheral expansion buses (such as GPU high-bandwidth VRAM).

Operating systems typically orchestrate and link virtual structures to hardware blocks at a granular page-level (with a standard page consuming 4096 bytes of memory), and the Linux framework follows this exact design. Every single 4 KB block of physical memory is linked to an individual tracker structure named struct page, defined as the physical page descriptor. This descriptor logs the real-time operational characteristics of that physical page frame, registering parameters such as its current kernel subsystem allocation type, active reference counts, and whether its contents can be safely swapped or recycled under memory pressure states. The localized storage layout and array alignment of these struct page tracking blocks differ strictly based on the system's selected memory tracking model; for example, the standard Flat Memory (FLATMEM) tracking architecture packages these descriptors sequentially inside a master global array named mem_map. For a detailed architectural breakdown of memory model configurations, developers can consult Section 8.2.15.8.1.

Architecture-Specific Initialization Function (setup_arch)

8.2 Architecture-Specific Initialization Function (setup_arch)

Following the early initialization of the security module, the start_kernel() function invokes setup_arch() to handle low-level operations specific to the underlying hardware architecture. The setup_arch() function processes the bootloader-supplied (e.g., U-BOOT) command line arguments string command_line to configure architecture-dependent peripherals, such as tuning the UART transmission baud rate. Because this function interfaces directly with the raw silicon layer, its internal program logic is completely distinct across different CPU families. When bringing up an entirely new CPU architecture, software engineers must develop this initialization suite from scratch. For the ARM architecture, the function is maintained within the architecture-specific source module linux/arch/arm/kernel/setup.c and is structured as follows:

void __init setup_arch(char **cmdline_p)
{
   const struct machine_desc *mdesc;
   setup_processor();
   mdesc = setup_machine_fdt(__atags_pointer);
   if (!mdesc)
       mdesc = setup_machine_tags(__atags_pointer, __machine_arch_type);
   if (!mdesc) {
       early_print("\nError: invalid dtb and unrecognized/unsupported machine ID\n");
       early_print("  r1=0x%08x, r2=0x%08x\n", __machine_arch_type,
           __atags_pointer);
       if (__atags_pointer)
           early_print("  r2[]=%*ph\n", 16, phys_to_virt(__atags_pointer));
       dump_machine_table();
   }
   machine_desc = mdesc;
   machine_name = mdesc->name;
   dump_stack_set_arch_desc("%s", mdesc->name);
   if (mdesc->reboot_mode != REBOOT_HARD)
       reboot_mode = mdesc->reboot_mode;
   init_mm.start_code = (unsigned long) _text;
   init_mm.end_code   = (unsigned long) _etext;
   init_mm.end_data   = (unsigned long) _edata;
   init_mm.brk        = (unsigned long) _end;
   strlcpy(cmd_line, boot_command_line, COMMAND_LINE_SIZE);
   *cmdline_p = cmd_line;
   early_fixmap_init();
   early_ioremap_init();
   parse_early_param();
#ifdef CONFIG_MMU
   early_mm_init(mdesc);
#endif
   setup_dma_zone(mdesc);
   xen_early_init();
   efi_init();
   adjust_lowmem_bounds();
   arm_memblock_init(mdesc);
   adjust_lowmem_bounds();
   early_ioremap_reset();
   paging_init(mdesc);
   request_standard_resources(mdesc);
   if (mdesc->restart)
       arm_pm_restart = mdesc->restart;
   unflatten_device_tree();
   arm_dt_init_cpu_maps();
   psci_dt_init();
#ifdef CONFIG_SMP
   if (is_smp()) {
       if (!mdesc->smp_init || !mdesc->smp_init()) {
           if (psci_smp_available())
               smp_set_ops(&psci_smp_ops);
           else if (mdesc->smp)
               smp_set_ops(mdesc->smp);
       }
      smp_init_cpus();
      smp_build_mpidr_hash();
   }
#endif
   if (!is_smp())
       hyp_mode_check();
   reserve_crashkernel();
#ifdef CONFIG_GENERIC_IRQ_MULTI_HANDLER
   handle_arch_irq = mdesc->handle_irq;
#endif
#ifdef CONFIG_VT
#if defined(CONFIG_VGA_CONSOLE)
   conswitchp = &vga_con;
#endif
#endif
  if (mdesc->init_early)
      mdesc->init_early();
}

The subsequent sections comprehensively detail the initialization mechanics and internal workflows executed across each underlying component within this architecture configuration routine.

8.2.1 Processor Architecture Setup

Processor architecture setup is initialized by invoking the setup_processor() function. This function first extracts the hardware CPU ID signature from the CP15 coprocessor space via the following macro definition block:

#define read_cpuid(reg) \
    ({ \
        unsigned int __val; \
        asm("mrc    p15, 0, %0, c0, c0, " __stringify(reg) \
            : "=r" (__val) \
            : \
            : "cc"); \
        __val; \
    })

Following this hardware register read, it calls lookup_processor() to scan the contiguous memory section bounded between the linker symbols __proc_info_begin and __proc_info_end to resolve the physical address hosting the processor descriptor structure struct proc_info_list. The binary layout and entries grouped within this link section are generated statically at link time based on the active platform target source files. The lookup_processor() wrapper routine references the underlying assembly function lookup_processor_type(), which is defined inside the architecture common assembly module linux/arch/arm/kernel/head-common.S as follows:

ENTRY(lookup_processor_type)
    stmfd    sp!, {r4 - r6, r9, lr}
    mov    r9, r0
    bl    __lookup_processor_type
    mov    r0, r5
    ldmfd    sp!, {r4 - r6, r9, pc}
ENDPROC(lookup_processor_type)

The underlying assembly loop __lookup_processor_type invoked here is the exact same routine previously executed during the low-level CPU mode initialization phase.

The proc_info_list descriptor resolved during this table scan is structured with the following fields:

struct proc_info_list {
   unsigned int             cpu_val;
   unsigned int             cpu_mask;
   unsigned long            __cpu_mm_mmu_flags;    	/* used by head.S */
   unsigned long            __cpu_io_mmu_flags;    	/* used by head.S */
   unsigned long            __cpu_flush;        	/* used by head.S */
   const char               *arch_name;
   const char               *elf_name;
   unsigned int             elf_hwcap;
   const char               *cpu_name;
   struct processor         *proc;
   struct cpu_tlb_fns       *tlb;
   struct cpu_user_fns      *user;
   struct cpu_cache_fns     *cache;
};

The proc_info_list structure aggregates vital system metadata required for central processor provisioning, including the Memory Management Unit (MMU) operational attributes, memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) attributes, compile-time target architecture name strings, and specific processor designation strings. The structural pointer field .proc targets a separate interface structure containing function vectors designed to route low-level platform behaviors, including data abort exceptions, prefetch abort traps, processor core initialization, hardware validation loops, deep sleep suspension, wake-up restoration, and cold reset sequences. The .proc field maps directly to the struct processor structure, declared as follows:

struct processor {
   void (*_data_abort)(unsigned long pc);
   unsigned long (*_prefetch_abort)(unsigned long lr);
   void (*_proc_init)(void);
   void (*check_bugs)(void);
   void (*_proc_fin)(void);
   void (*reset)(unsigned long addr, bool hvc) __attribute__((noreturn));
   int (*_do_idle)(void);
   void (*dcache_clean_area)(void *addr, int size);
   void (*switch_mm)(phys_addr_t pgd_phys, struct mm_struct *mm);
#ifdef CONFIG_ARM_LPAE
   void (*set_pte_ext)(pte_t *ptep, pte_t pte);
#else
   void (*set_pte_ext)(pte_t *ptep, pte_t pte, unsigned int ext);
#endif
   unsigned int suspend_size;
   void (*do_suspend)(void *);
   void (*do_resume)(void *);
};

The .tlb field contains a reference pointer targeting the struct cpu_tlb_fns structure. This interface provides an array of platform-specific Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) control pointers tasked with flushing user-space and kernel-space memory address caches. The tracking layout is defined as follows:

struct cpu_tlb_fns {
   void (*flush_user_range)(unsigned long, unsigned long, struct vm_area_struct *);
   void (*flush_kern_range)(unsigned long, unsigned long);
   unsigned long tlb_flags;
};

Within this function matrix, the .flush_user_range function pointer executes page flushes restricted to user virtual memory zones, while .flush_kern_range purges internal translation entries across the core kernel memory layout.

The processor architecture exposes specialized operations to copy or clear high-memory and low-memory page layouts across user virtual address zones via the .user reference field. These functions are encapsulated within the struct cpu_user_fns structure, which is structured as follows:

struct cpu_user_fns {
   void (*cpu_clear_user_highpage)(struct page *page, unsigned long vaddr);
   void (*cpu_copy_user_highpage)(struct page *to, struct page *from,
      unsigned long vaddr, struct vm_area_struct *vma);
};

The .cpu_clear_user_highpage handler zeroes out physical memory page maps associated with high-address user zones, while the .cpu_copy_user_highpage routine replicates the page content across separate user-space high-memory coordinates.

Hardware cache maintenance operations are registered via the .cache reference pointer, routing execution down to individual cache flushing mechanisms tracked inside the struct cpu_cache_fns structure:

struct cpu_cache_fns {
   void (*flush_icache_all)(void);
   void (*flush_kern_all)(void);
   void (*flush_kern_louis)(void);
   void (*flush_user_all)(void);
   void (*flush_user_range)(unsigned long, unsigned long, unsigned int);
   void (*coherent_kern_range)(unsigned long, unsigned long);
   int  (*coherent_user_range)(unsigned long, unsigned long);
   void (*flush_kern_dcache_area)(void *, size_t);
   void (*dma_map_area)(const void *, size_t, int);
   void (*dma_unmap_area)(const void *, size_t, int);
   void (*dma_flush_range)(const void *, const void *);
} __no_randomize_layout;

The specific low-level cache control operations can be directly deduced from their symbolic function names and are omitted here for brevity.

Within Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP) layouts, to isolate individual processing elements and minimize resource contention or cache bouncing across processing cores, the kernel reserves a dedicated, isolated data block memory area for each processor core, designed to archive core-specific execution variables (per-CPU sections). At this early juncture in the bootstrap lifecycle, secondary multi-core components have not yet completed their initial initialization passes.

However, the architecture-critical functions exposed via the .proc vectors must be executed before these secondary cores are formally initialized. Since these secondary cores lack active per-CPU storage windows at this stage, early state parameters cannot yet be written into core-specific segments.

To resolve this limitation, Linux establishes a centralized global lookup table matrix (cpu_vtable[]) to temporarily cache the processor core interface function vectors. Each logical core entry within this array initially points to an identical structure mapping. The inline routine init_proc_vtable(const struct processor *p) handles the creation of this global tracking array, declared as follows:

static inline void init_proc_vtable(const struct processor *p)
{
   unsigned int cpu = smp_processor_id();
   *cpu_vtable[cpu] = *p;
   WARN_ON_ONCE(cpu_vtable[cpu]->dcache_clean_area !=
      cpu_vtable[0]->dcache_clean_area);
   WARN_ON_ONCE(cpu_vtable[cpu]->set_pte_ext !=
       cpu_vtable[0]->set_pte_ext);
}

Upon finalizing the layout initialization of this global interface array, the setup_processor() function extracts the individual sub-system function pointers (tlb, user, cache, and elf_hwcap) exposed by the proc_info_list block and registers them inside the global variable structures cpu_tbl, cpu_user, and cpu_cache to make them globally available for downstream kernel operations.

The proc_info_list block also provides an .elf_hwcap capabilities bitmask field, which catalogues the native hardware features (such as hardware floating-point acceleration or advanced instructions support) available to applications compiled for the Executable and Linkable Format (ELF). Because different silicon revisions implement varying subsets of extensions, the kernel invokes cpuid_init_hwcaps() to perform hardware-specific capability matching and dynamically initialize these capability registers.

Following the initialization of the ELF capabilities registers, the setup_processor() routine sets the system's global default cache line eviction and mapping policy variable (cachepolicy) to match the explicit cacheability attributes passed through the __cpu_mm_mmu_flags word of the active proc_info_list.

Because cache controller microarchitectures vary significantly across different ARM generations, the function cacheid_init() interrogates the processor architecture to extract the exact hardware cache implementation profile, fully initializing the global configuration variable cacheid.

The terminal phase of the setup_processor() function coordinates the absolute initialization of the primary CPU core by invoking the cpu_init() routine. This function programs the CP15 coprocessor register TPIDRPRW (Thread ID Register, Privileged Read/Write) with the absolute base offset value designating the core's isolated per-CPU dedicated storage allocation region. Following this registration step, it fetches and calls the low-level processing initializer _proc_init() from the centralized cpu_vtable[] lookup table array to complete the core silicon-level hardware bring-up.

The structural execution pipeline tracking the setup_processor() function is mapped out in the technical flowchart below:

This concludes Section 8.2.1 and the complete technical translation of the processor setup subsystem.

8.2.2 Flattened Device Tree (FDT) Processing

When the system incorporates Device Tree support, the Linux kernel invokes the setup_machine_fdt() function to query and extract structural hardware platform definitions compiled within the tree. Upon completing this hardware parsing phase, it returns an authorizing pointer routing down to the specific struct machine_desc structure descriptor that maps out the baseline features of the system. The machine_desc structure is declared within the architecture-specific machine template header arch/arm/include/asm/mach/arch.h as follows:

struct machine_desc {
   unsigned int nr;                         /* Architecture numbers reference map */
   const char *name;                        /* Architecture name string */
   unsigned long atag_offset;               /* Tagged list offset (relative) */
   const char *const *dt_compat;            
/* Array of Device Tree 'compatible' strings */
   unsigned int nr_irqs;                    /* Total number of supported IRQs */
   phys_addr_t dma_zone_size;               /* Size boundary of the DMA-capable area */
   unsigned int video_start;                /* Absolute starting address of video RAM */
   unsigned int video_end;                  /* Absolute terminating address of video RAM */
   unsigned char reserve_lp0 :1;            /* Platform configuration flag for Low-Power Mode 0 */
   unsigned char reserve_lp1 :1;            /* Platform configuration flag for Low-Power Mode 1 */
   unsigned char reserve_lp2 :1;            /* Platform configuration flag for Low-Power Mode 2 */
   enum reboot_mode reboot_mode;            /* Default hardware reset action mode */
   unsigned l2c_aux_val;                    /* Level-2 Cache auxiliary control configuration word */
   unsigned l2c_aux_mask;                   /* Level-2 Cache auxiliary mask layout vector */
   void (*l2c_write_sec)(unsigned long, unsigned);
   const struct smp_operations *smp;        /* Core SMP operational callbacks framework */
   bool (*smp_init)(void);
   void (*fixup)(struct tag *, char **);
   void (*dt_fixup)(void);
   long long (*pv_fixup)(void);
   void (*reserve)(void);                   /* Core memory reservation block function pointer */
   void (*map_io)(void);                    /* Early static I/O peripheral routing table pointer */
   void (*init_early)(void);
   void (*init_irq)(void);
   void (*init_time)(void);
   void (*init_machine)(void);
   void (*init_late)(void);
   void (*handle_irq)(struct pt_regs *);
   void (*restart)(enum reboot_mode, const char *);
};

The core setup_machine_fdt() parsing handler is defined within the system architecture Device Tree framework file arch/arm/kernel/devtree.c as follows:

const struct machine_desc * __init setup_machine_fdt(unsigned int dt_phys)
{
   const struct machine_desc *mdesc, *mdesc_best = NULL;
   if (!dt_phys || !early_init_dt_verify(phys_to_virt(dt_phys)))
      return NULL;
   mdesc = of_flat_dt_match_machine(mdesc_best, arch_get_next_mach);
   if (!mdesc) {
       const char *prop;
       int size;
       unsigned long dt_root;
       early_print("\nError: unrecognized/unsupported "
           "device tree compatible list:\n[ ");
       dt_root = of_get_flat_dt_root();
       prop = of_get_flat_dt_prop(dt_root, "compatible", &size);
       while (size > 0) {
           early_print("'%s' ", prop);
           size -= strlen(prop) + 1;
           prop += strlen(prop) + 1;
       }
       early_print("]\n\n");
       dump_machine_table(); 		/* Execution freezes inside this block; does not return */
   }
   if (mdesc->dt_fixup)
       mdesc->dt_fixup();
   early_init_dt_scan_nodes();
   __machine_arch_type = mdesc->nr;
   return mdesc;
}

Within the fundamental kernel link script configuration template vmlinux.lds.S, a specific mapping directive is specified as:

.init.arch.info : {
        __arch_info_begin = .;
        *(.arch.info.init)
        __arch_info_end = .;
    }
