This alignment vector instructs the link manager to collect all input code sections matching the section syntax template *(.arch.info.init) and package them sequentially in memory bounded by the tracking markers __arch_info_begin and __arch_info_end. These target code blocks populate the system registry with the hardware descriptors of every individual motherboard revision supported by the compiled kernel binary.

The setup_machine_fdt() function interrogates these static tables by performing string matching between the descriptors linked between __arch_info_begin and __arch_info_end and the array of character keys declared under the global compatible root node property of the Flattened Device Tree. This step determines if the target central processor configuration is supported by the active kernel image. The greater the volume of character keys resolved during the verification pass, the more precise the structural compatibility mapping becomes.

During the discovery loop designed to isolate the optimal system hardware definition block, the setup_machine_fdt() function initially evaluates the binary integrity of the device tree payload by executing validation checks over the FDT magic signature word, the structure block length, the memory reservation list parameters, and the total strings module boundary. Following this integrity verification pass, it redirects execution into the specialized device tree macro parser of_flat_dt_match_machine() (within the kernel source layout, structural device tree processing handlers are uniformly prefixed with the of_ identifier, indicating Open Firmware inheritance, and are predominantly maintained within the subsystem module drivers/of/fdt.c).

This scanning utility matches the board descriptor tables with the string listings stored inside the FDT's root compatible array to extract the exact machine_desc record showcasing the highest structural compatibility rating. The core source module drivers/of/dev.c exports a vast matrix of matching device tree look-up wrappers prefixed with the of_ identifier, providing clean hooks to traverse the underlying .dtb architecture to parse nodes, hardware properties, and bus parameters.

Once a compatible system definition block matching the targeted board architecture has been successfully resolved, the setup_machine_fdt() function invokes the high-level tree scanning routine early_init_dt_scan_nodes(). This master scanning loop triggers distinct sub-node traversal callbacks, specifically early_init_dt_scan_chosen(), early_init_dt_scan_root(), and early_init_dt_scan_memory(), to parse the structural options wrapped inside the /chosen and /memory top-level tree branches.

  • Chosen Node Scanning (/chosen): If a valid /chosen container node is detected and its properties expose an active bootargs variable, the parser copies the contents of this text argument string straight into the system-wide command line tracker array boot_command_line. Concurrently, if the string properties register an initialized linux,initrd-start or linux,initrd-end field, the bootloader flags the system to support a temporary RAM-disk configuration and utilizes these physical address bounds to initialize the internal variables phys_initrd_start and phys_initrd_size.

  • Root Node Scanning (/): If the scanning loop targeting the baseline root node resolves valid #address-cells and #size-cells attributes, the system dynamically sets the operational boundaries for the variables dt_root_size_cells and dt_root_addr_cells.

  • Memory Node Scanning (/memory): When the parser processes a valid /memory block branch, confirming that its device_type identifier matches the literal definition "memory" and verifying the presence of an active linux,usable-memory or standard reg layout matrix, it extracts the memory bank parameters and appends these newly discovered coordinates straight into the kernel's active physical address allocator space, tracked via the .memory array inside the global memblock data structure (memblock.memory).

The memblock infrastructure acts as the primitive, early-stage boot allocation framework responsible for physical memory management and layout parsing long before the core virtual page or slab managers are active. The kernel relies on this tracking layer to chart the architecture partitions of physical memory. The structural layout definition of the memblock descriptor is configured as follows:

struct memblock {
   bool bottom_up;        /* Flag bit directing memory allocation trajectory (low-to-high vs high-to-low) */
   phys_addr_t current_limit;       /* Absolute boundary limit restricting early memory allocations */
   struct memblock_type memory;     /* Array tracking blocks registered as usable physical RAM */
   struct memblock_type reserved;   /* Array tracking blocks fenced off as protected, reserved memory */
};

If the physical target platform lacks Device Tree functionality, the upstream U-BOOT bootloader provides the runtime initialization parameters to the guest Linux kernel using the legacy atag parameter vector list format. As detailed in the preceding assembly bootstrap chapters, the absolute physical address pointer pointing to the base of this atag array is similarly passed to the kernel via register r2.

If the scanning engine fails to find a matching hardware descriptor block corresponding to the FDT string lists, or if the hardware environment does not implement a Flattened Device Tree, the system drops back from setup_machine_fdt() to call the legacy setup alternative setup_machine_tags() to provision the system context. The setup_machine_tags() routine compares the physical architecture number identifier __machine_arch_type against the hardcoded architecture indexes registered within every available machine_desc structure linked between the compilation boundaries __arch_info_begin and __arch_info_end. When an exact numeric match is successfully resolved, it binds that specific board structure to manage the hardware configuration. Upon securing this valid descriptor block, setup_machine_tags() initializes the reference points routing down to the target tags structure.

struct tag {
   struct tag_header hdr;
   union {
       struct tag_core        core;
       struct tag_mem32       mem;
       struct tag_videotext   videotext;
       struct tag_ramdisk     ramdisk;
       struct tag_initrd      initrd;
       struct tag_serialnr    serialnr;
       struct tag_revision    revision;
       struct tag_videolfb    videolfb;
       struct tag_cmdline     cmdline;
       struct tag_acorn       acorn;
       struct tag_memclk      memclk;
   } u;
};

If the first parameter passed to setup_machine_tags() is non-null, the pointer is initialized directly with that address value. Conversely, if the first input argument evaluates to null, the routine extracts the fallback baseline tracking pointer value from the matched machine_desc board descriptor structure. After initializing this tag context pointer, the kernel caches a persistent local backup copy of the tag block and invokes the corresponding parameter-specific parsing handlers to extract and process each constituent tag structure layout sequentially.

This concludes Section 8.2.2 and the deep technical translation of the early device parameter and tree-flattening interfaces.

8.2.3 Memory Subsystem Provisioning for the Initialization Process

Upon completing the Flattened Device Tree parsing routines, the setup_arch() function provisions the primary tracking structure init_mm utilized to coordinate memory management during the initialization phase. The init_mm structure is instantiated as a static global instance of type struct mm_struct, whose structural definition is maintained within the core memory abstractions header include/linux/mm_types.h.

This master descriptor sets the baseline parameters and tracking dimensions governing the virtual address space layout during early system bring-up; within this context, the root page table assignment init_mm.pgd = swapper_pg_dir is mapped out during the initial assembly phase of the MMU configuration.

During this architectural processing stage, setup_arch() binds the following four structural memory boundaries inside the init_mm structure to align with the linker symbols exported by the compiled kernel binary image:

  • init_mm.start_code: Initialized with the absolute virtual address matching the _text symbol, marking the absolute beginning of the executable .text instruction section.

  • init_mm.end_code: Initialized with the absolute virtual address matching the _etext symbol, marking the absolute termination boundary of the .text instruction section.

  • init_mm.end_data: Initialized with the absolute virtual address matching the _edata symbol, marking the absolute termination boundary of the initialized .data section.

  • init_mm.brk: Initialized with the absolute virtual address matching the _end symbol, marking the absolute termination boundary of the zero-filled uninitialized data (.bss) section and establishing the early heap boundary.

Following the initialization of these init_mm tracking fields, the setup_arch() function duplicates the character string payload from the global boot_command_line buffer into the primary local command-line array cmd_line to freeze it for downstream argument parsing routines.

8.2.4 Initializing the Fixed Mapping Region Memory (early_fixmap_init)

The Linux kernel safeguards a dedicated segment of virtual memory known as the fixed mapping region or fixmap, which begins at FIXADDR_START and terminates at FIXADDR_END. Prior to constructing the permanent runtime page tables, this isolated address space handles immediate I/O routing or highly specialized bare-metal operations. Once the final virtual memory hierarchy is operational, this region acts as the standard high-memory map framework (kmap), exposing temporary translation windows for the core kernel to manipulate high-memory pages. For a standard 32-bit ARM memory profile, this virtual window is located between 0xFFF00000 and 0xFFFC0000. Structurally, the real production fixmap allocations open at 0xFFFEF000, with the remaining block space down to 0xFFF00000 set aside as guard pages to prevent unmapped memory out-of-bounds page faults.

To interact with this dedicated address space during the earliest stages of the bootstrap process, the system must establish an early address mapping template within the active translation tables. The function early_fixmap_init() manages this process by writing early translation properties into the level-1 descriptors. Maintained within the memory management module git/arch/arm/mm/mmu.c, this function is defined as follows:

void __init early_fixmap_init(void)
{
	pmd_t *pmd;
	BUILD_BUG_ON((__fix_to_virt(__end_of_early_ioremap_region) >> PMD_SHIFT)
		     != FIXADDR_TOP >> PMD_SHIFT);
	pmd = fixmap_pmd(FIXADDR_TOP);
	pmd_populate_kernel(&init_mm, pmd, bm_pte);
	pte_offset_fixmap = pte_offset_early_fixmap;
}

It must be explicitly noted that these temporary configurations are only active during early boot phases; once the definitive, runtime page tables are generated down the line, this entire address translation matrix is overwritten.

On ARM Linux platforms enabling 40-bit large physical address extensions (LPAE), the MMU hardware drives a 3-tier translation flow. Conversely, on standard 32-bit ARM targets, each top-level PGD entry maps directly to a single PMD element, making the structural execution equivalent to a 2-tier page table walk (as shown in Figure 6-12). In the actual source tree implementation, the PGD table array and the PMD table array share an identical memory layout block.

The PGD mappings are registered into the processor co-processor registers (TTBR0 and TTBR1) during the early MMU configuration phase. The matching PMD offset vector is resolved by passing the top fixed coordinate address FIXADDR_TOP (0xFFFEF000) into the helper inline function fixmap_pmd(FIXADDR_TOP). The fixmap_pmd macro tracks back to the following definition:

static inline pmd_t * __init fixmap_pmd(unsigned long addr)
{
   return pmd_off_k(addr);
}

The underlying pointer evaluation routine pmd_off_k() is defined as follows:

static inline pmd_t *pmd_off_k(unsigned long va)
{
   return pmd_offset(pud_offset(p4d_offset(pgd_offset(&init_mm,va), va), va), va);
}

The cascading p*d_offset() macros parse the virtual address string va to calculate its specific numeric index inside that layer's page table directory. Because the standard ARM32 codebase completely collapses the intermediate software layers P4D and PUD, these translation steps are flattened to return the input reference pointer untouched:

p4d_offset(ptr, address) = ptr 
pud_offset(ptr, address) = ptr

Consequently, the operational flow inside pmd_off_k() simplifies down to:

static inline pmd_t *pmd_off_k(unsigned long va)
{
   return pmd_offset(pgd_offset(&init_mm, va), va);
}

Evaluating this pointer logic yields:

pgd_offset(&init_mm, va) 
= (&init_mm)->pgd + ((va >> PGDIR_SHIFT) & (PTRS_PER_PGD - 1))
pmd_offset(pgd_offset(&init_mm, va)) 
= (&init_mm)->pgd + ((va >> PGDIR_SHIFT) & (PTRS_PER_PGD - 1)) 
   + ((va >> PMD_SHIFT) & (PTRS_PER_PMD - 1))

Applying this calculation to resolve the target PMD coordinates for the fixmap region results in:

pmd = pmd_off_k(FIXADDR_TOP) 
    = (&init_mm)->pgd + ((FIXADDR_TOP >> PGDIR_SHIFT) & (PTRS_PER_PGD - 1)) 
      + ((FIXADDR_TOP >> PMD_SHIFT) & (PTRS_PER_PMD - 1))

Under an ARM32 short-descriptor model executing a 2-tier hardware lookup, the preprocessor shift constant PGDIR_SHIFT equals 21, the macro PTRS_PER_PGD evaluates to 2048, PMD_SHIFT is fixed to 21, and the single-element directory multiplier PTRS_PER_PMD maps to 1. This scales the calculation to:

pmd = init_mm.pgd + 0x7FF

During the initial bootstrap lifecycle, the standard ARM32 processor enforces section-based memory configurations where each physical descriptor maps out a 1 MB section. However, under Linux's software page directory alignment, each software PGD entry is designed to manage a 2 MB virtual address envelope. To cleanly map this 2 MB software logic onto the actual 1 MB structural requirements of the hardware, the Linux layout packages two consecutive physical page table descriptors (2 × 1 MB) into a single software PGD element; an odd index indicates that the access loop targets the upper 1 MB segment of the allocation window.

Once the intermediate page directory pointer (pmd) is resolved, early_fixmap_init() calls pmd_populate_kernel() to write the target descriptor properties into that slot. This mapping handler is defined inside the architecture header arch/arm/include/asm/pgalloc.h as follows:

static inline void pmd_populate_kernel(struct mm_struct *mm, pmd_t *pmdp, pte_t *ptep)
{
    __pmd_populate(pmdp, __pa(ptep), _PAGE_KERNEL_TABLE);
}
static inline void __pmd_populate(pmd_t *pmdp, phys_addr_t pte, pmdval_t prot)
{
   pmdval_t pmdval = (pte + PTE_HWTABLE_OFF) | prot;
   pmdp[0] = __pmd(pmdval);
   flush_pmd_entry(pmdp);
}

The underlying __pmd_populate() routine formats the target descriptor entry value to map exactly to (pte + PTE_HWTABLE_OFF) | prot. The subsequent chapters tracking fine-grained memory configuration explain why the system must adjust this layout offset to include PTE_HWTABLE_OFF rather than assigning a basic pte | prot bit mask.

Invoking pmd_populate_kernel(&init_mm, pmd, bm_pte) updates the level-1 page directory slot as follows:

pmd[0] = (__pa(bm_pte) + PTE_HWTABLE_OFF) | _PAGE_KERNEL_TABLE

As shown by this statement, pmd_populate_kernel() writes the absolute physical base address hosting the early Page Table Entry array bm_pte alongside its core memory attribute flags directly into the target PMD entry according to the formatting rules of the level-1 page directory. It then calls flush_pmd_entry() to force the cache controllers to clean this newly modified entry to memory, making the layout update active. This structural state update is visualized below:

Because the early bootstrap lifecycle enforces a single-tier section-level memory configuration, the primitive block management unit defaults to a 1 MB granularity. To execute fine-grained memory operations over smaller boundaries, the system introduces a specialized, early page table tracking array named bm_pte that encapsulates 512 standalone individual PTE slots. Within this 512-descriptor array, 256 entries are parsed exclusively to track software state flags for the Linux kernel, while the remaining 256 slots map directly to control bits checked by the ARM hardware. This design gives the early bootstrap framework a fine-grained translation resolution down to a standard 4 KB page limit.

As analyzed in Section 6.3.1, the binary bit alignment tracking a Short-descriptor PMD section descriptor follows this format:

The configuration constant _PAGE_KERNEL_TABLE (0b000110001) defines the target Domain field index and populates the control states for bits 4 and 0 within the descriptor word.

The data cache synchronization utility flush_pmd_entry(void *pmd) is maintained within the architecture tracking header arch/arm/include/asm/tblflush.h as follows:

static inline void flush_pmd_entry(void *pmd)
{
   const unsigned int __tlb_flag = __cpu_tlb_flags;
   tlb_op(TLB_DCLEAN, "c7, c10, 1        @ flush_pmd", pmd);
   tlb_l2_op(TLB_L2CLEAN_FR, "c15, c9, 1  @ L2 flush_pmd", pmd);
   if (tlb_flag(TLB_WB))
       dsb(ishst);
}

For ARM platforms, the flush_pmd_entry() handler expands via macro definitions to execute inline assembly instructions inside the C codebase. Upon compilation, the operations tlb_op(TLB_DCLEAN, ...) and tlb_l2_op(TLB_L2CLEAN_FR, ...) generate the following machine instructions:

mov rx, pmd
    ldr rt, [rx]
    mcr p15, 0, rt, c7, c10, 1        @ Clean data cache line by virtual address (MVA)
    mcr p15, 1, rt, c15, c9, 1        @ Clean L2 unified cache line by virtual address

Where rx and rt represent temporary working registers dynamically assigned by the compiler's optimization engine. The mcr coprocessor write commands copy the register data directly into the CP15 coprocessor control slots, forcing the cache controller to instantly clean the dirty memory descriptor from the L1/L2 cache blocks back out to physical RAM.

To clarify the precise data manipulation steps executed across this fixed memory mapping initializer, its comprehensive software processing path is presented in the flowchart below:

This concludes Section 8.2.4 and the deep architectural translation of the early fixmap subsystems.

8.2.5 Early I/O Remapping Initialization (early_ioremap_init)

As established previously, early-stage I/O operations rely on the fixed mapping (fixmap) region. For transactional use, this space is partitioned into seven contiguous segments indexed from 0 to 6. Each segment is designated as a tracking slot containing exactly 32 page table entries (PTEs). These slots store the virtual addresses allocated for active I/O peripheral configurations. By routing lookups through this fixmap framework, the kernel resolves the corresponding physical addresses of the target I/O registers. The relative index calculation for slot i is defined by the formula FIX_BTMAP_BEGIN - NR_FIX_BTMAPS * i, which evaluates to 32 * (7 - i).

The purpose of the early I/O remapping initializer early_ioremap_init() is to compute the exact virtual addresses corresponding to these relative slot configurations and archive them within the global tracking array slot_virt[]. This virtual address calculation is executed via the __fix_to_virt() preprocessor macro:

#define __fix_to_virt(x) (FIXADDR_TOP - ((x) \<\< PAGE_SHIFT))

The early_ioremap_init() function contains no architecture-specific dependencies; it calls the generic core Linux helper routine early_ioremap_setup(). Maintained within the memory module arch/arm/mm/ioremap.c, it is defined as follows:

void __init early_ioremap_init(void)
{
   early_ioremap_setup();
}

The core early_ioremap_setup() routine is implemented within the centralized memory management subsystem file mm/early_ioremap.c as follows:

void __init early_ioremap_setup(void)
{
	int i;
	for (i = 0; i < FIX_BTMAPS_SLOTS; i++)
		if (WARN_ON(prev_map[i]))
			break;
	for (i = 0; i < FIX_BTMAPS_SLOTS; i++)
		slot_virt[i] = __fix_to_virt(FIX_BTMAP_BEGIN - NR_FIX_BTMAPS * i);
}

The early I/O remapping pipeline manages its layout matrices using three centralized global tracking arrays: prev_map[], slot_virt[], and prev_size[]. Within this tracking matrix, prev_map[] stores the virtual base address of each active, in-use memory allocation, prev_size[] logs the linear size footprint of that allocation, and slot_virt[] records the starting virtual page address assigned to each individual slot. The architectural arithmetic relationship linking slot_virt[i] to its corresponding hardware slot index i is expressed as follows:

slot_virt[i] = FIXADDR_TOP - ((FIX_BTMAP_BEGIN - NR_FIX_BTMAPS*i) << PAGE_SHIFT)
             = 0xFFFEF000 – (FIX_BTMAP_END + 32 *  (7 - i) - 1) << PAGE_SHIFT
             = 0xFFFEF000 – （32 * (7 – i) << 12）

Under standard configuration templates, FIX_BTMAP_END evaluates to 1 and PAGE_SHIFT is fixed to 12 (representing a 4096-byte page size). The mapping layout and tracking dependencies linking the individual slots, page table entries, and physical memory frames are detailed in the schematic diagram below:

8.2.6 Boot Argument Parsing

The setup_arch() function copies the command-line boot parameters to the memory pointed to by the cmd_line pointer and invokes parse_early_options() to parse them. parse_early_options() internally calls parse_args() to evaluate all arguments supplied across the command line. The first input parameter of parse_args() is a string indicating the current phase; the second is a pointer to the arguments awaiting parsing; the third points to known parameters; the fourth defines the total number of arguments to check; the fifth and sixth specify the minimum and maximum parameter layers allowed; and the final argument points to a fallback callback function tasked with handling unrecognized parameters.

The argument parsing logic relies on parse_one(param, val, "early options", NULL, 0, 0, 0, NULL, do_early_param) to process each command-line variable sequentially. Because parse_args() passes a num_params value of 0 down to parse_one(), parse_one() itself skips basic command-line tokenization. Instead, it directly triggers the execution callback do_early_options() to inspect all historical parameters defined using legacy formats bounded between the linker symbols __setup_start and __setup_end. This legacy boot configuration structure is tracked via the struct obs_kernel_param descriptor block, which is declared as follows:

struct obs_kernel_param {
   const char *str;
   int (*setup_func)(char *);
   int early;
};

If the character string referenced by the .str pointer matches the active command-line argument parsed by the system, and the .early status flag bit evaluates to a non-zero value—or if the parsed argument context contains the sub-string "console" while a registered descriptor's .str field targets "earlycon"—the engine invokes the linked callback handler .setup_func to execute the corresponding peripheral configuration. If the compiled Linux kernel image lacks a dedicated .init.setup section, the parse_early_options() function completes without processing any operations.

8.2.7 Memory Attributes within the PMD Page Table Entries

For the ARM architecture, physical memory regions and memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) registers share a single consolidated address space. Specific regions or peripheral controllers require highly distinct hardware access attributes; for instance, certain RAM blocks support multiprocessor cache coherency sharing while others remain strictly isolated, and interrupt-driven peripheral input channels must bypass data caching entirely, whereas standard system memory relies heavily on write-back caching to optimize execution speeds. Based on these characteristics, the Linux kernel groups memory spaces into several distinct categories, ensuring that segments belonging to an identical class share uniform attributes and utilize identical page table entry flags. These native memory allocation classes are defined by the following enumeration block:

enum {
   MT_DEVICE = 0,
   MT_DEVICE_NONSHARED = 1,
   MT_DEVICE_CACHED = 2,
   MT_DEVICE_WC = 3,
   MT_MEMORY_RW_NS = 4,
   MT_UNCACHED = 5,
   MT_CACHECLEAN,
   MT_MINICLEAN,
   MT_LOW_VECTORS,
   MT_HIGH_VECTORS,
   MT_MEMORY_RWX,
   MT_MEMORY_RW,
   MT_ROM,
   MT_MEMORY_RWX_NONCACHED,
   MT_MEMORY_RW_DTCM,
   MT_MEMORY_RWX_ITCM,
   MT_MEMORY_RW_SO,
   MT_MEMORY_DMA_READY,
};

These highly specialized architectural mapping classes are modeled using the following structural metadata descriptor block:

struct mem_type {
	pteval_t prot_pte;
	pteval_t prot_pte_s2;
	pmdval_t prot_l1;
	pmdval_t prot_sect;
	unsigned int domain;
};

The function early_mm_init() invokes build_mem_type_table() to evaluate the current ARM generation, hardware platform extensions, and memory constraints. It parses the values assigned to the fields of individual mem_type records to determine the exact bit configurations tracking memory cacheability, shareability, and protection flags within the page table entries. The build_mem_type_table() routine is maintained within the memory module arch/arm/mm/mmu.c. Although the programmatic code footprint is extensive, the overwhelming majority of its logic branches handle conditional evaluations to verify the ARM processor family, flag active silicon errata workarounds, and check for 40-bit Large Physical Address Extensions (LPAE).

Following the completion of build_mem_type_table(), early_mm_init() calls the fallback routine early_paging_init(). This handler functions as a dynamic runtime patcher for platforms enabling large physical address translations. On legacy processors restricted to a standard 32-bit physical address space, if the system's machine_desc board descriptor explicitly provides a platform-specific .pv_fixup hook, early_paging_init() executes that callback; otherwise, it compiles directly down to a no-operation block.

8.2.8 DMA Allocation Zones Configuration

When subsystems allocate physical memory chunks using the kernel's memory management engines, they can pass the hardware allocation flag GFP_DMA to specify low-level requirements. The function setup_dma_zone() is invoked on startup to calculate and enforce the absolute physical upper boundary address permitted when a software routine issues a GFP_DMA allocation loop.

If this function is bypassed during architecture bring-up, or if the preprocessor build flag CONFIG_ZONE_DMA is omitted during compilation, the allocation subsystem defaults to imposing no physical address bounds over DMA requests. The setup_dma_zone() function enforces these boundary parameters globally across the platform by calculating and setting the core variables arm_dma_zone_size, arm_dma_limit, and arm_dma_pfn_limit.

8.2.9 Virtual Machine Monitor Subsystem (Xen)

Xen is a hypervisor-based virtualization technology that leverages a Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM, or Hypervisor) to allow multiple decoupled guest operating systems (Guest OS) to install and execute concurrently on a single hardware platform. The foundational structural relationship bridging the underlying hardware, the hypervisor, and the individual guest instances is mapped out in the schematic diagram below:

Within this topology, the distinct Virtual Machines (VMs) execute unprivileged user-space applications and run within the unprivileged DomU (User Domain) region. Conversely, Dom0 (Domain 0) operates as a highly privileged management layer whose architectural responsibility is to coordinate the global Xen engine, manage hardware allocations, and orchestrate the lifecycle or execution paths of guest domains. The hypervisor layer abstracts and executes low-level core scheduling, complex virtual memory management, and x-session management tasks—operations traditionally restricted to highly privileged execution modes.

Contemporary virtualization architectures implement hypervisors using two primary design methodologies. Type 1 Hypervisors execute bare-metal, running directly over the raw hardware platform without requiring an underlying host operating system. Consequently, a Type 1 hypervisor must implement a comprehensive suite of device drivers and resource management sub-blocks that are traditionally handled by an operating system core. Conversely, Type 2 Hypervisors sit as an application layer on top of a host operating system, leveraging the host's existing driver frameworks and infrastructure instead of re-implementing them. Because this model relies on the capabilities of an underlying operating system, it introduces the concept of a Host OS. The hypervisor utilizes the host kernel's core primitives to orchestrate physical machine virtualization. The structural block diagram below illustrates a Xen environment deployment leveraging a native Host OS configuration:

The Linux operating system can be deployed both as a native Host OS providing underlying hypervisor features, and as a Guest OS executing inside an isolated virtual machine window. Mainline ARM Linux kernels natively identify exactly three virtual domain operational states: XEN_NATIVE, XEN_PV_DOMAIN, and XEN_HVM_DOMAIN.

  • XEN_NATIVE: Indicates that the Linux kernel is running directly on the bare-metal hardware. Under this operational profile, the kernel entirely suppresses Xen virtualization and disables all hypervisor hooks.

  • XEN_PV_DOMAIN: Configures the kernel to run within a Paravirtualized (PV) environment. Paravirtualization represents an early virtualization technique that does not rely on hardware acceleration features. Instead, it uses software modifications to emulate core block disk interfaces, network drivers, interrupt controllers, and system timers. This model requires the guest kernel to issue specialized supervisor instructions and interact with the MMU via explicit service requests known as Hypercalls. Running a Linux subsystem under a PV architecture requires deep kernel modifications; to support PV configurations, the Linux image must embed specialized hypervisor interface logic alongside concrete Dom0 and DomU code layers. The schematic diagram below maps out the system architecture of a virtual machine deployed via PV mechanics:

  • XEN_HVM_DOMAIN: Configures the kernel to run within a Hardware Virtual Machine (HVM) environment. Under this operational profile, Linux leverages hardware virtualization extensions built into the CPU silicon to handle hypercall routines and trap executions automatically. The primary advantage of this model is that it dramatically accelerates execution speeds and allows standard, unmodified operating system binaries to run without kernel code adjustments. While the x86 architecture has historically provided comprehensive hardware extensions to assist virtual machine monitors, the ARM architecture also integrates high-performance virtualization hardware modules as a configurable option for silicon designers.

The Linux kernel registers and tracks whether the underlying hardware platform supports Xen virtualization using a specialized global tracking instance of type struct hyper_node. The structural declaration and default fallback assignments for this tracking variable are initialized as follows:

static __initdata struct {
   const char *compat;
   const char *prefix;
   const char *version;
   bool found;
} hyper_node = { "xen,xen", "xen,xen-", NULL, false };

The early initialization routine xen_early_init() handles the initial setup of this subsystem. It first invokes the flattened tree traversal manager of_scan_flat_dt() to sweep across the device tree nodes and utilizes the execution callback fdt_find_hyper_node() to scan the root tree branches for a node explicitly named "hypervisor". If a valid hypervisor node block is resolved, the engine checks its compatible string array to verify if it contains the required tracking tokens "xen,xen" or "xen,xen-". Matching these string filters confirms that the platform supports a Xen environment.

Upon successfully verifying hypervisor compatibility, the fdt_find_hyper_node() callback flags the .found field inside the global hyper_node structure to true. It then parses the trailing version numbers following the "xen,xen-" string literal within the FDT configuration and combines them with the .prefix string field to write the resulting version tracking parameters directly into the .version pointer field of the hyper_node database.

Once a valid hypervisor node has been parsed and authenticated from the device tree, the xen_early_init() function initializes the global state variable xen_domain_type to XEN_HVM_DOMAIN, directing the kernel to default to hardware-assisted HVM virtualization mode.

As analyzed in the low-level assembly bootstrap chapters, the early initialization sequence inside head.S implements the branch command bl __hyp_stub_install. If the underlying platform configuration supports hardware virtualization extensions, this command executes to call the __hyp_stub_install routine. This routine programs the ARM processor's hypervisor-mode coprocessor registers, including HVBAR (Hyp Vector Base Address Register), HCPTR (Hyp Coprocessor Trap Register), HSTR (Hyp System Trap Register), HSCTLR (Hyp System Control Register), HDCR (Hyp Debug Configuration Register), and SCTLR. Within this configuration block, HVBAR registers the absolute execution entry point routing to the hypervisor's exception and interrupt handlers, while the remaining control registers regulate the execution limits and virtualization boundaries of the ARM core. The __hyp_stub_install assembly loop is maintained within the architecture source module git/arch/arm/kernel/hyp-stub.S.

Following the configuration of the global xen_domain_type state variable, xen_early_init() invokes the feature discovery function xen_setup_features() to determine the exact matrix of virtualization features supported by the host environment, archiving the resulting capabilities bitmask inside the global array xen_features[].

To achieve this, xen_setup_features() calls the low-level wrapper HYPERVISOR_xen_version(), passing the explicit hypercall identifier constant __HYPERVISOR_xen_version (index 17) directly into register r12, and fires a hardware Hypervisor Call (hvc) exception instruction [1]. This forces an execution trap into the hypervisor's HVC exception service routine, allowing the kernel to query and audit the active features exported by the virtualization engine. The HYPERVISOR_xen_version() hypercall wrapper is defined within the architecture assembly module arch/arm/xen/hypercall.S.

Finally, if the validation pass confirms that the system is running as a privileged Dom0 management instance, xen_early_init() sets the global configuration flags within xen_start_flags. If the boot arguments have omitted an explicit console terminal definition for Dom0, the routine sets the default management console to route over the virtualized hypervisor console interface device (hvc).

8.2.10 Early Extensible Firmware Interface (EFI) Initialization

As noted in Section 4.1, the EFI System Partition (ESP) is a dedicated partition on the storage medium used to host bootloader programs formatted in the EFI standard. Regardless of whether the disk layout relies on a GUID Partition Table (GPT) or a legacy Master Boot Record (MBR), a motherboard platform executing a native UEFI-compliant boot sequence must contain an operational EFI partition, which is typically mounted under the /boot or /boot/efi directory path. (Note: Unlike standard desktop systems, native UEFI-compliant booting is rarely deployed within traditional embedded systems, which instead rely predominantly on direct U-BOOT execution paths).

The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) standardizes the low-level software layer bridging the underlying hardware platform and motherboard firmware with the guest operating system and its companion bootstrap loaders. A platform and firmware layer adhering strictly to the UEFI specification export a vast matrix of standard protocol interfaces and foundational hooks optimized across various storage media (including CD-ROMs, DVDs, USB mass storage, SD cards, SCSI disks, and network-based PXE interfaces). These services encompass standard partition layout parsers, secure boot verification paths, boot-time initialization services (Boot Services), and persistent runtime services (Runtime Services). The platform firmware also executes an internal Boot Manager engine to orchestrate the system-wide booting pipeline.

Consequently, any operating system or bootloader engineered to comply with the UEFI specification can initiate a clean boot cycle directly on a UEFI-compatible platform by invoking these standard service calls, completely abstracting away the granular silicon-level hardware configurations of the motherboard. Furthermore, UEFI allows the operating system loader and hardware properties to be indexed inside an interactive startup menu, enabling operators to choose dynamically from multiple distinct operating system targets. These independent operating systems can safely reside across entirely separate partitions spanning heterogeneous storage mediums.

When the platform firmware's early boot service loader LoadImage() finishes reading the operating system bootloader application binary into memory, it relinquishes execution control over to that bootloader. During this architectural handover, the platform firmware passes exactly two parameter arguments down to the operating system bootloader: the platform-assigned image handle matching the current loader instance and a master pointer targeting the primary System Table (System Table Pointer). The image handle serves as a specialized, unique interface identifier provided by the platform to service that specific loader thread. The System Table Pointer targets the master data block repository tracking the operational metrics of the current platform context; this table encapsulates entry pointers routing to standard character input/output device routines, a lookup pointer matrix targeting the structural Boot Services table, a secondary pointer matrix referencing the Runtime Services table, a master system configuration index table, and specific references to an array of secondary standardized description tables. Every data block compliant with the UEFI standard must strictly initiate its structure with a standardized table header, which is defined as follows:

struct {
	u64 Signature;
	u32 Revision;
	u32 HeaderSize;
	u32 CRC32;
	u32 Reserved;
}

The 64-bit .Signature field acts as a unique cryptographic key variable used to differentiate table classes; for example, the master System Table is hardcoded with the signature string 0x5453595320494249, the Boot Services matrix registers the identification signature 0x56524553544f4f42, and the specialized Runtime Services block is identified by the signature string 0x56524553544e5552.

The core architectural layout mapping the primary System Table is structured as follows:

struct {
	EFI_TABLE_HEADER Hdr;
	char16 *FirmwareVendor;
	u32 FirmwareRevision;
	EFI_HANDLE ConsoleInHandle;
	EFI_SIMPLE_TEXT_INPUT_PROTOCOL *ConIn;
	EFI_HANDLE ConsoleOutHandle;
	EFI_SIMPLE_TEXT_OUTPUT_PROTOCOL *ConOut;
	EFI_HANDLE StandardErrorHandle;
	EFI_SIMPLE_TEXT_OUTPUT_PROTOCOL *StdErr;
	EFI_RUNTIME_SERVICES *RuntimeServices;
	EFI_BOOT_SERVICES *BootServices;
	UINTN NumberOfTableEntries;
	EFI_CONFIGURATION_TABLE *ConfigurationTable;
}

The .NumberOfTableEntries parameter registers the total count of external configuration descriptors populated inside the array, while each element inside the Configuration Table adheres to the following structural format:

struct {
	EFI_GUID VendorGuid;
	void *VendorTable;
}

The early system routine efi_init() handles the initial stage-1 setup loops required to prepare the kernel context when booting from a UEFI interface. This function is maintained within the core firmware driver path git/drivers/firmware/efi/efi-init.c with the following definition:

void __init efi_init(void)
{
struct efi_memory_map_data data;
u64 efi_system_table;
/* Retrieve FDT (Flattened Device Tree) parameters and initialize memory mapping */
efi_system_table = efi_get_fdt_params(&data);
if (!efi_system_table) 
return;
/* Perform early initialization of the EFI memory map; panic on failure */
if (efi_memmap_init_early(&data) < 0) panic("Unable to map EFI memory map.\n");
/* Initialize UEFI system table and runtime services */
if (uefi_init(efi_system_table) < 0) {
	efi_memmap_unmap();
	return;
}
reserve_regions();         /* Reserve standard physical memory regions */
efi_esrt_init();           /* Initialize EFI System Resource Table (ESRT) for firmware updates */
efi_mokvar_table_init();   /* Initialize Machine Owner Key (MOK) variable table for Secure Boot */
/* Reserve the physical memory block occupied by the EFI memory map to prevent overwriting */
memblock_reserve(data.phys_map & PAGE_MASK,
	 PAGE_ALIGN(data.size + (data.phys_map & ~PAGE_MASK)));
init_screen_info();        /* Initialize screen display info (framebuffer, etc.) for early console */
#ifdef CONFIG_ARM
/* ARM architecture-specific handling: unmap early memory map */
efi_memmap_unmap();
if (cpu_state_table != EFI_INVALID_TABLE_ADDR) {
/* ... (Omitted specific status check code) */
}
#endif
}

The unified struct efi master database encapsulates global data tracking indicators, persistent system pointers, and abstract firmware service hooks, which are structured according to the following programmatic declaration:

extern struct efi {
   const efi_runtime_services_t     *runtime;               /* EFI Runtime Services Table pointer */
   unsigned int                     runtime_version;        /* Runtime services implementation version */
   unsigned int                     runtime_supported_mask;
   unsigned long                    acpi;                   /* ACPI Table absolute address (IA64 ext 0.71) */
   unsigned long                    acpi20;                 /* ACPI 2.0 Table absolute address */
   unsigned long                    smbios;                 /* SMBIOS Table address (32-bit entry point) */
   unsigned long                    smbios3;                /* SMBIOS Table address (64-bit entry point) */
   unsigned long                    esrt;                   /* EFI System Resource Table address */
   unsigned long                    tpm_log;                /* TPM2 Event Log tracking table base */
   unsigned long                    tpm_final_log;          /* TPM2 Final Event Log tracking table base */
   unsigned long                    mokvar_table;           /* Machine Owner Key (MOK) configuration table */
   efi_get_time_t                   *get_time;
   efi_set_time_t                   *set_time;
   efi_get_wakeup_time_t            *get_wakeup_time;
   efi_set_wakeup_time_t            *set_wakeup_time;
   efi_get_variable_t               *get_variable;
   efi_get_next_variable_t          *get_next_variable;
   efi_set_variable_t               *set_variable;
   efi_set_variable_t               *set_variable_nonblocking;
   
efi_query_variable_info_t        *query_variable_info;
   efi_query_variable_info_t        *query_variable_info_nonblocking;
   efi_update_capsule_t             *update_capsule;
   efi_query_capsule_caps_t         *query_capsule_caps;
   efi_get_next_high_mono_count_t   *get_next_high_mono_count;
   efi_reset_system_t               *reset_system;
   struct efi_memory_map            memmap;
   unsigned long                    flags;
};

Upon completing the device tree scanning pass, the efi_get_fdt_params() internal routine parses the FDT nodes to extract the firmware memory allocation parameters. This early structure maps out the memory map metadata as follows:

struct efi_memory_map_data {
   phys_addr_t     phys_map;        /* Absolute physical address of the EFI memory map */
   unsigned long   size;            /* Linear size byte-count of the memory allocation map */
   unsigned long   desc_version;    /* EFI memory descriptor structural version format */
   unsigned long   desc_size;       /* Byte size dimension of an individual memory descriptor */
   unsigned long   flags;           /* Operational memory trait configuration flags */
};

After validating this memory map structure, efi_init() calls efi_memmap_init_early() to instantiate temporary page table mappings over this data region within the virtual fixmap zone. This sequence maps the virtual addresses directly down to their matching physical coordinates and utilizes the resolved mappings to fully populate the internal .memmap attribute tracking cluster inside the master efi global database. The structural tracking context of the .memmap nested block is organized as follows:

struct efi_memory_map {
   phys_addr_t     phys_map;        /* Absolute physical base address of the memory allocation map */
   void            *map;            /* Local virtual base address pointing to the memory map */
   void            *map_end;        /* Virtual boundary marking the end of the memory map block */
   int             nr_map;          /* Total count of valid descriptor segments mapped in the array */
   unsigned long   desc_version;
   unsigned long   desc_size;
   unsigned long   flags;
};

As detailed in the preceding section, the platform firmware utilizes the System Table pointer to expose and pass baseline parameters to the guest operating system kernel. By mapping and analyzing the configuration metrics supplied via this device tree system table node, the kernel can safely evaluate and override default hardware initializations.

Once the early memory map translation entries are fully operational inside the fixmap architecture, the efi_init() master handler shifts execution down to invoke uefi_init() to process the primary UEFI System Table. Maintained within the specialized driver framework file drivers/firmware/efi/efi-init.c, uefi_init() initially utilizes the __early_ioremap() routing utility to construct dedicated look-up paths over the System Table virtual region inside the fixmap area.

It then calls efi_systab_check_header() to execute integrity checks validating the System Table's signature words and revision tracking version, verifying that the payload data structures match specifications supported by the running kernel tree. Following this validation loop, the routine reads the metadata tracking parameters embedded inside the FDT's system table representation to initialize the global .runtime service function pointer block inside the master efi structure, registers the active .runtime_version constant, and outputs core diagnostic strings to log the hardware vendor name and firmware platform revision parameters to the console device.

Having successfully finalized the System Table configurations, the uefi_init() routine steps forward to parse the general configuration table array, which is statically tracked via the common_tables[] variable:

static const efi_config_table_type_t common_tables[] __initconst = {
	{ ACPI_20_TABLE_GUID, &efi.acpi20, "ACPI 2.0" },
	{ ACPI_TABLE_GUID, &efi.acpi, "ACPI" },
	{ SMBIOS_TABLE_GUID, &efi.smbios, "SMBIOS" },
	{ SMBIOS3_TABLE_GUID, &efi.smbios3, "SMBIOS 3.0" },
	{ EFI_SYSTEM_RESOURCE_TABLE_GUID, &efi.esrt, "ESRT" },
	{ EFI_MEMORY_ATTRIBUTES_TABLE_GUID, &efi_mem_attr_table, 
"MEMATTR" },
	{ LINUX_EFI_RANDOM_SEED_TABLE_GUID, &efi_rng_seed, "RNG" },
	{ LINUX_EFI_TPM_EVENT_LOG_GUID, &efi.tpm_log, "TPMEventLog" },
	{ LINUX_EFI_TPM_FINAL_LOG_GUID, &efi.tpm_final_log, "TPMFinalLog" },
	{ LINUX_EFI_MEMRESERVE_TABLE_GUID, &mem_reserve, 
"MEMRESERVE" },
	{ EFI_RT_PROPERTIES_TABLE_GUID, &rt_prop, "RTPROP" },
#ifdef CONFIG_EFI_RCI2_TABLE
	{ DELLEMC_EFI_RCI2_TABLE_GUID, &rci2_table_phys },
#endif
#ifdef CONFIG_LOAD_UEFI_KEYS
	{ LINUX_EFI_MOK_VARIABLE_TABLE_GUID, &efi.mokvar_table, "MOKvar" },
#endif
	{},
};

This array encapsulates critical architecture parameters, including the Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) matrices and the hardware entropy seed vectors used to initialize the early kernel random number generation engines. Each array element binds a unique 128-bit Global Unique Identifier (GUID) key string to its corresponding physical target table pointer address.

The uefi_init() parser handles these fields by first invoking __early_ioremap() to construct early virtual pathways mapping the table configurations inside the fixmap layout, then routes execution straight into efi_config_parse_tables() to loop across and unpack the contents of the sub-tables. If the specific GUID token (VendorGuid) matching an incoming table entry is not matched inside this global common_tables[] database but is instead matched inside the architecture-dependent table array arch_tables[], the parsing engine dynamically replaces the target reference pointer inside arch_tables[] with the new .VendorTable base pointer provided by the device tree, cleanly executing a live firmware configuration override.

Upon completing this table parsing loop, if parameters like efi_rng_seed, mem_reserve, or rt_prop contain valid address locations rather than evaluating to the initialization constant EFI_INVALID_TABLE_ADDR, it signifies that the device tree configuration has successfully supplied valid hardware entropy pools, protected memory layouts, or specialized runtime performance properties that must be applied to configure the kernel environment.

Under this condition, efi_config_parse_tables() updates the underlying memory constraints by calling early_memremap(), modifying the mapping attributes of these specific pages to match the standard memory page type FIXMAP_PAGE_NORMAL. It then maps these tables straight into the kernel's virtual addressing space via __early_ioremap(). Finally, if the initialization parameters demand that physical memory regions be permanently walled off to secure persistent firmware tracking tables, the parsing handler triggers the memblock_reserve() memory manager to flag those specific coordinates as reserved physical RAM blocks, shielding them from general kernel allocations.

If the hardware architecture executes a native UEFI boot sequence, the accompanying Flattened Device Tree must also supply the memory allocation table characteristics, which describe how the UEFI System Table, configuration matrices, and transient runtime contexts are structured inside physical RAM. An individual entry within this memory allocation map is explicitly modeled using the following structural memory descriptor block:

struct {
        u32 type;               /* Memory allocation type (e.g., usable RAM, boot code, or reserved firmware blocks) */
        u32 pad;                /* Formatting padding field */
        u64 phys_addr;          /* Physical address */
        u64 virt_addr;          /* Virtual address */
        u64 num_pages;          /* Number of pages */
        u64 attribute;          /* Memory attribute */
};

Upon completing the uefi_init() function loop, efi_init() routes execution down to invoke the reserve_regions() routine. This helper function parses the individual memory descriptor parameters supplied by the device tree's memory allocation table attributes to dynamically register and append these active firmware memory regions straight into either the usable physical RAM block array (memblock.memory) or the protected, walled-off section tracking table (memblock.reserved) deployed during the early Linux bootstrap phase.

Starting with specification version 2.3, the UEFI standard introduces native framework support to coordinate low-level firmware updates. To manage these updates cleanly, the specification defines the EFI System Resource Table (ESRT), which is organized according to the following layout:

struct efi_system_resource_table {
        u32    fw_resource_count;
        u32    fw_resource_count_max;
        u64    fw_resource_version;
        u8     entries[];
};

Within this layout, the .entries[] block acts as a contiguous array composed of the following structural v1 system resource entries:

struct efi_system_resource_entry_v1 {
        efi_guid_t    fw_class;
        u32           fw_type;
        u32           fw_version;
        u32           lowest_supported_fw_version;
        u32           capsule_flags;
        u32           last_attempt_version;
        u32           last_attempt_status;
};

The function efi_esrt_init() initially determines whether a valid System Resource Table is present in the platform context. If the platform exposes an active resource table, the routine scans across the primary memory allocation maps to resolve the matching memory descriptor matching the ESRT tracking parameters. After validating the structural integrity and physical alignment of this system resource memory descriptor, it calls early_memremap() to instantiate early translation page table entries mapping this table inside the virtual fixmap zone. Finally, it assigns the resolved virtual address of the resource table straight to the global tracking variable esrt_data and writes the absolute table size byte-count into the global variable esrt_data_size.

Furthermore, the UEFI standard formalizes cryptographic Secure Boot protocols. When a platform enforces Secure Boot parameters, the motherboard firmware restricts execution exclusively to operating system kernels and third-party hardware device drivers that carry authenticated signatures authorized by the machine owner. To execute this secure verification pipeline, Linux defines a specialized global user credential database named the MOK (Machine Owner Key) Variable Table, where individual entries are structured according to the following descriptor format:

struct efi_mokvar_table_entry {
	char name[256];    		/* Cryptographic key signature identifier name string */
	u64  data_size;    		/* Exact byte-size dimension consumed by the key payload */
	u8   data[];        	/* Raw cryptographic key binary array */
};

When a secure, cryptographically guarded hardware platform boots, the system's global table registry (common_tables[]) contains a dedicated MOKvar descriptor entry, and a matching memory tracking descriptor is populated inside the primary memory allocation maps. The efi_init() master routine invokes efi_mokvar_table_init() to audit whether Secure Boot mechanisms are active on the platform. If the verification pass confirms Secure Boot alignment, it interrogates the memory allocation maps to locate the memory descriptor tracking the base of the user credential database. Upon resolving this target descriptor, efi_mokvar_table_init() sweeps across the embedded keys to inspect their relative data size bytes and authenticate their individual structural integrity. Once validated, it maps the entire database into virtual space by constructing temporary page table entries inside the fixmap region and permanently fences off this memory zone by adding its coordinates to the global memblock.reserved tracking array.

Once the system finishes instantiating the early translation page table paths mapping every required UEFI table payload into memory, the uefi_init() routine dynamically updates the system structures to flag the physical memory blocks occupied by the primary memory allocation map itself as completely reserved physical RAM.

When a platform launches via UEFI pipelines, it can leverage an EFI-native graphic frame buffer display infrastructure. If the platform initializes an EFI display layout, the kernel intercepts the physical address range matching the linear frame buffer base coordinate (lfb_base) and explicitly registers this region as non-direct-mapped kernel memory. Fencing off this graphics window prevents the core kernel's memory management engines from mapping standard direct virtual address translation entries over the frame buffer cells. This physical baseline coordinate is archived inside the global display telemetry structure struct screen_info.

The architecture-specific global hardware description table targeting ARM systems encapsulates a default screen info configuration profile. UEFI-driven boot routines parse this table to configure and register the primary display terminal.

Low-level infrastructure utilities tasked with parsing and executing core EFI transactions—such as efi_config_parse_tables() and efi_systab_check_header()—are defined within the core firmware processing module /drivers/firmware/efi/efi.c. Concurrently, the overarching initialization functions, memory re-mapping loops, and memory reservation allocation subroutines tracking this subsystem are maintained within the source file /drivers/firmware/efi/efi-init.c. The end-to-end technical flowchart tracking the operational stages of the efi_init() function is presented in the schematic below:

8.2.11 Core Architectural Concepts of Address Translation

8.2.11.1 Early Boot-Stage Memory Allocator (memblock)

During the early bootstrap phase of the Linux kernel, system components continuously demand physical memory spaces to complete system staging or release transient tracking arrays. However, because the final virtual page table hierarchy has not yet been built and the highly capable main page and slab management frameworks are not yet active, the kernel must rely on a primitive direct address allocation tracking mechanism known as the Memblock Allocator to coordinate its early physical address mappings. By initializing and populating the early translation page tables during this bootstrap window, the allocator establishes the mandatory prerequisites for subsequent runtime Linux memory management. This section details the process through which Linux brings up its early page table configurations.

The early boot lifecycle relies exclusively on the global memblock variable instance to track and govern physical memory partitions. The memblock allocator is instantiated as a data structure of type struct memblock, whose core layout is configured as follows:

struct memblock {
/* Flag defining the direction of early memory allocation (low-to-high vs high-to-low) */
        bool bottom_up; 
/* Enforces the absolute maximum physical ceiling address permitted for allocations */
        phys_addr_t current_limit;  
/* Sub-structure tracking all physical blocks registered as usable RAM */
        struct memblock_type memory;   
/* Sub-structure tracking all physical blocks fenced off as protected memory */
        struct memblock_type reserved; 
};

Within this layout, the .bottom_up boolean variable dictates the trajectory algorithm utilized to isolate unallocated memory pools, and .current_limit restricts the upper physical addressing boundaries. Early system memory partitions are strictly divided into usable physical RAM blocks (registered via the .memory context domain) and protected memory windows (tracked via the .reserved context domain). Both the usable and reserved memory matrices are driven by the struct memblock_type structure, configured according to the following programmatic layout:

struct memblock_type {
        unsigned long cnt;           /* Count of distinct, non-contiguous physical memory regions currently in the array */
        unsigned long max;        /* Maximum array limit threshold allowed for region tracking slots */
        phys_addr_t total_size; /* Combined linear volume of all tracked blocks inside the array measured in bytes */
/* Reference base pointer targeting the primary array of memblock region descriptors */
        struct memblock_region *regions; 
        char *name;             /* Descriptive text identification string assigned to the memory type */
};

The parameter .cnt tracks the real-time count of isolated, non-contiguous memory segments currently linked to the array, .max defines the allocation threshold bounding the array slice, and .total_size captures the total byte capacity aggregated across all active elements. The .regions pointer targets the absolute base of an allocated array composed of individual struct memblock_region descriptor records, mapping out every discrete memory block belonging to that memory category. An individual memory block region is tracked using the following structural layout:

struct memblock_region {
        phys_addr_t base;            /* Absolute starting physical address of the specific memory block */
        phys_addr_t size;            /* Linear byte-size capacity or length of the memory block region */
        enum memblock_flags flags;   /* Architectural allocation trait masks applied to the memory block */
        int nid;     /* Numerical identifier index mapping the region to its target hardware NUMA node */
};

The physical block layout and structural cross-references governing the early memblock subsystem are presented in the schematic below:

The early kernel exports an array of dedicated, minimalist allocation wrappers optimized for use during the earliest phases of architecture bring-up. Upon successfully carving out a physical block pool to fulfill an allocation request, the subsystem automatically invokes the tracking handler memblock_reserve() to permanently add the target block coordinates to the global .reserved list, protecting the memory from being overwritten by subsequent allocations.

As detailed in the fields of the region structure, each distinct memory block is explicitly mapped using its base boundary address, its linear length parameter, its specific allocation flags, and its hardware NUMA Node Identification token (nid). The specific architectural characteristics tracking a region's configuration flags can be set to manage standard RAM targets, identify volatile columns supporting dynamic physical insertion, mirror high-reliability zones, or shield specific blocks from kernel direct-mapping lookups, as defined by the following bitmask enumeration:

enum memblock_flags {
        MEMBLOCK_NONE     = 0x0,    /* Standard memory allocation profile containing no specialized layout constraints */
        MEMBLOCK_HOTPLUG  = 0x1,    /* Fences off the target region as a volatile memory block supporting physical hot-plug operations */
        MEMBLOCK_MIRROR   = 0x2,    /* Identifies mirrored physical RAM blocks duplicated for fault-tolerant reliability extensions */
        MEMBLOCK_NOMAP    = 0x4,    /* Restricts the block to prevent the kernel from instantiating direct virtual translation maps over it */
};

8.2.11.2 Linux Linked Lists

Heaps, stacks, singly linked lists, doubly linked lists, circular linked lists, and queues are fundamental data structures that are extensively utilized across the entire software engineering paradigm. To streamline data tracking and optimize cross-subsystem messaging, the Linux kernel defines a comprehensive suite of native macros and inline handlers to manipulate data lists. The generic, doubly linked list operations are declared within the master framework header git/include/linux/list.h. Concurrently, highly optimized list primitives capable of executing concurrent Read-Copy-Update operations are maintained within the synchronization header git/include/linux/rculist.h, while other specialized lists are distributed across dedicated subsystem headers.

The core Linux architecture relies almost entirely on formal list abstractions to implement higher-level sequential structures; data paradigms such as software queues, stacks, and FIFO (First-In, First-Out) buffers are constructed using fundamental list manipulation macros such as list_add_tail() or list_add().

A standard kernel list is structurally anchored by a master list head and composed of multiple sequential element nodes. The structural anchor is declared using the primitive struct list_head layout, which encapsulates forward and backward tracking references:

struct list_head {
    struct list_head *next, *prev;
};

The literal variable name assigned to this list head identifier serves as the global key tracking the entire database chain, enabling kernel routines to traverse the underlying nodes from this entry point. Typically, developers invoke the initialization macro LIST_HEAD(name) to instantiate and declare an empty list anchor named name.

An individual list node encapsulates the payload metadata required by the subsystem, composed of an embedded member of type struct list_head paired with one or more operational data fields. For example, the following block maps out a standard virtual memory tracking entry:

struct static_vm {
    struct vm_struct vm;
    struct list_head list;
};

In the majority of kernel data layouts, the .list tracking field is placed at the absolute front of the custom container structure to simplify lookups and accelerate relative offset calculations. The physical tracking configurations and pointer links governing these sequential structural paradigms are illustrated in the schematics below:

8.2.11.3 Linux I/O Virtual Memory Management

The Linux kernel tracks and coordinates the virtual address windows allocated to peripheral memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) controllers using a global linked list named static_vmlist paired with a master reference tracking pointer named vmlist. An individual node inside the static_vmlist hierarchy is instantiated as a data structure of type struct static_vm, while the global vmlist tracking pointer references an underlying struct vm_struct instance. The vm_struct descriptor block is declared within the virtual memory abstractions header as follows:

struct vm_struct {
	struct vm_struct    *next;    /* Pointer link to the subsequent vm_struct node in the chain */
	void                *addr;      /* Base virtual address of the allocated memory window */
	unsigned long       size;       /* Combined linear size footprint of the allocation in bytes */
	unsigned long       flags;      /* System configuration allocation capability flags */
	struct page         **pages;    /* Array of physical page descriptors mapping back the allocation */
	unsigned int        nr_pages;   /* Total number of physical page frames managed by the segment */
	phys_addr_t       phys_addr;  /* Absolute physical address boundary matching the I/O region */
	const void         *caller;    /* Reference tracking the invoking subsystem or device driver */
};

The matching struct static_vm container node encapsulating this database is structured as follows:

struct static_vm {
	struct vm_struct vm;    	/* Nested allocation metadata structure */
	struct list_head list;    	/* standard doubly linked tracking list pointers */
};

The structural linkage and multi-dimensional tracking layers joining static_vmlist and the global vmlist database are organized as illustrated in the schematic diagram below:

Because the .next field embedded inside the vm_struct definition explicitly references the subsequent vm_struct instance, the global vmlist tracking pointer effectively anchors and traverses the absolute head node of this structural memory chain.

The platform architecture routine iotable_init() handles the initial setup of these I/O translation layers. It first creates permanent, level-1 translation page table descriptors for the virtual address channels requested via an incoming struct map_desc array. It then utilizes the configuration metrics provided by the mapping parameters to seamlessly insert the compiled vm_struct allocation blocks into both the static_vmlist and vmlist lookup chains. The map_desc parameter layout is declared as follows:

struct map_desc {
	unsigned long virtual;      /* Intended target virtual base address of the I/O channel */
	unsigned long pfn;          /* PFN marking the boundary of the hardware I/O resource */
	unsigned long length;       /* Linear byte-size capacity or width of the mapping window */
	unsigned int  type;         /* Memory attribute classification index matching the memory type */
};

This descriptor tracks the absolute starting virtual coordinate, the hardware-mapped Page Frame Number (PFN), the total allocation length, and the specific memory caching traits matching the targeted I/O layout.

For each individual map_desc element passed to the function, iotable_init() first claims a raw memory slice from the early boot-stage allocator to hold the static_vm descriptor tracking block. Following this allocation step, it parses the metadata parameters inside map_desc to initialize the various field assignments tracking the static_vm instance. Finally, the function inserts this newly configured static_vm descriptor into the master static_vmlist doubly linked list and wires its internal .vm.next pointer fields to insert the node directly into the centralized tracking chain anchored by the global vmlist reference pointer.

8.2.11.4 Linux Resource Management Subsystem

To implement a unified framework for managing peripheral components, the Linux kernel categorizes physical hardware resources into discrete operational infrastructure classes, including MEM (Memory-mapped IO), IO (I/O Ports), REG (Registers), IRQ (Interrupt Requests), DMA (Direct Memory Access Channels), and BUS configurations. The kernel maps and monitors each individual tracking asset through the following struct resource descriptor layout:

struct resource {
        resource_size_t start;       /* Absolute physical starting address boundary of the resource */
        resource_size_t end;         /* Absolute physical terminating address boundary of the resource */
        const char *name;            /* Descriptive identification string assigned to the resource */
        unsigned long flags;         /* Bitmask tracking resource type attributes and access capabilities */
        unsigned long desc;          /* Additional system configuration description flags */
        struct resource *parent, *sibling, *child; /* Hierarchical tree management pointer links */
};

Before an individual peripheral hardware module or integrated controller driver can execute programmatic I/O transactions, it must first file a reservation request with the core resource manager to claim its intended address range.

The CPU interfaces with physical peripheral microarchitectures using one of two primary hardware access methodologies.

  • I/O Port-Mapped Architecture: The CPU drives dedicated, independent read/write control signaling lines to manage peripheral transactions. Under this setup, the address space allocated to hardware peripherals is entirely decoupled from the address window mapping system RAM, allowing overlapping numeric coordinates to coexist without conflict. This isolated peripheral boundary space is traditionally designated as I/O Ports.

  • Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) Architecture: The CPU shares a unified bus control signaling matrix to coordinate read/write operations for both standard system memory and peripherals. Peripherals and system RAM share a single, consolidated address plane, meaning a peripheral register address must be unique and cannot cross-allocate or collide with a physical RAM coordinate. This integrated peripheral space is designated as Peripheral Memory or I/O Memory (iomem).

To track these distinct access models, Linux instantiates two global framework tracking variables of type struct resource: iomem_resource and ioport_resource. The iomem_resource variable monitors all memory-mapped peripherals, tracking an address envelope starting from physical coordinate 0x0 up to -1 (which translates to the maximum addressable boundary 0xFFFFFF series based on the processor's word width). Concurrently, the ioport_resource tracks port-mapped assets, mapping a baseline port range from index 0 up to IO_SPACE_LIMIT.

The global core declarations and fallback boundaries for iomem_resource and ioport_resource are initialized as follows:

struct resource iomem_resource = {
	 .name  = "PCI mem",
	 .start = 0,
	 .end   = -1ULL,
	 .flags = IORESOURCE_MEM,
};
struct resource ioport_resource = {
	.name  = "PCI IO",
	.start = 0,
	.end   = IO_SPACE_LIMIT,
	.flags = IORESOURCE_IO,
};

These baseline allocations establish the maximum total address envelopes manageable across both hardware categories. Each overarching address space can be subdivided into multiple secondary sub-spaces to be distributed among various peripheral configurations. These sub-allocations can be further partitioned down to track individual registers or internal IO blocks.

By precisely wiring the structural parent (.parent), sibling (.sibling), and child (.child) reference pointer fields embedded within each descriptor, the resource allocation blocks form a strict hierarchical tree topology. Within this structure, iomem_resource and ioport_resource serve as the definitive root nodes anchoring two independent trees, as illustrated in the schematic below:

When a device driver files an allocation request to claim a hardware resource range, it must initially specify which root node to target and supply the absolute starting and terminating boundary coordinates, along with appropriate type configuration bitmasks. Based on the requested physical address bounds, the core allocation function request_resource() identifies the appropriate location to insert the candidate node along the resource tree.

The insertion algorithm strictly mandates that child nodes nested beneath a common parent must be arranged in an ascending linear sequence from the first child across all subsequent sibling nodes, sorting the address blocks from lowest to highest. If the traversal loop fails to resolve a vacant slot matching the coordinates without overlapping an operational node, the kernel rejects the block allocation as an address conflict. If a valid, vacant position is secured, the engine safely hooks the new resource descriptor into the database tree. The following sequential schematics map out different structural scenarios when adding a new peripheral resource to the tree, where the newly inserted node is highlighted in red:

The low-level allocation routing logic executing this tracking validation pass is driven by the internal function __request_resource():

static struct resource * __request_resource(struct resource *root, struct resource *new)
{
        resource_size_t start = new->start;
        resource_size_t end = new->end;
        struct resource *tmp, **p;
        if (end < start)
            return root;
        if (start < root->start)
            return root;
        if (end > root->end)
            return root;
        p = &root->child;
        for (;;) {
            tmp = *p;
            if (!tmp || tmp->start > end) {
                new->sibling = tmp;
                *p = new;
                new->parent = root;
                return NULL;
            }
            p = &tmp->sibling;
            if (tmp->end < start)
                continue;
            return tmp;
    }
}

This management routine is defined within the core kernel subsystem module git/kernel/resource.c. If an address overlap or allocation conflict is caught during the execution loop, the function returns a pointer tracking the conflicting peripheral resource block. If the verification pass confirms the request is completely safe, the entry is linked into the tree, and the function returns a null pointer (NULL). Furthermore, the resource.c module contains an array of baseline utilities tasked with handling resource deletion (release_resource), configuration queries, and database walk loops.

8.2.12 Low-Memory and High-Memory Boundary Adjustments (adjust_lowmem_bounds)

When the absolute physical address space of system RAM approaches or scales past the linear bounds of the kernel's virtual address space, the architecture establishes the conceptual layout of High Memory (highmem) and Low Memory (lowmem). High memory refers explicitly to the physical address blocks that are not permanently covered or mapped by the kernel's early direct-mapping translation page tables. Conversely, low memory defines the physical address envelope that is directly covered by the persistent, fixed virtual page tables, enabling the kernel core to access these page frames directly without temporary translation overlays. The precise partitioning boundary separating low memory from high memory is governed by explicit hardware configurations and silicon platform constraints.

Because the early fixed page tables cannot directly reach high memory zones, any programmatic read/write loop targeting a high-memory physical frame must construct a transient virtual page map on the fly. The kernel exports a dedicated suite of access handlers to coordinate these short-lived high-memory lookups, such as the kmap_local_page() interface. For detailed architectural guidelines, developers can reference the Linux Kernel API Reference Manual.

The adjust_lowmem_bounds() routine analyzes the topological state of the system by inspecting the struct memblock and struct memblock_region arrays to systematically tune the division line separating low memory from high memory. The allocator initially evaluates all physical memory blocks registered as usable RAM that carry no specialized layout restrictions (where the allocation mask matches MEMBLOCK_NONE) to isolate the region sitting at the absolute highest physical address bound.

The algorithm then takes the absolute terminating physical address of this highest block, compares it against the kernel configuration variable vmalloc_min (under standard ARM platform layouts, vmalloc_min defaults to 0xF0000000), isolates the lesser of these two numeric words, and executes a bitwise AND operation with the bitmask mask 0xFFF00000. The resulting calculation defines the definitive lowmem/highmem division boundary. Once this threshold is calculated, the adjust_lowmem_bounds() routine writes this parameter directly into the system-wide global variable arm_low_limit.

8.2.13 Early Boot-Stage Memory Allocator Initialization (arm_memblock_init)

The arm_memblock_init() function is an architecture-specific initializer deployed across the ARM tree to protect core memory spaces used during the early bootstrap lifecycle, explicitly registering them as reserved physical RAM to prevent subsequent boot operations or template loaders from overwriting or corrupting active data. Maintained within the initialization module arch/arm/mm/init.c, this routine is structured as follows:

void __init arm_memblock_init(const struct machine_desc *mdesc)
{
	memblock_reserve(__pa(KERNEL_START), KERNEL_END - KERNEL_START);
	arm_initrd_init();
	arm_mm_memblock_reserve();
	if (mdesc->reserve)
		mdesc->reserve();
	early_init_fdt_reserve_self();
	early_init_fdt_scan_reserved_mem();
	dma_contiguous_reserve(arm_dma_limit);
	arm_memblock_steal_permitted = false;
	memblock_dump_all();
}

The underlying subroutines and allocation tracking fences operate according to the following design parameters:

  • The primary statement memblock_reserve() claims the physical memory footprint occupied by the active executable kernel binary image, copying these exact boundary coordinates straight into the .reserved tracking array of the master memblock data structure.

  • If the target platform boot parameters configure an initial RAM-disk sequence, arm_initrd_init() isolates the memory footprint staging the compressed initrd payload and flags those blocks as protected reserved RAM. The explicit layout coordinates and linear width tracking this initrd space are parsed dynamically from the device tree parameters.
