		set_smp_ops_by_method(cpus);
	if (!bootcpu_valid) {
		pr_warn("DT missing boot CPU MPIDR[23:0], fall back to default cpu_logical_map\n");
		return;
	}
	for (i = 0; i < cpuidx; i++) {
		set_cpu_possible(i, true);
		cpu_logical_map(i) = tmp_map[i];
	}
}

As established previously, once the device tree is unflattened, every node on the device tree is represented by a struct device_node structure. Thus, both the cpu and cpus pointers in the function point to struct device_node structures.

The function arm_dt_init_cpu_maps() first determines whether the system supports symmetric multiprocessing booting. The system provides two methods to configure SMP booting: one method is configured via the compilation switch CONFIG_SMP, and the other method is configured via the compilation switch CONFIG_SMP_ON_UP (Uniprocessor). The first method is suitable for hardware architectures that are natively symmetric multi-core systems, whereas the second method is geared toward single-core hardware systems that intend to execute an SMP-enabled operating system. If the system supports SMP booting, the mpidr (Multiprocessor Affinity Register) value is read from the cp15 c0 c5 register; if SMP booting is not supported, the mpidr is cleared to zero.

After reading the hardware mpidr value, the function obtains a pointer to the /cpus node by invoking of_find_node_by_path("/cpus"). Then, utilizing this pointer, it iterates through each individual CPU node enclosed within the /cpus node to read the value of the reg property of each CPU node, which represents the physical ID of that CPU node. Upon reading the physical ID of a CPU node, the function verifies whether the physical ID is valid. The retrieved property value is considered invalid if any of the following conditions are met:

  • The CPU node does not contain a reg property.

  • The number of bytes contained within the reg property value is less than 4.

  • The upper 8 bits of the reg property value do not equal 0.

  • The exact same property value appears in more than one (inclusive of two) CPU nodes.

After validating the legitimacy of the property value, if this property value matches the mpidr value read from the hardware, the CPU currently being traversed is identified as the boot CPU. Under this circumstance, the physical ID of this CPU node must be written into the first position of the logical relationship table. If it does not equal the value of mpidr, the physical ID values read from the device tree are written into the logical relationship table sequentially starting from the second position, following the traversal order of the CPU nodes.

During the traversal of the various CPUs, the function arm_dt_init_cpu_maps() also invokes set_smp_ops_by_method(). This allows developers to configure customized SMP CPU initialization routines for each CPU, which include functions such as smp_init_cpus(), smp_prepare_cpus(), smp_secondary_init(), smp_boot_secondary(), as well as hotplug-related operations like cpu_kill(), cpu_die(), cpu_can_disable(), and cpu_disable(). The system is notified to utilize its self-contained initialization routines by specifying the enable-method property within the CPU nodes of the device tree file.

Concurrently with the construction of the cpu_logical_map array, the function arm_dt_init_cpu_maps() also builds a bitmask _cpu_possible_mask for all discovered CPUs. That is, if the (id)-th CPU node exists in the device tree, the (id)-th bit of _cpu_possible_mask is set to 1; otherwise, it is cleared to 0.

8.2.18.2 PSCI Initialization

PSCI is the abbreviation for Power State Coordination Interface. New generation ARM architectures, such as ARMv8-A, provide a power management interface designed to interface directly with the operating system. Linux utilizes the structure:

struct psci_operations {
	u32 (*get_version)(void);
	int (*cpu_suspend)(u32 state, unsigned long entry_point);
	int (*cpu_off)(u32 state);
	int (*cpu_on)(unsigned long cpuid, unsigned long entry_point);
	int (*migrate)(unsigned long cpuid);
	int (*affinity_info)(unsigned long target_affinity, unsigned long lowest_affinity_level);
	int (*migrate_info_type)(void);
};

to define the interface between the operating system and the PSCI module. Device manufacturers can define their own PSCI operations according to the respective function signatures outlined within this structure, or provide Linux with the necessary information, thereby achieving compatibility support for Linux. Before the various functionalities provided by PSCI can be utilized, Linux must populate the supported fields within the psci_operations structure. The function that assigns values to the psci_operations structure is implemented in the file git/drivers/firmware/psci/psci.c, and the functions executing the diverse capabilities of PSCI are defined within the exact same file.

During the execution of architecture-based hardware initialization, setup_arch() invokes the function psci_dt_init() to traverse the hierarchical device tree to search for nodes possessing the "arm,psci-1.0" property. Nodes carrying this property natively support PSCI functionalities. The PSCI device driver supplied by the vendor provides the starting memory address of the init_fn() function via the data field of the of_device_id structure, which is leveraged to initialize the PSCI functional modules. By executing init_fn(), the function completes the corresponding initialization of the PSCI modules for all nodes that support PSCI capabilities. The definition of the psci_dt_init() function is as follows:

int __init psci_dt_init(void)
{
	struct device_node *np;
	const struct of_device_id *matched_np;
	psci_initcall_t init_fn;
	int ret;
	np = of_find_matching_node_and_match(NULL, psci_of_match, &matched_np);
	if (!np || !of_device_is_available(np))
		return -ENODEV;
	init_fn = (psci_initcall_t)matched_np->data;
	ret = init_fn(np);
	of_node_put(np);
	return ret;
}

The function of_find_matching_node_and_match() within this routine traverses the device tree starting from the root node to locate all nodes with properties matching "arm,psci-1.0". The of_device_is_available() function subsequently verifies whether the value of the status property of the matched node evaluates to "ok" or "okay". The init_fn function is supplied directly by the hardware manufacturer.

8.2.18.3 SMP CPU PSCI Function Initialization

If the system supports a symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) CPU boot mechanism, it must initialize both the SMP CPUs and the various functional modules required by the SMP PSCI capabilities. As explained in the previous section, the function addresses for the diverse PSCI functional modules are supplied by the psci_operations structure, whereas the function addresses for the modules required by SMP CPU booting are supplied by the structure:

struct smp_operations {
#ifdef CONFIG_SMP
	void (*smp_init_cpus)(void);
	void (*smp_prepare_cpus)(unsigned int max_cpus);
	void (*smp_secondary_init)(unsigned int cpu);
	int  (*smp_boot_secondary)(unsigned int cpu, struct task_struct *idle);
#ifdef CONFIG_HOTPLUG_CPU
	int  (*cpu_kill)(unsigned int cpu);
	void (*cpu_die)(unsigned int cpu);
	bool  (*cpu_can_disable)(unsigned int cpu);
	int  (*cpu_disable)(unsigned int cpu);
#endif
#endif
};

For systems supporting hotplugging, multi-core CPUs require additional capabilities such as cpu_kill(), cpu_die(), and cpu_disable().

To utilize the features provided by multi-core symmetric CPUs, Linux first needs to assign the addresses of these respective functions to the corresponding fields of smp_ops, a static variable of type struct smp_operations. Prior to configuring the SMP CPUs, the setup_arch() function checks whether the machine descriptor mdesc provides an SMP CPU initialization routine smp_init. If the machine descriptor provides an initialization routine, the system uses the functions supplied by the machine descriptor to configure the various fields of smp_ops. If it is not provided, the fields of smp_ops are configured via the function smp_set_ops() using the respective function addresses provided by either psci_smp_ops or mdesc->smp. If PSCI is online, priority is given to the function addresses of psci_smp_ops defined in git/arch/arm/kernel/psci_smp.c.

After assigning values to smp_ops, setup_arch() invokes the function smp_init_cpus(), which is defined as follows:

void __init smp_init_cpus(void)
{
	if (smp_ops.smp_init_cpus)
		smp_ops.smp_init_cpus();
}

This function invokes the platform-dependent smp_init_cpus() routine to initialize each individual CPU core. For the i.MX6 Solo processor, a machine descriptor named __mach_desc_IMX6Q is statically defined via the macro DT_MACHINE_START(), and its smp field is initialized with the address of the function imx_smp_init_cpus() (defined in git/arch/arm/mach-imx/mach-imx6q.c). That is to address that the system provides the SMP CPU initialization routine via mdesc. The finalized result of expanding the DT_MACHINE_START macro is as follows:

static const struct machine_desc __mach_desc_IMX6Q __used
__section(".init.arch.info") = {
	.nr = ~0U, /* Or the corresponding board ID, typically ~0U in Device Tree (DT) mode */
	.name	= "Freescale i.MX6 Quad/DualLite (Device Tree)",
	.l2c_aux_val 	= 0,
	.l2c_aux_mask	= ~0,
	.smp	= &imx_smp_ops, /* Pointer after macro expansion of smp_ops(imx_smp_ops) */
	.map_io		= imx6q_map_io,
	.init_irq	= imx6q_init_irq,
	.init_machine	= imx6q_init_machine,
	.init_late      = imx6q_init_late,
	.dt_compat	= imx6q_dt_compat,
};

The function imx_smp_init_cpus(), defined in git/arch/arm/mach-imx/platsmp.c, is implemented as follows:

static void __init imx_smp_init_cpus(void)
{
	unsigned long arch_type;
	int i, ncores;
	asm volatile(
		".align 4\n"
		"mrc p15, 0, %0, c0, c0, 0\n"
		: "=r" (arch_type)
	);
	/* MIDR[15:4] defines ARCH type */
	__mxc_arch_type = (arch_type >> 4) & 0xfff;
	if (arm_is_ca7()) {
		unsigned long val;
		/* CA7 core number, [25:24] of CP15 L2CTLR */
		asm volatile("mrc p15, 1, %0, c9, c0, 2" : "=r" (val));
		ncores = ((val >> 24) & 0x3) + 1;
	} else {
		ncores = scu_get_core_count(scu_base);
	}
	for (i = ncores; i < NR_CPUS; i++)
		set_cpu_possible(i, false);
}

Its primary operations include:

  • Reading the MIDR register of the CP15 coprocessor via the assembly instruction mrc to identify the processor architecture, where bits [15:4] define the CPU model.

  • Acquiring the CPU core count. If it is a Cortex-A7 (such as i.MX7D), it reads the L2CTLR register. If it is another architecture (such as i.MX6Q/DL, Cortex-A9), it retrieves the CPU core count by reading the SCU register.

  • Updating the kernel CPU bitmap cpu_possible_mask.

8.2.18.4 Initialization of the SMP MPIDR Hash Table

A hash table is a fundamental concept in data structures and is extensively applied in the computer domain. It is a technique capable of storing and querying large tables through a smaller set of keys, thereby optimizing memory utilization. When generating or querying a hash table, a hash function is first employed to map a key into an index value, which is then utilized to look up the data corresponding to that key.

In practical applications, because the range of potential keys is far larger than the actual size of the hash table, different keys may resolve to the exact same index value when computed by the hash function. This gives rise to a phenomenon known as a hash collision. Diverse methodologies exist to resolve this issue, such as utilizing a linked list to store all keys and their corresponding values mapped to the same index; when a collision occurs, the target data is retrieved by traversing this linked list with the specific key.

Linux employs a hash table designated as mpidr_hash. This hash table stores the CPU states prior to entering sleep, which is leveraged by the system when entering low-power sleep states or during system wakeup. The purpose of the macro MPIDR_LEVEL_BITS is to initialize several fundamental parameters of this hash table.

As established from previous descriptions, the ARM mpidr encoding scheme is divided into three segments: aff0, aff1, and aff2. The rationale behind this tripartite division is to facilitate thread scheduling by choosing CPUs based on varying affinity preferences. One can define aff0 as the thread ID, aff1 as the CPU ID, and aff2 as the cluster ID; alternatively, aff0 can be defined as the CPU ID, aff1 as the cluster ID, and aff2 can be cleared to zero. Linux adopts the first configuration. During process scheduling, matching the configuration of aff0, aff1, and aff2 allows the system to set the priority level for a process when selecting a CPU core, such as binding a specific process to a designated core.

Linux leverages the value of mpidr as the key to generate and query this hash table. The index value is generated by a hash function named compute_mpidr_hash through bitwise shifting and OR operations on the mpidr values of the respective CPUs. This hash function is defined as a macro written in assembly language within the file git/arch/arm/kernel/sleep.S. The inputs to this function are rs0, rs1, rs2, along with aff0, aff1, and aff2, where rs0, rs1, and rs2 represent the right-shift bit counts for aff0, aff1, and aff2 respectively, while aff0, aff1, and aff2 are the values of the individual segments of the CPU mpidr. The functionality implemented by this macro is:

$$index = aff0 > > rs0|aff1 > > rs1|aff2 > > rs2$$

It should be pointed out here that utilizing this specific hash function guarantees that no collision phenomena will occur, even though the hash table generated via this approach is not the absolute minimal hash table possible.

When initializing the hash table, rs0, rs1, and rs2 are configured by the function smp_build_mpidr_hash() based on the mpidr values of all available CPUs. The definition of the smp_build_mpidr_hash() function is as follows:

static void __init smp_build_mpidr_hash(void)
{
	u32 i, affinity;
	u32 fs[3], bits[3], ls, mask = 0;
	for_each_possible_cpu(i)									
		mask |= (cpu_logical_map(i) ^ cpu_logical_map(0));
	for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
		affinity = MPIDR_AFFINITY_LEVEL(mask, i);
		ls = fls(affinity);
		fs[i] = affinity ? ffs(affinity) - 1 : 0;
		bits[i] = ls - fs[i];
	}
	mpidr_hash.shift_aff[0] = fs[0];
	mpidr_hash.shift_aff[1] = MPIDR_LEVEL_BITS + fs[1] - bits[0];
	mpidr_hash.shift_aff[2] = 2*MPIDR_LEVEL_BITS + fs[2] - (bits[1] + bits[0]);
	mpidr_hash.mask = mask;
	mpidr_hash.bits = bits[2] + bits[1] + bits[0];
	if (mpidr_hash_size() > 4 * num_possible_cpus())
		pr_warn("Large number of MPIDR hash buckets detected\n");
	sync_cache_w(&mpidr_hash);
}

This function first iterates through each available CPU. By executing a bitwise XOR operation against the mpidr of the boot CPU, it identifies all bits that flip across the mpidr registers of the diverse CPUs, and stores the intermediate result into the variable mask. It then combines the results of all CPUs together via bitwise OR operations. Consequently, a bit with a value of 1 within mask denotes that this specific bit has flipped in at least one CPU—meaning the value of this bit does not match the value of the corresponding bit in the boot CPU mpidr. The finalized mask value is utilized to determine the bitmask for index generation.

Since a bit with a value of 0 within mask indicates that the value of this bit in the mpidr remains unchanged across all CPUs, it can be inferred that this bit contributes nothing to the generation of the hash table index. By leveraging such a bitmask, the hash function can isolate the index generation from the influence of non-flipped bits, thereby reducing the memory footprint of the hash table.

To ensure that the LSB (Least Significant Bit) positions of aff0, aff1, and aff2 all align to bit 0, once the positions of the flipped bits across all CPU mpidr registers are determined, the macro definition MPIDR_AFFINITY_LEVEL(mask, i) shifts the LSB positions corresponding to each individual segment of aff0, aff1, and aff2 within the mask down to bit 0.

Through right-shifting, Linux discards the contiguous trailing zero segments starting from the LSB. The purpose of this operation is to further shorten the length of the keys used during lookups, thereby decreasing the storage space occupied by the hash table. The shift bit counts to be discarded for aff0, aff1, and aff2 are stored respectively in the shift_aff[0], shift_aff[1], and shift_aff[2] arrays of the mpidr_hash structure, whereas the total count of flipped bits is stored in the bits field of mpidr_hash. The mask bitmask required for calculating the index value is stored in the mask field of mpidr_hash.

When establishing the right-shift bit counts necessary for calculating the hash table index, the used variable fs[0] represents the position of the first flipped bit in aff0, fs[1] represents the position of the first flipped bit in aff1, and fs[2] represents the position of the first flipped bit in aff2. Due to the hardware encoding format of the ARM mpidr, fs[1] and fs[2] must be additionally shifted by MPIDR_LEVEL_BITS and 2 * MPIDR_LEVEL_BITS bits respectively, where the value of MPIDR_LEVEL_BITS evaluates to 8.

8.2.19 HYP Mode Check

As is established, ARM architecture CPUs possess multiple modes to provide users with varying levels of hardware access privileges. The primary CPU operating modes include User mode, System mode, Supervisor mode, Abort mode, FIQ mode, IRQ mode, Hypervisor mode (HYP mode), and Monitor mode. In terms of security partitioning, the CPU can operate in either a Secure state or a Non-secure state. When the CPU operates in the Non-secure state, it features three privilege levels: PL0, PL1, and PL2, wherein only Hypervisor mode possesses the PL2 privilege level. When the CPU operates in the Secure state, it features two privilege levels: PL0 and PL1. Hypervisor mode and Secure mode depend on hardware extensions. When the CPU is equipped with Virtualization hardware extensions, the system supports Hypervisor mode, whereas when the CPU is equipped with Security hardware extensions, the system supports Secure mode.

During the boot phase, the CPU typically operates in Supervisor mode or Hypervisor mode. If the system is an asymmetric multi-core system, the setup_arch() function invokes the Hypervisor check function hyp_mode_check() to verify whether the boot mode configuration is logical. This function is exclusively utilized for CPUs with Virtualization hardware extensions and is defined within the file git/arch/arm/kernel/setup.c. The function definition is as follows:

void __init hyp_mode_check(void)
{
#ifdef CONFIG_ARM_VIRT_EXT
	sync_boot_mode();
	if (is_hyp_mode_available()) {
		pr_info("CPU: All CPU(s) started in HYP mode.\n");
		pr_info("CPU: Virtualization extensions available.\n");
	} else if (is_hyp_mode_mismatched()) {
		pr_warn("started in wrong/inconsistent modes (primary CPU mode 0x%x)\n",
		__boot_cpu_mode & MODE_MASK);
		pr_warn("CPU: This may indicate a broken bootloader or firmware.\n");
	} else
		pr_info("CPU: All CPU(s) started in SVC mode.\n");
#endif
}

The function hyp_mode_check() acquires the boot mode by reading the value of the variable __boot_cpu_mode, wherein the function sync_boot_mode() flushes the cache prior to reading the value of the variable __boot_cpu_mode. The function is_hyp_mode_available() checks whether the mode portion of __boot_cpu_mode evaluates to HYP_MODE, whereas the function is_hyp_mode_mismatched() verifies whether the primary CPU mode is HYP mode while the remaining respective CPUs are configured to the exact same mode (all CPUs must be configured to identical modes). By checking the values of these two components, the system determines whether the HYP mode configuration is appropriate. The value of __boot_cpu_mode is populated during the U-Boot phase by the function __hyp_stub_install via the function store_primary_cpu_mode. These two functions are defined within the file git/linux/arch/arm/kernel/hyp-stub.S. As established in section 8.1.12, the __hyp_stub_install() function is invoked within the head.S file.

8.2.20 Reserving Memory for Kernel Crash Dump Information

Linux provides kernel crash data capturing and service tools such as kdump and kexec. When a kernel crash occurs, the capturing tool collects diagnostics data and generates a core dump file. Production-grade Linux distributions generally include these utilities; if omitted from the release artifacts, users can download and install them manually using package management tools.

Before starting the kdump or kexec services, a dedicated chunk of memory must be reserved for them. The required memory capacity can be configured via the cmdline string within the /chosen/bootargs node of the device tree file in the U-Boot source, or inside other corresponding configuration files. There are three formats for configuring the memory required by the capturing utility via cmdline: crashkernel = size,[high|low], crashkernel = size[@offset], and crashkernel = ramsize-range:size[,...][@offset]. Examples include crashkernel=192M,high, crashkernel=192M@16M, and crashkernel=512M-2G:64M,2G-:128M.

The routine responsible for parsing and configuring the kdump command is implemented as follows:

static void __init reserve_crashkernel(void)
{
	unsigned long long crash_size, crash_base;
	unsigned long long total_mem;
	int ret;

	total_mem = get_total_mem();
	ret = parse_crashkernel(boot_command_line, total_mem, &crash_size, &crash_base);
	if (ret)
		return;
	if (crash_base <= 0) {
		unsigned long long crash_max = idmap_to_phys((u32)~0);
		unsigned long long lowmem_max = __pa(high_memory - 1) + 1;
		if (crash_max > lowmem_max)
			crash_max = lowmem_max;
		crash_base = memblock_find_in_range(CRASH_ALIGN, crash_max, crash_size,  
 CRASH_ALIGN);
		if (!crash_base) {
			pr_err("crashkernel reservation failed - No suitable area found.\n");
			return;
		}
	} else {
		unsigned long long start;
		start = memblock_find_in_range(crash_base, crash_base + crash_size, crash_size, 
       SECTION_SIZE);
		if (start != crash_base) {
			pr_err("crashkernel reservation failed - memory is in use.\n");
			return;
		}
	}
	ret = memblock_reserve(crash_base, crash_size);
	if (ret < 0) {
		pr_warn("crashkernel reservation failed - memory is in use (0x%lx)\n",
(unsigned long)crash_base);
		return;
	}
	crashk_res.start = crash_base;
	crashk_res.end = crash_base + crash_size - 1;
	insert_resource(&iomem_resource, &crashk_res);
	if (arm_has_idmap_alias()) {
		static struct resource crashk_boot_res = {
			.name = "Crash kernel (boot alias)",
			.flags = IORESOURCE_BUSY | IORESOURCE_MEM,
		};
		crashk_boot_res.start = phys_to_idmap(crash_base);
		crashk_boot_res.end = crashk_boot_res.start + crash_size - 1;
		insert_resource(&iomem_resource, &crashk_boot_res);
	}
}

The function parse_crashkernel() within this procedure scans boot_command_line to detect whether it contains the "crashkernel" substring. If the "crashkernel" substring is present, it parses "crashkernel=" and its trailing parameters according to the three predefined formats described above to establish the designated memory size and address offset. The evaluated memory magnitude and offset address are then returned via crash_size and crash_base. total_mem denotes the aggregate memory dimension available for kdump operations.

Upon receiving the evaluated values of crash_size and crash_base, reserve_crashkernel() passes distinct sets of parameters to the function memblock_find_in_range() based on whether crash_base evaluates to zero, thereby selecting an appropriate block within the available memory pool. It subsequently reserves this memory block for kdump by calling the function memblock_reserve(), and registers the reserved block into the iomem_resource subsystem.

Certain ARM systems incorporate specialized hardware extensions intended for identity mapping (ID mapping). When the system features such ID mapping hardware extensions, it must export this specific information to utilities like kexec via the crashk_boot_res structure.

8.2.21 Machine Descriptor-Based Initialization

Upon completing the majority of the architecture-based hardware configurations, if the machine descriptor provides a generic interrupt service routine, a VGA console driver, or an early initialization routine, the architecture-based hardware subsystem will execute these initialization routines or assign their entry memory addresses to the corresponding variables.

chapter 9 Kernel Boot - Boot Configuration

Bootconfig File

9.1 Bootconfig File

During the boot process, Linux can configure kernel parameters via the cmdline string. The cmdline originates from the tag structures passed by U-Boot to the kernel boot procedure. It is a text string containing multiple configuration options, such as console and video. Among these options, variables containing the = delimiter are utilized to configure environment variables for the init() process, whereas variables lacking the = delimiter represent command-line variables passed to the init() process, and variables succeeding the -- marker are explicitly forwarded to the init() process.

If the cmdline string contains the keyword "bootconfig", it denotes that the Linux system supplies supplemental kernel parameters via a bootconfig file. The bootconfig file is appended immediately to the end of the initrd image, as illustrated in the figure below:

The bootconfig file is an ASCII text file placed directly adjacent to the initrd. Succeeding the bootconfig file is its total size in bytes, followed by the size of the checksum block and the checksum value itself, each occupying 4 bytes. Finally, a 12-byte magic string "#BOOTCONFIG\n" concludes the block to serve as the signature identifier for the bootconfig file.

The structural syntax for each entry within a bootconfig file is formatted as: KEY[.WORD[...]] = VALUE[, VALUE2[...]][;]. The keyword (KEY) denotes the variable intended for configuration, such as video or console. A WORD is also designated as a subkey, which is utilized to further compartmentalize a keyword. Keywords must only consist of alphanumeric characters, hyphens (-), or underscores (_). The parameter assignment (VALUE) must consist solely of printable characters or spaces, excluding delimiters such as ,, ;, newlines, #, and }. To incorporate these explicit delimiters within a value assignment, the value must be encapsulated within single ('') or double ("") quotation marks. When writing the file, entries sharing identical subkey path segments can be grouped together. For instance, the variable foo.bar.baz and the variable foo.bar.qux.quux can either be expressed as:

foo.bar.baz = value1
foo.bar.qux.quux = value2

or grouped and expressed as:

foo.bar {
		baz = value1
		qux.quux = value2
}

or:

foo.bar { baz = value1; qux.quux = value2 }

In this context, foo acts as the parent key for bar, while bar represents the subkey of foo. Similarly, foo.bar acts as the parent key path for baz and qux.quux.

The grammatical rules of the bootconfig file dictate that the exact same keyword cannot be repeatedly assigned distinct values. Concurrently, a single keyword cannot simultaneously possess both a direct value assignment and child subkeys. Consequently, the following two scenarios:

foo = bar, baz
foo = qux

or

foo = value1
foo.bar = value2

are strictly forbidden.

The first scenario attempts duplicate assignments to the variable foo, while the second scenario configures foo to simultaneously possess the direct value value1 and the child subkey bar.

The bootconfig specification permits appending supplemental values to an existing variable via the += operator, as shown below:

foo = bar, baz
foo += qux

Parsing the Bootconfig File

9.2 Parsing the Bootconfig File

The Linux kernel initialization process start_kernel(), upon completing the framework-based hardware configurations, invokes the function setup_boot_config() to prepare for the configuration of supplemental kernel parameters. The function setup_boot_config() is defined in the file git/lib/bootconfig.c, and its definition is as follows:

static void __init setup_boot_config(const char *cmdline)

{

static char tmp_cmdline[COMMAND_LINE_SIZE] __initdata;

const char *msg;

int pos;

u32 size, csum;

char *data, *copy, *err;

int ret;

data = get_boot_config_from_initrd(&size, &csum);

strlcpy(tmp_cmdline, boot_command_line, COMMAND_LINE_SIZE);

err = parse_args("bootconfig", tmp_cmdline, NULL, 0, 0, 0, NULL, bootconfig_params);

if (IS_ERR(err) || !bootconfig_found)

return;

if (err)

initargs_found = true;

if (!data) {

pr_err("'bootconfig' found on command line, but no bootconfig found\n");

return;

}

if (size >= XBC_DATA_MAX) {

pr_err("bootconfig size %d greater than max size %d\n", size, XBC_DATA_MAX);

return;

}

if (boot_config_checksum((unsigned char *)data, size) != csum) {

pr_err("bootconfig checksum failed\n");

return;

}

copy = memblock_alloc(size + 1, SMP_CACHE_BYTES);

if (!copy) {

pr_err("Failed to allocate memory for bootconfig\n");

return;

}

memcpy(copy, data, size);

copy[size] = '\0';

ret = xbc_init(copy, &msg, &pos);

if (ret < 0) {

if (pos < 0)

pr_err("Failed to init bootconfig: %s.\n", msg);

else

pr_err("Failed to parse bootconfig: %s at %d.\n", msg, pos);

} else {

pr_info("Load bootconfig: %d bytes %d nodes\n", size, ret);

extra_command_line = xbc_make_cmdline("kernel");

extra_init_args = xbc_make_cmdline("init");

}

return;

}

The variable passed to this function by start_kernel() is command_line. This function first invokes get_boot_config_from_initrd() to obtain the trailing boundary address of the initrd, and reads 12 bytes of data from the position corresponding to the magic string within the kernel image payload. If the retrieved payload matches the string "#BOOTCONFIG\n", it indicates that a bootconfig file is appended after the initrd; otherwise, no bootconfig file is attached. Upon identifying the bootconfig file, the function get_boot_config_from_initrd() reads the checksum block and the file size attribute from the image file to determine the starting address of the bootconfig file. If this established address is smaller than the trailing boundary address of the initrd, it indicates a structural fault within the bootconfig metadata layout. If all verifications pass, get_boot_config_from_initrd() stores the file size and checksum value into the variables size and csum respectively, and returns the base address of the bootconfig file. In the event of a failure, the function returns a null pointer.

After retrieving the base address of the bootconfig file, the contents of boot_command_line are copied into tmp_cmdline, and the function parse_args() is employed to traverse and tokenized the string payload within tmp_cmdline. For ARM-based architectures, boot_command_line preserves the string data supplied by the cmdline field originating from the U-Boot ATAGs/tag infrastructures. boot_command_line is leveraged for parameter orchestration during system boot operations and typically reflects the default environment configuration criteria, which is populated by the function setup_machine_tags() during tag parsing blocks.

parse_args() passes the entry address of the function bootconfig_params() to parse_one(), executing the bootconfig_params routine to determine whether the "bootconfig" token is enclosed within boot_command_line. It should be noted here that because parse_args() specifies a num argument value of 0 when invoking parse_one(), parse_one() bypasses the logic path intended to confirm whether the parameters encapsulated within tmp_cmdline are secure. Instead, it exclusively executes the bootconfig_params routine. Consequently, when parse_one() is triggered through parse_args(), its role is simplified to merely detecting the presence of the "bootconfig" string to determine whether supplemental parameter orchestration needs to be processed.

When the requirement for supplemental parameter configuration is confirmed, and the presence of a valid bootconfig file within the image payload is established, setup_boot_config() utilizes boot_config_checksum() to ensure the data integrity of the bootconfig file payload.

After creating a copy of the bootconfig file, the system parses the bootconfig file through the function xbc_init(), and constructs a tree topology designated as the XBC tree based on the text payload to describe the relationship hierarchy between the diverse variables. The nodes of this tree architecture are composed of keys and values, which are represented by the structure:

struct xbc_node {

u16 next;

u16 child;

u16 parent;

u16 data;

} __attribute__ ((__packed__));

The next field stores the index value of the next node, child stores the index value of its child node, and parent stores the index value of its parent node. The lower 15 bits of the data field store the index value of either the key or the value, while the most significant bit (MSB) is utilized to distinguish between a key and a value. When the MSB evaluates to 1, it indicates that the address corresponding to data stores a value; when the MSB evaluates to 0, it signifies that the address corresponding to data stores a key.

During the process of parsing the bootconfig file, if a syntax error is discovered within the file, the error message is preserved in emsg, and the position where the error occurred is preserved in epos. Upon completing the syntax parsing of the bootconfig file, the function xbc_verify_tree() is invoked to ensure that the constructed tree structure is free of issues, and then a value of 0 is returned.

{width=“2.038031496062992in” height=“2.388059930008749in”}{width=“1.7238801399825021in” height=“2.3800634295713037in”}

Figure 9-2 Bootconfig File and Corresponding Tree Structure

For the bootconfig file illustrated on the left side of Figure 9-2, xbc_init() generates the tree structure illustrated on the right side of the figure.

When parsing a bootconfig file, the xbc_init() procedure first searches for characters possessing special significance, such as {, }, =, +=, ;,
=, \n, and #, to determine the syntax format of the variables. If the symbol =, +=, or := is located, it indicates that the variable syntax follows a value assignment format—meaning the left side of the symbol represents the variable name and the right side represents the variable value—which requires invoking the function xbc_parse_kv() to parse the key-value pair. If the symbol located is #, it indicates that this portion represents a comment, under which circumstance all characters starting from # to the end of the line are ignored. If the symbol located is ; or \n, it must be succeeded by a key, which triggers a call to xbc_parse_key() to parse the key. If the character located is { or }, it indicates that entries sharing identical key segments are enclosed between { and }, which requires invoking xbc_open_brace() and xbc_close_brace() to parse the contents enclosed within.

Since a key can contain subkeys delimited by ., the functions xbc_parse_kv(), xbc_parse_key(), and xbc_open_brace() all invoke the internal function __xbc_parse_keys(), which sequentially searches for the . symbol to determine each individual subkey. Upon locating each subkey (including the root key itself) or confirming a value, __xbc_parse_keys() invokes the function __xbc_add_key(). If the current variable tree structure does not yet contain this key or value, it appends this key or value as a child node of its upper-level key. If they already reside within the XBC tree, they will not be added to the XBC tree again; instead, the routine merely records the upper-level node of that key or value.

After establishing the hierarchical parameter tree structure, setup_boot_config() traverses the XBC tree by invoking the function xbc_make_cmdline() to check whether the bootconfig file contains the "kernel" and "init" keys. If the "kernel" key is present, it assigns the string "kernel:" along with its corresponding variable values to the global variable extra_command_line. If the kernel key possesses subkeys, it likewise appends "kernel.subkey1...subkeyn:" and its corresponding variable values to extra_command_line. Similarly, it assigns "init:" and its values to extra_init_args, making them available for use by the kernel and the init() process.

Command-Line Parameter Merging

9.3 Command-Line Parameter Merging

After retrieving the supplemental command-line parameters and initialization variables, these additional parameters and variables must be merged with the command-line parameters and variables passed by U-Boot, eventually being globally provided to the kernel and the init() process. The function setup_command_line() merges the string within extra_command_line with the string within boot_command_line and the string within extra_init_args, and subsequently saves the combined result into the variable saved_command_line. Concurrently, it merges the string stored within command_line with the string within extra_command_line, saving the resulting combination into the variable static_command_line.

chapter 10 CPU Configuration under Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP) Boot Mode

Configuring the Number of CPU Cores

10.1 Configuring the Number of CPU Cores

For multi-core systems, the number of CPU cores is tightly coupled with subsequent parameter configurations; therefore, it is imperative to determine the exact number of CPUs encompassed within the hardware architecture. Establishing the core count is relatively straightforward and is accomplished by identifying the bit position of the last set bit (value of 1) within the cpu_possible_mask variable, which was previously determined during the hardware configuration phase. The function that determines the CPU count is defined within the file git/kernel/smp.c, and its definition is as follows:

void __init setup_nr_cpu_ids(void)
{
	nr_cpu_ids = find_last_bit(cpumask_bits(cpu_possible_mask), NR_CPUS) + 1;
}

Allocating a Private Memory Block for Each Core

10.2 Allocating a Private Memory Block for Each Core

10.2.1 Private Memory Allocation Strategy

Because the Linux operating system utilizes page translation tables to execute transformations between virtual addresses and physical addresses, it must continuously access these page tables throughout its operation. To enhance memory access efficiency, Linux typically establishes a fundamental minimum unit when allocating memory, rather than performing memory allocation on a raw byte granularity. The choice of this minimum unit directly dictates the overall efficiency of memory utilization. This minimum unit is generally a page.

The private memory for each individual CPU primarily comprises the static memory blocks generated by the compiler and linker, situated between the symbols __per_cpu_start and __per_cpu_end. Combined with the reserved memory blocks designated for loadable modules and a dedicated portion allocated for dynamic runtime usage, these three components are collectively referred to as the minimum required allocation memory. Because memory allocation constraints enforce a minimum allocation unit size (atom_size), the actual allocated memory space must evaluate to an integer multiple of this atomic size. Consequently, the actual magnitude of allocated memory (alloc_size) is generally larger than the baseline minimum required allocation memory.

For uniprocessor (UP) systems, memory utilization efficiency can reach its theoretical maximum when memory is partitioned using this minimum allocation unit. Conversely, for systems featuring a Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) architecture, private memory blocks are allocated within the explicit memory zone of a NUMA node for all CPUs designated to access that specific node. Under this scenario, if the system stubbornly adheres to the default minimum allocation unit to carve out memory for each individual CPU, it can introduce substantial memory waste. For instance, consider a scenario where 7 CPUs access a specific node, and each CPU requires 10 KiB of memory. If the minimum allocation unit evaluates to 4 KiB, each CPU demands 3 allocation units, leading to a total requirement of 21 allocation units across all 7 CPUs, which equates to 84 KiB of memory. Since the 7 CPUs only strictly require 70 KiB of payload memory, 14 KiB of memory is lost to fragmentation waste. Mathematically, allocating exactly 72 KiB of memory for the 7 CPUs is sufficient to satisfy the alignment constraint that the aggregate allocation must be an integer multiple of the allocation unit. Therefore, when allocating memory for each CPU corresponding to a NUMA node, dropping the operational allocation granularity down to 2 KiB allows the system to allocate exactly 72 KiB of memory across the 7 CPUs, thereby elevating memory utilization efficiency.

When Linux allocates private memory blocks for CPUs within a NUMA-based architecture, it establishes an optimal finalized allocation granularity, designated as Units Per Allocation (UPA), by continuously decrementing the allocation unit step-by-step. This algorithmic approach guarantees that the aggregate memory volume allocated to each individual NUMA node scales strictly as an integer multiple of the atomic minimum unit, while simultaneously maintaining peak memory utilization efficiency.

10.2.2 Private Memory Allocation Execution

For multi-core systems, the runtime operating states and executing tasks of each individual CPU may vary. Consequently, CPU-private variables (per_cpu variables) are required to preserve distinct variables to differentiate each processor from the others. Since private memory is restricted to a single CPU, under most circumstances, a CPU can access its own private variables without requiring locks. Linux provides the macro definition #define DEFINE_PER_CPU(type, name) DEFINE_PER_CPU_SECTION(type, name, "") to declare these CPU-private variables. Each CPU's private variables are stored within its own dedicated storage area, which is allocated via the function setup_per_cpu_areas(). For uniprocessor (UP) systems or symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) systems, this function is defined within the file git/mm/percpu.c. For NUMA systems, the function is defined inside git/arch/yourprocessorname/mm/numa.c (e.g., git/arch/arm64/mm/numa.c).

The function definition for uniprocessor (UP) systems is as follows:

void __init setup_per_cpu_areas(void)
{
	const size_t unit_size = roundup_pow_of_two(
		max_t(size_t, PCPU_MIN_UNIT_SIZE, PERCPU_DYNAMIC_RESERVE));
	struct pcpu_alloc_info *ai;
	void *fc;
	ai = pcpu_alloc_alloc_info(1, 1);
	fc = memblock_alloc_from(unit_size, PAGE_SIZE, __pa(MAX_DMA_ADDRESS));
	if (!ai || !fc)
		panic("Failed to allocate memory for percpu areas.");
	kmemleak_free(fc);
	ai->dyn_size = unit_size;
	ai->unit_size = unit_size;
	ai->atom_size = unit_size;
	ai->alloc_size = unit_size;
	ai->groups[0].nr_units = 1;
	ai->groups[0].cpu_map[0] = 0;
	pcpu_setup_first_chunk(ai, fc);
	pcpu_free_alloc_info(ai);
}

The function definition for symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) systems is as follows:

void __init setup_per_cpu_areas(void)
{
	unsigned long delta;
	unsigned int cpu;
	int rc;
	rc = pcpu_embed_first_chunk(PERCPU_MODULE_RESERVE, PERCPU_DYNAMIC_RESERVE,PAGE_SIZE, NULL, pcpu_dfl_fc_alloc, pcpu_dfl_fc_free);
	if (rc < 0)
		panic("Failed to initialize percpu areas.");
	delta = (unsigned long)pcpu_base_addr - (unsigned long)__per_cpu_start;
	for_each_possible_cpu(cpu)
		__per_cpu_offset[cpu] = delta + pcpu_unit_offsets[cpu];
}

ARM64 supports NUMA architectures, and its function definition is as follows:

void __init setup_per_cpu_areas(void)
{
	unsigned long delta;
	unsigned int cpu;
	int rc;
	rc = pcpu_embed_first_chunk(PERCPU_MODULE_RESERVE, PERCPU_DYNAMIC_RESERVE, 
				  PAGE_SIZE, NULL, pcpu_dfl_fc_alloc, pcpu_dfl_fc_free);
	if (rc < 0)
		panic("Failed to initialize percpu areas.");
	delta = (unsigned long)pcpu_base_addr - (unsigned long)__per_cpu_start;
	for_each_possible_cpu(cpu)
		__per_cpu_offset[cpu] = delta + pcpu_unit_offsets[cpu];
}

To facilitate memory management, Linux defines the structures struct pcpu_alloc_info and struct pcpu_group_info for the private memory allocation management subsystem. Among these, the pcpu_alloc_info structure preserves diverse metrics regarding memory sizes, memory grouping, and memory allocation granularities. It is defined as:

struct pcpu_alloc_info {
	size_t		static_size;
	size_t		reserved_size;
	size_t		dyn_size;
	size_t		unit_size;
	size_t		atom_size;
	size_t		alloc_size;
	size_t		__ai_size;
	int		nr_groups;
	struct pcpu_group_info	groups[];
}

Within this block, unit_size signifies the number of memory bytes allocated to a single CPU, and alloc_size represents the number of memory bytes actually allocated. The meanings of the remaining fields are clear and will not be individually described.

The structure struct pcpu_group_info is defined as:

struct pcpu_group_info {
	int			nr_units;
	unsigned long	base_offset;	
	unsigned int		*cpu_map;
};

It preserves the CPU grouping status, wherein nr_units represents the actual number of UPAs (Units Per Allocation) assigned to the corresponding node. base_offset stores the memory offset allocated for the node, where the offset of the first node evaluates to 0. cpu_map is an array that records the logical IDs of all CPUs associated with the current node.

With a basic understanding of private memory, the allocation process becomes easier to comprehend. For uniprocessor (UP) systems, the function setup_per_cpu_areas() first invokes the function pcpu_alloc_alloc_info(int nr_groups, int nr_units) to allocate memory for the structures pcpu_alloc_info and pcpu_group_info themselves, where nr_groups represents the number of NUMA nodes and nr_units represents the number of UPAs. Obviously, for a uniprocessor system, both nr_groups and nr_units equal 1.

After allocating memory for these two structures, setup_per_cpu_areas() directly calls the memblock memory allocator encountered previously to allocate sufficient CPU-private memory.

By comparing the setup_per_cpu_areas() function of symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) systems with that of NUMA systems, it can be observed that their function definitions are fundamentally identical. The only distinction lies in the final three parameters passed to the memory allocation function pcpu_embed_first_chunk(). An SMP system invokes it via pcpu_embed_first_chunk(PERCPU_MODULE_RESERVE, PERCPU_DYNAMIC_RESERVE, PAGE_SIZE, NULL, pcpu_dfl_fc_alloc, pcpu_dfl_fc_free), whereas a NUMA system invokes it via pcpu_embed_first_chunk(PERCPU_MODULE_RESERVE, PERCPU_DYNAMIC_RESERVE, PAGE_SIZE, pcpu_cpu_distance, pcpu_fc_alloc, pcpu_fc_free). The final three parameters of the pcpu_embed_first_chunk() function—cpu_distance_fn, alloc_fn, and free_fn—are callbacks utilized to determine the distance between each CPU and the different NUMA nodes, allocate memory, and free memory respectively. The memory allocation and deallocation functions resolve to the memblock allocation and deallocation routines (memblock_alloc_try_nid and memblock_free). Because all CPUs in an SMP system share an identical distance to the memory nodes—meaning there is only a single NUMA node—the distance determination callback passed to the pcpu_embed_first_chunk() function is specified as null.

An analysis of pcpu_embed_first_chunk() reveals that for SMP systems, its role is to invoke the function pcpu_build_alloc_info() to determine the number of units allocated per CPU (UPA—units per allocation), allocate memory for the structures pcpu_alloc_info and pcpu_group_info (by invoking the function pcpu_alloc_alloc_info()), perform initialization, and finally invoke the callback function alloc_fn() to allocate the private memory. When invoking pcpu_alloc_alloc_info(), nr_groups = 1, and nr_units represents the required number of units to be allocated (a multiple of UPA).

Aside from the memory allocation and deallocation functions, the callbacks passed to pcpu_embed_first_chunk() by a NUMA system include an additional function cpu_distance_fn(), which is utilized to determine the distance between a CPU and each memory node. pcpu_build_alloc_info() leverages this function to partition the CPUs into multiple groups (effectively grouping together the CPUs that access the exact same NUMA node).

pcpu_build_alloc_info() first determines the maximum value of UPA, then utilizes cpu_distance_fn() to group the CPU cores, and subsequently searches for an optimal UPA value. Following this, it allocates memory for the structures pcpu_alloc_info and pcpu_group_info via the function pcpu_alloc_alloc_info(), and finally initializes the two aforementioned structures.

After the function pcpu_build_alloc_info() returns, pcpu_embed_first_chunk() invokes the callback function alloc_fn() to sequentially allocate private memory for each group, and the allocated memory addresses are stored within the areas array. If the memory allocation callback function fails to execute successfully, the already allocated memory can be released via the callback function free_fn().

Following the allocation of private memory, if the hardware architecture is based on an SMP topology or a NUMA topology, the setup_per_cpu_areas() function must also initialize the contents of the __per_cpu_offset array to establish the precise locations of the per_cpu variables for each CPU within the private memory space.

Preparing the Boot CPU

10.3 Preparing the Boot CPU

The preparation of the boot CPU is tightly coupled with the specific hardware architecture. Under the ARM architecture, the function responsible for preparing the boot CPU is defined within the file git/arch/arm/kernel/smp.c, and its definition is as follows:

void __init smp_prepare_boot_cpu(void)
{
	set_my_cpu_offset(per_cpu_offset(smp_processor_id()));
}

Within this routine, the return value of smp_processor_id() evaluates to 0, which designates the first CPU core to act as the boot CPU. The function per_cpu_offset() is implemented as a macro definition, expressed as #define per_cpu_offset(x) (__per_cpu_offset[x]), and is leveraged to retrieve the base memory offset address of a specific CPU's per_cpu variables within the private memory space. The function set_my_cpu_offset writes this retrieved offset address of the per_cpu variables into the TPIDRPRW register of the CP15 coprocessor. Therefore, the primary objective of the function smp_prepare_boot_cpu(void) is to write the private memory address offset of the first CPU into the CP15 TPIDRPRW register. The TPIDRPRW register preserves the base memory address utilized for storing thread-specific diagnostics and state information.

CPU Hotplug State Initialization

10.4 CPU Hotplug State Initialization

To provide architectural support for hotplugging capabilities, Linux declares a _per_cpu variable named cpuhp_state within the private memory zone of each individual CPU core. The type of this variable is defined by the structure struct cpuhp_cpu_state, as shown below:

struct cpuhp_cpu_state {
	enum cpuhp_state	state;
	enum cpuhp_state	target;
	enum cpuhp_state	fail;
	struct task_struct	*thread;
	bool			should_run;
	bool			rollback;
	bool			single;
	bool			bringup;
	struct hlist_node	*node;
	struct hlist_node	*last;
	enum cpuhp_state	cb_state;
	int			result;
	struct completion	done_up;
	struct completion	done_down;
};

Because the first CPU has already commenced the boot sequence, the system must update its local hotplug tracking variable cpuhp_state to mark the state field, which signifies the current operational phase of the hardware component, as online. The function responsible for initializing this initial hotplug state is implemented as follows:

void __init boot_cpu_hotplug_init(void)
{
#ifdef CONFIG_SMP
	cpumask_set_cpu(smp_processor_id(), &cpus_booted_once_mask);
#endif
	this_cpu_write(cpuhp_state.state, CPUHP_ONLINE);
}

Within this procedure, the function cpumask_set_cpu() sets the corresponding bit belonging to the first CPU inside the bitmask cpus_booted_once_mask. Concurrently, this_cpu_write() marks the state field of the per_cpu variable cpuhp_state of the first CPU as CPUHP_ONLINE. By breaking down the ARM-specific implementation of the this_cpu_write(pcp, val) function, it can be determined that this_cpu_write(pcp, val) evaluates as functionally equivalent to:

*(&pcp + _my_cpu_offset()) = val;

Here, _my_cpu_offset() represents the offset value read directly from the TPIDRPRW register of the CP15 coprocessor. As established in the preceding section, the TPIDRPRW register preserves the private memory base offset address of the first CPU; consequently, this_cpu_write() successfully writes the targeted numerical value directly into the private variable space of the first CPU.

chapter 11 Memory Node and Zone Initialization

Nodes and Zones

11.1 Nodes and Zones

The architectural concepts of nodes and zones were introduced in Chapter 8. Within a Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) topology, physical memory is partitioned into multiple distinct nodes. Each individual node can be structurally segmented into several zones of varying types (see §8.8.1), and each zone can be further categorized into a sequence of granular pages. A node is represented by the struct pglist_data (pg_data_t) structure, a zone is represented by the struct zone structure, and an individual page is represented by the struct page structure. The hierarchical relationship among nodes, zones, and pages is illustrated in the figure below:

The primary fields of the pglist_data structure, which describes a memory node, were outlined briefly in §8.1.1. Leveraging either the node_zonelists[0] pointer or the node_zones array embedded within this structure allows the system to access all architectural zones belonging to that specific node. Several highly critical fields within struct zone that are routinely utilized include zone_start_pfn, zone_end_pfn, node, zone_pgdat, _watermark, spanned_pages, managed_pages, present_pages, and free_area. Among these, zone_start_pfn and zone_end_pfn designate the starting and ending Page Frame Numbers (PFNs) encompassing the targeted zone, respectively. The node field identifies the numerical index of the node hosting this zone. The zone_pgdat pointer references the parent pglist_data structure of the node to which this specific zone belongs.

The _watermark array is utilized to track the residual free memory constraints within the zone. This array comprises three discrete watermark indexes: WMARK_MIN, WMARK_LOW, and WMARK_HIGH. The memory allocation subsystem leverages these three explicit thresholds to orchestrate memory allocation and reclamation constraints. When the number of available free pages drops below _watermark[WMARK_LOW], the asynchronous memory management background daemon (kswapd) is activated to scan for and reclaim pages that can be safely evicted. Conversely, when the number of available free pages rises above _watermark[WMARK_HIGH], the memory reclamation task enters a low-power sleep state. The operating system enforces a strict runtime constraint dictating that the volume of available free pages must not drop below the threshold configured at _watermark[WMARK_LOW].

spanned_pages represents the aggregate span of pages covered by the zone from its lowest to highest PFN. present_pages denotes the actual volume of physical memory present within the zone, which mathematically evaluates to the total spanned pages minus any memory holes (non-existent physical pages). managed_pages signifies the total pool of pages actively managed by the buddy memory allocation system, which equals the present pages minus any platform-reserved pages. free_area is an array of free_area structures tracking all free memory chunks within the zone. Following predefined memory allocation granularities, Linux partitions this free space into distinct tracking arrays scaling by orders of 1 page, 2 pages, 4 pages, up to $2^{11}$ pages. For instance, the region tracked by free_area[0] is utilized to allocate chunks of a 1-page magnitude, whereas free_area[11] is utilized to allocate continuous memory chunks of a $2^{11}$-page magnitude.

Following system boot, continuous runtime allocation and deallocation operations inevitably cause physical memory to become highly fragmented into non-contiguous, small-sized address spaces—a phenomenon designated as memory fragmentation. Certain high-performance application scenarios mandate physically contiguous memory blocks; therefore, it is imperative to consolidate heavily fragmented memory blocks back into larger, continuous address spaces. The structural process of consolidating fragmented memory chunks into physically contiguous zones is designated as memory compaction. This operation relies on page migration mechanisms, which physically relocate the raw data contents of pages from one tracking block to another. To facilitate this, the struct zone structure declares specialized variables related to memory compaction tracking, such as compact_init_migrate_pfn.

To record the operational status of individual nodes, Linux defines a global bitmask array designated as node_states. This tracking subsystem preserves seven distinct sets of bitmasks: N_POSSIBLE, N_ONLINE, N_NORMAL_MEMORY, N_HIGH_MEMORY, N_MEMORY, N_CPU, and N_GENERIC_INITIATOR. Each individual bit within these masks maps explicitly to a unique node index. If a specific bit within a tracking mask is set to 1, it indicates that the corresponding node currently satisfies the operational criteria of that mask. The underlying meaning of each mask category can be inferred directly from its name; for instance, the node_states[N_ONLINE] mask logs all nodes that are currently online, while node_states[N_NORMAL_MEMORY] tracks nodes that contain a valid ZONE_NORMAL memory region. The concrete programmatic definitions can be reviewed inside the header file git/include/linux/nodemask.h.

A page represents the fundamental tracking block for physical memory management, and the Memory Management Unit (MMU) interfaces with physical memory via translation page tables. In the virtual address space, the Linux buddy memory management framework handles physical allocation via the page structure (the physical page descriptor). The struct page structure is declared within the file git/include/linux/mm_types.h. Although the hardware dimensions of memory pages remain identical—typically evaluating to 4096 bytes—the concrete definition of struct page changes dynamically depending on the active execution context. For instance, the definition of a page structure utilized within the SLOB allocator varies from one utilized within the SLAB allocator, and the definition utilized within the core buddy allocator diverges from both the SLOB and SLAB tracking formats. These architectural variances are achieved programmatically via nested C language constructs known as unions. The specific definitions regarding distinct page variations are outlined across subsequent sections.

To prevent multiple CPU cores from contending for global locks when frequently allocating and freeing individual memory pages (Order-0 pages), the kernel establishes localized memory caches for each individual CPU core. This specific category of localized memory cache is described by the Per-CPU Pages (PCP) mechanism via the per_cpu_pages structure.

During the early stages of kernel boot before the full dynamic memory allocation infrastructure is active, Linux defines a temporary buffer array designated as the boot_pageset of the PCP type. This provides uniform memory allocation code paths and serves as the underlying structural support for single-page (Order-0) allocations. The operations of the memory management framework are tightly bound to the specific CPU utilizing that memory. The definition of the tracking structure struct per_cpu_pageset is as follows:

struct per_cpu_pageset {
	struct per_cpu_pages pcp;
#ifdef CONFIG_NUMA
	s8 expire;
	u16 vm_numa_stat_diff[NR_VM_NUMA_STAT_ITEMS];
#endif
#ifdef CONFIG_SMP
	s8 stat_threshold;
	s8 vm_stat_diff[NR_VM_ZONE_STAT_ITEMS];
#endif
}

The per_cpu_pageset structure incorporates the per_cpu_pages structure, which is defined as follows:

struct per_cpu_pages {
	int count;
	int high;
	int batch;
	struct list_head lists[MIGRATE_PCPTYPES];
};

The count variable denotes the number of memory pages that the CPU can currently release. The high field is utilized to configure the threshold for batch memory reclamation; memory pages are released only when the number of reclaimable pages exceeds this threshold value. batch signifies the number of pages sequentially added or freed by this specific CPU during a single batch operation within the memory management subsystem. lists is an array of linked list heads, where the linked lists are used to preserve the memory pages (Order-0 pages) that can be directly utilized by the CPU without contending for global locks. Depending on the migration types of the memory pages, pages are preserved within distinct linked lists respectively. It can be observed from this setup that the directly usable memory pages are all migration-ready pages, which encompasses MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE, MIGRATE_MOVABLE, and MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE. (In the latest version of Linux, the definition of the PCP list has been revised to struct list_head lists[MIGRATE_PCPTYPES][NR_PCP_LISTS]. After upgrading to a two-dimensional array, the introduction of NR_PCP_LISTS allows the system to preserve not only Order-0 memory pages but also higher-order free physical pages of continuous blocks of 2, 4, or 8 pages, thereby enabling small-amount, multi-page allocations to benefit from the extreme performance of lockless access).

To ensure the normal operation of the memory management subsystem, the initialization of the pglist_data, zone, and page structures must be executed during the boot phase. The initialization of pglist_data commences immediately following the termination of the previously described paging_init() procedure. In this chapter, we will outline the initialization process of the zone structures and the page allocation subsystem.

Zone Structure Initialization

11.2 Zone Structure Initialization

The initialization of zone structures is performed by the function build_all_zonelists(), which is defined within the file git/mm/page_alloc.c. Omitting print diagnostics, the function can be simplified as follows:

void __ref build_all_zonelists(pg_data_t *pgdat)
{
	unsigned long vm_total_pages;
	if (system_state == SYSTEM_BOOTING) {
		build_all_zonelists_init();
	} else {
		__build_all_zonelists(pgdat);
	}
	vm_total_pages = nr_free_zone_pages(gfp_zone(GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE));
	if (vm_total_pages < (pageblock_nr_pages * MIGRATE_TYPES))
		page_group_by_mobility_disabled = 1;
	else
		page_group_by_mobility_disabled = 0;
}

As inferred from its name, the primary objective of this function is to construct a continuous list of zones. Because the system is currently in its early booting phase, the argument passed to build_all_zonelists() evaluates to a null pointer. This function triggers the initial zone routing map configuration via build_all_zonelists_init(). The build_all_zonelists_init() function is likewise defined within the page_alloc.c file and is implemented as follows:

static noinline void __init build_all_zonelists_init(void)
{
	int cpu;
	__build_all_zonelists(NULL);
	for_each_possible_cpu(cpu)
		setup_pageset(&per_cpu(boot_pageset, cpu), 0);
	mminit_verify_zonelist();
	cpuset_init_current_mems_allowed();
}

The internal function __build_all_zonelists(NULL) leverages the raw data structures provided by each individual pglist_data node to initialize the node_zonelists array embedded inside every parent pg_data_t structure, thereby building the fallback node zone lists. The architectural layout of the node_zonelists array for each individual node is illustrated in Figure 11-2 below:

The node_zonelists array is composed of zonelist elements. A zonelist is constructed from an array of zoneref structures, each consisting of a pointer to a specific zone along with an integer index (idx) that signifies its matching zone type. The total dimension of the node_zonelists array maps to the total count of online NUMA nodes, while the entry count within a zonelist maps directly to the diverse zone types supported by the operating system.

Stripping out non-essential compilation blocks and inactive operational paths, __build_all_zonelists() can be simplified as follows:

static void __build_all_zonelists(void *data)
{
	int nid;
	int __maybe_unused cpu;
	pg_data_t *self = data;
	static DEFINE_SPINLOCK(lock);
	spin_lock(&lock);
#ifdef CONFIG_NUMA
	memset(node_load, 0, sizeof(node_load));
#endif
	for_each_online_node(nid) {
		pg_data_t *pgdat = NODE_DATA(nid);
		build_zonelists(pgdat);
	}
	spin_unlock(&lock);
}

Its primary operation is to iterate over every online node and leverage the function build_zonelists() to construct the corresponding node_zonelists fallbacks. The NODE_DATA macro is utilized to retrieve the base memory address of node nid from the global node_data tracking table, thereby granting access to its target pglist_data structure. The build_zonelists() routine is implemented as follows:

static void build_zonelists(pg_data_t *pgdat)
{
	static int node_order[MAX_NUMNODES];
	int node, load, nr_nodes = 0;
	nodemask_t used_mask = NODE_MASK_NONE;
	int local_node, prev_node;

	local_node = pgdat->node_id;
	load = nr_online_nodes;
	prev_node = local_node;
	memset(node_order, 0, sizeof(node_order));
	while ((node = find_next_best_node(local_node, &used_mask)) >= 0) {
		if (node_distance(local_node, node) != node_distance(local_node, prev_node))
			node_load[node] = load;
		node_order[nr_nodes++] = node;
		prev_node = node;
		load--;
	}
	build_zonelists_in_node_order(pgdat, node_order, nr_nodes);
	build_thisnode_zonelists(pgdat);
}

The function build_zonelists() first sorts the individual memory nodes based on their physical distance relative to the target node along with other affinity weight metrics. This generates an ordered node array node_order[] that isolates remote nodes from the local node context. Following this, the routine invokes build_zonelists_in_node_order() to append all valid zones belonging to the remote nodes sorted within the node_order array directly into the current node's node_zonelists array.

build_zonelists_in_node_order() internally relies on build_zonerefs_node(). The role of build_zonerefs_node() is to construct a discrete zonelist link for an individual node targeted inside the node_order array. Throughout the composition of this fallback link, the routine loops through all valid zone types. If the node from node_order effectively supports the current zone type being evaluated—indicated by a non-zero managed_pages metric—the corresponding zoneref metadata composed of this zone and its matching index type is appended onto the zonelist.

Because build_zonelists_in_node_order() only processes and appends zones belonging to distinct, remote nodes into the target node_zonelists array, build_zonelists() must invoke build_thisnode_zonelists() at the conclusion of its runtime logic path to append the node's local zones onto its primary index slot, saving the finalized tracking links inside node_zonelists[0].

Core memory management procedures require access to the CPU-private variable boot_pageset. Consequently, once the node_zonelists arrays have been constructed for all valid nodes, __build_all_zonelists() must invoke setup_pageset() to initialize the individual fields of the per_cpu_pages structure embedded inside each CPU's boot_pageset allocation. setup_pageset() initializes the internal linked list heads of per_cpu_pages via pageset_init(), while forcing the batch field assignment to evaluate to 1 and the high field threshold to evaluate to 0 via pageset_set_batch().

As outlined in §7.3, system administrators can leverage the cgroup subsystem to govern and coordinate the hardware resources allocated to active tasks, within which the cpuset subsystem explicitly dictates task allocation boundaries across CPU cores and memory nodes. Throughout thread scheduling passes, a task is strictly constrained to execute only on the CPU cores and memory nodes permitted by its assigned cpuset. Through tactical configuration, a CPU core can be explicitly matched to access localized memory nodes situated closest to its physical execution context, thereby drastically minimizing inter-node bus cycles and optimizing memory access latency metrics.

Upon successfully configuring the fallback node_zonelists tracking tables across all active nodes, the build_all_zonelists_init() routine invokes mminit_verify_zonelist() to log and audit the layout of each node zone map, followed by a call to cpuset_init_current_mems_allowed(). Via the internal routine nodes_setall(), the mems_allowed bitmask field inside the root configuration of the initial setup task (init_task) is filled with the comprehensive mask 0xFFFFFFFF,FFFFFFFF, denoting that the bootstrap context possesses unrestricted authorization to allocate from any memory node. At this juncture, the initial initialization tasks for memory nodes and architectural zones are complete.

Memory Hotplug Management Initialization

11.3 Memory Hotplug Management Initialization

The hotplug functionality of most memory hardware devices operates independently of the CPU; however, certain NUMA memory hardware devices mandate architectural CPU support to execute hotplug operations. Consequently, Linux must implement a NUMA memory hotplug management infrastructure to accommodate these NUMA memory components that cannot achieve standalone hotplug capabilities.

Linux divides the CPU hotplug management sequence into multiple explicit phases or states, which can be broadly classified into several operational stages: offline, silent, prepare, and online. Each stage is further segmented into diverse, granular steps, whose precise categorization can be reviewed inside the definition of the cpuhp_state enum class located within the file git/include/linux/cpuhotplug.h. Linux leverages the previously introduced cpuhp_cpu_state structure to record the runtime state of a CPU across different phases. This encompasses multiple structural fields tracking the CPU's current state, target state, currently running hotplug daemon thread, and whether it is undergoing a bringup or teardown transition.

Throughout hotplug management execution, a CPU residing at any given state possesses the potential to enter a low-power sleep phase, or be woken up and restored from distinct conditions. Similarly, a CPU might encounter exceptions or recover from faults at any state block. Therefore, each discrete state must be paired with corresponding startup and teardown routines. To preserve these platform-specific startup and teardown handlers defined in the form of callback functions under diverse states, Linux declares a global array named cpuhp_hp_states of type struct cpuhp_step. This array is defined within the source file git/kernel/cpu.c.

The definition of the cpuhp_step structure is as follows:

struct cpuhp_step {
	const char		*name;
	union {
		int		(*single)(unsigned int cpu);
		int		(*multi)(unsigned int cpu, struct hlist_node *node);
	} startup;
	union {
		int		(*single)(unsigned int cpu);
		int		(*multi)(unsigned int cpu, struct hlist_node *node);
	} teardown;
	struct hlist_head	list;
	bool			cant_stop;
	bool			multi_instance;
};

This structure is hosted within git/kernel/cpu.c, wherein the list field represents a hash linked list head used to preserve all active entities (instances) that invoke the matching startup() and teardown() callbacks of this specific tracking node.

Upon initializing the architectural zone structures of the available NUMA nodes, the start_kernel() process invokes page_alloc_init(). This routine triggers cpuhp_setup_state_nocalls() to register the teardown handler for the mm/page_alloc:dead step under the CPUHP_PAGE_ALLOC_DEAD hotplug state, assigning it to the function address of page_alloc_cpu_dead(). Structurally, this sets the name field of the cpuhp_step structure located at index slot cpuhp_hp_states[CPUHP_PAGE_ALLOC_DEAD] to "mm/page_alloc:dead", maps the teardown.single field to point to the entry address of the function page_alloc_cpu_dead(), sets the multi_instance flag to 0, and initializes the remaining tracking fields to NULL.

The function page_alloc_cpu_dead() acts as the memory reclamation interface within the core memory management subsystem. Its primary technical objective is to drain and release the cached memory pages archived inside the diverse local LRU (Least Recently Used) lists of the target dead CPU core. It drains these cached pages back into the fallback free_area tracking arrays of their respective architectural zone structures, and subsequently updates the corresponding __lruvec tracking field within the parent pglist_data node framework. The __lruvec field is of type struct lruvec and records the active runtime Least Recently Used (LRU) statistics of the physical memory block.

To facilitate high-efficiency memory reclamation passes, Linux partitions physical memory frames across distinct LRU tracking lists based on their exact active usage criteria (for instance, evaluating whether a page is backed by an active disk filesystem block or mapped onto an anonymous swap area). The struct lruvec structure acts as a composite wrapper grouping these diverse categories of LRU tracking links; interested readers can consult specialized Linux memory management documentation for comprehensive architectural analysis.

Throughout memory management operations, Linux utilizes the page structure as the definitive abstract descriptor to represent physical memory frames. Because distinct runtime execution paths and functional workloads alter the core characteristics of a page along with the explicit tracking variables required to audit it, the structural configuration of the page structure must adapt dynamically. Linux achieves this modular variance by composing the page structure with nested C language union datatypes, which facilitates the reuse of a single descriptor canvas across multiple distinct allocation sub-modules. The page structure is declared within the file git/include/linux/mm_types.h.

Every variation of the page structure preserves the flags field as its leading member. Each individual bit within this field represents an explicit operational bitmask, which logs whether a physical page frame fits into a particular category or resides at a specific management phase. These bitmasks are primarily leveraged to determine if a page represents a compound page component, belongs to a specialized SLAB allocation block, acts as a highly active caching node, maps directly onto a file storage object versus an anonymous swap slice, or features contents that can be safely migrated to different nodes. The comprehensive set of page tracking bitmasks supported by Linux is declared within the header file git/include/linux/page-flags.h.

Manipulating these flags typically requires invoking dedicated processing routines to handle runtime testing, bit setting, and clearing passes. When searching for these specific bit manipulation interfaces using tracking utilities, developers often discover that these functions lack explicit definitions inside the source trees. This architecture exists because these interfaces are generated dynamically via macro expansion routines. For instance, the macro execution PAGEFLAG(Unevictable, unevictable, PF_HEAD) generates the complete family of helper functions used to manipulate the PG_unevictable bit flag. The blueprint definition of the PAGEFLAG macro is as follows:

#define PAGEFLAG(uname, lname, policy)					\
	TESTPAGEFLAG(uname, lname, policy)				\
	SETPAGEFLAG(uname, lname, policy)					\
	CLEARPAGEFLAG(uname, lname, policy)

The matching blueprint definitions for the underlying TESTPAGEFLAG, SETPAGEFLAG, and CLEARPAGEFLAG macros are implemented as:

#define TESTSETFLAG(uname, lname, policy)					\
static __always_inline int TestSetPage##uname(struct page *page)			\
	{ return test_and_set_bit(PG_##lname, &policy(page, 1)->flags); }
#define SETPAGEFLAG(uname, lname, policy)					\
static __always_inline void SetPage##uname(struct page *page)			\
	{ set_bit(PG_##lname, &policy(page, 1)->flags); }

and

#define CLEARPAGEFLAG(uname, lname, policy)				\
static __always_inline void ClearPage##uname(struct page *page)			\
	{ clear_bit(PG_##lname, &policy(page, 1)->flags); }

From this macro expansion architecture, it can be determined that evaluating PAGEFLAG(Unevictable, unevictable, PF_HEAD) dynamically expanding code generates the three inline helper functions TestSetPageUnevictable(), SetPageUnevictable(), and ClearPageUnevictable() to execute atomic testing, bitwise setting, and bitwise clearing passes on the PG_unevictable bit mask, respectively. These generated helper functions resolve programmatically to:

static __always_inline int TestSetPageUnevictable(struct page *page)
{
	return test_and_set_bit(PG_unevictable, &PF_HEAD(page, 1)->flags);
}
static __always_inline void SetPageUnevictable(struct page *page)		
{ 
	set_bit(PG_unevictable, &PF_HEAD(page, 1)->flags);
}
static __always_inline void ClearPageUnevictable(struct page *page)		
{ 
	clear_bit(PG_unevictable, &PF_HEAD(page, 1)->flags);
}

chapter 12 Jump Label Initialization

Jump Label Modification

12.1 Jump Label Modification

In all computer programs, branch execution is an indispensable control flow instruction. However, executing a branch operation usually demands multiple machine cycles. Frequent invocation of branch instructions—particularly conditional branch instructions—inevitably penalizes execution throughput. In many execution flows, the mathematical probability of a branch being taken versus flowing sequentially varies drastically. In certain execution tracks, the likelihood of a program branching is far greater than that of raw sequential processing, whereas under alternative constraints, sequential tracking happens far more frequently than branching paths. Since branching costs more processor pipeline cycles than straight-line sequential execution, programmers can often anticipate which logical side exhibits the higher probability. Through specialized source structure designs, code paths with lower execution profiles can be shunted to the taken side of the branch, while high-probability hot code sequences can be positioned along the straight-line sequential track. This arrangement accelerates execution velocity and optimizes microarchitectural performance. To support this paradigm, GCC supplies the likely(x) and unlikely(x) macro definitions. When x evaluates to 0, both macros return 0; when x does not evaluate to 0, both macros return 1. The difference lies in their compiler hints: likely() predicts that the value of x will be non-zero, whereas unlikely() predicts that the value of x will resolve to 0. The exact definitions of likely(x) and unlikely(x) are implemented as follows:

#define likely(x)      	__builtin_expect(!!(x), 1) 
#define unlikely(x)    	__builtin_expect(!!(x), 0)

The intrinsic __builtin_expect(x,y) represents a built-in helper function provided by the GCC compiler. It seamlessly returns the actual value of x, while informing the compiler infrastructure that the statistical expectation of x is predicted to match y.

By utilizing likely() and unlikely(), software architects can explicit signal to the compiler infrastructure which execution paths exhibit high probability profiles and which blocks feature low execution frequencies.
