Armed with these microarchitectural weight hints, the compiler places the high-probability payload (likely code) straight down the sequential pipeline track (the fast path), while segregating the low-probability blocks (unlikely code) over to the taken side of the branch (the slow path). The canonical usage pattern is structured as follows:

if (likely(x)) {		/* Executed identically to standard if (x) logic */
	/* likely code - Positioned down the straight-line sequential track */
} else {
	/* unlikely code - Shunted onto the taken side of the branch */
}

or alternatively:

if (unlikely(x)) {
	/* unlikely code - Shunted onto the taken side of the branch */
} else {
	/* likely code - Positioned down the straight-line sequential track */
}

If the compiler can definitively compute the final value of x at compile time before evaluating the likely(x) or unlikely(x) optimization passes, the conditional branch statement transitions into an unconditional jump instruction, enabling the optimizer to prune dead blocks and emit code solely for the active logical path. Programmers are free to choose between the likely or unlikely format, as both arrive at equivalent structural optimization targets. It must be explicitly emphasized that neither likely() nor unlikely() exerts any influence over the logical behavior of the software flow; their singular technical purpose is to aid the compiler in code generation optimization.

Another optimization paradigm arises when the branching behavior can be definitively resolved at runtime or compile-time without constant evaluation, such as determining whether to print diagnostic debug tracking lines. Building two independent monolithic image variants to handle verbose versus quiet execution states is an inefficient engineering choice. The codebase must simultaneously support both silent and verbose modalities. Another clear analogy is network profiling: the system must execute one specific code block when network functionalities are fully enabled, and trace an entirely separate code path when networking configurations are absent. If this architectural toggle relies on standard conditional branching, the pipeline spends countless cycles continually re-evaluating the tracking variable. To address this overhead, Linux introduces a runtime code modification technology designated as static jump label patching.

The foundational design of this jump label patching technique is to plant an atomic NOP instruction at the explicit control position where a jump might eventually be required, immediately followed by the high-probability sequential code path. If a runtime state change later mandates a branch at that junction, the bootloader or core kernel hot-patches this specific NOP placeholder, converting it into a concrete, executable branch instruction (as illustrated in Figure 12-1). The target instruction address of the NOP placeholder to be modified, alongside its matching destination branch address, is recorded within a dedicated jump entry metadata structure (struct jump_entry). These descriptor blocks are grouped by the linker toolchain within a bounded memory segment situated precisely between the symbols __start_jump_table and __stop_jump_table. The exact boundaries of __start_jump_table and __stop_jump_table, along with the metadata payload of the individual jump entries, are generated automatically by the compiler based on the source code directives.

Foundational Principles of Optimizing Program Performance via Label Modification

12.2 Foundational Principles of Optimizing Program Performance via Label Modification

The jump label modification technique primarily utilizes two central data structures—the jump entry (struct jump_entry) and the static key (struct static_key)—to perform code patching. These two data structures are defined in the file include/linux/jump_label.h as follows:

struct jump_entry {
	jump_label_t code;	
	jump_label_t target;
	jump_label_t key;	
};
struct static_key {
	atomic_t enabled;
	union {
		unsigned long type;
		struct jump_entry *entries;
		struct static_key_mod *next;
	};
};

Within struct jump_entry, the code field stores the address of the instruction that needs to be modified, while the target field stores the destination address of the branch instruction. The key field, after its lowest two bits are cleared, yields the base memory address of the static_key structure corresponding to this jump entry. The least significant bit (b0) of the key field serves as the branch flag; a value of 0 indicates a low branch probability (referred to as unlikely in Linux terminology), while a value of 1 indicates a high branch probability (referred to as likely in Linux terminology).

The static_key structure contains two primary fields. The first is enabled, and the second is a multi-purpose field of type unsigned long shared within a union. Bit b0 of this shared field represents the type bit, where 0 indicates that the key is initialized to false and 1 indicates that the key is initialized to true. Bit b1 is utilized to distinguish whether this entry stores the address of a jump_entry or a static_key_mod; 0 indicates it points to a jump_entry address, and 1 indicates it points to a static_key_mod address. The type bit is leveraged during the compilation phase to emit code, whereas the enabled field is used at runtime to dynamically toggle the routing direction of the branch instruction.

The precise relationships among the fields of jump_entry, static_key, and the executable program code are illustrated in Figure 12-2.

During the compilation phase, the compiler performs an XOR operation between the type bit and the branch bit to generate the initial instruction according to the matrix below:

Table 12-1 Determination of Patch Instructions by type and branch

type \ branchlikelyunlikely
trueNOPjump
falsejumpNOP

If the XOR product of type and branch evaluates to 0, a NOP instruction is generated. If the XOR product of type and branch evaluates to 1, an unconditional jump instruction is generated.

At compile time, relying purely on the type and branch bits only emits either a NOP or an unconditional jump instruction, meaning the execution path remains static and only one section (either the likely or unlikely path) will be executed. To dynamically toggle the branching path at runtime, the kernel must leverage the value of the enabled field to hot-patch the code inline while the program is running.

When code patching is triggered, an XOR operation is performed between the enabled field of the static key and the branch bit. The patch instruction type is determined based on Table 12-2, and an appropriate patch instruction is subsequently generated. If the resolved patch type is a NOP, the memory address pointed to by the code field of the jump entry is overwritten with a hardware NOP instruction. If the resolved patch type is a branch instruction, the system calculates the relative jump displacement using the instruction address in the code field (which typically acts as the Program Counter reference value) and the destination address in the target field. This computed branch instruction is then written directly into the memory location designated by code, thereby successfully patching the instruction. This type of patching work is commonly executed during the system boot phase.

Table 12-2 Determination of Patch Instructions by enabled and branch

enabled \branchtrue(likely)false(unlikely)
trueNOPjump
falsejumpNOP

Generation of the jump_entry

12.3 Generation of the jump_entry

As discussed in the preceding section, generating branch instructions requires the utilization of a static key to establish the instruction type, the branch target address, and the memory address of the instruction that needs to be modified. How, then, are these static keys generated? This section outlines the structural generation process of the static key.

When a specific block of code requires a dynamic toggle of its branching path, a global static key must be defined for that explicit toggle via the macro definitions:

DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_TRUE(name)

or

DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_FALSE(name)

A static key defined by the DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_TRUE macro is initialized to a default value of true, whereas a static key defined by DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_FALSE(name) is initialized to a default value of false.

The core macro blueprints for DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_TRUE and DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_FALSE are implemented as follows:

#define DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_TRUE(name) struct static_key_true name = STATIC_KEY_TRUE_INIT
#define DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_FALSE(name) struct static_key_false name = STATIC_KEY_FALSE_INIT

The finalized output of expanding these two macros defines the variable name respectively as:

struct static_key name =  {.enabled = {1}, {.entries = (void*) 1UL}}
struct static_key name = {.enabled = {0}, {.entries = (void*) 0UL}}

The functions static_branch_likely(key) and static_branch_unlikely(key) leverage the specified key to switch the execution routing direction of the branch. As established from Table 12-2, regarding the static_branch_likely() function, if the enabled field of the static key is true, static_branch_likely() returns a true value, prompting the compiler to emit a NOP instruction at compile time. Conversely, if the enabled field of the static key is false, static_branch_likely() returns a false value, prompting the compiler to emit a jump instruction at compile time. The function static_branch_unlikely() operates analogously to static_branch_likely().

The functional definitions of static_branch_likely() and static_branch_unlikely() are implemented as follows:

#define static_branch_likely(x)							\
({										\
	bool branch;								\
	if (__builtin_types_compatible_p(typeof(*x), struct static_key_true))		\
		branch = !arch_static_branch(&(x)->key, true);			\
	else if (__builtin_types_compatible_p(typeof(*x), struct static_key_false)) 	\
		branch = !arch_static_branch_jump(&(x)->key, true);		\
	else									\
		branch = ____wrong_branch_error();				\
	likely(branch);								\
})
#define static_branch_unlikely(x)							\
({										\
	bool branch;								\
	if (__builtin_types_compatible_p(typeof(*x), struct static_key_true))		\
		branch = arch_static_branch_jump(&(x)->key, false);		\
	else if (__builtin_types_compatible_p(typeof(*x), struct static_key_false)) 	\
		branch = arch_static_branch(&(x)->key, false);			\
	else									\
		branch = ____wrong_branch_error();				\
	unlikely(branch);								\
})

Within these blocks, x denotes the static key controlling the execution routing direction of the branch. These two macros leverage arch_static_branch() and arch_static_branch_jump() to determine the evaluation of branch via the static key x, and subsequently employ likely(branch) and unlikely(branch) to instruct the compiler infrastructure where to position the code blocks. During compilation, if the static_branch_likely() function is utilized, the compiler places the hot code succeeding the macro on the straight-line sequential track, while shunting the code block following the else statement onto the taken side of the branch. Similarly, if static_branch_unlikely() is invoked, the compiler places the code succeeding the macro onto the taken side of the branch, while shunting the code block following the else statement onto the straight-line sequential track.

The underlying routines arch_static_branch() and arch_static_branch_jump() are highly dependent on the CPU architecture of the system. For the ARM architecture, these two functions are defined respectively as follows:

static __always_inline bool arch_static_branch(struct static_key *key, bool branch)
{
	asm_volatile_goto("1:\n\t"
		 WASM(nop) "\n\t"
		 ".pushsection __jump_table,  \"aw\"\n\t"
		 ".word 1b, %l[l_yes], %c0\n\t"	
		 ".popsection\n\t"
		 : :  "i" (&((char *)key)[branch]) :  : l_yes);
	return false;
l_yes:
	return true;
}
static __always_inline bool arch_static_branch_jump(struct static_key *key, bool branch)
{
	asm_volatile_goto("1:\n\t"
		 WASM(b) " %l[l_yes]\n\t"
		 ".pushsection __jump_table,  \"aw\"\n\t"
		 ".word 1b, %l[l_yes], %c0\n\t"
		 ".popsection\n\t"
		 : :  "i" (&((char *)key)[branch]) :  : l_yes);
	return false;
l_yes:
	return true;
}

The composition of these two routines adopts the syntax of embedding assembly language instructions within C code. WASM is a helper macro utilized to construct assembly statements. WASM(nop) and WASM(b) define the ARM hardware instructions NOP and b (unconditional branch), respectively. The physical memory location occupied by these two instructions represents the precise location where code patching must be executed. The .pushsection and .popsection compiler directives instruct the GCC toolchain to sequentially place the enclosed code blocks into the specialized __jump_table section. Similarly, the directive .word 1b, %l[l_yes], %c0 acts as an ARM GCC compilation instruction whose purpose is to allocate a discrete jump_entry item, assigning local label 1, label l_yes, and the memory address of the static key to the code, target, and key fields of that jump_entry structure, respectively.

Usage Methodology of Static Keys

12.4 Usage Methodology of Static Keys

To implement dynamic toggling of program branching paths via a static key, a global static key with a default status of true or false must first be defined via either DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_TRUE(key) or DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_FALSE(key). Following this, the function static_branch_likely(key) or static_branch_unlikely(key) is invoked at the location where routing manipulation is required, as demonstrated below:

if (static_branch_likely(&key)) {
	/* likely code */
} else {
	/* unlikely code */
}

or alternatively:

if (static_branch_unlikely(&key)) {
	/* unlikely code */
} else {
	/* likely code */
}

The function static_branch_enable(&key) sets the enabled field of the static key to 1, whereas static_branch_disable(&key) clears the enabled field of the static key to zero. Invoking the function static_branch_enable(&key) prompts the program flow to execute a branch alteration, whereas invoking static_branch_disable(&key) terminates that specific routing modification. If a gradual reference-counted change to the branch routing direction is required, static_branch_inc(&key) and static_branch_dec(&key) can be called. While static_branch_enable() and static_branch_disable() explicitly force the static key's enabled field to 1 or 0, static_branch_inc() and static_branch_dec() serve to increment or decrement the value of the enabled field by 1, respectively. When the enabled counter decrements down to 0, the program branching direction undergoes a structural transformation. The following snippet illustrates a code sequence utilized by the SLAB memory allocation algorithm when carving out memory for sockets:

#ifdef CONFIG_NET
DECLARE_STATIC_KEY_FALSE(memalloc_socks_key);
static inline int sk_memalloc_socks(void)
{
	return static_branch_unlikely(&memalloc_socks_key);
}
#else
static inline int sk_memalloc_socks(void)
{
	return 0;
}
#endif
/* ... Execution Context ... */
if (sk_memalloc_socks()) {
	void *obj = cache_alloc_pfmemalloc(cachep, n, flags);
	if (obj)
		return obj;
}

When network functionality support is enabled via the compilation flag CONFIG_NET, the value of memalloc_socks_key is declared as false via DECLARE_STATIC_KEY_FALSE(). Because memalloc_socks_key defaults to false, the return value of sk_memalloc_socks() evaluates to false, and the CPU does not enter the inner branch of the if statement. When the system enters a memory reclamation state and needs to activate pfmemalloc sockets, the kernel invokes static_branch_enable(&memalloc_socks_key) to alter the state of memalloc_socks_key. At this point, sk_memalloc_socks() returns true during runtime execution, causing the code flow to enter the inner branch of the if statement and execute cache_alloc_pfmemalloc() to allocate memory.

The concrete assembly language execution workflow is as follows: the compiled assembly instruction at the if (sk_memalloc_socks()) check location resolves to a single hardware NOP instruction, enabling the CPU to stream directly down the straight-line sequential track without executing any conditional branching evaluations, thereby perfectly avoiding pipeline stalls triggered by CPU branch mispredictions. When memory reclamation becomes active and the pfmemalloc sockets must be energized, the kernel leverages functions such as text_poke() to dynamically hot-patch the original NOP placeholder into a concrete branch instruction at runtime.

Initializing the Jump Table

12.5 Initializing the Jump Table

Based on the descriptions provided across the preceding sections, it can be observed that during the source compilation process, the compiler toolchain only initializes the static keys and emits the __jump_table section. It arranges the branch-related segments at their respective code paths but does not execute instruction hot-patching on the placeholder sites based on the evaluation of the static keys. The task of performing instruction patching is handled by an initialization routine, a requirement executed by the function jump_label_init(). Upon completing the memory node and architectural zone initialization workflows, the start_kernel() process invokes jump_label_init(). This routine leverages each individual jump entry structure situated between __start___jump_table and __stop___jump_table, along with the runtime value of the static key referenced by that structure, to generate either a NOP instruction or a branch instruction. If the generated instruction type resolves to a NOP, the instruction location referenced by the code field of that jump entry is overwritten with a hardware NOP instruction. The function jump_label_init() is defined inside the source file linux/kernel/jump_label.c, and its definition is as follows:

void __init jump_label_init(void)
{
	struct jump_entry *iter_start = __start___jump_table;
	struct jump_entry *iter_stop = __stop___jump_table;
	struct static_key *key = NULL;
	struct jump_entry *iter;
	if (static_key_initialized)
		return;
	cpus_read_lock();
	jump_label_lock();
	jump_label_sort_entries(iter_start, iter_stop);
	for (iter = iter_start; iter < iter_stop; iter++) {
		struct static_key *iterk;
		if (jump_label_type(iter) == JUMP_LABEL_NOP)
			arch_jump_label_transform_static(iter, JUMP_LABEL_NOP);
		if (init_section_contains((void *)jump_entry_code(iter), 1))
			jump_entry_set_init(iter);
		iterk = jump_entry_key(iter);
		if (iterk == key)
			continue;
		key = iterk;
		static_key_set_entries(key, iter);
	}
	static_key_initialized = true;
	jump_label_unlock();
	cpus_read_unlock();
}

This routine first utilizes the function jump_label_sort_entries() to sort the jump entries located between __start___jump_table and __stop___jump_table in ascending order based on the magnitude of their code field values. Following this sorting pass, it iterates through all available jump entries. The function jump_label_type() is utilized to evaluate the truth table outlined in Table 12-2, executing an XOR bitwise operation to determine the exact patch instruction type. The definition of this function is as follows:

static enum jump_label_type jump_label_type(struct jump_entry *entry)
{
	struct static_key *key = jump_entry_key(entry);  	
	bool enabled = static_key_enabled(key);
	bool branch = jump_entry_is_branch(entry);	
	return enabled ^ branch;
}

If the value of the static key's enabled field is greater than zero, static_key_enabled() returns a value of 1; otherwise, it returns a value of 0. jump_entry_is_branch(entry) returns the value of the least significant bit (b0) of the key field within the target jump entry.

The function arch_jump_label_transform_static() is responsible for updating the instruction target referenced by the entry's code field to the format specified by the type parameter. If the designated target type is JUMP_LABEL_NOP, this routine writes a hardware NOP instruction into the address designated by code. If the instruction type resolves to a branch target, the function leverages the values of the entry's code field and target field to generate a valid branch instruction, and subsequently writes the generated instruction into the address referenced by the code field.

The code sequence init_section_contains() verifies whether the instruction address referenced by the entry's code field resides within the initialization code segment (bounded between __init_begin and __init_end). If the target address resides within the initialization segment, it invokes the function jump_entry_set_init() to set bit b1 (the second bit) of the key field inside the jump entry, denoting that the initialization pass for this jump entry has completed. Following the initialization of this jump entry, the routine leverages static_key_set_entries() to map the entries field within the matching static key to store the base address of this jump entry.

After traversing all jump entries within the static jump label array, the program sets the global variable static_key_initialized to 1, indicating that the initialization phase for the jump table has completed successfully.

If a subsequent operational flow requires toggling a NOP placeholder into a concrete branch instruction, this transformation can be executed at runtime by invoking arch_jump_label_transform_static(iter, JUMP_LABEL_JMP).

chapter 13 Command-Line Parameter Parsing

Kernel Command-Line Parameters

13.1 Kernel Command-Line Parameters

As established in the section covering boot parameter analysis and command-line parameter merging, U-Boot supplies command-line parameters via the command_line variable, which encompasses both core kernel command-line parameters and miscellaneous environment parameters. When tokenizing these command-line arguments, the kernel exclusively parses parameters preceding the -- delimiter, while explicitly forwarding all arguments succeeding the -- marker directly to the init() process. Throughout this parsing procedure, if the kernel encounters an unrecognized parameter that does not contain a . symbol, it likewise hands that parameter over to the init() process. The init() process subsequently treats parameters containing the = symbol as its local environment variables, whereas parameters lacking the = symbol are handled as standard command-line variables for the init() process. All parameters placed after the -- marker are parsed as variables for the init() process.

Via these kernel command-line parameters, the system dynamically enables or disables specific capabilities. When a designated argument is present within the kernel command-line string, the system activates the operational functionality associated with that parameter. Common kernel parameters include AGP, ALSA, APM, DRM, and IPV6, which map respectively to Accelerated Graphics Port, Advanced Linux Sound Architecture, Advanced Power Management, Direct Rendering Manager, and Internet Protocol Version 6. A comprehensive register of available parameters can be reviewed within official Linux technical documentation.

Command-line kernel arguments can also be leveraged to assign variable values to specific modules. For example, configuring the following command-line argument:

"usbcore.blinkenlight=1"

assigns a value of 1 to the variable blinkenlight belonging to the usbcore module, thereby enabling the kernel to support USB LED blinking capabilities.

The formatting layout of the command-line parameters is structured as:

"log_buf_len=1M print-fatal-signals=1" "foo=bar,bar2 baz=fuz wiz"

or alternatively:

"log-buf-len=1M print_fatal_signals=1"

Each pair of double quotation marks encapsulates a distinct group of variables, and the quotation groups are separated from one another via whitespace characters. Hyphens (-) and underscores (_) are treated as functionally equivalent characters by the parser.

Early Option Parsing

13.2 Early Option Parsing

For ARM systems, the primary function of parsing early kernel parameters is to configure specific attributes for the early console (earlyconsole). The function responsible for executing this early argument parsing is parse_early_param(), which is decorated with the __init attribute and defined within the source file git/init/main.c. Its definition is implemented as follows:

void __init parse_early_param(void)
{
	static int done __initdata;
	static char tmp_cmdline[COMMAND_LINE_SIZE] __initdata;
	if (done)
		return;
	strlcpy(tmp_cmdline, boot_command_line, COMMAND_LINE_SIZE);
	parse_early_options(tmp_cmdline);
	done = 1;
}

After copying the command-line arguments from boot_command_line into a temporary staging buffer, parse_early_param() invokes the function parse_early_options() to process the text string. This function acts as a wrapper around the generalized parse_args() routine and is declared inside git/init/main.c as follows:

void __init parse_early_options(char *cmdline)
{
	parse_args("early options", cmdline, NULL, 0, 0, 0, NULL, do_early_param);
}

Within this scope, "early options" represents the descriptive target identity used to print verbose debugging traces. cmdline points to the raw command-line string payload targeted for parsing. The callback function do_early_param is specifically provided to handle variables that the core kernel parameter registry cannot natively identify.

The definition of the core parse_args() routine is hosted within the source file git/kernel/params.c and is implemented as follows:

char *parse_args(const char *doing, 
                char *args, 
                const struct kernel_param *params, 
                unsigned num, 
                s16 min_level, 
                s16 max_level, 
                void *arg, 
                int (*unknown)(char *param, char *val, const char *doing, void *arg)) 
{
	char *param, *val, *err = NULL;
	args = skip_spaces(args);
	if (*args)
		pr_debug("doing %s, parsing ARGS: '%s'\n", doing, args);
	while (*args) {
		int ret;
		int irq_was_disabled;
		args = next_arg(args, &param, &val);	
		if (!val && strcmp(param, "--") == 0)	
			return err ?: args;
		irq_was_disabled = irqs_disabled();
		ret = parse_one(param, val, doing, params, num, min_level, max_level, arg, unknown);
		if (irq_was_disabled && !irqs_disabled())
			pr_warn("%s: option '%s' enabled irq's!\n", doing, param);
		switch (ret) {
		case 0:
			continue;
		case -ENOENT:
			pr_err("%s: Unknown parameter `%s'\n", doing, param);
			break;
		case -ENOSPC:
			pr_err("%s: `%s' too large for parameter `%s'\n", doing, val ?: "", param);
			break;
		default:
			pr_err("%s: `%s' invalid for parameter `%s'\n", doing, val ?: "", param);
			break;
		}
		err = ERR_PTR(ret);
	}
	return err;
}

The function next_arg(args, &param, &val) scans the string payload referenced by args (the cmd_line data) to isolate the position of the next parameter group, and returns a pointer tracking that next block. param captures the target address of the variable currently being parsed. val points to the specific parameter value corresponding to the current variable—meaning the text string segment trailing the = delimiter. If the assignment delimiter = cannot be located, the value defaults to a null pointer. next_arg() isolates the boundaries of the active variable group and the succeeding token block by parsing special control characters such as ", -, --, and = inside the cmd_line string. It strips out leading and trailing whitespaces enclosing the parameter group and overwrites the literal characters " and = with null terminators ('\0'). The function next_arg() is defined inside the file git/lib/cmdline.c.

The function parse_one(param, val, doing, params, num, min_level, max_level, arg, unknown) handles the parsing logic for a single variable pair. param represents a standalone variable extracted from the command line, while val references the corresponding text value assigned to that variable. doing is a text string marking the active operational phase, which is primarily leveraged to print debugging traces. params represents an array composed of elements of type struct kernel_param, which enumerates the valid variables that this routine is authorized to handle. Any command-line arguments that fall outside the explicit boundary constraints specified within the params registry are handed off to the unknown function callback (provided as the final argument input) for customized processing. The definition of the kernel_param structure is implemented as follows:

struct kernel_param {
	const char *name;
	struct module *mod;
	const struct kernel_param_ops *ops;
	const u16 perm;
	s8 level;
	u8 flags;
	union {
		void *arg;
		const struct kparam_string *str;
		const struct kparam_array *arr;
	};
};

This structure outlines the parameter name, the specific kernel module ownership mapping, and the operational callback table used to set and get the underlying value. The perm field determines whether the module parameter is exposed visually within the sysfs filesystem infrastructure. The level field dictates the execution priority level of the module during the initcall stabilization passes. The generalized concept of initcall execution tracks will be analyzed across subsequent chapters. The flags field configures the safety and security attributes of the parameter, where bit 0 indicates whether setting this parameter will taint the active kernel instance, and bit 1 establishes whether it is permissible to configure this parameter under hardware lockdown constraints. These two specific bit definitions correspond to:

enum {
	KERNEL_PARAM_FL_UNSAFE    = (1 << 0),
	KERNEL_PARAM_FL_HWPARAM   = (1 << 1),
};

The routines utilized to assign and read the parameter parameters are grouped inside the kernel_param_ops structure, which is structured as follows:

struct kernel_param_ops {
	unsigned int flags;	
	int (*set)(const char *val, const struct kernel_param *kp);
	int (*get)(char *buffer, const struct kernel_param *kp);
	void (*free)(void *arg);
};

Within this layout, the flags field indicates whether a null or empty value configuration is valid for this specific variable. The available bitmask flag resolves to:

enum {
	KERNEL_PARAM_OPS_FL_NOARG = (1 << 0)
};

The set field points to the callback routine used to configure the variable value, while the get field points to the callback routine used to read back the active variable value.

The function parse_one() is declared as follows:

static int parse_one(char *param, 
    char *val, 
    const char *doing, 
    const struct kernel_param *params, 
    unsigned num_params, 
    s16 min_level, 
    s16 max_level, 
    void *arg, 
    int (*handle_unknown)(char *param, char *val, const char *doing, void *arg))
{
	unsigned int i;
	int err;
	for (i = 0; i < num_params; i++) {
		if (parameq(param, params[i].name)) {
			if (params[i].level < min_level || params[i].level > max_level)
				return 0;	
			if (!val && !(params[i].ops->flags & 
   KERNEL_PARAM_OPS_FL_NOARG))
				return -EINVAL;
			pr_debug("handling %s with %p\n", param, params[i].ops->set);
			kernel_param_lock(params[i].mod);
			if (param_check_unsafe(&params[i]))
				err = params[i].ops->set(val, &params[i]);
			else
				err = -EPERM;
			kernel_param_unlock(params[i].mod);
			return err;
		}
	}
	if (handle_unknown) {
		pr_debug("doing %s: %s='%s'\n", doing, param, val);
		return handle_unknown(param, val, doing, arg);
	}
	pr_debug("Unknown argument '%s'\n", param);
	return -ENOENT;
}

The parse_one() function is defined within the source file git/kernel/params.c.

parse_one() initially verifies whether the specific parameter designated by param is contained within the variable registry specified by params. If the argument falls outside this registered scope, param is handed off to the handle_unknown callback function (which maps to do_early_param). Conversely, if the argument is found within the specified registry, parse_one() determines whether the initcall level of the variable falls within the boundaries bounded by the maximum and minimum levels. If the priority constraints are satisfied, the function proceeds to check whether the flags field of this parameter evaluates to KERNEL_PARAM_FL_UNSAFE. Provided that the configuration does not negatively compromise kernel runtime safety, it further evaluates whether the variable value is a null value. In the event of a null value configuration, the routine checks whether the parameter's operational flags permit an empty value assignment. Upon passing all validation blocks, parse_one() invokes the customized set callback provided by the variable itself to apply the parameter value. The initcall tier establishes the exact scheduling and execution sequence of a given initialization routine. The internal execution topology of these initialization layers will be comprehensively analyzed when introducing the underlying initcall operational mechanics.

For ARM architectures, the specific manifestation of invoking the parse_args() function is executed as:

    parse_args("early options", cmdline, NULL, 0, 0, 0, NULL, do_early_param)

Because this explicit invocation supplies no structural array enumerating the targeted variables to be parsed, the parse_one() function directly triggers the do_early_param handler callback to process the incoming param variable. The do_early_param function is declared within the file git/init/main.c, and its definition is as follows:

static int __init do_early_param(char *param, char *val, const char *unused, void *arg)
{
	const struct obs_kernel_param *p;
	for (p = __setup_start; p < __setup_end; p++) {
		if ((p->early && parameq(param, p->str)) || (strcmp(param, "console") == 0
 		    && strcmp(p->str, "earlycon") == 0)) {
			if (p->setup_func(val) != 0)
				pr_warn("Malformed early option '%s'\n", param);
		}
	}
	return 0;
}

The structure definition for obs_kernel_param is implemented as:

struct obs_kernel_param {
	const char *str;
	int (*setup_func)(char *);
	int early;
};

The do_early_param function first evaluates whether the memory segment bounded precisely between __setup_start and __setup_end encloses a tracking descriptor matching the argument passed via param. It checks whether this descriptor explicitly enables the early attribute flag, or whether the param string matches "console" while the __setup_start to __setup_end table contains the "earlycon" tracking signature. If either condition is structurally satisfied, it invokes the corresponding parameter initialization callback setup_func() to initialize the configuration targeted by param.

As established from the preceding layout description, the function parse_early_param() executes no operations on parameters it cannot structurally identify, deliberately leaving those unparsed tokens to be resolved by subsequent backend processing stages.

If an exception or parsing failure occurs throughout the tokenization of a given variable pair, the parse_args() function immediately terminates the evaluation of any remaining command-line components, translates the resulting error code (situated between -1 and -4095) into a pointer pointing to a void type, and returns it. If the entire string payload is successfully processed without errors, it returns the precise memory address pointing to the double-hyphen delimiter "──" within the command line.

The complete function execution call graph for parsing kernel command-line parameters during the early system boot phase is illustrated in Figure 13-1.

Separation of Command-Line Options and Environment Variables

13.3 Separation of Command-Line Options and Environment Variables

The preceding section introduced the parameter parsing function parse_args(). After evaluating the early command-line parameters, the start_kernel() function invokes parse_args() once again, utilizing the unknown_bootoption() function to handle unknown options encountered during the boot sequence. In this secondary execution path, start_kernel() invokes parse_args() in the following manner:

after_dashes = parse_args("Booting kernel", static_command_line, __start___param, __stop___param - __start___param, -1, -1, NULL, &unknown_bootoption)

The descriptive identity tracking string designated for log diagnostics is "Booting kernel". The pointer tracking the target string to be parsed is static_command_line, which encapsulates the combined contents of extra_command_line and command_line, wherein the contents of command_line append directly to the end of extra_command_line. The registry of valid options that this routine is authorized to handle is specified by the pointer __start___param, and the total count of these listed variables evaluates to __stop___param - __start___param. Because the maximum and minimum initcall levels passed to the routine are both specified as -1, all incoming parameters are directly routed to the unknown_bootoption() callback function for custom parsing.

The unknown_bootoption() function is defined within the source file git/init/main.c, and its definition is implemented as follows:

static int __init unknown_bootoption(char *param, char *val, const char *unused, void *arg)
{
	size_t len = strlen(param);
	repair_env_string(param, val);
	if (obsolete_checksetup(param))
		return 0;
	if (strnchr(param, len, '.'))
		return 0;
	if (panic_later)
		return 0;
	if (val) {
		unsigned int i;
		for (i = 0; envp_init[i]; i++) {
			if (i == MAX_INIT_ENVS) {
				panic_later = "env";
				panic_param = param;
			}
			if (!strncmp(param, envp_init[i], len+1))
				break;
		}
		envp_init[i] = param;
	} else {
		unsigned int i;
		for (i = 0; argv_init[i]; i++) {
			if (i == MAX_INIT_ARGS) {
				panic_later = "init";
				panic_param = param;
			}
		}
		argv_init[i] = param;
	}
	return 0;
}

As established from previous descriptions, the helper routine next_arg() replaces the literal structural characters = and " within arguments formatted as param=val and param="val" with null characters ('\0'). To restore this data, unknown_bootoption() first invokes the function repair_env_string(param, val) to uniformly reconstitute the target tokens back into the explicit param=val schema. If the original format matched the param="val" schema, repair_env_string() also strips out the extraneous embedded null markers.

Following this repair pass, it invokes obsolete_checksetup() to ensure that the processed command-line argument does not rely on an outdated format specification. Once the parameter syntax format is validated to satisfy all layout constraints, unknown_bootoption() begins separating the parameters from their matching values. If the parameter value field val evaluates to a non-null pointer—meaning the parameter satisfies the explicit param=val schema—this argument is classified as an environment variable. Under this scenario, if the environment variable tracking array envp_init possesses available slots and the current parameter has not yet been registered, the parameter string is saved directly into envp_init.

Conversely, if the parameter lacks an associated value assignment—meaning it follows the raw param schema—it is classified as a command-line option. Similarly, if the command-line option tracking array argv_init contains unallocated slots and the argument does not yet exist within that repository, the param pointer is saved directly into argv_init. If the routing logic fails to discover a valid unallocated index slot inside either envp_init or argv_init, the unknown_bootoption routine populates the tracking variables panic_later and panic_param to trigger a kernel panic fault at a later execution phase.

Upon concluding this variable separation workflow, if an execution fault occurs, parse_args() returns the memory address of the matching exception handling handler. If the command line payload is processed successfully without errors, the function returns the exact memory address pointing immediately after the double-hyphen delimiter -- inside the static_command_line string. Therefore, provided that the command-line arguments conform to the required syntax and the arrays envp_init and argv_init possess sufficient storage space, the after_dashes pointer tracks the string sequence placed after the -- marker, meaning it maps directly to the explicit variables forwarded to the user-space init() process. The structural workflow of separating command options from environment variables is illustrated in Figure 13-2.

Option Processing for the Init Process

13.4 Option Processing for the Init Process

After processing the parameters preceding the -- marker, the start_kernel() function utilizes the macro definition IS_ERR_OR_NULL() to determine whether the after_dashes pointer evaluates to null or falls within the exception range between -1 and -4095. If it is a valid pointer, the kernel invokes the parse_args() function once again to tokenize the parameters trailing the -- delimiter within static_command_line. If these arguments conform to the required syntax layout, they are stored directly into the argv_init array. The function is invoked in the following manner:

parse_args("Setting init args", after_dashes, NULL, 0, -1, -1, NULL, set_init_arg);

Similarly, due to the parameter configuration passed to parse_args(), the parse_args() function bypasses internal table lookups and hands the variables tracked by after_dashes directly to the set_init_arg() function for parsing. This function is located within the file git/init/main.c and is defined as follows:

static int __init set_init_arg(char *param, char *val, const char *unused, void *arg)
{
	unsigned int i;
	if (panic_later)
		return 0;
	repair_env_string(param, val);
	for (i = 0; argv_init[i]; i++) {
		if (i == MAX_INIT_ARGS) {
			panic_later = "init";
			panic_param = param;
			return 0;
		}
	}
	argv_init[i] = param;
	return 0;
}

Upon invoking the function repair_env_string(param, val) to uniformly restore arguments structured as param=val or param="val" back into the explicit param=val schema, the routine verifies if the argv_init array contains sufficient unallocated slots. If space is available, each individual parameter is appended into the argv_init array. If the array bounds are exceeded, the routine populates the tracking variables panic_later and panic_param accordingly.

Furthermore, if the supplemental init process variable string extra_init_args is present, start_kernel() invokes parse_args() one final time, leveraging the set_init_arg() function to archive the diverse variables pointed to by extra_init_args into the argv_init array.

chapter 14 Buffer and Exception Handler Initialization

Log Buffer Configuration

14.1 Log Buffer Configuration

During the boot phase, the system has not yet completed its core initialization routines, nor has it loaded device drivers. Consequently, messages cannot be exported via standard subsystem drivers. To track the boot sequence, print fault diagnostics, and output debugging traces, the Linux kernel provides the printk() function to facilitate fundamental message logging capabilities during the system bootstrap phase.

Linux utilizes a circular queue topology to store tracking messages targeted for display during the boot sequence. The kernel implements diverse functions to orchestrate queue movement, read operations, write operations, and storage space allocation, all of which are leveraged by the printk() engine. The following sections outline the architecture and operations of this circular queue framework to clarify the log buffer initialization process.

14.1.1 Ring Buffer

The Linux kernel describes the ring structure utilized by the printk engine via the following structural abstraction:

struct printk_ringbuffer {
	struct prb_desc_ring	desc_ring;
	struct prb_data_ring	text_data_ring;
	atomic_long_t		fail;
};

This structure defines the primary header control block of the ring buffer queue. The desc_ring field describes the descriptor ring tracking metadata records, while the text_data_ring field represents the primary data ring buffer used to preserve the literal string text targeted for printing. The fail variable tracks the cumulative count of read or write anomalies encountered.

The layout of the ring buffer header control block is illustrated in Figure 14-1.

The collective blueprint of the entire ring buffer architecture is illustrated in Figure 14-2.

14.1.1.1 The Descriptor Ring Buffer

The concrete array elements composing the metadata descriptor ring are specified by the following data type:

struct prb_desc_ring {
	unsigned int			count_bits;
	struct prb_desc		*descs;
	struct printk_info		*infos;
	atomic_long_t		head_id;
	atomic_long_t		tail_id; 
};

Within this tracking control block, count_bits establishes the exact magnitude of the descs array—defining the bit width utilized to index elements inside the descs repository. The literal size of the descs array evaluates to DESC_COUNT = 2^count_bits^. The descs member points to an array of type struct prb_desc, which Linux accesses via a modulo-based circular methodology. Each standalone entry in this array corresponds to a discrete tracking payload, mapping out the base boundary, tail boundary, and active state of the associated record. The infos array stores supplemental metadata descriptors associated with the log entries. Its indices correspond one-to-one with the elements of the descs array, meaning records sharing an identical index value track the exact same message payload. head_id represents the logical sequence index of the most recent descriptor record committed into the descs array, while tail_id tracks the logical index of the oldest valid record retained within the matrix.

The individual elements inside the descs array are formatted as:

struct prb_desc {
	atomic_long_t			state_var;
	struct prb_data_blk_lpos		text_blk_lpos;
};

The upper two bits of the state_var variable serve as explicit state bitmasks used to track the operational phase of the matching descriptor entry. This metadata state field accepts the discrete evaluation properties desc_reusable, desc_reserved, desc_committed, and desc_finalized. These represent free space available for reuse, storage space actively held by a writer context, data committed by a writer context but not yet fully visible, and data finalized and available for read consumption, respectively.

The programmatic definitions for these entry state parameters are structured as follows:

enum desc_state {
	desc_miss		=  -1,		/* ID mismatch (pseudo state) */
	desc_reserved	= 0x0,		/* reserved, in use by writer */
	desc_committed	= 0x1,		/* committed by writer, could get reopened */
	desc_finalized	= 0x2,		/* committed, no further modification allowed */
	desc_reusable	= 0x3,		/* free, not yet used by any writer */
};

The tracking symbol desc_miss is never preserved inside the literal state_var flag; it merely acts as a programmatic pseudo-state denoting that a matching descriptor entry cannot be located within the ring metadata table.

The remaining bits of state_var specify the logical identification sequence number of the descriptor, whose scale extends far beyond the physical array limits of the ring list. Computing the logical identifier modulo the total array dimension yields the physical array slot location: index = ((state_var << 2) >> 2) % DESC_COUNT. This logical sequence token is concurrently stored at the leading boundary of the corresponding text data block payload.

The structure type for text_blk_lpos is implemented as:

struct prb_data_blk_lpos {
	unsigned long	begin;	
	unsigned long	next;
};

begin represents the absolute starting memory tracking position of the text payload corresponding to this descriptor block. next indicates the starting position of the subsequent data payload block. By analyzing the values of begin and next, the core subsystem can determine the location and size of the text data described by this entry.

The infos array tracks supplemental metadata records belonging to the matching entry data payload, and its structure is defined as follows:

struct printk_info {
	u64	seq;				/* sequence number */
	u64	ts_nsec;			/* timestamp in nanoseconds */
	u16	text_len;			/* length of text message */
	u8	facility;			/* syslog facility */
	u8	flags:5;			/* internal record flags */
	u8	level:3;			/* syslog level */
	u32	caller_id;			/* thread id or processor id */
	struct dev_printk_info	dev_info;
};

The most critical parameters inside this layout are the chronological sequence token seq and the message priority property level. The sequence number is utilized to index and interface with this ring list infrastructure, while users can leverage the log level to filter the specific content targeted for output display.

During initial execution, the element situated at index 0 of the infos repository initializes with a sequence value of 0, whereas all subsequent items possess sequence tokens that match their literal array index slots. Because this framework wraps as a circular loop sequence, each tracking slot is recycled and rewritten multiple times. When an individual slot is reallocated for a new log entry, its sequence number increments by adding DESC_COUNT onto the baseline sequence metric.

The structural arrangement of the descriptor ring queue is illustrated in the diagram below.

4.1.1.2 The Data Ring Buffer

The data ring buffer is utilized to preserve the literal tracking text targeted for output display. The underlying elements composing this ring queue are described by the following structure:

struct prb_data_ring {
	unsigned int			size_bits;
	char				*data;
	atomic_long_t			head_lpos;
	atomic_long_t			tail_lpos;
};

Within this tracking structure, size_bits defines the total bit width required to represent the index values used to access elements within the data queue. The queue data container data is implemented as a character array whose absolute capacity evaluates to DATA_SIZE = 2^size_bits^, inside of which the actual string payload is saved. This tracking container is likewise processed using modulo-based circular access logic, where the physical array index is calculated as:

data_index = lpos%DATA_SIZE

Here, lpos represents the logical tracking address of the raw data block, and its boundary scale extends far beyond the physical constraints of DATA_SIZE.

14.1.2 Ring Buffer Operations

The Linux kernel implements a robust suite of functions dedicated to manipulating the core components of the printk ring buffer infrastructure. The function prb_init(struct printk_ringbuffer *rb, char *text_buf, unsigned int textbits, struct prb_desc *descs, unsigned int descbits, struct printk_info *infos) is responsible for initializing a target ring buffer instance rb. Within this interface, text_buf, descs, and infos represent externally allocated backing storage structures supplied to the ring subsystem, which act respectively as the raw text data ring buffer, the descriptor array, and the metadata info array. The parameter descbits configures the bit width utilized to index elements inside the descs tracking structure, while textbits defines the bit width utilized to index elements inside the data array within the data ring structure. This initialization routine hooks the pointers text_buf, descs, and infos onto the corresponding tracking fields of rb, establishes the initial operational bounds of the descriptor and info queues via descbits, and configures the initial limits of the text data ring via textbits.

Once the structural scaffolding of the ring buffer has been established, the subsystem can execute concurrent read and write operations against it. Prior to executing a write operation against an existing ring buffer instance rb, a tracking variable r of the following type must be declared:

struct printk_record {
	struct printk_info	*info;
	char			*text_buf;
	unsigned int		text_buf_size;
};

Following the declaration of r, the function prb_rec_init_wr(&r, len) is invoked to configure the text_buf_size field to match the explicit buffer size allocation requirements specified by len. The function prb_rec_init_wr() is implemented as follows:

void prb_rec_init_wr(struct printk_record *r, unsigned int text_buf_size)
{
	r->info = NULL;
	r->text_buf = NULL;
	r->text_buf_size = text_buf_size;
}

As demonstrated by the implementation snippet, the role of this routine is to establish the dimensions of the write staging buffer by initializing the text_buf_size field of the printk_record structure tracking variable r.

After initializing the tracking variable r, the system invokes the function prb_reserve(struct prb_reserved_entry *e, struct printk_ringbuffer *rb, struct printk_record *r) to reserve the necessary structural storage space for both the metadata descriptor and raw text data entries inside the ring buffer rb for the calling thread context. It subsequently assigns the internal infos pointer of the newly carved descriptor element and the internal data pointer of the allocated text payload element directly onto the info and text_buf fields of the tracking variable r, respectively. The function prb_reserve() records the remaining operational metadata belonging to this reserved block within a separate context variable e of type struct prb_reserved_entry. This metadata tracking structure captures a pointer rb mapping back to the parent ring buffer, the logical tracking identification token id of the newly reserved descriptor, and the absolute size metrics of the memory space consumed by the data block. Upon completing these alignment and registration tasks, the calling context can execute its concrete write transaction against the ring buffer by streaming data directly into the memory buffer referenced by the text_buf field of variable r.

The kernel further exports a higher-level abstract write interface designated as add_to_rb(struct printk_ringbuffer *rb, struct printk_record *r). This utility automatically orchestrates the underlying calls to prb_rec_init_wr() and prb_reserve() to allocate descriptor and text data blocks, copies the diverse data streams referenced by r.info and r.text_buf directly into the corresponding storage blocks reserved inside the ring buffer infrastructure, and subsequently invokes the routine prb_final_commit() to transition the state bitmask of the data block to a readable phase. Finally, it returns the total memory footprint consumed by the archived record payload.

When executing a read transaction against a target ring buffer, a tracking variable of type struct printk_record must similarly be declared. In contrast to the write sequence, the subsystem must explicitly allocate two standalone staging memory zones prior to reading, which are leveraged to preserve the data payload streams retrieved from the text data queue and the metadata descriptor queue respectively. Before reading from the ring list, the printk_record tracking variable r must be initialized with the physical base memory addresses and size limits of these two independent staging zones. The function responsible for initializing this tracking context is implemented as follows:

void prb_rec_init_rd(struct printk_record *r, struct printk_info *info, char *text_buf, unsigned int text_buf_size)
{
	r->info = info;
	r->text_buf = text_buf;
	r->text_buf_size = text_buf_size;
}

Within this initialization wrapper, the pointer info tracks the base address of the staging zone allocated to hold descriptor metadata records, text_buf points to the base address of the staging zone allocated to hold text data payloads, and text_buf_size specifies the absolute memory limit of the text data staging allocation.

Following the configuration of the tracking variable r, the core subsystem can read back the ring buffer data payloads and associated info records by evaluating the contents hosted at the target memory locations referenced by the distinct pointers inside r.

The Linux kernel additionally implements a variety of supplemental helper functions to handle display updates, scale the log buffer capacity dynamically for auxiliary secondary CPU cores, validate the structural integrity of the ring lists, read out record states, and execute mathematical transformations to map logical identifiers and locations (id and lpos tokens) into literal array indices. These specialized routines are defined across the source code trees located within the files git/kernel/printk/printk_ringbuffer.h and git/kernel/printk/printk_ringbuffer.c.

14.1.3 Data State Transition

As established in the preceding sections, the upper two bits of the state_var field within the descriptor ring describe the operational phase of its corresponding entry. The state can be read via the function desc_read() by providing a specific logical index. If the descriptor ring cannot locate an entry that matches the specified logical index, the function returns the desc_miss pseudo-state.

The active lifecycle of an entry comprises four core states: desc_reusable, desc_reserved, desc_committed, and desc_finalized. Upon system initialization, all entries default to the desc_reusable state. When a writer context triggers a log allocation, it invokes the function prb_reserve() to lock down the necessary storage space inside the ring buffer. The descriptor subsystem scans for available slots starting from head_id + 1. If the structural distance between head_id and tail_id reaches the maximum physical dimension of the descriptor array, prb_reserve() advances the tail position of the circular list, thereby evicting the stale record occupied at the old tail boundary. Once the writer context successfully claims a descriptor slot, it invalidates and frees up the physical space consumed by the oldest records inside the data ring. This data space allocation is executed by the internal routine data_alloc(). This routine scans for unallocated space starting from the begin_lpos boundary of the data ring. Upon claiming the necessary data blocks, data_alloc() marks the old associated descriptor entries as invalid and updates tail_lpos to guarantee that the active data bounds within the text array remain valid. After successfully reserving the memory blocks, the state bitmask of the matching entry transitions from desc_reusable to desc_reserved. The prb_reserve() routine can only claim memory from entries that reside in the desc_reusable state. Once the memory block is reserved, the writer context can stream data into the ring buffer. Upon completing the write transaction, calling the function prb_commit() transitions the entry status to desc_committed. Alternatively, if the write operation is concluded and no further modifications are required, calling the function prb_final_commit() transforms the state directly from desc_reserved to desc_finalized.

The structural state transition rules are governed by a strict unidirectional lifecycle: desc_reusable can only transition to desc_reserved; desc_reserved can transition to either desc_committed or desc_finalized; desc_committed can only transition to desc_finalized; and desc_finalized can only revert to desc_reusable. This means that storage allocation can only be carved out from elements residing in the desc_reusable pool. Before any data can be committed to the ring buffer, the memory must be explicitly reserved. Furthermore, only elements that have reached the desc_finalized state are eligible to be invalidated and recycled by the system.

14.1.4 Initialization of the Log Buffer

The printk subsystem utilizes two categories of ring buffers: a temporary early buffer and a standard dynamic ring buffer. During the initial booting phase, printk leverages a temporary staging queue that is programmatically set up at runtime. The standard persistent ring buffer is activated during later boot stages and post-boot execution, declared and instantiated via the macro definition _DEFINE_PRINTKRB(name, descbits, avgtextbits, text_buf). Within this macro blueprint, name specifies the identifier of the ring buffer instance, descbits configures the bit width utilized to index the elements of the descriptor array, avgtextbits dictates the bit width for the text data block sizing metrics, and text_buf points to the externally allocated static backing buffer designated to store the raw text data strings.

The macro responsible for instantiating this ring buffer architecture is defined as follows:

#define _DEFINE_PRINTKRB(name, descbits, avgtextbits, text_buf)			\
static struct prb_desc _##name##_descs[_DESCS_COUNT(descbits)] = {		\
	[_DESCS_COUNT(descbits) - 1] = {					\
		.state_var		= ATOMIC_INIT(DESC0_SV(descbits)),		\
		.text_blk_lpos	= FAILED_BLK_LPOS,			\
	},									\
};										\
static struct printk_info _##name##_infos[_DESCS_COUNT(descbits)] = {		\
	[0] = {									\
		.seq = -(u64)_DESCS_COUNT(descbits),				\
	},									\
	[_DESCS_COUNT(descbits) - 1] = {					\
		.seq = 0,								\
	},									\
};										\
static struct printk_ringbuffer name = {						\
	.desc_ring = {								\
		.count_bits	= descbits,					\
		.descs		= &_##name##_descs[0],			\
		.infos		= &_##name##_infos[0],			\
		.head_id		= ATOMIC_INIT(DESC0_ID(descbits)),		\
		.tail_id		= ATOMIC_INIT(DESC0_ID(descbits)),		\
	},									\
	.text_data_ring = {							\
		.size_bits	= (avgtextbits) + (descbits),					\
		.data		= text_buf,					\
		.head_lpos	= ATOMIC_LONG_INIT(BLK0_LPOS((avgtextbits) + (descbits))),\
		.tail_lpos	= ATOMIC_LONG_INIT(BLK0_LPOS((avgtextbits) + (descbits))),	\
	},									\
	.fail			= ATOMIC_LONG_INIT(0),			\
}

This macro instantiates a monolithic ring buffer structural instance under the designated name name (where name represents the literal string sequence supplied by the caller). Concurrently, it allocates static tracking matrices name_descs and name_infos with a capacity scaling to 2^descbit^ to serve respectively as the backing descs descriptor array and the infos metadata array. The text storage component of the data ring utilizes the externally supplied text_buf memory container. The internal trackers head_id, tail_id, and seq belonging to the descriptor infrastructure are initialized to predefined architectural defaults, while the tracking fields head_lpos and tail_lpos within the text data ring are similarly anchored to default base indices (typically resolving to 0 or -1).

The specific ring buffer instance leveraged by the printk engine is designated as printk_rb_static, which is instantiated via the statement _DEFINE_PRINTKRB(printk_rb_static, CONFIG_LOG_BUF_SHIFT - PRB_AVGBITS, PRB_AVGBITS, &__log_buf[0]). The data ring container specified in this declaration utilizes the core log buffer memory asset __log_buf, which is implemented as a global character array.

The _DEFINE_PRINTKRB() macro merely executes the initial compile-time structural initialization for the printk_rb_static ring buffer topology. Before the printk() function can reliably stream logs into this queue, supplemental initialization settings must be orchestrated at runtime. The start_kernel() process handles this requirement by invoking the function setup_log_buf(0) to finalize the log buffer configuration. The function setup_log_buf(int early) is defined across the source files git/include/linux/printk.h and git/kernel/printk/printk.c, and its definition is implemented as:

void __init setup_log_buf(int early)
{
	struct printk_info *new_infos;
	unsigned int new_descs_count;
	struct prb_desc *new_descs;
	struct printk_info info;
	struct printk_record r;
	size_t new_descs_size;
	size_t new_infos_size;
	unsigned long flags;
	char *new_log_buf;
	unsigned int free;
	u64 seq;
	if (!early)
		set_percpu_data_ready();
	if (log_buf != __log_buf)
		return;
	if (!early && !new_log_buf_len)
		log_buf_add_cpu();
	if (!new_log_buf_len)
		return;
	new_descs_count = new_log_buf_len >> PRB_AVGBITS;
	if (new_descs_count == 0) {
		pr_err("new_log_buf_len: %lu too small\n", new_log_buf_len);
		return;
	}
	new_log_buf = memblock_alloc(new_log_buf_len, LOG_ALIGN);
	if (unlikely(!new_log_buf)) {
		pr_err("log_buf_len: %lu text bytes not available\n", new_log_buf_len);
		return;
	}
	new_descs_size = new_descs_count * sizeof(struct prb_desc);
	new_descs = memblock_alloc(new_descs_size, LOG_ALIGN);
	if (unlikely(!new_descs)) {
		pr_err("log_buf_len: %zu desc bytes not available\n", new_descs_size);
		goto err_free_log_buf;
	}
	new_infos_size = new_descs_count * sizeof(struct printk_info);
	new_infos = memblock_alloc(new_infos_size, LOG_ALIGN);
	if (unlikely(!new_infos)) {
		pr_err("log_buf_len: %zu info bytes not available\n", new_infos_size);
		goto err_free_descs;
	}
	prb_rec_init_rd(&r, &info, &setup_text_buf[0], sizeof(setup_text_buf));
	prb_init(&printk_rb_dynamic, new_log_buf, ilog2(new_log_buf_len), new_descs, 
ilog2(new_descs_count), new_infos);
	logbuf_lock_irqsave(flags);
	log_buf_len = new_log_buf_len;
	log_buf = new_log_buf;
	new_log_buf_len = 0;
	free = __LOG_BUF_LEN;
	prb_for_each_record(0, &printk_rb_static, seq, &r)
		free -= add_to_rb(&printk_rb_dynamic, &r);
	prb = &printk_rb_dynamic;
	logbuf_unlock_irqrestore(flags);
	if (seq != prb_next_seq(&printk_rb_static)) {
		pr_err("dropped %llu messages\n", prb_next_seq(&printk_rb_static) - seq);
	}
	pr_info("log_buf_len: %u bytes\n", log_buf_len);
	pr_info("early log buf free: %u(%u%%)\n", free, (free * 100) / __LOG_BUF_LEN);
	return;
err_free_descs:
	memblock_free(__pa(new_descs), new_descs_size);
err_free_log_buf:
	memblock_free(__pa(new_log_buf), new_log_buf_len);
}

During execution, the printk() function needs to acquire the console_lock. If this lock is successfully acquired, printk() invokes the console drivers to output messages to the console hardware. If the console_lock cannot be obtained, printk() preserves the messages inside the __log_buf staging area. Prior to writing into the __log_buf area, printk() must acquire the logbuf_lock.

Under Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) conditions, it is impossible for printk() to safely acquire the logbuf_lock. To prevent message loss in multi-CPU hardware architectures, the Linux kernel allocates a dedicated private buffer for each individual CPU core. When a CPU fails to acquire the logbuf_lock, it streams the data into its own private staging buffer. Subsequently, an interrupt service routine drains the data from these per-CPU private staging buffers back into the main ring buffer used by printk() at an appropriate time. The function set_percpu_data_ready() calls printk_safe_init() to establish these private buffers for each CPU. It registers the function __printk_safe_flush() as the deferred interrupt handling task responsible for flushing data from the private buffers into the main ring buffer, and sets the per-CPU flag __printk_percpu_data_ready to indicate that this mechanism is fully operational. __printk_safe_flush() is defined in the source file git/kernel/printk/printk_safe.c.

The ring buffer instantiated via the macro definition _DEFINE_PRINTKRB() can initially only be utilized by a single CPU. When the system incorporates multiple CPU cores, an equivalent volume of storage space must be allocated for the other CPUs to handle log messages. The function setup_log_buf() first evaluates the aggregate log buffer capacity demanded across all active CPUs via new_log_buf_len(). Following this evaluation, it leverages the memblock_alloc() memory allocation function to independently carve out chunks of memory for the text data area, the descs descriptor array, and the infos metadata array.

As established previously, performing a read operation against the ring buffer requires an external staging area. The Linux kernel declares a global character array designated as setup_text_buf[LOG_LINE_MAX]. The setup_log_buf() function utilizes the address and size of this array to initialize the read staging record r via prb_rec_init_rd(). Upon completing these preparatory tasks, setup_log_buf() creates a new ring buffer instance named printk_rb_dynamic by binding the newly allocated memory zones and their respective capacities, which serves as the log queue during the early phase of the system bootstrap.

After establishing the printk_rb_dynamic ring buffer infrastructure, setup_log_buf() invokes the function add_to_rb() to copy the archived log payload out of the static ring buffer printk_rb_static over into the new printk_rb_dynamic repository, while simultaneously computing the absolute residual free space remaining within the log buffer.

Inside the setup_log_buf() routine, prb is a static pointer variable declared outside the function scope of type struct printk_ringbuffer *, whose default target address references printk_rb_static. By executing the assignment statement prb = &printk_rb_dynamic, the setup_log_buf() function hot-swaps the underlying queue utilized by the printk() engine over to printk_rb_dynamic. Consequently, it can be stated that during the early system boot phase, the kernel switches to this dynamic ring buffer architecture to manage and display system diagnostics.

Virtual File System Buffer Initialization

14.2 Virtual File System Buffer Initialization

14.2.1 Introduction to the Virtual File System

The Virtual File System (VFS) is a software layer within the kernel designed to provide a uniform file interface to user space. In Linux, everything is handled as a file. Linux files include disk files, pipes, sockets, and I/O devices. To uniquely identify a file, Linux utilizes an index node (inode) to represent it. An inode stores file metadata, which primarily encompasses the file size, device ID, user ID, group ID, file read/write modes, user access permissions, physical storage location, the reference count of users currently accessing the file, and file protection flags. The filename and the raw contents of the file itself are not stored within the inode. The definition of the inode structure is located in the file git/include/linux/fs.h and contains a large array of fields to facilitate diverse file operations and ensure file system access security.

User-space file operations involve a significant amount of directory path lookup procedures. To maximize lookup efficiency, Linux carves out a fallback caching zone in memory named the Dentry Cache (dcache). Each tracking entry within this cache block consists of a structure of type struct dentry, which is utilized to preserve frequently accessed path components. The dentry structure is declared within the file git/include/linux/dcache.h. When a user invokes a file operation, Linux first queries the dcache buffer to find a matching dentry for the targeted path or filename. A dentry encloses a direct pointer to its corresponding inode, thereby mapping out the concrete file represented by that entry. If a matching dentry cannot be located, Linux traverses upward through the directory hierarchy step-by-step from the parent node to resolve the file's inode. Upon successfully locating it, Linux instantiates a new dentry entry inside the dcache, which drastically accelerates future path resolution routines.

14.2.2 Hash Tables

Because the absolute number of files contained within a Linux file system can be exceptionally massive, it is impossible to cache the dentry descriptors for all files simultaneously inside the active buffer zone. To circumvent this scale barrier, Linux manages the dcache buffer by structuring it as a hash table. Querying a filename or path component within the cache can then be executed by passing the tokens through a specialized hash function.

A hash table is an extensively applied data structure characterized by its ability to store a large, unpredictable volume of indexed data within a relatively small set of fixed storage slots, while maintaining a baseline query time that remains fundamentally constant. The fundamental building block of a hash table is a bucket, with each bucket preserving explicit lookup keys alongside their corresponding data payload records. One primary challenge present in hash table architectures is the phenomenon of hash collisions—where distinct keys map onto the exact same index location within the table. Diversified strategies exist to resolve hash collisions, one of which is the chained list methodology. When chaining is employed to resolve collisions, each bucket encloses an additional structural pointer referencing a subsequent bucket. When a collision manifests, the colliding key and its associated payload are appended into a newly linked bucket slot down the chain.

When querying a hash table, the engine first runs a hash function to map the user-supplied lookup key into a target hash table index. If the key enclosed inside the bucket referenced by that index matches the target lookup key, the query result is immediately returned. If the keys diverge, the lookup tracking routine traces down the linked chain to evaluate the subsequent bucket slots, repeating this pass until the target key is matched or the tail boundary of the chain is reached. If the matching key cannot be located anywhere along the index's chained list, the query operation evaluates as a failure.

When executing an insertion operation, the key and the hash function are leveraged to compute the appropriate hash table index. If the bucket referenced by this index or any subsequent bucket down its linked chain is currently empty, the key and its corresponding data payload are written directly into that vacant slot. If no empty bucket is found along the existing chain, the subsystem allocates a brand-new bucket descriptor block, records the key and data payload within it, and appends the base address of this new bucket onto the pointer field of the preceding bucket in the chain. The layout of a hash table utilizing chained buckets is illustrated in Figure 14-4.

As demonstrated by the diagram above, a hash table is functionally composed of an array of independent linked lists, where each specific list encapsulates all entries that map to an identical hash table index value.

14.2.3 Initializing the Virtual File System Caches

The start_kernel() function performs the initialization of the memory buffers utilized by the virtual file system by invoking vfs_caches_init_early(). The routine vfs_caches_init_early() is defined within the source file git/fs/dcache.c, and its definition is implemented as follows:

void __init vfs_caches_init_early(void)
{
	int i;
	for (i = 0; i < ARRAY_SIZE(in_lookup_hashtable); i++)
		INIT_HLIST_BL_HEAD(&in_lookup_hashtable[i]);
	dcache_init_early();
	inode_init_early();
}

This function first utilizes the macro definition INIT_HLIST_BL_HEAD to initialize the bucket pointers of the hash table in_lookup_hashtable (i.e., the linked list heads) to null. The type of this linked list head is a pointer to a struct hlist_bl_head structure, which is declared as:

struct hlist_bl_head {
	struct hlist_bl_node *first;
};

It contains only a single tracking pointer field named first, whose data type resolves to a pointer referencing a structure of type:

struct hlist_bl_node {
	struct hlist_bl_node *next, **pprev;
};

The first field of the hash table bucket points to the initial element of the dentry list, which is of type struct hlist_bl_node. Linux leverages the d_hash member to chain together all colliding bucket elements that resolve to an identical index location, thereby composing the explicit linked list for that hash index. When the hash table is fully established, if a bucket corresponding to a particular index contains valid entries, the first pointer of the corresponding hash header points directly to the leading dentry of that index's list—specifically capturing the base memory address of the first dentry's d_hash field.

The next and pprev pointers within the d_hash field of the list components reference the base memory addresses of the d_hash fields belonging to the subsequent and preceding dentry entries, respectively. The pprev pointer of the very first element points back to the parent list head pointer itself, which maps to in_lookup_hashtable. The detailed configuration of the hash table framework adopted by the VFS is illustrated in Figure 14-5.

Following the initialization of these hash table headers, vfs_caches_init_early() invokes the routine dcache_init_early() to initialize the dcache buffer zone. The dcache_init_early() function is declared within git/fs/dcache.c and is implemented as:

static void __init dcache_init_early(void)
{
	if (hashdist)
		return;
	dentry_hashtable = alloc_large_system_hash("Dentry cache",sizeof(struct hlist_bl_head), 
       dhash_entries,13,HASH_EARLY | HASH_ZERO,&d_hash_shift,NULL,0,0);
	d_hash_shift = 32 - d_hash_shift;
}

This routine first tests the runtime value of the global variable hashdist to determine whether the hash table elements must be distributed across the distinct nodes of a NUMA architecture. If the configuration dictates that the hash table should be distributed across varying nodes, the early initialization pass is deferred, and dcache_init_early() exits immediately. Conversely, if the hash table components are centralized together, the routine invokes alloc_large_system_hash() to allocate a memory tracking buffer named "Dentry cache". The prototype signature of alloc_large_system_hash() is specified as follows:

void *__init alloc_large_system_hash(const char *tablename,
                                     unsigned long bucketsize,
                                     unsigned long numentries,
                                     int scale,
                                     int flags,
                                     unsigned int *_hash_shift,
                                     unsigned int *_hash_mask,
                                     unsigned long low_limit,
                                     unsigned long high_limit);

Within this tracking interface, tablename references the target string identity assigned to the cache buffer. bucketsize dictates the explicit capacity of an individual bucket, measured in raw bytes. numentries configures the total number of entries contained within the dcache hash table, which is supplied by the global variable dhash_entries. The default value of dhash_entries evaluates to 0, though it can be overridden to alternative constraints via the kernel command line parameters utilizing the option "dhash_entries=" during device tree processing. Currently, few hardware platforms explicitly define dhash_entries via command line arguments, and the vast majority rely on the default evaluation.

The function alloc_large_system_hash() can be triggered during early bootstrap initialization or invoked at later execution stages. It can wipe the allocated memory allocations to zero or fill the allocation blocks with -1. The memory allocation tracking algorithms differ depending on whether the call happens during early boot or late stages. When the flags parameter enables the bitmask flag HASH_EARLY, the system employs the early boot-stage block memory allocator framework; otherwise, it defaults to standard regular runtime allocation utilities. If invoked at later stages, the function allocates a cache area within the kernel's virtual memory space dedicated to caching dentry structures, whose base address is logged at dentry_cache. Diverging from the primary hash table tracking array, this memory zone preserves the literal dentry cache structures themselves, and is typically aligned to optimize Level 1 (L1 cache) high-speed cache lines. The buckets of the hash table store only the pointer members related to the underlying linked list architecture, whose sole purpose is to establish the memory storage locations of the cached dentry elements. When the system executes a cache query, it queries the dentry cache allocation first, which occupies a smaller memory footprint and delivers faster execution response times.
