When the flags parameter enables the bitmask flag HASH_ZERO, the routine calls block memory allocation functions that zero out the memory payload; otherwise, it invokes memblock_alloc_raw() to allocate raw blocks and fills the payload with -1.

The scale argument determines the size scaling factor relative to memory pages. _hash_shift captures the bit width utilized to right-shift hash values when computing index mappings via the hash function. low_limit and high_limit specify the maximum and minimum capacity boundaries enforced on the hash table allocation space, while _hash_mask returns the bitmask utilized to isolate hash index values.

Upon initializing the dcache buffer infrastructure, the vfs_caches_init_early() function invokes inode_init_early() to allocate a separate tracking cache for the virtual file system designated as "Inode-cache". inode_init_early() is defined within the source file git/fs/inode.c, and its definition is implemented as follows:

void __init inode_init_early(void)
{
	if (hashdist)
		return;
	inode_hashtable = alloc_large_system_hash("Inode-cache", sizeof(struct hlist_head),
     ihash_entries,14,HASH_EARLY|HASH_ZERO, &i_hash_shift, &i_hash_mask,0,0);
}

The programmatic structure of this routine is functionally identical to the statements executed during dcache configuration. The Inode Cache acts as the target hash table used when querying file index nodes (inode structures). Similarly, the individual buckets of this hash table store only the pointer tracking elements related to the underlying linked list architecture, which are leveraged to determine the precise memory locations of the cached inode entries.

Exception Handler Queueing

14.3 Exception Handler Queueing

Upon initializing the VFS buffers, the start_kernel() process invokes the function sort_main_extable(). Certain hardware architectures allow explicit instructions to trigger hardware exceptions throughout their execution path. Diverging from standard exceptional interrupts, when these specific exceptions manifest, the program flow can transition to a designated recovery routine to resume execution. These specialized exception handlers are arranged within a bounded memory segment situated precisely between the symbols __start___ex_table and __stop___ex_table.

Certain hardware platforms mandate that these routines must be sorted in ascending order based on their memory addresses, whereas for alternative hardware architectures, sorting these procedures from lowest to highest address during the boot phase significantly accelerates runtime lookup operations. The purpose of the function sort_main_extable() is to sort the exception handlers in ascending address order if required by the underlying architecture. Strictly speaking, this specific routine bears little relation to core memory initialization; however, because the logic is exceptionally straightforward, it is briefly outlined here.

Trap Initialization

14.4 Trap Initialization

The trap initialization routine is executed by the function trap_init(), which is heavily dependent on the specific hardware architecture. Its primary objective is to initialize the hardware components associated with trap execution and configure the trap interrupt vector tables. This function is defined within the respective architecture subdirectories; for instance, the trap_init() function for ARM systems is defined within git/arch/arm/kernel/traps.c, whereas the trap_init() function for PowerPC architectures is hosted within git/arch/powerpc/kernel/traps.c. For ARM-based hardware architectures, the trap_init() routine is implemented as an empty function block.

Chapter 15 Linux Memory Initialization

Fundamental Concepts

15.1 Fundamental Concepts

After executing the exception handler initialization, start_kernel() invokes the mm_init() function to allocate memory for several buffers utilized by memory management and to initialize the associated variables and structures. To better comprehend the memory initialization procedure, this section first introduces the fundamental concepts utilized in memory management, memory allocation algorithms, page extensions (page_ext), and bounce buffer technologies. Following this, it outlines the execution process of mm_init() and the basic functionalities of the functions it invokes.

Across the preceding chapters, we have progressively introduced concepts used in memory management, such as Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA), nodes, memory zones, page migration, and memory compaction. Furthermore, memory management encompasses concepts including huge pages, compound pages, and memory reclamation.

Currently, mainstream computer architectures utilize 4096 bytes as a standard page and execute memory allocation via the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) cache. However, with the evolution of computer architectures, many computer systems have surpassed the 4 GiB address space barrier. Under these circumstances, if 4096 bytes is stubbornly maintained as the page size, the cache hit rate will degrade. To mitigate this issue, many computer architectures have adopted memory management hardware with larger page dimensions. The page sizes adopted by this hardware can reach 2 MiB or even 1 GiB. Linux designates pages larger than 4 KiB as huge pages.

A compound page is a collection of multiple contiguous memory pages utilized to describe a SLAB allocation that is larger than a single physical memory page. The first memory page therein is designated as the head page of the compound page, while the remaining pages act as tail pages. The head page is flagged within the flags field of its page structure; when the PG_head bit (bit 16) of flags evaluates to 1, it indicates that this memory page represents the head page of a compound page. A tail page is identified by the least significant bit of the compound_head field within its page structure, where a value of 1 signifies that the page is a tail page. The remaining bits of compound_head preserve the base memory address of the head page belonging to the compound page hosting that tail page. The first tail page is unique, as it preserves supplemental metadata including the order of the compound page, the total number of memory pages enclosed within the compound page, and the associated destructor function.

Throughout different phases of system runtime operation, a single page of physical memory can be utilized to store distinct categories of data. Much of this data either has an existing backup in an external storage space like a hard disk drive, or can be paged out into an external swap area. Memory pages preserving this specific category of data are classified as reclaimable memory pages, and the physical space occupied by reclaimable memory pages can be safely released. The operation of releasing reclaimable memory pages is designated as memory page reclamation.

Memory Allocation Algorithms

15.2 Memory Allocation Algorithms

Previously, we introduced the block memory allocation strategy adopted during the early boot phase. This method is relatively simple and does not represent an efficient approach to memory management. Once boot initialization is complete, Linux transitions to highly efficient memory management mechanisms.

Memory allocation in Linux is executed hierarchically. The vmalloc() memory allocation function leverages the page allocator to allocate memory spaces larger than a single memory page, ensuring that the virtual addresses are contiguous even if the physical addresses are non-contiguous. The page memory allocator employs the buddy system to partition contiguous physical memory into 4096-byte pages, performing memory allocation on a page-level granularity. [[1], [2], [3]]

Various kmalloc() functions operate on top of the memory pages allocated by the page allocator. They leverage the SLOB, SLAB, or SLUB memory allocators to manage memory spaces smaller than a single page. The kmalloc() memory allocation functions primarily serve the internal memory allocation needs of the kernel. [[1], [2]]

  • SLOB (Simple List of Blocks) was adopted in early versions. It has been deprecated in desktop systems and is currently utilized primarily in embedded operating systems. [[1], [2]]

  • SLAB is a relatively complex algorithm. Its primary advantage is minimal memory fragmentation, but its disadvantage is the requirement to preserve a massive amount of management metadata. As of the [Linux 6.8] release, the legacy SLAB allocator has been completely removed from the kernel. [[1], [2], [3]]

  • SLUB improves upon the SLAB algorithm by mitigating the disadvantage of storing substantial amounts of management metadata. [[1]]

The buddy system is utilized inside the page allocator, primarily to allocate physical memory spaces larger than a single page. Both the SLAB and SLUB allocators request memory blocks from the buddy allocator to form their slabs. The hierarchical relationships among these distinct memory management modules are illustrated in Figure 15-1. [[1], [2]]

15.2.1 SLOB Allocation Algorithm

SLOB is one of the earliest memory management algorithms adopted by Linux. It is primarily utilized to allocate memory spaces smaller than a single page from the SLOB heap. Its minimum allocation granularity can reach 2 bytes, though it typically evaluates to 4 bytes. When the requested memory space is smaller than a single page, kmalloc()-type functions leverage the SLOB allocator to carve out memory from the SLOB heap. Conversely, when the requested space reaches the size of a single page, kmalloc() bypasses the heap and directly invokes alloc_pages() to acquire the memory. [[1], [2], [3]{.underline}]

The SLOB heap is structurally composed of three independent linked lists, with each list consisting of multiple memory pages: [[1]]

  • The first linked list is utilized to allocate memory requests smaller than 256 bytes. [[1]]

  • The second list is utilized to allocate memory requests smaller than 1024 bytes. [[1]]

  • The final list is reserved for all other standard allocation cases. [[1]]

Each page corresponding to these three linked lists maintains its own sub-list composed of the available free memory blocks within that page. This sub-list is arranged in ascending order based on the physical starting addresses of the individual blocks. When a memory block is released, it is inserted into the appropriate sorted position within the linked list according to its address, rather than simply being appended to the end of the list. [[1]]

When executing a memory allocation request, the algorithm first identifies the first page with sufficient free space within the appropriate page linked list. It then traverses that page's internal sub-list to locate the first free memory block that satisfies the requested capacity constraint and assigns it to the requesting context. The primary advantage of the SLOB algorithm is its simplicity and its minimal requirement for storing management metadata. However, the disadvantages of this algorithm are also conspicuous: it introduces exceptionally severe memory fragmentation, resulting in relatively low overall memory utilization efficiency.

15.2.2 SLAB Memory Allocation Algorithm

Memory allocation and deallocation are the most universal operations within the kernel, making rapid and effective allocation strategies paramount to overall operating system performance. To optimize these paths, Linux adopted the SLAB memory allocator starting with version 2.1.23. The SLAB architecture was originally designed and implemented within the Solaris operating system.

The defining characteristic of the SLAB allocator is that the data structures required to manage kernel memory are cached as "objects" within dedicated high-speed lookaside caches. When allocating memory, if a required data object does not exist, it is instantiated. If the object already resides within the lookaside cache, the allocator merely retrieves the memory from the cache and increments the data object's reference count. Under this paradigm, if the existing cache footprint is insufficient, the allocator can request additional backing pages without needing to re-instantiate or re-initialize the underlying object structures. Conversely, during memory deallocation, if an object's reference count is greater than 1, the memory is returned to the lookaside cache and the reference count is decremented. Only when the reference count drops to 1 will the memory be fully released and the tracking object destroyed.

Memory reclamation refers to the explicit process of freeing memory blocks owned by the lookaside caches and destroying the allocator data objects within them. Because objects are only initialized and destroyed during large-scale reclamation sweeps rather than on a per-allocation basis, the kernel avoids repetitive allocation, initialization, and breakdown routines. This drastically minimizes computational overhead and accelerates individual memory allocation and deallocation cycles.

The SLAB allocator infrastructure within Linux is structured as a collection of caches implemented by struct kmem_cache objects, with each cache tuned to service a specific size and type of memory. The managed slots scale logarithmically across intervals spanning 0-1, 1-2^2^-1, 2^2^-2^3^-1, …, 2^25^-2^26^-1 bytes. The primary allocation types encompass KMALLOC_NORMAL, KMALLOC_RECLAIM, and KMALLOC_DMA. These individual caches are woven together via the list field of struct kmem_cache to form a global, doubly linked circular list designated as slab_caches. Every cache within this list operates independently to manage objects belonging to a specific functional category. Each cache contains an array of pointers referencing localized cache nodes (struct kmem_cache_node), where each array index corresponds to a unique NUMA node.

The kmem_cache_node structure contains three distinct list heads: slabs_full, slabs_partial, and slabs_free. These point respectively to linked lists composed of entirely allocated slabs, partially allocated slabs, and completely vacant slabs. These lists are threaded together using the slab_list field inside the corresponding struct page structures. The page structure serves as the core physical descriptor canvas adopted by the SLAB allocator to track backing physical memory.

Every kmem_cache instance manages multiple underlying slabs, with each individual slab consisting of 2^n^ physically contiguous memory pages. Slabs spanning more than a single page are structurally managed as compound pages. Each slab is partitioned into equally sized chunks designated as objects. To prevent ambiguity within this architectural context, these objects are referred to as memory blocks. The baseline dimension of these blocks is dictated by the size field of kmem_cache, while the total count of blocks per slab is governed by the num field.

The struct page utilized for this category of memory allocation incorporates an s_mem pointer, which references the starting memory address of the first block within that slab. Because a slab is guaranteed to consist of physically contiguous pages, this base pointer provides access to all individual blocks across all pages within the slab. The precise memory address of a given block is derived as:

$$p = s_{_}mem + size*（idx - 1）$$

Where p represents the target address of the idx-th block, and idx represents the sequential block index number.

The page structure also encloses a pointer named slab_cache that references the parent kmem_cache instance managing that backing page. Concurrently, the slabs_full, slabs_partial, and slabs_free lists inside kmem_cache_node are populated by threading together the slab_list fields of the active memory pages. This dual linkage enables the kmem_cache manager to seamlessly locate any memory page under its jurisdiction, while enabling any given memory page to resolve its managing cache via the s_mem mapping.

To fulfill a request, the SLAB allocator first selects the appropriate kmem_cache lookup slot from the slab_caches pool based on the requested block magnitude and the execution flags (GFP masks) passed by the calling thread. It then evaluates the target NUMA node via per-CPU topological variables to locate the matching kmem_cache_node. Following this, it traverses the slab_list chains across the slabs_full, slabs_partial, and slabs_free lists to select a candidate slab, ultimately deriving the exact destination memory block via the page's s_mem pointer and the target block index $idx$. This multi-stage address resolution workflow is detailed in Figure 15-3.

The kmem_cache object is defined within the header file git/include/linux/slab_def.h, where its leading field is the cpu_cache pointer. This pointer maps to a per-CPU private variable (per_cpu), ensuring that its evaluated target remains unique to each individual processor core. The pointer references a structure of type array_cache, whose internal entry pointer array caches the specific block indices allocated locally to that CPU core.

When a processor core requests memory, it first queries its local array_cache to see if a free object is readily available. If a vacant slot exists, the memory block is instantly fulfilled from this local cache. If the local cache is exhausted, the allocator evaluates whether a shared array_cache is configured with available objects. If the shared tier is also empty, the engine falls back to inspect the slabs_partial and slabs_free chains hosted inside the node's kmem_cache_node. If a vacant object is discovered at this tier, the indices of the acquired blocks are pulled up to populate the CPU's local array_cache entry array. Finally, if no vacant space can be harvested from these lists, the allocator invokes the low-level page allocator (alloc_pages()) to carve a fresh backing page from virtual memory and append it to the kmem_cache tracking lists. If the underlying page allocator cannot fulfill the raw page request, an out-of-memory (OOM) error is triggered.

The SLAB mechanism is heavily optimized to service memory allocations that fall below a single-page threshold. The comprehensive suite of core kernel kmalloc() routines relies entirely on this underlying allocation logic.

15.2.3 SLUB Memory Allocation Algorithm

The kmem_cache object used by the SLAB allocator maintains a significant volume of metadata. For each NUMA node, a corresponding kmem_cache_node structure is present, and each kmem_cache_node manages three independent linked lists. Managing this metadata is inherently complex and consumes a considerable amount of CPU cycles. To further enhance memory allocation efficiency, Christoph Lameter implemented the SLUB memory allocation algorithm in 2008 within kernel version v2.6.23. Today, SLUB has become the primary memory allocator for Linux, and the widely utilized kmalloc subsystem is built directly upon the SLUB algorithm.

The SLUB allocator optimizes several shortcomings of the SLAB memory allocator. It redefines the kmem_cache and kmem_cache_node structures, removing much of the superfluous management metadata. At runtime, it only utilizes a single partial list, while the full list is exclusively enabled when debugging is required. In the SLUB allocator, individual CPU cores no longer rely on arrays; instead, they utilize the local partial list and a freelist pointer to manage their active slabs and the internal memory objects within those slabs, respectively. When a CPU releases an active object, it puts it back onto its local freelist chain to facilitate immediate, lockless reuse.

SLUB still manages memory blocks using the slab as a fundamental unit, and the layout dimension of a slab is dictated by the size field of the kmem_cache structure. Every individual slab is partitioned into multiple equally sized memory modules, designated as objects, whose baseline footprint is defined by the object_size field of the structure. In contrast to the SLAB allocation algorithm, each slab within SLUB can encapsulate supplemental debugging information; however, these tracking fields are entirely optional. Figure 15-4 illustrates the structural layout of a single object utilized within SLUB. The RED zone left padding, RED zone, SLUB allocation information, and KASAN allocation information segments are completely optional components that are only enabled by kernel or driver developers during debugging sessions. The precise physical positioning of each segment is governed by the individual fields within the kmem_cache structure.

The RED zone Left Padding ensures that the physical starting address of the active memory object strictly satisfies alignment criteria. The Red Zone is partitioned into a left zone and a right zone; it is utilized to execute memory out-of-bounds validation by filling a specific memory region with a dedicated magic number (such as 0xBB). The left zone is positioned immediately preceding the object payload, while the right zone succeeds the object payload. The Object Content represents the actual usable memory footprint granted to the user or kernel application request. When the object resides in a vacant state, the Free Pointer stores the memory address referencing the subsequent free object down the chain. The SLUB Allocation Information logs the specific function call or call stack responsible for allocating or freeing the object, a tracking capability typically exposed via CONFIG_SLUB_DEBUG. The KASAN Allocation Information represents metadata reserved exclusively for KASAN (Kernel Address Sanitizer), which logs highly precise call stacks for asynchronous allocations and deallocations to troubleshoot advanced vulnerabilities such as Use-After-Free (UAF). Finally, the Padding segment trails all metadata structures to align the total physical size of the unified object to a specific hardware alignment boundary.

A slab is still fundamentally backed by the page structure. The page structure configuration adopted by the SLUB allocator encloses tracking fields such as slab_list, partial, next, pages, and counters. The next pointer of the slab_list field chains the individual slabs together to form a linked list. The explicit next pointer shares an identical memory slot with the next sub-field of slab_list, referencing the subsequent slab down the chain. The tracking fields pages and pobjects overlay the memory slot typically reserved for the prev pointer of slab_list, and are leveraged to log the cumulative number of slabs attached to the CPU's local partial list along with the total count of vacant objects contained within them. freelist is a standalone pointer that references the memory location preserving the starting address of the next free object within that specific slab. The counters variable shares its memory alignment with a trailing anonymous union; structurally, counters can be interpreted as a composite element composed of three sections: inuse, objects, and frozen. inuse occupies the upper 16 bits, tracking the number of memory objects that are currently allocated. The lower 16 bits are split between objects and frozen. objects utilizes the upper 15 bits of this lower half to represent the absolute count of objects partitioned within the slab. frozen utilizes the least significant bit (b0) to signify the structural condition of the slab; when this bit evaluates to 1, the slab is frozen, meaning only the specific CPU core that froze it possesses authorization to manipulate its object links.

Each CPU maintains a local tracking variable of type struct kmem_cache_cpu, whose fields are mapped out as follows:

  • The freelist pointer references the memory address preserving the next available free object.

  • The partial pointer references the linked list head capturing the partially vacant slabs.

  • The page pointer references the active slab currently being consumed, which the CPU leverages to fulfill real-time memory allocations.

When allocating memory, the CPU first attempts to harvest a vacant object directly from its local freelist. If a free object cannot be located within the active CPU's freelist, the allocator falls back to fetch a partially vacant slab from its local partial list and subsequently extracts the required memory chunk from that slab. If no free space can be harvested from the local partial list, the engine queries the global partial list hosted inside the node's kmem_cache_node. If this path also fails, the allocator invokes the underlying page allocator (page_allocator) to carve a fresh slab out of system memory.

Both the CPU's local partial list and the cache node's global partial list enforce strict capacity thresholds that are defined inside the parent kmem_cache structure. When the total number of slabs attached to a list surpasses this specified limit, the list is evaluated as full. When a CPU attempts to fetch a slab from its local partial list and finds it full, it flushes and releases all slabs residing on that local list back over to the node's global partial list. If the node's global list is also full during this synchronization pass, the surplus slabs are completely released back to the system memory allocator.

Upon successfully acquiring a fresh slab, if the CPU's local page field evaluates to null, the slab is assigned directly to the page field. Conversely, if the page field is already occupied, the incoming slab is appended onto the CPU's local partial list. Figure 15-5 illustrates the list structure of partial slabs utilized by SLUB.

Figure 15-6 details the operational tracking chains utilized locally by each individual CPU core.

15.2.4 Buddy Memory Allocation Algorithm

During the continuous process of allocating and freeing memory modules of varying sizes, the physical memory inevitably fragments into dispersed blocks of arbitrary capacities—a phenomenon known as memory fragmentation. Contiguous physical memory addresses not only accelerate memory read/write cycles but also represent a hard architectural constraint for certain operations such as Direct Memory Access (DMA). When fragmentation becomes severe, it increases access latency and can cause memory allocation failures even when aggregate free space is mathematically sufficient. Mitigating memory fragmentation is a fundamental requirement for any memory allocator. The buddy allocator is specifically designed to address memory fragmentation. Operating at the lowest layer of the core memory management hierarchy, it enforces a minimum allocation granularity of one page and handles the allocation of single or multi-page physical memory chunks. Its core design philosophy is to maximize the size of physically contiguous free memory spaces.

As established in previous chapters, the Linux buddy allocator partitions the physical memory of each NUMA node into 11 distinct groups (orders), where each group is composed of equally sized, physically contiguous memory blocks. The capacities of these memory blocks scale across orders of 1 page, 2 pages, 4 pages, 8 pages, 16 pages, 32 pages, and so forth, with the final group managing block chunks of 1024 pages. These groups are explicitly utilized to service allocation demands of 1 page, 2 pages, 4 pages, up to 1024 pages, respectively. The struct zone configuration for each individual NUMA node manages an array named free_area composed of 11 elements (spanning Order-0 to Order-10) of type struct free_area, which preserves the allocation metadata for these 11 explicit orders. The free_area structure encloses an array of linked list heads named free_list with a capacity of MIGRATE_TYPES, alongside an nr_free tracking field that records the cumulative number of vacant memory blocks available within that specific order. Each element within the free_list array corresponds to a discrete migration type, tracking the available free blocks classified under that type. The migration types supported by Linux are defined within the header file git/include/linux/mmzone.h. Figure 15-7 illustrates the memory grouping topology utilized by the buddy allocator inside the page allocator subsystem.

The core buddy memory management engine is implemented within the source file git/mm/page_alloc.c. Full page allocations are dispatched via the interface alloc_pages(), which is declared within git/include/linux/gfp.h. When NUMA support is enabled in the system, alloc_pages() routes the request to alloc_pages_current(). This routine first reads the memory allocation policy constraint specified by the current process within struct task_struct->mempolicy. If the calling thread specifies explicit policies such as MPOL_BIND (forcing allocation to a strict subset of specific nodes), MPOL_INTERLEAVE (alternating allocations across nodes in a round-robin loop), or MPOL_PREFERRED (preferring local node allocation), alloc_pages_current() evaluates these criteria to derive an ordered list of candidate zones (Zonelist) before requesting pages from the buddy infrastructure. Depending on the resolved memory allocation policy, alloc_pages_current() triggers either alloc_page_interleave() or __alloc_pages_nodemask(), with alloc_page_interleave() ultimately falling back to invoke __alloc_pages_nodemask().

Conversely, if NUMA support is disabled, alloc_pages() routes the request to alloc_pages_node(). Because multi-node concepts are absent under this constraint, numa_node_id() permanently returns the index of the singular, local physical node (typically Node 0). The kernel bypasses all policy verification execution paths and directly leverages the globally unique node zone list to execute lockless or locked buddy allocation passes. Under this uniprocessor constraint, alloc_pages_node() calls __alloc_pages_node(), which likewise resolves to invoke __alloc_pages_nodemask().

The function __alloc_pages_nodemask() represents the definitive core routine for memory allocation workloads. It evaluates real-time memory availability by calling either get_page_from_freelist() or __alloc_pages_slowpath(). Depending on the gravity of the allocation constraints, __alloc_pages_slowpath() triggers paths including get_page_from_freelist(), __alloc_pages_direct_compact() (direct memory compaction), __alloc_pages_direct_reclaim() (direct page reclamation), or __alloc_pages_may_oom() (Out-Of-Memory execution). It can fulfill the request directly, or invoke iterative compaction and reclamation sweeps before attempting allocation. The primary task of get_page_from_freelist() is core allocation orchestration, and it serves as the ultimate execution funnel for all alternative allocation handlers; structurally, it is get_page_from_freelist() that executes the physical page acquisition. Throughout the allocation attempt, get_page_from_freelist() manages memory pools via node_reclaim() and extracts page blocks from the target lists via rmqueue().

When extracting pages, rmqueue() leverages the mathematical buddy relationship to first attempt allocation from the smallest order group that can fully satisfy the requested capacity constraint. If free space is unavailable within the current order group, the routine searches upward through larger order groups. Upon a successful match in a higher order, the algorithm splits the block to satisfy the request while preserving the largest possible contiguous address spaces, shunting the residual split chunks down into the appropriate lower-order groups.

The inverse process of releasing a page block back to the allocator is handled by the function __free_one_page(). Throughout this deallocation path, if the algorithm detects two physically contiguous memory blocks belonging to the same order, it combines them into a single larger block and moves the merged entity up into the subsequent higher-order group. Physically contiguous memory blocks of identical order that can be merged in this manner are designated as buddies. Figure 15-8 provides an execution example of a buddy memory allocation sequence. In this scenario, we assume a calling context requests a single page of memory (Order-0), while the system can only discover sufficient free blocks at Order-5 (the 32-page group).

The allocation engine first identifies an available high-order block buddy5-0 containing sufficient tracking space via the appropriate free_list. It splits buddy5-0 in half, generating two distinct Order-4 buddies designated as buddy4-0 and buddy4-1. The routine inserts buddy4-0 directly into an Order-4 free_list chain, while further bisecting buddy4-1 into two Order-3 buddies designated as buddy3-0 and buddy3-1. This algorithmic bisection loops continuously until the block is successfully broken down into two Order-0 buddies named buddy0-0 and buddy0-1. Finally, the engine appends buddy0-0 onto an Order-0 free_list tracking chain and fulfills the request by returning buddy0-1 to the calling user context.

The inverse memory consolidation pipeline operates conversely to the allocation workflow, as demonstrated by the step-by-step example in Figure 15-8. When a physical page frame is released back to the allocator, the subsystem first evaluates whether its corresponding companion block (buddy) is currently vacant and eligible for consolidation. If the criteria are met, the released block merges with its companion to compose a single unified block of the subsequent higher order. This merging tracking loop executes recursively until it encounters a companion block that is active or ineligible for consolidation. Figure 15-9 details the complete consolidation workflow for a single physical page. Similarly, we assume a calling context releases an Order-0 page frame measuring 4096 bytes; upon reaching Order-5, the consolidated block encounters a companion that cannot be further merged, concluding the deallocation pass.

Throughout allocation passes, the system references a predefined fallback tracking topology formatted as follows:

static int fallbacks[MIGRATE_TYPES][3] = { /* fallback list */
	[MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE]   = { MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE, MIGRATE_MOVABLE,   
      MIGRATE_TYPES },
	[MIGRATE_MOVABLE]     = { MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE, MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE, 
      MIGRATE_TYPES },
	[MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE] = { MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE,   MIGRATE_MOVABLE,   
      MIGRATE_TYPES },
#ifdef CONFIG_CMA
	[MIGRATE_CMA]         = { MIGRATE_TYPES }, /* Never used */
#endif
#ifdef CONFIG_MEMORY_ISOLATION
	[MIGRATE_ISOLATE]     = { MIGRATE_TYPES }, /* Never used */
#endif
};

Each explicit row within this fallback matrix maps out a prioritized search hierarchy (Fallback List) to guide allocation borrowing when the primary requested migration type faces exhaustion. The values defined inside the array establish the descending precedence sequence for cross-type borrowing, which terminates upon encountering the MIGRATE_TYPES marker boundary.

Fulfilling an allocation request demands the resolution of a topologically suitable memory node. A candidate node is classified as unsuitable if it is explicitly bound to a separate CPU thread context that prohibits external allocation, if its internal dirty page volume surpasses permitted system thresholds, or if its real-time residual capacity drops beneath safety watermarks. If a target node's allocation metrics breach these safety watermarks, the engine first evaluates whether it can harvest fresh memory blocks by pulling in pages whose initialization was deferred during early boot. If this path is exhausted, it ultimately determines if the free block count can be replenished by triggering active page reclamation (including invoking cross-node memory reclamation passes) alongside targeted compaction passes. Once an eligible node passes these validation blocks, the physical allocation is committed within its boundaries.

Red-Black Trees

15.3 Red-Black Trees

A Red-Black Tree is a self-balancing binary search tree (see Figure 15-10). It achieves approximate balance by adding a storage bit to each node representing its "color" (either red or black), combined with a series of mandatory constraint rules that ensure no single path from the root to a leaf is more than twice as long as any other.

A red-black tree must strictly adhere to the following five properties; otherwise, it is not a valid red-black tree:

  1. Every node is either red or black.

  2. The root node must be black.

  3. All leaf nodes (NIL nodes, which are empty nodes) are black.

  4. If a node is red, then its child nodes must be black (meaning two consecutive red nodes are forbidden).

  5. All paths from any given node to its matching leaf nodes must contain the exact same number of black nodes.

The red-black tree achieves an excellent trade-off between its balancing precision and structural manipulation overhead:

  • In both average and worst-case scenarios, the time complexity for lookup, insertion, and deletion operations evaluates to $O(log n)$.

  • Compared to strictly balanced AVL trees, red-black trees require fewer rotation operations, which yields superior performance in scenarios involving frequent insertions and deletions.

When an insertion or deletion violates any of the properties, the red-black tree restores its structural balance via the following remedies:

  • Color Flipping: Changing the red or black status of the nodes.

  • Left Rotation: Rotating the node to the left, causing its right child to become the new parent node.

  • Right Rotation: Rotating the node to the left, causing its left child to become the new parent node.

Within the Linux kernel, the red-black tree (rbtree) acts as a highly critical, high-performance self-balancing binary search tree. It is widely deployed across core subsystems including virtual memory management, process scheduling, and I/O monitoring. It has undergone deep optimizations tailored for kernel environments, setting its architecture significantly apart from textbook implementations.

The rbtree implementation within Linux (hosted within lib/rbtree.c) pursues extreme execution throughput and memory utilization efficiency via the following paradigms:

  • No Indirection Layer: Distinct from traditional paradigms where "the tree contains the payload data," Linux adopts an architecture where "the payload data embeds the tree node." Each struct rb_node is directly embedded within its target parent data structure. This eliminates supplemental memory allocations and pointer indirections, which dramatically elevates CPU cache hit rates.

  • Pointer Pointer-Packing Trick: To minimize the storage footprint, Linux compresses the node's color metadata into the lower bits of the parent node pointer (since memory pointers are always hardware-aligned, the least significant bits are naturally 0). This optimization saves 8 bytes of space per node on 64-bit systems.

  • No Built-in Search Callbacks: The kernel does not supply a unified comparison handler function. Instead, users write custom search and insertion logic tailored to specific key types (such as process IDs or virtual memory addresses), which completely eliminates function call overheads.

Furthermore, Augmented Red-Black Trees (augmented rbtree) support storing accumulated statistics (such as the maximum value within a sub-tree) inside the individual nodes. This capability is useful for implementing Interval Trees, which are deployed to handle overlap detection during virtual memory region management.

The red-black tree serves as the backbone for multiple time-sensitive tasks within the Linux kernel:

  • Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS): CFS leverages an rbtree to manage all runnable processes. The search key used within this tree is the process's vruntime (virtual runtime). The scheduler can continuously insert a new process at an $O(log n)$ execution cost and quickly locate the process that demands the CPU most urgently.

  • Virtual Memory Management (VMA): The kernel utilizes red-black trees to track every single vm_area_struct (memory segment) belonging to a process. When a page fault exception manifests, the kernel traverses the red-black tree to resolve the corresponding memory region within an $O(log n)$ time window.

  • epoll Subsystem: The epoll engine implements an rbtree to manage all file descriptors (FDs) monitored by user space. Even when monitoring tens of thousands of active connections, operations to add, delete, or modify an FD consistently maintain stable logarithmic complexity.

  • High-Resolution Timers (hrtimers): All pending timer requests are sorted by their precise expiration timestamps and stored within a red-black tree, guaranteeing that the system can process massive volumes of timed tasks both accurately and efficiently.

Page Swapping and Virtual Memory Mapping

15.4 Page Swapping and Virtual Memory Mapping

Within the Linux system, each process possesses its own unique virtual memory space, and the available virtual memory capacity within each space is completely unconstrained by the literal size of the physical memory. When the memory footprint demanded by the active processes surpasses the physical memory capacity, the operating system writes portions of the physical memory that are currently unutilized out onto an external storage device. This external storage space dedicated to temporarily preserving physical memory payloads is designated as the swap partition. To facilitate seamless file swapping operations, Linux reserves specific lookaside buffers within the virtual memory space for disk file swapping consumption.

Because Linux natively supports multi-process execution, files or library functions loaded into memory might be concurrently utilized by multiple independent processes. If these files or library functions had to be re-read from the hard disk drive upon every single invocation, it would drastically degrade program execution velocity. To circumvent this bottleneck, Linux also carves out dedicated tracking buffers utilized to preserve this shared data.

Throughout their execution lifecycles, programs generate a substantial volume of temporary runtime data. Due to the microarchitectural characteristics of computer hardware, aggregating this data together not only optimizes overall memory utilization efficiency and streamlines memory management but also enables the CPU to access data via immediate addressing or direct addressing modes rather than indirect pointing mechanisms. This effectively minimizes address arithmetic overhead and elevates program processing throughput, giving rise to the concepts of the heap and the stack. Each individual process maintains an independent heap and stack, which serve as localized buffers for tracking temporary data.

Although the lookaside buffers dedicated to disk file swapping vary slightly from the standard process heap and stack setups, these two categories of memory regions share a core characteristic: their raw physical targets cannot be interfaced with directly via unmapped virtual addresses, meaning their high-level buffer management workflows share significant commonality. Consequently, Linux adopts a unified infrastructure to manage both buffer categories, introducing variances solely within their concrete architectural mapping methodologies.

To streamline buffer orchestration, Linux categorizes virtual memory tracking structures into two primary functional types. The first type is dedicated to storing data consumed dynamically by running applications; this category of virtual memory region is designated as anonymous memory. Both the process heap and stack belong to the anonymous memory classification. The alternative memory type is dedicated to executing data swapping passes with the hard disk drive, a category designated as file-backed memory. File-backed memory zones are utilized to cache files read from or written to disks, swap partition files, shared library functions, and the binary execution code of the program itself. Figure 15-11 illustrates the explicit mapping relationships between various file types and the virtual address canvas.

Linux differentiates between anonymous memory and file-backed memory by evaluating the least significant bit (b0) of the mapping field enclosed within the physical page frame descriptor struct page. When this least significant bit (the PAGE_MAPPING_ANON bit) is set to 1, it indicates that the current page frame maps to anonymous memory; under this scenario, the mapping pointer references a specialized structural backbone named struct anon_vma (see §15.4.2). Conversely, when this least significant bit evaluates to 0, it signifies that the current page frame maps to file-backed memory, under which constraint the mapping field acts as a valid pointer referencing an address space tracking structure (struct address_space).

15.4.1 Memory Eviction and Page Release

When utilizing file-backed memory, the physical memory capacity constraints require the processes to frequently execute data swapping passes with disk storage (encompassing both regular files and swap partition files). An efficient file swapping mechanism minimizes the frequency of disk read/write cycles, thereby enhancing overall program execution throughput. Linux achieves this by managing five fixed-length Least Recently Used (LRU) lists classified into three operational categories to guide page swapping operations. These five LRU lists encompass anon_active, anon_inactive, file_active, file_inactive, and unevictable. Among them, anon_active and anon_inactive are dedicated to orchestrating page swapping for anonymous memory; file_active and file_inactive handle page swapping for file-backed memory; and the unevictable list preserves pages that are structurally prohibited from being evicted to disk storage. For instance, when Linux mounts a ramfs filesystem, the files contained within it must remain permanently resident in physical memory throughout the system runtime lifecycle.

When a process executes a memory read operation, if the targeted page frame already resides on an active list, the subsystem promotes this page to the head boundary of that active list, shunting the preceding entries downward by one slot position. If the targeted page is located on an inactive list, the system similarly promotes this page to the head boundary of the corresponding active list, while shunting the pages originally preceding it on the inactive list downward by one slot position. If a page fault exception manifests—indicating that the requested payload data is completely absent from physical memory—the operating system's page fault handler evicts and releases the page frame situated at the tail boundary of the corresponding inactive list (xx_inactive) (see §15.6) and reads the correct data block back from disk storage. Upon initially loading a page from disk, the newly fetched page frame is positioned at the head boundary of the inactive list, pushing the remaining elements on that list downward by one slot position. To maintain clarity, this overview simplifies the operational tracking loops of the LRU subsystem. In practical execution, additional metrics are factored in; for instance, when deciding whether to promote a page from an inactive list to an active list, the allocator evaluates the chronological interval between two consecutive accesses to the exact same page, thereby preventing thrashing where a single page is repeatedly evicted and re-read. These lists are similarly manipulated during large-scale page reclamation passes. Figure 15-12 illustrates several common structural state changes across the LRU lists.

The majority of LRU list structural topologies and memory eviction routines are defined within the source file git/mm/swap.c. The internal state transformation and relocation loops across these lists are executed by the function mark_page_accessed(). Readers interested in pursuing deeper architectural specifics can review the source code contained within that file.

15.4.2 Mapping Between Virtual Addresses and Caching Buffers

Both anonymous memory and file-backed memory reside within dedicated private caching buffers. The execution program is unable to interface with these buffers directly via unmapped virtual addresses; instead, it must employ a mapping layer to bind virtual addresses or file offsets to the caching buffer space, thereby ensuring the correct dataset can be retrieved. To achieve structural mappings from disk files and anonymous memory domains into the runtime caching buffers, Linux defines four core data structures. Their primary structural technical objective is to govern the process's virtual memory intervals, and to enable the system—upon encountering a page eviction or a Copy-on-Write (CoW) cycle—to rapidly perform a reverse lookup from a physical page frame back to all referencing virtual memory areas.

These primary architectural structures encompass:

  • struct mm_struct (The mm Structure):
    The memory descriptor canvas. Exactly one instance is assigned to each individual process, which encapsulates fields tracking the localized cache areas consumed by the thread context, the root node of the process's VMA red-black tree, the aggregate address space footprint, the cumulative number of virtual page frames, the precise boundary markers for the heap, stack, data, code, and uninitialized variable (bss) segments, a structural tracking pointer referencing the standalone VMA sequential linked list, environment variable segments, alongside diverse runtime statistic counters and memory watermarks. The VMA red-black tree is structurally composed of all vm_area_struct instances tied to this parent mm_struct.

  • struct vm_area_struct (The VMA Structure):
    The virtual memory area descriptor. It delineates a single physically non-contiguous but virtually continuous block of memory space assigned to a process. It primarily contains the sequential pointer hooks vm_next and vm_prev utilized to thread together the process's absolute buffer chain, the virtual address starting boundary, the virtual address ending boundary, the structural red-black tree node tracking member vm_rb used to hook the VMA instance directly onto the mm_struct parent tree, a pointer tracking back to the owner mm_struct, an rb tracking node utilized to attach the VMA container into the global interval tree address_space->i_mmap tracking backed disk files, a pointer targeting the explicit anon_vma context managing this caching zone, a list head tracking member anon_vma_chain grouping all anon_vma_chain bridge structures intersecting this VMA node, and a vm_file structural file pointer referencing the backing file descriptor (which evaluates as a null pointer when tracking anonymous memory blocks).

  • struct anon_vma (The AV Structure):
    While resolving a virtual address down to its corresponding physical address is efficiently handled via forward page table walks, the inverse sequence—mapping a raw physical address back to its referencing virtual addresses (known as reverse mapping or rmap)—represents a significant microarchitectural challenge due to the unidirectional design of page tables. A critical application context for reverse mapping manifests during memory eviction passes: the kernel must perform an rmap lookup to discover every virtual address referencing the target physical page frame, and subsequently modify those page table entries to point directly to the page's slot within the swap partition.
    The primary functional purpose of the anon_vma structure is to facilitate high-performance reverse mapping queries. It encapsulates 6 distinct fields, where the root field points to the definitive root node of the active anon_vma ancestry tree, and the parent field references the corresponding anon_vma context of the parent process that invoked the original fork() cycle. Across multi-generational process hierarchies, parent-child memory sharing paths introduce complex exclusive versus shared memory mapping boundaries. To streamline tracking, Linux arranges these process structures hierarchically into an ancestry tree, where all descendant anon_vma instances resolve their lineage back to the initial ancestral root via the root pointer.
    The degree counter field logs the total count of direct child anon_vma structures; when degree evaluates to less than 2, the current structure is eligible to serve as the immediate parent anon_vma framework for a subsequent child process layer.
    The rb_root field anchors the root node of a specialized interval red-black tree composed of anon_vma_chain bridge structures, which links all VMAs intersecting the current anon_vma instance. This specific interval tree structure aggregates all referencing VMAs across the entire system that currently map this chunk of anonymous memory (achieved structurally via the intermediary anon_vma_chain components). This binary search tree links all concurrent VMAs belonging to distinct processes (or threads) that share access to the same anonymous physical memory frames. Consequently, it encompasses not only the local process VMA but also the VMAs of all child and grandchild descendant processes generated via fork() cycles, provided these descendants continue to share this specific memory interval. If a descendant process triggers a Copy-on-Write (CoW) exception, Linux creates a fresh memory block and hooks a newly instantiated anon_vma structure onto its local red-black interval tree, thereby transitioning it to manage its own isolated anonymous memory pages.

  • struct anon_vma_chain (The AVC Structure):
    The primary architectural role of the anon_vma_chain structure is to act as a bridge establishing a clean intersection between the anon_vma context and individual VMAs, which it accomplishes by configuring its vma and anon_vma fields to point directly to their respective target structures. Furthermore, this structure serves a dual purpose as a standard list node labeled same_vma (hooked onto the list head anchored at the VMA's local anon_vma_chain field) and as an active binary tree node labeled rb (hooked into the interval red-black tree anchored at the anon_vma structure's rb_root field).
    The AVC tracking chains are woven together via the same_vma list element, and the base head of this chain is managed within the anon_vma_chain field of the corresponding VMA structure, thereby logging all distinct anon_vma contexts intersecting that specific VMA container. Concurrently, the interval red-black tree is threaded together via the rb node element, tracking all distinct VMAs that are managed under the jurisdiction of the specified anon_vma structure.
    Within the reverse mapping subsystem of the Linux memory management framework, the anon_vma and anon_vma_chain structures work in tandem to solve the core architectural problem of discovering every virtual memory area mapping a given anonymous physical page frame. The internal red-black tree managed inside the anon_vma instance preserves a comprehensive index of all VMAs that could potentially map the same physical page frames.

Figure 15-13 details the structural linkages and pointer topologies mapped out across these distinct descriptor blocks, providing a clear visualization of how these structures interact.

As illustrated in Figure 15-13, the initial vm_area_struct instance belonging to a process can be directly resolved from its parent mm_struct. Evaluating this VMA structure yields multiple parameters regarding the address space footprint currently consumed by the process. Furthermore, via the mm_struct, the system can interface with the global VMA red-black tree, allowing the kernel to rapidly look up a specific VMA instance of interest.

Figure 15-14 shows the contiguous tracking chain composed of all VMAs assigned to a process. Traversing this sequential list enables the kernel to inspect every VMA structure registered under the process context. The primary drawback of this linear structure is its high search latency, making it ideal only for scenarios that mandate a full sweep across all VMAs.

When a new process is created within the system, a corresponding anon_vma_chain (AVC) bridge structure is instantiated and bound directly to the process's local VMA structure. When this process subsequently forks a child process, it invokes the routine dup_mmap() to clone the VMA structures (for deeper analysis, developers can consult the implementation flow encompassing kernel_clone(), fork_idle(), copy_process(), copy_mm(), dup_mm(), and dup_mmap() within the source file git/kernel/fork.c). After cloning the parent process's VMA structures, the routine duplicates the parent's page table entries into the translation tables of the child process. This architectural optimization guarantees that the child process initially consumes no new backing physical memory. A fresh physical page block is allocated to the child process only when it generates a write transaction targeting the memory interval mapped by that VMA.

Following the VMA duplication stage, the kernel invokes anon_vma_fork(), which calls anon_vma_clone() to traverse the parent process's internal AVC linked list (anchored at the list head anon_vma_chain). For each AVC encountered during this sweep, a corresponding AVC structure is instantiated for the child context. The newly created AVC is populated with the parent's matching anon_vma reference alongside the child's newly cloned VMA reference. Following this configuration, the routine appends this new AVC instance onto the list headed by the child VMA's anon_vma_chain field, and inserts it into the interval red-black tree rooted at the anon_vma's rb_root field. This multi-stage cloning pipeline replicates the parent's anon_vma tracking chains over to the child process context. The explicit technical purpose of this setup is to establish an appropriate anon_vma mapping relationship for the child's new VMA, enabling the parent and child processes to share the underlying anonymous physical page frames while seamlessly supporting Copy-on-Write (CoW) exceptions and rmap reverse lookups.

Figure 15-15 illustrates the linked list layout anchored at the VMA's anon_vma_chain field, which aggregates all AVC components intersecting that singular VMA node. This specific list is threaded together sequentially via the same_vma field. Figure 15-16 illustrates the interval red-black tree rooted at the anon_vma structure's rb_root field, which aggregates all AVC elements mapped under its jurisdiction. This binary search tree scales dynamically as a byproduct of process fork cycles, and the attached AVC elements map back to all VMAs across different address spaces that intersect this root anon_vma node. Figure 15-17 diagrams the structural layout of the child process's AVC linked list prior to encountering a Copy-on-Write (CoW) transaction.

The structural interconnections among the VMA, AVC, and AV descriptors can be visualized as an intersection network in Figure 15-18. Here, the AVC functions analogously to an intersection switch array, establishing a flexible, clean many-to-many relationship mapping between individual VMAs and anon_vma contexts.

The programmatic routines responsible for identifying every virtual memory region mapping a common physical page frame are encapsulated inside central reverse mapping handlers such as page_referenced_anon(). Its standardized execution logic is executed as follows:

  • Extracting the target anon_vma from the physical page descriptor (page->mapping):
    The page->mapping pointer of an anonymous physical page frame does not link directly to a filesystem inode; instead, it points to the managing anon_vma structural backbone.

  • Traversing each individual AVC element hosted inside the anon_vma interval red-black tree:
    The kernel iterates over the tree entries to step through the intersecting references.

  • Resolving the specific VMA linked to each candidate AVC:
    The routine extracts a valid VMA mapping that shares access to that physical page block.

By continuously traversing all AVC entities attached to the anon_vma interval red-black tree, the memory subsystem can resolve every virtual memory area mapping that identical physical page block.

Beyond its role in orchestrating basic reverse memory mappings, this interval red-black tree—rooted at the anon_vma's rb_root field—is leveraged by the Kernel Same-page Merging (KSM) subsystem. The KSM engine scans the tree structure to evaluate identical physical memory pages that are eligible to be safely consolidated into a single shared page to optimize the system's memory footprint.

15.4.3 Mapping Anonymous Memory to Caching Buffers

Mapping anonymous memory to caching buffers involves designating a specified virtual memory range as a cache block. Following initial parameter compliance validations, the primary technical objective of this routine is to initialize the diverse fields of the vm_area_struct (VMA) container, aligning the VMA with the targeted memory area and ensuring it satisfies all required protection and operational attributes. Figure 15-19 illustrates the systematic workflow for mapping a specified memory region into a caching buffer.

Throughout this mapping procedure, the subsystem often needs to search through existing VMAs to determine whether the starting address of the designated region already resides within a virtual memory space allocated to another VMA. This lookup tracking sequence traverses the global red-black tree (whose root is anchored at the vm_rb field) managed within the process's mm_struct. It compares the target starting virtual address address against the vm_start and vm_end boundary flags of each VMA encountered during the tree walk. If the comparison satisfies the condition vma->vm_start <= address < vma->vm_end, it indicates that the virtual memory space managed by that specific VMA encapsulates the target starting address. The topological relationships among the various data structures involved in this lookup process are illustrated in Figure 15-20.

15.4.4 Mapping File-Backed Memory to Caching Buffers

File-backed memory is utilized to cache disk files into designated regions of physical memory. Because disk files, unlike anonymous memory, do not natively reside within the virtual address space, the operating system must employ a specialized mechanism to link disk files with virtual memory. This linkage is achieved via the address space structure (struct address_space), which is defined within the header file git/include/linux/fs.h. The address space structure works in tandem with the kernel-space file descriptor (struct file) and the index node structure (struct inode) to accomplish the mapping of disk files into the virtual memory space.

The address space structure defines objects that can be cached and mapped. It encloses multiple tracking fields, including the host object owning this structure (either an inode or a block storage device) and the total number of cached pages. It also encapsulates up to 22 operational callbacks, such as writing pages, reading pages, setting dirty page flags, page isolation, and page migration. Among these, the field responsible for tracking mapping relationships is i_mmap. This field serves as the root of an interval red-black tree composed of all VMAs cached within this memory buffer. The VMA nodes within this binary tree are threaded together via the shared.rb node member enclosed within each vm_area_struct. During the execution of a file-backed mapping, the system invokes the function vma_link_file() to insert the VMA node into this red-black tree, thereby binding the file to the VMA. Utilizing this binary tree allows the kernel to query the VMAs corresponding to a specific file and determine the mapped addresses of the file within the backing memory buffer. Figure 15-21 illustrates the interval red-black tree utilized for this caching mechanism.

Another highly critical field inside the address space structure is i_pages. This field is implemented as an extensible array (XArray), which encapsulates the descriptors of all cached physical pages (in kernel versions 5.15 and earlier; newer versions store pointers to struct folio data structures instead). Utilizing the diverse helper functions provided by the XArray subsystem, the kernel can directly perform read, write, and flag modification operations on the cached page descriptors using the index field of the physical page frames.

The kernel-space file descriptor (struct file) describes files that have been opened within the system, supporting user-space operations such as opening, reading, writing, and closing files via functions like fopen(). This structure encompasses fields including the file path structure f_path, a pointer to the index node structure f_inode, and a pointer to the address space structure f_mapping. It also specifies an operational method table via f_op, which defines handlers for file operations such as open, close, read, write, position querying (llseek), memory mapping (mmap), and retrieving unmapped areas (get_unmapped_area). The explicit components leveraged for cache mapping are f_mapping, f_inode, the mmap() method, and the get_unmapped_area() method. The mmap() method is responsible for mapping the file into the targeted VMA, while get_unmapped_area() is utilized to resolve an available unallocated starting address within the virtual memory space.

The index node structure (struct inode) stores file metadata and serves as the primary repository for file diagnostics within Linux. It records extensive data including the file mode, User ID (uid), Group ID (gid), file size, file type, file modification time, last access time, several pointers referencing underlying disk blocks, and general administrative metadata. It also exposes localized methods for manipulating the file and the index node structure itself. The actual raw data contents of the file are not preserved inside the inode. The methods for executing file operations utilize the handlers exposed by the file descriptor, whereas the methods for manipulating the index node structure primarily encompass directory table lookups, link(), unlink(), mknod(), rmnode(), mkdir(), rmdir(), and setattr(). The specific field within the index node structure utilized for memory mapping is i_mapping, which acts as a pointer targeting the explicit address_space structure. The definitive architectural interconnections among these distinct descriptors and the interval red-black tree are detailed in Figure 15-22.

15.4.5 Reverse Mapping from Physical Addresses to Virtual Memory Addresses

Due to process forking and memory sharing, a single physical page may be concurrently mapped to multiple distinct virtual addresses. Figure 15-23 illustrates a scenario where, through a multi-generational process tree, a single physical memory page is mapped to three different virtual memory regions. When a child process is forked, it bridges multiple translation domains: its local VMA's anon_vma_chain links both to the parent's inherited anon_vma (utilized for reverse-mapping older, shared pages) and to a fresh, dedicated anon_vma instantiated specifically for the child during the fork() lifecycle (utilized for tracking future exclusive pages).

As established in the preceding sections, forward address translation relies on navigating the page tables; by evaluating a virtual address through the page table entries (PTEs), the system resolves the matching physical Page Frame Number (PFN) along with its corresponding physical page descriptor (struct page). Conversely, reverse mapping (rmap) denotes the inverse process of tracing from a physical page descriptor back to its referencing virtual addresses. Because page tables are strictly unidirectional routing structures, even in the simplest scenario where a physical page maps to exactly one virtual memory page, the system cannot directly extract the mapped virtual address or the governing PTE from the struct page alone. This bottleneck is magnified because a single physical page frame can be simultaneously mapped to multiple virtual pages across distinct process address spaces. This reverse lookup capability is a mandatory prerequisite when the memory subsystem evicts page content out to the swap partition or releases physical pages back to the allocator.

In kernel versions prior to Linux 2.4, executing a reverse lookup required the system to traverse the page tables of every single process running in the system to identify all PTEs mapping a target physical address—a brute-force scanning pipeline that was exceptionally time-consuming. To resolve this architectural bottleneck, Rik Van Riel pioneered the conceptual framework of reverse mapping and proposed adding direct pointer networks to realize the lookups. However, Rik's initial design introduced significant memory overhead and proved suboptimal for production scaling.

To refine this approach, Dave McCracken introduced object-based reverse mapping. This method was primarily tailored for file-backed memory reverse lookups, and the mmap() system call architecture leverages this paradigm. For a file-backed mapping, Dave enabled object-based rmap by routing the physical page descriptor's mapping pointer to reference its parent address_space structure.

However, for anonymous mappings, the struct page's mapping field initially remained unassigned. To extend reverse mapping capabilities to anonymous memory domains, Andrea Arcangeli proposed routing the mapping field to reference a target VMA directly. Yet, this simple relationship broke down during process replication: when a process forks, a single inherited VMA maps to multiple disjoint page table domains across different address spaces, meaning a single physical address maps to multiple distinct virtual addresses. Consequently, mapping anonymous memory via a direct, singular pointer from page->mapping to a VMA was architecturally unviable.

To overcome this structural barrier, Andrea defined the anon_vma (AV) and anon_vma_chain (AVC) structures. Each process utilizes AVC bridge elements to bind its local VMA instances to the appropriate anon_vma contexts. Via the unified anon_vma_chain linked lists, a process simultaneously tracks the shared anonymous pages inherited from its parent ancestry alongside its own exclusive, locally generated anonymous pages. The definitive structural mechanics of these tracking meshes have been detailed across the preceding sections introducing the AV and AVC subsystems.

15.4.6 Reverse Mapping from Anonymous Memory to Virtual Memory

During anonymous memory mapping, the mapping field of the physical page descriptor points directly to its corresponding anon_vma structure. To execute a reverse mapping lookup, the system leverages this mapping pointer to resolve the target anon_vma context and accesses the interval red-black tree rooted at its rb_root field. By traversing the individual anon_vma_chain (AVC) entries within this binary search tree, the kernel can identify all VMAs that map this specific physical page descriptor page, thereby resolving every referencing virtual memory page across the system. Furthermore, by evaluating the index field of the page structure, the engine determines the exact page offset within the virtual address space managed by each VMA. The architectural connections among these structures and the red-black tree are illustrated in Figure 15-24.

15.4.7 Reverse Mapping from Files to Memory

As established previously, Dave McCracken enabled reverse mapping for file-backed memory by routing the mapping field of the physical page descriptor to point directly to its parent address space structure. The system leverages the physical page descriptor's mapping field to locate the corresponding address_space structure. Via the i_mmap pointer of this address space structure, the engine accesses the interval red-black tree composed of all referencing VMAs. By traversing the diverse VMA nodes within this binary tree, the system resolves every VMA mapping that specific physical page frame, and subsequently tracks back to the target physical file descriptor via the VMA's vm_file field. Figure 15-25 illustrates this multi-stage reverse mapping pipeline for file-backed memory.

Page Migration

15.5 Page Migration

Page migration is a technology leveraged by Linux to improve program execution efficiency. Through page migration, the system can alter the physical memory location mapped by a virtual address while guaranteeing that the process's virtual address remains unchanged. This serves to expand physically contiguous memory blocks or ensure that the physical memory occupied by a process resides as close as possible to the CPU running that process. Page migration permits the relocation of physical memory mapped by virtual addresses from one node to another, and also allows physical memory to be migrated between different processes. For instance, when the system leverages cpusets for process and resource management, CPU cores are typically bound to specific memory nodes. When the system switches a process from one cpuset to another, it must concurrently migrate the corresponding memory to the newly bound nodes.

After determining that a page is suitable for migration, the foundational operation of page migration is to locate all page table entries (PTEs) mapping that specific physical memory page via forward and reverse mappings, modify the contents of these entries to point to the new physical memory, and concurrently update the page descriptor (struct page) tracking that physical memory page while modifying its mapping-related fields. Of course, page migration is not that simple; the migration pipeline must first establish whether a memory page is eligible for migration, and isolate the targeted page to prevent other CPU cores from releasing or manipulating it while the migration is underway.

Linux supplies functions such as migrate_pages(), sys_move_pages(), handle_pte_fault(), and handle_mm_fault(). migrate_pages() is utilized internally by the kernel for page migration. sys_move_pages() acts as a system call interface enabling users to manually migrate pages from user space. handle_pte_fault() and handle_mm_fault() serve as the handler routines for page table faults and process address space faults, both of which invoke internal migration routines provided by the kernel to relocate memory.

As established previously, Linux maintains several LRU lists to coordinate memory swapping. To process these LRU lists efficiently, each CPU utilizes a local pagevec vector structure to temporarily stage memory pages destined for the LRU lists; these independently batched pages are flushed onto the main LRU lists only during list synchronization loops. Prior to executing a page migration, the system must flush these temporarily staged pages from each CPU's page vector onto the appropriate LRU lists. Below, we outline the general procedural steps of page migration using the kernel_move_pages() function as an execution example.

Before invoking the page migration routine, the targeted pages must first be isolated via isolate_movable_page(), and these pages must satisfy the criteria for movable pages. The page migration process encompasses the following sequential steps:

  • Upon entering the page isolation procedure, the system first flushes all pages temporarily staged inside each CPU's local pagevec structure onto the primary LRU lists.

  • It scans all pages specified during the invocation of the page migration process to determine the specific home node of each page.

  • Via the process identifier (pid), it resolves the process address space descriptor mm_struct and the memory nodes available to the task.

  • It aggregates all migration-targeted pages residing on the identical memory node into a migration page linked list, and isolates these target pages via the function isolate_lru_page().

  • After collecting all target pages belonging to a specific node, the system executes a batched migration of these pages to their new destinations. This concrete migration workload is performed by the function migrate_pages(), whose primary operations encompass:
    a) Clearing specific operational flags within the original page descriptor's flags field based on the exact context.
    b) If the migration target is a dirty page, flushing its contents out to external storage; depending on the active migration mode, the system might not wait for this writeback cycle to complete.
    c) Configuring the flags field of the new page descriptor based on the status of the original page's flags, and copying the original index and mapping field values over to the new page descriptor.
    d) Copying the raw data payload from the original memory page over to the new physical memory page.
    e) Modifying the contents of all page table entries currently mapping the original page, routing them to point directly to the new physical page.
    f) Recording the explicit reason or trigger for the page migration.
    g) Removing the original page frame from the primary LRU tracking lists.
    h) Appending the newly allocated page frame onto the primary LRU tracking lists.
    i) Clearing the entire flags field of the original page descriptor and releasing the original page frame back to the allocator.

Upon successfully migrating all target pages across the respective memory nodes, the migration task concludes. Figure 15-26 provides a simplified execution flowchart of the page migration process. For the sake of visual clarity and structural conciseness, extensive exception handling blocks and divergent logic paths for specialized page categories (such as unmovable pages, cached pages, and huge pages) are omitted from this diagram.

Memory Reclamation

15.6 Memory Reclamation

During the Linux initialization sequence, the system spawns an asynchronous kernel daemon designated as kswapd(), which remains in a low-power sleep state under normal operations. If memory resources experience severe contention or fragmentation bottlenecks throughout the system runtime, this background daemon is awakened. It processes the five globally managed LRU tracking lists to release portions of the allocated physical memory, subsequently invoking compaction routines to optimize the residual pools. This complete operational pipeline of freeing allocated frames is designated as memory reclamation.

The kswapd() daemon orchestrates memory freeing operations via the routine balance_pgdat(). When the volume of anonymous pages residing on the inactive list (the cold chain) drops beneath safety thresholds, balance_pgdat() invokes age_active_anon() to transition a portion of the active anonymous memory frames (the hot chain) down into the inactive pool. If the Memory Resource Controller (memcg) subsystem is enabled, system administrators can configure explicit soft limit thresholds for corporate memory consumption profiles. When the volume of free system memory drops below these benchmarks, balance_pgdat() triggers mem_cgroup_soft_limit_reclaim() to free physical memory allocations from the specific memcg instance that breaches its soft limit by the widest margin within that node. Concurrently, kswapd_shrink_node() focuses eviction routines on reclaiming blocks from the highest-indexed eligible memory nodes. Following the conclusion of a memory reclamation cycle, balance_pgdat() invokes wakeup_kcompactd() to alert the background memory compaction daemon. Furthermore, the kernel exposes the synchronous functions do_try_to_free_pages() and node_reclaim(), which can be explicitly called by running processes to perform direct, foreground memory reclamation passes. The core engine managing the memory reclamation subsystem is declared within the source file git/mm/vmscan.c.

Memory Compaction

15.7 Memory Compaction
